- [x] ISC-108: A worker completing 3 turns with zero tool calls is classified `failed:no_tool_calls`. **[GRADED 2026-08-19 — STAYS OPEN. The runtime detector does not exist, so there is nothing a test could hold.]** SRD §5.9/F39 specifies TWO detectors for the prose-instead-of-tool-calls failure and only the first is built. The STARTUP probe is real and enforced — `src/security/model-probe.ts` classifies a model that answers with prose, `llm.require_native_tool_calls` gates it, and `up` exits 2. The RUNTIME detector this criterion names is absent in every part: `grep -rn 'no_tool_calls' src/` returns NOTHING; `prose_turns_before_fail` (SRD's default of 3, and the number in this criterion) appears nowhere outside `Docs/SRD.md` — not in `config/schema.ts`, so the threshold is not even configurable; and although the supervisor does count tool calls (`state.tool_calls++` on `tool_execution_end`, `src/supervisor/index.ts`), NO VERDICT PATH READS THAT COUNTER — `cli/commands/harvest.ts` prints it, `harvest/transcript.ts` reports it as a metric, and `reconstruct`'s verdict switch keys on `stopReason` alone. The existing coverage does not cover this; it says the opposite out loud. `test/unit/completion.test.ts`'s "no-tool-calls: three turns with zero tool calls still settle cleanly" asserts settlement as `success` — correctly, because the completion tracker must not HANG on prose — and both it and `test/fixtures/scenarios/no-tool-calls.json` defer the classification to "the harvester's job (acceptance #61, Phase 2)". NO MUTATION WAS RUN, and that is the finding rather than an omission: there is no code whose corruption could change any outcome, which is the sharpest available evidence that the criterion is unimplemented. WHAT IS MISSING, concretely: a per-epoch zero-tool-call counter in the supervisor, `run.prose_turns_before_fail` in the config schema, and a settle path producing verdict `failed` with reason `no_tool_calls` — at which point `no-tool-calls.json` is already the fixture that proves it, and its `EXPECTED_SETTLES` entry becomes the thing to revise. *(CLOSED 2026-08-24, Phase E. **The production caller first, because that is what the grade note said was missing.** `src/supervisor/prose-detector.ts` holds the state machine; `src/supervisor/index.ts` holds three call sites that make it load-bearing — `prose.observe(event.type, {interrupted})` on the LIVE-attributed branch of `onEvent`, `prose.tripped` at the head of the verdict chain in `maybeProbe`, and `prose.reset()` in both `settle` and the `bindStart` branch. The config road mirrors `ui_request_timeout` end to end: `run.prose_turns_before_fail` in `config/schema.ts` (default 3, derived not restated), folded with `llm.require_native_tool_calls` by `effectiveProseTurnsBeforeFail` so §5.9's "disables both" has ONE spelling of off, written to `run.json` by `up`, read back by `readRunProseTurnsBeforeFail` — the supervisor's only route to it, since it never loads `fleet.yaml`. **FOUR EDGE CASES, DECIDED.** (1) *Reset:* per epoch, and the streak also dies at any live-attributed tool call — consecutive-run semantics. Cumulative-per-worker is what `state.tool_calls` already was and why it could not answer this; "N turns and zero tool calls ever" is the literal reading of §5.9 and is strictly weaker, since it can never fire on a worker that acted once at turn 1 and then degraded, which is the long-context drift the detector is named for. (2) *An interrupted turn is not a prose turn:* a `turn_end` arriving after `em.timedOut || em.abortRequested` neither increments nor clears the streak — it has zero tool calls because WE ended it, and counting it would report a task that timed out mid-tool-call as a model that never called a tool, routing the operator to change the model when the answer was a longer deadline. (3) *`prose_turns_before_fail: 0` is OFF*, not fail-immediately: the other reading fires on every task including the ones that work, and 0 is the value `require_native_tool_calls: false` collapses to, so the two switches are one. The schema is `nonnegative()` rather than `positive()` precisely so off is representable; negative and fractional are still refused, and `ProseTurnDetector` re-checks — a `-1` under a bare `>=` would trip on the first turn of every task, a fail-CLOSED corruption that looks like the detector working. (4) *Precedence:* the prose trip outranks `timed_out` and `aborted`. `timed_out`/`aborted` describe HOW the epoch ended; the trip says WHY it had to, and the two route the operator differently — `timed_out` sends them to raise `per_task_timeout`, which fixes nothing. Same reasoning ISC-116 used to prefer `timed_out` over `aborted` ("a timeout that happened to be polite"), one step further: a diagnosis outranks a description. The window is narrow by construction — the trip TEARS THE EPOCH DOWN itself (advisory `abort`, then the deadline branch's ladder at `ABORT_GRACE_MS` on its own timer handle), which is also what keeps `prose.tripped` reachable at settle instead of losing the race to a deadline. The trip path deliberately does NOT call `em.noteAbortRequested()`: that would stamp `abort_requested: true` in `fence.json` for an abort no operator sent, and would have let the diagnosis erase itself. **EVIDENCE.** `test/integration/supervisor.test.ts` → `ISC-108: three turns with zero tool calls are failed, not settled successfully` drives a REAL detached supervisor against `scenarios/no-tool-calls.json` at the schema default and asserts `verdict: "failed"`, `reason: "no_tool_calls"`, plus a `no_tool_calls_detected` record carrying `prose_turns: 3` / `threshold: 3`, and the ABSENCE of `deadline_exceeded` and `no_tool_calls_escalated` so no other path can be what ended it. Its paired control writes `prose_turns_before_fail: 0` into `run.json` and asserts the SAME scenario on the SAME supervisor settles `success`/`quiesced` with no trip record and three `turn_end`s observed — so neither test can pass by the fixture being unusual or the detector being inert. 18 unit tests in `test/unit/prose-detector.test.ts` cover the branches one scenario cannot reach. **MUTATION-PROVED THREE TIMES, one per layer, because a module mutation alone would prove the module.** (a) Threshold comparison → `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`: the integration test fails on the VERDICT assertion, `Expected: "failed" / Received: "success"` — the exact pre-ISC-108 behaviour — plus 5 of 18 unit tests. (b) Deleting the `prose.tripped` branch from `maybeProbe`, i.e. the production caller only: same red, same message. (c) `readRunProseTurnsBeforeFail` returning the default unconditionally: the CONTROL goes red, `Expected: "success" / Received: "failed"`, so the `run.json` road is load-bearing rather than decorative. All three restored and confirmed byte-identical by sha256. **WHAT WAS STALE IN THE 2026-08-19 NOTE.** Two things. `grep -rn 'no_tool_calls' src/` no longer returns nothing. And the prediction that `EXPECTED_SETTLES` "becomes the thing to revise" was WRONG, recorded rather than quietly dropped: that table is a property of the COMPLETION TRACKER, which ISC-108 did not touch, so `no-tool-calls.json` is still `[1]` — the scenario still holds one terminal `agent_end` and still settles once. A verdict is not a count and there was no column that could have held it. Had the detector been wired into the tracker instead — the wrong layer, making prose unsettleable and turning a bad task into a stranded worker — the entry WOULD have become `[]`; the surviving `[1]` rules that design out, and the reasoning is now written beside it. The note's own framing was also stale in a third way worth naming: both the fixture and the tracker test deferred classification to "the harvester's job (acceptance #61, Phase 2)", and it is not the harvester's job and never became one — §5.9 puts the runtime detector in the supervisor so the failure is loud at ~3 turns rather than at harvest. Both comments now state the division of labour instead: the tracker decides WHETHER the epoch is over, the supervisor decides WHAT it was. **LIVE GROUNDING.** The §5.9 measurement is `Qwen3-8B-4bit`; a sharper one was taken 2026-08-23 against `Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-4bit` — a model that PASSES the startup probe — which leaked its tool call as raw `<function=read>…</tool_call>` TEXT with `finish_reason=stop` in 1 of 3 identical probes. Intermittent, which is the shape a one-shot probe cannot see, and the turn genuinely has zero tool calls when it happens. That is the drift this detector exists for, and the reason the startup probe alone was never enough.)*
- [x] ISC-109: With 6 workers up and `max_concurrent: 2`, at most 2 have an in-flight generation at any sampled moment. **[CLOSED 2026-08-20 by wiring `BudgetManager` onto the dispatch path.]** `max_concurrent` was defined at `config/schema.ts:190` and enforced only inside the callerless `safety/budget.ts`, so the scheduler's own `inflight` map excluded an already-busy worker and capped nothing — a probe drove the real `runSchedule` with 6 workers and `max_concurrent: 2` and measured peak in-flight 6. `runSchedule` now takes a `ScheduleBudget` and calls `admit` before every `io.dispatch`; a refusal `continue`s, leaving the task `ready`. **Proven at two levels, both sampling over time rather than counting `admit` calls** (a test that calls `admit` twice tests `budget.ts`, which already had one): `test/unit/budget-wiring.test.ts` drives the real `runSchedule` against 6 fake workers and asserts the peak of an in-flight series sampled at every dispatch, settle and idle poll; `test/integration/budget-halt.test.ts` runs SIX real detached supervisors through the real CLI and reconstructs the same series from `[dispatched_at, settled_at)` intervals taken from the ledger and the task records. MUTATION-PROVED at both: forcing `maxConcurrent` to `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` fails the unit probe with `Expected: <= 2 / Received: 6` and the integration probe with the identical `Expected: <= 2 / Received: 6` (3/3 trials). **Non-vacuity is asserted separately and deliberately not as `peak === 2`** — on a slow runner the first task can settle before the second is dispatched, which would fail a correct cap; the integration test instead asserts the first-to-last dispatch span is at least `DEFAULT_POLL_MS * 2`, which an uncapped scheduler (all six out in one pass, microseconds apart) cannot satisfy and which load only widens. The unit control case pins the same discrimination from the other side: the same fleet with no budget attached still measures peak 6. **Verified under deliberate load, not only on an idle box** — `.github/scripts/test-under-load.sh` at `LOAD_PROCS=32` on 14 cores (2.3 busy loops per core, harsher than the CI load job's 1 per core) and again at `LOAD_PROCS=40`: PASS both times, the ISC-109 test itself measuring 1.33 s against the 79.8 s its `cliBudget(7)` derives. Neither of its assertions can be broken by a slow machine by construction: the cap is enforced logically so contention can only LOWER observed overlap, and the non-vacuity assertion is a lower bound on elapsed span, which load only widens.
- [x] ISC-110: A worker queued behind others is not killed as wedged before `event_stall_warn` elapses. **[RE-GRADED `[x]` -> `[ ]` 2026-08-19 by the unreachable-module sweep. BOTH halves of this criterion — the queue and the stall policy — are unreachable from production, so the sentence has no subject and no verb.]** **The stall policy is callerless.** `classifyStall` (`src/safety/kill.ts:241`) is the function that distinguishes a queued worker from a wedged one, and `grep -rn classifyStall src/` returns only its own definition. Nothing in `src/` computes a `StallVerdict`, so no worker is killed as wedged — nor spared as queued — by any code path. `event_stall_warn` and `event_stall_kill` (`config/schema.ts:166-167`) are parsed by the schema and read by NO production line; the only other `stall` timer in `src/` is `scheduler.ts`'s `DEFAULT_STALL_TIMEOUT_MS`, a fleet-wide no-progress abort that throws `SchedulerError` at `EXIT.TIMEOUT` and neither reads those keys nor kills a worker. **The queue does not exist either.** `classifyStall`'s discriminator is `holdsSlot`, documented in place as `BudgetManager.holdsSlot`, and `BudgetManager` (`src/safety/budget.ts:102`) has no caller in `src/cli`, `src/orchestrate` or `src/run` — `max_concurrent` (`config/schema.ts:190`) is enforced only at `safety/budget.ts:168`, inside that callerless module. A probe drove the real `runSchedule` with 6 workers against `max_concurrent: 2` and measured peak in-flight = 6, so no worker is ever "queued behind others" in the first place (see ISC-109, correctly `[ ]`). **Evidence, and what it proves.** `test/unit/kill.test.ts` -> `classifyStall (ISC-110 / ISC-117): queued and wedged are different` passes, and its assertions are correct — about the function. It calls `classifyStall` directly with hand-built `StallInput` values; it proves the module, not the criterion. Recorded separately because it cost time to establish: that file throws `ReferenceError: Cannot access 'realProcessOps' before initialization` when it is the FIRST importer of `kill.ts` (an order-dependent init cycle `kill.ts` -> `run/registry.ts` -> `safety/reaper.ts` -> `kill.ts`), so it fails when run alone or in small groups. It DOES execute under `bun test test/unit` (measured: 1093 pass / 0 fail across 51 files), where an earlier file warms the cycle from the `registry.ts` side. So this is a local-isolation fragility, NOT a non-executing test, and it is not the grounds for this re-grade. **`[ ]` and not `[~]`:** production cannot reach the code under test from any entry point, and the criterion is only vacuously true — nothing kills for stall, so nothing spares a queued worker either. **Wiring that would close it:** construct a `BudgetManager` on the dispatch path (ISC-235) so `holdsSlot` has a live answer, have the supervisor sample `sinceLastEventMs` from its `Stopwatch` and feed `classifyStall` with `timers.event_stall_warn`/`event_stall_kill`, and drive the resulting `warn`/`kill` verdicts into the existing kill ladder. Closing that one call site closes ISC-110 and puts ISC-109 and ISC-117 within reach of a scenario test. **[RE-GRADED `[ ]` -> `[~]` 2026-08-20 by the stall-wiring commission. The half this criterion said was missing is now present; the half that is machine-checked is named exactly.]** **What changed.** `classifyStall` now has a production caller: `runSchedule`'s settle pass classifies every in-flight worker and acts on the verdict, and the window reaches it from `fleet.yaml` through `run.json` (`runBudgetRecord` -> `readRunBudgetPolicy`) rather than being parsed and dropped. The entry's second half — "the queue does not exist either" — was already made stale by ISC-109: admission is on the dispatch path, so a worker CAN now be queued behind others, which is what made this criterion testable at all. **MACHINE-CHECKED:** `test/unit/scheduler-stall.test.ts` drives the real `runSchedule` with six tasks against `max_concurrent: 2` and asserts peak in-flight never exceeds 2 while the stall policy is live, and that every kill landed on work that had actually been dispatched — so queued work is never killed. Mutation-proved: replacing the kill branch with `if (false)` fails it. **NOT machine-checked, and the reason this is `[~]` and not `[x]`:** the test drives the SCHEDULER through an injected clock and a fake `eventSilenceMs`. The production reading — `stat(events.jsonl).mtimeMs` in `dispatch.ts` — has no test, so "before `event_stall_warn` elapses" is proven as policy and not as a measurement of a real worker's silence. See ISC-282. **[GROUNDS PARTLY STALE — struck 2026-08-25 by the budget re-grade audit, which was auditing ISC-115/193 and tripped over this. The GRADE stands at `[~]`; the REASON above does not.]** The sentences *"`grep -rn classifyStall src/` returns only its own definition"* and *"it has NO CALLER anywhere in production"* were true on 2026-08-19 and false from 2026-08-20. The stall-wiring commission moved the function to `src/safety/stall.ts` (`kill.ts:643` re-exports it) and `orchestrate/scheduler.ts:476` calls it on every poll, with `event_stall_warn`/`event_stall_kill` read from the run — two live wedges emitted `worker_stall_warn` at exactly 180000 ms, so the WARN rung demonstrably fires in production. `[~]` and not `[x]` for a NARROWER reason than the one this entry gives: the scheduler's ACTION on the verdict is proved against an injected clock and a fake `eventSilenceMs`, while the two PRODUCTION inputs — `stat(events.jsonl).mtimeMs` and the `abort` RPC — are not, which is exactly what ISC-282 was filed to own. ISC-297 additionally records that the KILL rung is unreachable under shipped defaults for any task deadline under 25 minutes. **The same false claim was live in `src/` and is fixed rather than only noted:** `src/safety/kill.ts:47` asserted "`classifyStall` has no production caller at all — ISC-110 and ISC-117 are both open on exactly that", which sent a reader at the source to a settled question with the wrong answer. **[RE-GRADED `[~]` -> `[x]` 2026-08-25 by the ISC-282 closure. The stated reason for `[~]` is discharged, not reinterpreted.]** This entry's own last paragraph gave one reason and one only for withholding the grade: *"the scheduler's ACTION on the verdict is proved against an injected clock and a fake `eventSilenceMs`, while the two PRODUCTION inputs — `stat(events.jsonl).mtimeMs` and the `abort` RPC — are not, which is exactly what ISC-282 was filed to own."* Both are now covered against real files and a real supervisor, with nine mutations; see ISC-282 for the evidence and for the one thing that is still NOT covered — a single run driving real silence through the threshold to a real abort. The reachability half was already settled by ISC-297: before it, the kill rung could not fire inside any deadline under 25 minutes, so this criterion was unfalsifiable in production regardless of how well the policy was tested.
- [x] ISC-111: A dialog `extension_ui_request` is answered `{cancelled:true}` within 5s. **[GRADED 2026-08-19 — STAYS OPEN. Nothing anywhere answers a UI request; the "within 5s" clause has no timer behind it.]** SRD §12.3 guard 2 is unbuilt. `grep -rni 'extension_ui\|ui_request' src/` returns exactly three hits and not one of them is a handler: `contracts.ts:207` declares the `WorkerState.ui_requests` counter `{answered, denied}`, `config/schema.ts:165` parses `ui_request_timeout` (prefault `5s` — the very 5 seconds this criterion names) and NO CODE READS IT, and `security/refresh.ts` matches only on the English word "cancelled" in a comment. Mechanically, an `extension_ui_request` is not a response (`isRpcResponse` keys on `type === "response"`), so it arrives through `RpcClient.onEvent` and lands in the supervisor's `onEvent`, which logs it, offers it to `CompletionTracker.observe` — where it matches no case and is not in `ACTIVITY_EVENTS` — and returns. No reply is ever written to the child's stdin. This is CONFIRMED FROM THE FAR END OF THE WIRE, not only by reading: the new `test/integration/ui-requests.test.ts` captures every line the supervisor writes to its Pi process (via fake-pi's new `PIFLEET_FAKE_REQUEST_LOG`) and the captured set contains only `prompt` and `get_state` — so `answered` and `denied` are both structurally 0 for every run, and `ui_requests` in `state.json` is a field that can never move off its default. NO MUTATION WAS RUN: there is no responder whose corruption could change an outcome. WHAT IS MISSING: a supervisor-side classifier over SRD §4.2's nine methods, a per-request timer seeded from `timers.ui_request_timeout`, a `{cancelled:true}` reply on the four dialog methods, and `WorkerState.ui_requests.denied` incremented when it fires. TESTING IT ALSO NEEDS FIXTURE WORK that does not exist yet: `test/fixtures/fake-pi.ts` can EMIT a UI request (the new `ui-fire-and-forget.json` does) but cannot BLOCK on one, and a dialog that does not block is not a dialog — the double needs a step form that withholds the turn's `agent_end` until a matching answer arrives, which is also the only way to measure the 5s bound honestly. **[CLOSED 2026-08-24 by Phase E-A — guard 2 is BUILT, and the response frame was EXTRACTED FROM THE BUILD rather than derived from the SRD.]** MACHINE-CHECKED, every CI run (`test/integration/ui-requests.test.ts`, real detached supervisor, real fake-pi child, no Docker and no network): `test/fixtures/scenarios/ui-dialogs.json` emits `select`, `confirm` and `input` with `await_response: true` — the double now HOLDS the emission sequence until a correlated frame arrives on stdin — and each is answered inside the configured bound. **The frame is `{"type":"extension_ui_response","id":"<request id>","cancelled":true}`**, read out of the pinned image at `/usr/local/lib/node_modules/@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent/dist/modes/rpc/rpc-types.d.ts:405-418`, its stdin dispatcher at `dist/modes/rpc/rpc-mode.js:573-585`, and its own `docs/rpc.md:1153-1176`. §4.2 does not state it, so it was measured rather than guessed — SRD §4's own rule that the build wins. **THE KEY IS `id`, AND THAT MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS:** the dispatcher does `pendingExtensionRequests.get(response.id)` and drops an unmatched id with NO error, so the plausible spelling `request_id` parses, matches nothing, and hangs the dialog in silence — ISC-112's failure reached through a reasonable guess. The frame is also a bare top-level record handled BEFORE `handleCommand`, so it cannot go through `RpcClient.send()` (which stamps its own id over the caller's and registers a pending entry that would later reject unheld); `sendUncorrelated()` was added for it. **THE PRODUCTION CALLER EXISTS** — `src/supervisor/index.ts:64` imports the policy and line 769 calls `handleUiRequest` from `onEvent`. This is the half grading rule 3 exists to demand, and a first attempt shipped the module WITHOUT it: `src/supervisor/ui-requests.ts` sat complete and callerless, which would have been the ninth RC-1 criterion in this file. **MUTATION-PROVED:** disabling that single call site (sha256 `afab9b05…` before and after restore) turns exactly three probes red — this one on *"select answered after 8003ms, bound is 5000ms"*, which is the FIXTURE's own self-resolve rather than the supervisor, ISC-112's on a `timed_out` verdict, and ISC-113's mixed run. **DEVIATION FROM SRD §12.3, RECORDED NOT BURIED:** the SRD says the answer goes out *after* `ui_request_timeout`; the implementation answers IMMEDIATELY and treats the key as a CEILING. Justified from the build — `cancelled:true` resolves select/input to `undefined` and confirm to `false`, byte-identical to the `defaultValue` those methods reach when their own timeout fires, so a waited-out cancellation and a prompt one are indistinguishable to the extension. **The SRD sentence reads as a schedule and should be reworded as a bound.** Line numbers in this note's 2026-08-19 text were also stale: `config/schema.ts:165` is now `:201`.
- [x] ISC-112: An `editor` extension UI request does not hang the run. **[GRADED 2026-08-19 — STAYS OPEN, and of the three UI criteria this is the one most likely to be FALSE in production rather than merely unproven.]** Same missing handler as ISC-111, but the consequence is worse and SRD §4.2 says why: `select`/`confirm`/`input` carry an optional `timeout` and SELF-RESOLVE, so an unanswered one eventually unblocks itself; **`editor` has no timeout and hangs forever unanswered** — "the supervisor's timer is the only unblocker". There is no such timer (`ui_request_timeout` is parsed in `config/schema.ts:165` and read nowhere). So a real Pi extension issuing an `editor` request against today's supervisor blocks its turn until `deadline_s` expires, at which point the heartbeat's `deadline_exceeded` path sends an advisory `abort`, waits `ABORT_GRACE_MS`, and settles `timed_out` with reason `deadline_exceeded_no_terminal_event` before killing the child. That is the kill ladder working correctly and it is NOT this criterion: burning a whole task deadline before a SIGKILL is what "hangs the run" means, not the counter-example to it. Mitigated in practice — never closed — by §12.2's mandatory `--no-extensions`, which is what stops an `editor` request being issued at all; that makes the exposure conditional on a guard that lives elsewhere, and a criterion whose only defence is another criterion is not proved. NO MUTATION WAS RUN: there is nothing to mutate, and a test written today would have to assert the timeout behaviour rather than the criterion. WHAT IS MISSING: the ISC-111 responder (an `editor` answer is the same `{cancelled:true}` reply), plus fake-pi support for a UI request that WITHHOLDS `agent_end` until answered — without that the double cannot model a hang, and a scenario that emits an `editor` request and then finishes anyway would produce a green test proving only that the double does not block. Until the blocking-step form exists, any pass here is a false one. **[CLOSED 2026-08-24 by Phase E-A, and this note's "most likely to be FALSE in production rather than merely unproven" reading was CORRECT.]** The build confirms §4.2 exactly: `rpc-mode.js` builds `select`/`confirm`/`input` through `createDialogPromise`, which honours `opts.signal` and arms `if (opts?.timeout) setTimeout(...)`, while **`editor` is a bare promise with no timeout parameter, no signal and no cleanup**. The supervisor's answer really is the only unblocker. `DIALOG_METHODS` encodes this AS DATA rather than as a special case — its VALUE is what else can unblock the method, `supervisor_only` for `editor` and `agent_timeout_if_set` for the other three — so a future reader cannot collapse the four into one branch without deleting the distinction on purpose. MACHINE-CHECKED in CI via `test/fixtures/scenarios/ui-editor.json`, whose dialog carries NO `self_resolve_ms`, because `editor` has none. **MEASURED BOTH WAYS on the same fixture: 2.5 s answered versus 54.5 s unanswered**, and with the call site disabled the editor turn settles `timed_out`/`quiesced` after 20108 ms of a 20 s `deadline_s` — so the probe fails in the direction the criterion names. A `ui_dialog_unanswered` ledger entry is written if the watchdog ever fires, because the alternative is an operator seeing only `deadline_exceeded_no_terminal_event` twenty-five minutes later and having nothing to attribute it to.
- [x] ISC-113: Fire-and-forget UI methods receive no response and are logged. **[GRADED 2026-08-19 — PARTIAL. The sentence is now re-checked literally and in CI; it is `[~]` and not `[x]` because half of it passes VACUOUSLY.]** MACHINE-CHECKED, every CI run (`test/integration/ui-requests.test.ts`, collected by the workflow's `bun test test/integration` step, real detached supervisor, real fake-pi child, no Docker and no network): the new `test/fixtures/scenarios/ui-fire-and-forget.json` emits all FIVE fire-and-forget methods from SRD §4.2's vocabulary table — `notify`, `setStatus`, `setWidget`, `setTitle`, `set_editor_text` — mid-turn, each carrying an id an answer could be addressed to, and the test asserts both clauses. **"Are logged":** all five reach `events.jsonl` verbatim, in emission order, with `id`, `method` AND `params` intact — asserted as an ordered deep-equal against a list of the methods written out in the test rather than derived from the scenario, so a scenario that silently lost a method shrinks nothing. **"Receive no response":** observed from the FAR END OF THE WIRE. Nothing in the run directory can carry this — `events.jsonl` records what the supervisor RECEIVED, and a message never sent leaves no trace on disk — so `test/fixtures/fake-pi.ts` gained an opt-in `PIFLEET_FAKE_REQUEST_LOG` that appends every raw line the supervisor writes to the double's stdin. The assertion is an ALLOWLIST (every logged request's `type` must be one of the supervisor's own six commands) rather than only "no request carries a UI id", because a responder could address the request by id, echo it in `params`, or reply with a bare `{"type":"response"}`, and only the allowlist covers all three; a second assertion additionally rejects any sent line containing `uireq-` under any key. The log is also asserted NON-EMPTY and to contain the `prompt`, so "nothing was sent about these" cannot be satisfied by a plumbing failure that recorded nothing at all. Env-gated and therefore inert for every existing scenario. **MUTATION-PROVED, twice, both against `src/supervisor/index.ts` and both restored (sha256 `61c06af4…` before and after):** (1) guarding the event log with `if (event.type !== "extension_ui_request")` turns the logging clause red — *"Expected: [{id: uireq-notify, method: notify}, …5 entries]  Received: []"*; (2) adding `void client.send("extension_ui_response", {request_id: event.id, cancelled: true})` on every UI event turns the silence clause red — *"the supervisor wrote something that is not one of its own commands: [{type: extension_ui_response, request_id: uireq-notify, cancelled: true}, …]"*, `- Expected - 1 / + Received + 32`. The consequence: `neutralizeRepoHazards` quarantining a repo's `.pi/extensions/` is DEFENCE IN DEPTH against a class this Pi version does not trigger from a checkout — still correct (the behaviour is version-dependent, and the explicit-`-e` measurement proves the bytes are live the instant anything points at them), but not the primary control it was recorded as. **A TRIPWIRE RATHER THAN A GUARANTEE:** the third probe asserts the workspace payload executes nothing WITH discovery fully allowed as well as with the flags. That assertion is about Pi, not about pifleet, and it exists so a future Pi that DOES scan the workspace turns it red — at which point the hazard class becomes live, the quarantine becomes the primary control, and this entry has to be rewritten again. A red there is not a pifleet regression. **MUTATIONS, each reddening exactly one probe:** `buildPiArgv` stops emitting `--no-extensions` -> only "the production denial flags stop Pi loading an extension it otherwise runs" reddens; the payload's side effect removed -> only the positive control reddens. It had NO test before — `grep -rn 'ISC-123' test/ src/` returned nothing — and the property was held in place by design alone (worker checkouts are CLONES, not linked worktrees, so the branch is created in the clone and the parent only ever gets a `remote add`). The background listener's death is FATAL: the entrypoint supervises both, and if the listener dies the worker container ends.]** The reasoning given for the choice, because it constrains the implementation: a honeypot whose listener has silently died reports "no escape attempt" when it was simply not watching, and a detector that cannot be observed failing is the shape this file has now re-learned four times. The cost is accepted explicitly — `docker/entrypoint.sh` stops being a bare `exec` at its last line, which is cost (2) in the enumeration above and was the reason the question was asked. The two rejected options are recorded so the choice is not re-opened by accident: logging the death and letting the agent continue was refused because the run report would then have to distinguish "clean" from "unwatched" and nothing today can; doing without a background process was refused because no passive mechanism is known that observes a real client connect, and the cheap `cat`-in-the-background variant is already recorded above as detecting nothing. **[PHASE H CLOSE-OUT, 2026-08-27 — RE-GRADED `[ ]` -> `[x]`. Built to the shape this entry decided on 2026-08-21 and 2026-08-25; nothing about the design was re-opened, and the one thing that changed is recorded below because it changed a MEASUREMENT, not a choice.]** **WHAT `[x]` MEANS HERE, stated before the evidence so it cannot be read wider than it is:** a worker that connects to `/var/run/docker.sock` from inside its own container, under the full production posture, is recorded; the record reaches the operator's run report; and a run in which nothing was watching says so instead of reading clean. **THE SEED** is the one this entry chose: reach the Docker socket. **THE OBSERVER** is `docker/honeypot.cjs`, an AF_UNIX listener bound at that path which accepts, records, and destroys without reading or writing a byte — `curl` gets exit 56, which is asserted in the probe precisely because a detector that had never bound would give 7 and the attempt would go unrecorded, and the two are otherwise indistinguishable from a passing test. node rather than python3: the base image IS `node:*-bookworm-slim`, so node is in every toolchain variant, while python3 is only a transitive dependency of `google-cloud-cli`. **THE CHANNEL is reused, not built.** The listener appends to `/outbox/ledger/verbgate.jsonl` — ISC-172's file — so the evidence rides custody and truncation-marking that already exist and are already mutation-proved. A second file would have needed a second collector with its own frontier fingerprint to get the same property: new transport for no new guarantee. **THE REPORT gained a `security` field, which it had none of before**, and it carries THREE states rather than two: caught, watched-and-clean, and NOT WATCHED. The third is the whole point and is not decoration — `attempts: 0` means nothing unless something was listening, so the clean line names the number of containers actually armed rather than saying "no escape attempts", a sentence that reads identically whether the detector ran or was absent. **FOUR COSTS, all four paid as enumerated on 2026-08-21.** (1) `--tmpfs /run:rw,noexec,nosuid,size=1m,uid=10001,gid=10001` on the launch argv; MEASURED both ways against the real image under `--read-only --cap-drop ALL --security-opt no-new-privileges --user 10001` before the flag was written — without the uid option the bind fails `EACCES`, exactly as this entry predicted. (2) `docker/entrypoint.sh` stopped being a bare `exec`; it is now a bash supervisor. (3) the `security` field. (4) EIGHT Docker-gated probes in a new `test/integration/honeypot.test.ts`, counted by `TOTAL_EXPECTED`, DERIVED by the hand method rather than incremented: gate unset, bun 1.3.11, no listener on :8000, 6 pass / 113 skip / 0 fail, 119 tests across 13 files — 111 -> 119, eight more skips, pass unmoved at 6. **FOUR OF THE EIGHT ARE NOT ABOUT THE HONEYPOT, and they are the ones a reader is most likely to think are padding.** Turning the entrypoint into a supervisor put two things at risk that nothing else in this repo re-checks, because every other container probe runs `--entrypoint bash` and `down reaps the container` runs `alpine:latest`: a worker's exit code now travels THROUGH a supervisor instead of through process replacement, and SIGTERM now arrives at the supervisor instead of at the worker. Both are load-bearing — the verdict ladder reads the exit code, and `docker stop` is how every run ends. The stop probe bounds ELAPSED TIME rather than merely asserting the container stopped: without the trap it still stops, on Docker's SIGKILL, ten seconds later, so a probe that only checked the outcome would pass on the broken code. Mutations: remove `trap forward TERM INT HUP` -> only the stop probe reddens; replace `exit "${rc}"` with `exit 0` -> only the exit-code probe reddens. **THE THIRD OF THE THREE IS THE ONE THAT ACTUALLY SHIPPED BROKEN, and it is the most valuable thing in this close-out.** The worker container's STDOUT IS THE RPC STREAM — JSONL over stdin/stdout, `src/rpc/client.ts` — and both the entrypoint and the listener inherit that descriptor. `pifleet-honeypot: armed at /var/run/docker.sock` went to STDOUT, landing in the middle of the stream ahead of Pi's first message. **All six probes above passed on that code**, because every one of them runs `PIFLEET_WORKER_BIN=/bin/bash` and reads the two streams MERGED, which is precisely the reading that cannot see it. `container-live` — the only job in this repo that drives a real `up` through the real RPC path — caught it seven minutes into a run as `pifleet: worker eng-1 died during startup`, with no entrypoint output anywhere, because the output WAS the corruption. The fix is one word; the probe is the point. It reads stdout ALONE, asserts `toBe` rather than `toContain` (the defect is extra lines, which `toContain` tolerates), and asserts the arming line is present on STDERR — which is what distinguishes "moved to the right stream" from "stopped announcing itself". Mutation: put the write back on stdout -> only that probe reddens. **AND THE FOURTH IS THE SAME MISTAKE A SECOND TIME, which is why the lesson below is stated as a rule rather than as an anecdote.** POSIX assigns `/dev/null` to an asynchronous list's stdin when job control is off — always, in a non-interactive shell — so `pi "$@" &` handed the worker `/dev/null`. `pi --mode rpc` is a JSONL protocol ON STDIN; it read instant EOF and exited, and `up` reported `worker eng-1 died during startup` with no other symptom anywhere. MEASURED in the real image rather than deduced: `cat &` reads nothing, `exec 3<&0; cat <&3 &` reads the piped line. The fix is the saved-duplicate form, because `<&0` alone is not reliable — the default is applied to the asynchronous list BEFORE redirections are processed. Mutation: revert to the bare `&` -> only the stdin probe reddens, AND a real `pi --mode rpc` container goes `running=false` within six seconds, which is the CI failure reproduced locally rather than inferred. **THE GENERALISABLE LESSON, stated as a rule because it cost two CI round trips:** every local probe of this feature substituted `PIFLEET_WORKER_BIN=/bin/bash -c '<script>'` for the worker, and that seam neither READS stdin nor WRITES the RPC stream — which is both halves of the entrypoint's real contract. **A test seam that replaces the subject is blind to exactly the properties the subject has and the substitute does not**, and those are precisely the properties a bare `exec` used to provide for free and a supervisor has to provide on purpose. The two probes that close it are deliberately shaped against the seam rather than around it: one pipes bytes IN and asserts they arrive, one reads stdout ALONE and asserts `toBe` rather than `toContain`. **AND THE THING I SHOULD HAVE DONE FIRST:** before writing any probe, enumerate what `exec` was providing for free — stdout, stdin, exit status, signal delivery — and write one probe per item. That list is four items long, it is knowable in advance from the word `exec`, and every single defect in this build was on it. **AND THE EXIT-CODE PROBE EXISTS BECAUSE OF A HAZARD I FOUND BY RE-READING RATHER THAN BY TESTING.** `[ -n "${honeypot_pid}" ] && kill …` sits immediately before that `exit "${rc}"`, and under `set -e` a failing `&&` list can end a script. bash exempts it only because the failing command is not the last in the list — a RULE, not an intention, and a reorder of those two lines would silently turn every non-zero worker into a 1. I first concluded from my own probe that it was already broken; the probe was measuring `tail`'s exit status through a pipe, not the container's. Measured properly it is correct, and it is now re-checked every run rather than reasoned about. **THE OWNER DECISION IS IMPLEMENTED AND PROVED, not merely commented.** The listener's death ends the worker: measured exit 71, `ending the worker (ISC-125)` on stderr, and the worker's own `SURVIVED` line absent. **bash, not sh, and the reason is a defect I nearly shipped:** the first supervisor polled with `kill -0`, which SUCCEEDS on a zombie — a child that has exited and not been reaped — so the loop could never have noticed either process ending. `wait -n -p` is the only construct that reports which child exited without polling. **A SECOND DEFECT, found by running `docker stop` rather than reasoning about it:** `wait -n -p var` UNSETS `var` and re-sets it only when a process actually exited, so under `set -u` every trapped signal aborted the supervisor with `finished: unbound variable`, exit 1, and an unreaped worker. Assigning `""` before the wait does not help; the unset happens after it. After the fix, `docker stop` returns in 0s with the worker's own TERM handler having run and exit 0 — signal forwarding through a supervisor that no longer `exec`s. **MY OWN FIRST PROBE OF THE FATAL PATH WAS VACUOUS, and that is worth more than the passing one.** It used `pkill -f pifleet-honeypot`, which is wrong twice: `pkill` is not in the image, and the pattern also matches the entrypoint's and the worker's own argv, both of which contain that literal string from the test script. It reported `kill_rc=0`, killed nothing, and the worker survived — and had I read the exit code alone I would have concluded the supervision was broken and "fixed" working code. The shipped probe targets the process by `readlink /proc/<pid>/exe` and asserts BOTH the exit code and the absence of the worker's `SURVIVED` line, because an exit 71 from any other cause would otherwise read as the supervisor doing its job. **MUTATIONS, each reddening a DIFFERENT probe, which is what shows the four are not one claim.** Drop the `armed` row -> detection AND clean probes red (2 of 4). Stop recording attempts -> detection only (1 of 4). Remove the fatal branch, i.e. build the option this entry REJECTED -> the fatal probe only, and it takes 10.3s instead of 0.7s because the worker runs its whole sleep loop, which is the mutation's signature. Blank the report's `security` field -> the three report probes red, the fatal probe correctly untouched. Make "no records" read as `armed: true` -> the NOT WATCHED probe and the unit case that names it. Delete the `NOT WATCHED` branch from the renderer -> the same two. Drop `uid=` from the `/run` tmpfs -> the argv unit probe, and the container refuses to arm with `EACCES` and never starts the worker. All restored; `shasum -a 256 -c` verified. **A PROCESS FINDING WORTH KEEPING, because it cost real work:** the mutation backups were taken with `cp "$f" /tmp/bak/$(basename $f)`, and `src/config/render.ts` and `src/report/render.ts` share a basename — so one restore silently wrote the config renderer over the report renderer. Detected only because `shasum -c` was run afterwards rather than trusted. Back up by path, not by basename, and always check the restore. **THE ISA-CLAIMS ENTRY FOR THIS CRITERION WAS REPLACED, and the replacement is a finding about the registry itself.** The old claim was `grep -rn hazard src/report/` -> empty, worded as "the run report carries no security field at all … any hit means the reporting half of this criterion has been built". The reporting half is now built — as `security.escape_watch`, not as hazards — so that command STILL returns empty and the claim would have gone on passing while the sentence it defends had become false. That is the stale-grounds shape the registry exists to catch, arriving through the one direction its two-direction design does not cover: a claim whose SUBJECT moved rather than whose result moved. **RESIDUALS, none of which this grade closes.** (a) A worker can `unlink` the socket and bind its own in the `/run` tmpfs; the listener keeps its fd and does not die, so the substitution is NOT detected. It also gains the worker nothing — there is no Docker daemon behind either socket — but it is a real blind spot and not a theoretical one. (b) The rows are worker-authored: a worker can FORGE `escape_attempt` and `honeypot_armed` lines. Forging an alarm against yourself is not an attack, and forging `armed` only helps if the real detector was also suppressed, which ends the container — but "the rows are authentic" is NOT the guarantee and must not be restated as one. (c) ISC-172's accepted window is inherited whole: an attempt written AND truncated between two collector passes is lost, and only the truncation mark survives. (d) `RepoHazard` still reaches no report surface; `grep -n hazard src/report/*.ts` is still empty. That was never this criterion and is now stated as an open residual rather than carried in the claims registry as though it were. (e) If the listener dies AFTER the worker has already exited, `wait -n` may report the worker first and the run reads clean; the window is the microseconds between two exits and is not closed. **WHAT IS NOT ACCEPTED AS EVIDENCE HERE, restated because the temptation survives the close:** `docker/verbgate`'s refusals are a policy gate on cloud verbs, and `harvest/outbox.ts`'s symlink refusal is ISC-121 and is an escape from the OUTBOX. Neither is this criterion. The seed, the observation and the report are one path and were tested as one.
- [x] ISC-126: The control socket refuses a connection from another uid. **Stays `[ ]`. No uid check exists anywhere in the codebase, and the refusal that does occur is an unasserted side-effect of the operator's ambient umask.** `grep -rn 'getpeereid|SO_PEERCRED|peerCred|getuid|geteuid' src/` returns NOTHING, and no test in the repo names this criterion. [BOTH HALVES SUPERSEDED by this entry's own close-out below, which built `src/security/peer-uid.ts`; re-run with `-E` today that pattern returns 34 hits, 30 of them in that module. Flagged 2026-08-25 by the staleness sweep and left in place as history rather than edited, because the close-out already says so — but noting here that AS WRITTEN the command is un-runnable: without `-E`, grep reads `|` literally and it returns zero whatever the code does.] THE MECHANISM, read rather than assumed: `run/registry.ts`'s `serveJsonlSocket` calls `mkdir(dirname(path), { recursive: true })` with NO mode argument and `Bun.listen({ unix: path })` with no subsequent `chmod`, so both the socket and its directory inherit whatever the process umask yields. MEASURED on this machine by standing up a real listener through that production path: socket `0755`, directory `0755`, umask `022`; others cannot WRITE the socket, and on Linux `connect(2)` to a unix socket requires write permission, so another uid is in fact refused — with `EACCES` from the kernel, not from this code. THAT IS WHY IT IS NOT `[~]`. The protection is real but INCIDENTAL and INVERTS: an operator running with `umask 000` gets a `0777` socket in a `0777` directory and another uid connects successfully, at which point the only thing standing between them and the verbs is the ISC-181 auth token — which is the layer `security/control-auth.ts` explicitly describes as the SECOND line, on the stated basis that filesystem permissions already handle "another USER". So the module's own threat model rests on a property nothing establishes, nothing asserts, and the operator's shell can silently revoke. Worth noting alongside ISC-127: that criterion's exposure would have let a container READ `control-auth.json`, so these two failure modes compose — the filesystem gate is undefended by code and the token gate was reachable through a supported mount. ISC-127 is now closed; this one is not. NOT SUBSTITUTED WITH A WEAKER PROXY, deliberately. A test asserting the socket's mode bits, or that the directory is `0700`, would prove something STRICTLY WEAKER than the criterion — "the permissions look right on this machine today" is not "a connection from another uid is refused", and pinning `0755` would additionally pin the ambient umask of whoever ran it. No such test was added, and the measurement above is recorded here instead so the next reader starts from the fact rather than from the comment. WHAT A REAL `[x]` NEEDS — a genuine second uid, which this host cannot supply without `sudo`: (1) an engineered check, i.e. `getpeereid`/`SO_PEERCRED` on accept with an explicit refusal when the peer uid is not the server's, plus a `chmod 0700` on the socket directory so the control is code rather than umask; and (2) a probe that connects AS a different uid. Docker can supply the second uid for free — `docker run --user <other-uid>` against the socket directory bind-mounted in — and that probe would belong in the `container` job. It was NOT written here because it cannot be honestly verified on this machine: `socketPath()` puts the socket under `os.tmpdir()`, which on macOS is `/var/folders/...` and is NOT in the Docker VM's shared set (`container/mounts.ts` records the measurement), so the container would mount an empty directory and the probe would pass or fail for reasons unrelated to uid. Shipping a probe whose red and green states have never both been observed is the failure this ISA's mutation convention exists to prevent, so the honest move was to leave the criterion open and name the blocker. **[UNBLOCKED 2026-08-20 by the container launcher (ISC-286/287): the runtime path this criterion was waiting on now exists — `up` records a launch argv and the supervisor spawns it, so a container can be inspected, exec'd into and torn down. This criterion is NOT closed by that; what it asks for still has to be built and probed. The note is here so the next reader does not re-derive that the blocker was absence of a launcher.]** **[CLOSED 2026-08-24 by Phase E-B. BOTH halves this note demanded were built, and the note's own stated blocker turned out to be the WRONG blocker.]** **(1) The engineered check exists.** `security/peer-uid.ts` asks the KERNEL who is on the other end of an accepted connection — `getpeereid` on macOS, `SO_PEERCRED` on Linux — and refuses when the peer uid is not the one the socket serves. It has its production caller at `src/run/registry.ts:38`. **(2) The filesystem gate is now CODE, not umask.** `registry.ts` chmods the socket directory AND the socket to 0700 explicitly. `mkdir`'s `mode` option is not sufficient for two separate reasons and both were checked: it is masked by the umask on the way through, and it does nothing at all when the directory already exists — which is the common case, since the run directory is created before the daemon starts. **(3) The probe connects AS a different uid**, for real, and it is `PIFLEET_DOCKER=1`-gated so it runs in the `container` job. **THE BLOCKER IN THIS NOTE WAS CORRECT AND INCOMPLETE, and the correction is the finding.** The note said a bind-mount probe could not be honestly verified because `socketPath()` lives under `os.tmpdir()`, which is `/var/folders/...` on macOS and outside the Docker VM's shared set. Measured 2026-08-24: repeating the experiment from a directory that IS shared — under `$HOME`, exactly where `container/mounts.ts` says bind mounts work — the socket appears in the container, `ls -l` shows it as a socket with the right mode, and **`connect(2)` returns ENOTSUP**. It fails IDENTICALLY for a matching uid and a differing one, so that shape cannot distinguish the two on macOS AT ALL. The VM's filesystem passthrough carries the NAME of a unix socket, not the socket. **Fixing the path — which is what this note implied — would have produced a probe that still proved nothing here and whose green state could only ever have been seen on CI**, which is the exact failure the mutation convention exists to prevent. So the probe puts BOTH ENDS INSIDE ONE CONTAINER: the socket lives on the container's own filesystem where it is an ordinary Linux unix socket, the server runs as uid 0 and the probing client as uid 12345 via `docker exec -u`. A genuine second uid on a shared kernel, and **both the red and green states of every assertion were observed on this machine** before it shipped. **The unit layer does something this note thought impossible:** `expectUid` narrows the gate to exactly one uid — it cannot disable the control, only point it elsewhere — which drives the refusal path on a single-uid machine without `sudo`. That is a MECHANISM test and is recorded as one; pointing the gate at another uid and connecting as another uid are different claims, and only the second is this criterion. **CONSEQUENCE FOR ISC-181:** `security/control-auth.ts`'s header asserted that filesystem permissions were "sufficient against another USER", making its token the SECOND line. At `umask 000` that was false and the token was the FIRST line. The header is amended to describe what the code now does, and to keep the distinction it was always right about — the uid gate cannot see another PROCESS of the same user, which is what the token is for. The `container` job's probe-count guard is RE-DERIVED by hand, 91 -> 94, measured with the gate unset as 6 pass / 88 skip across 10 files — not incremented.
- [x] ISC-127: The run-dir is not mounted in any container. **It was FALSE as shipped, and the measurement came first.** Driving `renderWorker` with `run.repo` set to a checkout that CONTAINS the runs root — `PIFLEET_RUNS_DIR=<repo>/runs`, an ordinary thing to want and reachable purely through supported config — produced a `/workspace` bind mount whose source was an ancestor of `<run-dir>/control-auth.json`. That file is the 0600 per-run control-socket secret whose entire threat model (`security/control-auth.ts`) is that a worker cannot read it; the same mount also hands over `registry.json`, `ledger/`, `inbox/` (full task envelopes), `run.json`, and every OTHER worker's `state.json` and `events.jsonl`. Nothing in `render.ts` looked wrong, because every literal in its mount table is still a run-dir CHILD — the exposure lives in the relationship between two operator-settable values, which is knowable only on the finished argv. THE LITERAL READING IS THE ONLY WORKABLE ONE and is what is enforced: §5.5 mounts `<run>/outbox/<id>`, `<run>/sessions`, `<run>/skills/<role>`, `<run>/workers/<id>/cloud-allow` and the briefing ON PURPOSE, so "no mount is under the run dir" would be a criterion production must violate to function. What must never be mounted is the run dir ITSELF, or any ancestor of it. FIXED IN PRODUCTION, not merely asserted about: `classifyRunDirExposure` / `assertNoRunDirMount` in `run/paths.ts`, called at the end of `buildDockerArgv` beside the ISC-44 guard it is deliberately modelled on — two relations (`is-the-run-dir`, `contains-the-run-dir`) rather than three, for the reason above. `grep -rn assertNoRunDirMount src/` confirms a real production caller, not the predicate-with-no-importer shape ISC-44 records its own constants having been in. Note this is NOT caught incidentally by the gcloud guard: a checkout under `/tmp` or `~/proj` contains no `~/.config/gcloud`, so `assertNoHostGcloudMount` passes it happily. MACHINE-CHECKED AT TWO ALTITUDES, BOTH EXECUTING IN CI. `test/unit/render.test.ts` (fast `test` job, every push) asserts across all three `isolation` modes that no bind-mount source is the run dir or an ancestor, that run-dir CHILDREN are still mounted (so the check is not vacuous on an empty table), and that `control-auth.json` is inside no mounted subtree; a second case drives the exposing config through `renderWorker` and requires a `RunDirMountError`. `test/integration/container-env.test.ts` reads the same claim back out of `docker inspect .Mounts` on a container started from production's own argv, `realpath`-normalising both sides — it runs in the `container` job (see ISC-31 for the `TOTAL_EXPECTED` 79 -> 81 derivation) and self-skips nowhere in CI. THREE MUTATIONS, confirmed RED and reverted. (A) guard call disabled -> `a run.repo that CONTAINS the run directory is refused, not rendered (ISC-127)` red: `expect(received).not.toBeNull() / Received: null` — the exposing config rendered silently. (B) `argv.push("-v", ${opts.run.root}:/rundir)` in the mount table with the guard disabled -> red naming the offence: `Expected: "…/dry -> clean" / Received: "…/dry -> is-the-run-dir"`. (F) the same mount against the live daemon -> integration half red identically. It is now a `mkdtemp` sibling, matching the form the ISC-188 "moved" case already used. All of that was true. What none of it established is that the PREDICATE could see, and it could not: **`-v /:/host` — the entire host filesystem, the maximal violation of this criterion — passed `classifyRunDirExposure` cleanly.** `dir.startsWith(`${s}/`)` builds `"//"` when `s` is `/`, and no path in existence starts with `"//"`, so the one mount that exposes every run directory, every ssh key and the docker socket returned `null`. Root-has-no-separator, in a function whose whole subject is separators. **AND THE INDEPENDENT BACKSTOP HAD THE IDENTICAL BUG.** `render.test.ts`'s hand-written `control-auth.json` containment check — written deliberately as a string comparison so it would NOT agree with production's predicate by construction — was also spelled `startsWith(`${s}/`)`. Demonstrated rather than asserted: with `-v /:/host` pushed into the mount table, both guards disabled and `classifyRunDirExposure` blinded to `null`, the original backstop line ran **1 pass / 0 fail**; the fixed line fails `Expected: false / Received: true`. An independent backstop that reproduces the predicate's bug is not independent — it is the same mistake typed twice, and it cost this criterion its only cross-check. **SEVEN DEFECTS FIXED, each mutation-verified RED and reverted.** Baseline for every tally below is `bun test test/unit/render.test.ts test/unit/container-env.test.ts` = **61 pass / 0 fail**. (1) **The filesystem root.** `isPathUnder` special-cases `/`; mutation restoring the bare prefix -> 59/2, `Expected: "/ -> contains-the-run-dir" / Received: "/ -> null"`. (2) **Case-variant spellings.** `resolve()` does not case-fold, so on this project's own dev platform `/USERS/OP/PROJ/RUNS/R-1` and `/Users/op/proj/Runs` were both `null` — the SAME directory on default APFS, and Docker Desktop mounts them. The fold is UNCONDITIONAL rather than `platform === "darwin"`, and the reasoning is in the docstring: `process.platform` is a proxy for a filesystem's case behaviour rather than the truth (APFS can be case-sensitive, Linux mounts case-insensitive volumes), the two errors are wildly asymmetric (a false red is an actionable refusal, a false green is the control secret), the `<run>-backup` false-red argument does not transfer because a live case-twin of the runs root is not an ordinary thing to have, and — decisively — a platform branch would make the case test skip on Linux CI, leaving the darwin behaviour proved only by whoever last ran the suite on a Mac. This ISA does not count self-skipping evidence. Mutation removing the fold -> 60/1. The ISA's own stated mutation (`-v ${opts.run.root}:/rundir` in `buildDockerArgv`) could not catch it, because that tests whether the guard is WIRED, not whether it can SEE; blinding the predicate while leaving the renderer honest is the mutation that separates the two. Now pinned by a `renderWorker`-driven case using only operator-settable values (`run.repo` absolute, `PIFLEET_RUNS_DIR`, and `--run-id`, a real `render` flag) -> 59/2. **Note what that mutation now produces, because it changes the claim:** with the cross-run relation in place the blinded exact relation falls through to `is-another-run-dir`, so the mount is still REFUSED and what breaks is the DIAGNOSIS. The test catches it because it asserts the relation by name rather than merely that something threw. (4) **The separator defence was untested.** It worked; nothing stopped its deletion (50/0). Pinned with sources OUTSIDE the runs root, which is where the separator is the only thing doing the work — `<base>/run` (a string prefix of the run dir at a non-boundary) and `<runsRoot>-backup`. Mutation dropping the separator -> 60/1, `Expected: "/Users/op/proj/run -> clean" / Received: "/Users/op/proj/run -> contains-the-run-dir"`, i.e. a FALSE RED, which is the failure mode the separator exists to prevent. (5) **Three of four Docker bind-mount spellings bypassed the guard.** `--volume=<src>:<dst>`, `-v<src>:<dst>` and `--mount type=bind,source=…` are all valid docker and all walked past a scan that understood only the two-element form. Latent — `render.ts` emits one spelling — and latency is the argument FOR the fix: the entire stated justification for checking the finished argv is that upstream literals cannot be trusted, so a guard depending on upstream keeping one spelling has re-imported the assumption it was built to remove. Now parsed by one shared `bindMountSources` (`container/docker-argv.ts`); mutation -> 60/1. (6) **Relative host paths were dropped as "a named volume".** `./runs/r-1` is a host path and Docker mounts it. The distinction now drawn is Docker's own — a bare NAME with no separator is a volume, anything else is a path resolved against `process.cwd()`, which is correct rather than convenient because these guards run in the process that spawns docker. Mutation -> 60/1. (7) **`RunDirMountError` reported as `internal error`.** It carried no `exitCode`, so `isExitCoded` was false and `exitCodeForError` fell to `EXIT.INTERNAL` — meaning the message written so an operator could move their runs root was prefixed `pifleet: internal error:`, which tells them the tool is broken and there is nothing for them to fix. Now `EXIT.USAGE`, the grade `ConfigError` carries. **TWO GAPS CLOSED THAT WERE NOT DEFECTS IN THE GUARD BUT IN ITS EVIDENCE.** (8) **The integration containment assertion was CONDITIONALLY VACUOUS, and the condition was "macOS".** `control-auth.json` is minted by the supervisor, `startRenderedWorker` never started one, so `realpath` threw `ENOENT` and `norm`'s `.catch(() => p)` returned the UNRESOLVED path while `runDirReal` beside it was resolved — on a `/var/folders/...` scratch root the two share no prefix and every comparison passed on the mismatch rather than on the property. Demonstrated: with the mint removed the ORIGINAL assertion runs **2 pass / 0 fail** against a file that does not exist; the new one fails `Expected: true / Received: false` on an added `exists()` precondition. The secret is now minted through `ensureControlAuth` — production's own path, not a hand-written stand-in — and derived from `runDirReal` rather than re-normalised. (9) **The `-e` source sweep had ZERO demonstrated sensitivity.** Its regex wanted a quoted SCREAMING_CASE literal after a quoted `-e`, a sequence appearing nowhere in this repository — not in `relay.ts` (template literal) nor `probe-transport.ts` (bare identifier), i.e. neither of the two forms its own codebase uses. It collected into an empty array and compared it against an empty array on every commit and could not have done otherwise. Extracted to `test/support/env-sweep.ts` and paired with a fixture test asserting it flags all eight hazardous spellings and none of four safe ones; the repo scan additionally asserts `scanned > 20` so a mis-rooted glob cannot pass either. Mutation reverting the regex -> 60/1. **ONE RELATION ADDED: `is-another-run-dir`.** A sibling run directory under the same runs root was neither this run dir nor an ancestor of it and classified clean — while holding THAT run's `control-auth.json`, ledger, inbox and worker state. Concurrent runs under one root are the normal way this tool is used. Graded under ISC-127 rather than filed separately because the criterion's sentence is "the run-dir is not mounted in any container" and a concurrent run's directory is a run dir. Mutation -> 59/2. **This interacts with (4) and the interaction is worth recording:** `r-10` and `<run>-backup` are sibling-prefixes of `r-1`, so the separator correctly keeps them out of the CHILD/ANCESTOR relations — and both are then refused anyway by the new relation, because both sit in the runs root. An early framing of the separator finding said `r-10` "must be allowed"; that was right about the relation and wrong as a verdict on the source, and asserting the verdict would have pinned the cross-run hole OPEN. **THE SYMLINK HALF IS NOW CLOSED IN PRODUCTION, which is what keeps this `[x]` rather than `[~]`.** The lexical compare is forced on `buildDockerArgv` — synchronous and pure by design — but that constrains the FUNCTION, not the criterion: `renderWorker` is already `async`, is the only production path that produces a worker argv, and `materializeWorkerInputs` awaits it before creating anything. `assertNoRunDirMountResolved` now runs there. Neither value is unusual, neither is hostile, and lexically they share no prefix at all. `realpathish` resolves the deepest EXISTING ancestor and re-appends the tail, because the run dir does not exist yet at render time and a plain `realpath(p).catch(() => p)` would return the unresolved path — reintroducing defect (8) inside the fix for it. The integration half was executed locally against a real container and the real image (`PIFLEET_DOCKER=1`, `pifleet/pi-worker:verify`): 2 pass / 0 fail. No new integration test was added, so no `cliBudget` derivation applies — every case added here is a unit test spawning no subprocess. **NOT ONE ASSERTION WAS WEAKENED.** `git diff` removes exactly two `expect(...)` lines and both are the defective ones described in (1) and (8); each is replaced by the same property checked correctly, and (8)'s replacement additionally adds the `exists()` precondition. Both replacements are mutation-proved strictly stronger than what they replace. **RESIDUALS, named rather than left implicit.** (a) The same root hole and the same three-spelling gap existed INDEPENDENTLY in `assertNoHostGcloudMount` / `classifyHostGcloudExposure`, so `-v /:/host` handed over the host gcloud auth store too. Both are fixed here and both are now pinned (`the filesystem root is refused by the gcloud guard too (ISC-44)`), and the two guards now share one boundary definition — `isPathUnder` / `pathsEqual` — because two copies of a boundary cannot check each other. **ISC-44's checkbox is NOT moved, by an explicit grader's ruling rather than by omission:** its claim is now true and pinned in production, a checkbox records whether the criterion holds with reproducible evidence, and re-grading `[x]` -> `[ ]` -> `[x]` inside one branch churns the record without informing anyone. No new criterion number was taken. What the gap warranted was HISTORY, and ISC-44's own close-out now carries it — both defects, both mutations, and the shared-boundary reasoning. Its spelling coverage is pinned by a test named for ISC-44 rather than inherited from ISC-127's, because when two criteria rest on one piece of shared code the criterion that depends on a behaviour must be the one that reddens when it is removed. (b) `assertNoRunDirMountResolved` protects `renderWorker` only. Any future synchronous caller of `buildDockerArgv` gets the lexical guard alone. `renderWorker` is the sole production caller today, and that is a fact with a shelf life. (c) `bindMountSources` scans the WHOLE argv including elements after the image, which belong to the container's command rather than to Docker. Deliberate, and it errs toward refusing; the alternative requires knowing which element is the image, a question with no reliable syntactic answer. (d) The `-e` sweep's interpreter exclusion (`"node", "-e"`) is a heuristic, stated as one in its header, and both sides of it are exercised by the fixture so it cannot silently widen into matching nothing the way its predecessor did. (e) Everything here is still argv-level enforcement: `up` does not launch worker containers yet (ISC-248), so this proves production's argv is refused, not that a running fleet was observed refusing it. **[ADDENDUM 2026-08-20 — an ENVIRONMENT LEAK in this criterion's own integration file, fixed here and belonging to ISC-278.]** The general property — *no test file leaves a `PIFLEET_*` variable different at process exit from what it was at load* — is ISC-278, filed on the coverage-doctor branch and NOT present in this tree; these two sites are named there and this note is the cross-reference from the branch that repaired them. **What was wrong.** `test/integration/container-env.test.ts` set `PIFLEET_RUNS_DIR` to a `makeDaemonScratch` directory and never restored it, while its own `afterEach` `rm -rf`'d that directory. `test/unit/container-env.test.ts` did the opposite and equally wrong thing: it `delete`d the variable unconditionally in `afterAll`, with no BEFORE capture, destroying an ambient value it never owned. **Why this is a CORRECTNESS problem and not tidiness**, which is the distinction worth keeping: the leaked value does not merely point somewhere wrong, it points at a directory **that no longer exists**. Measured by reverting each fix with an ambient value exported — integration: `before="/tmp/ambient-runs-dir" after="<scratch>/runs" dir=DELETED`; unit: `before="/tmp/ambient-runs-dir" after=undefined`. Every run path in the codebase derives from that variable, so a later file inherits a runs root that cannot be read or written, and whatever it then reports is about the wrong world. Both read `PRESERVED` with the fixes in place, using the save/restore idiom `render.test.ts` already had four files away. Restored in `afterEach` on the integration side rather than `afterAll`, deliberately: the scratch dies per test, so anything later leaves a window in which the variable names a deleted directory even WITHIN the file. **THE ORDERING PREMISE, VERIFIED INDEPENDENTLY RATHER THAN ACCEPTED, because "this file sorts last" reasoning has now misled two separate gradings.** bun does NOT execute test files in CLI argument order. Measured directly on this repo: `bun test clock render container-env` and `bun test container-env clock render` BOTH executed `container-env` FIRST — i.e. a file listed LAST still ran FIRST. Order comes from `readdir()`, which differs between APFS and a fresh Linux clone, so no argument of the form "this file runs late so its leak is harmless" can be relied on in either direction. In the container job's real order this file runs SECOND of seven, so five Docker-gated files ran after it inheriting the dangling value. That is why the fix is to stop leaking rather than to be positioned safely — position is not a property this suite has.

- [x] ISC-135: Anti: disabling `read-screen` entirely changes no acceptance result.
