- [x] ISC-138: Anti: no code path uses `readline` or `split(/\r?\n/)` on an RPC or session stream. **[CLOSED 2026-08-19 — a GRADING correction, not new work.]** The coverage already existed and had existed for some time: `test/unit/rpc-client.test.ts` carries a block headed "Static anti-criteria (ISC-137, ISC-138)" which scans every file under `src/**/*.ts` for four readline usage forms (`from "node:readline"`, `require(...)`, dynamic `import(...)`, and any `createInterface(`) and for the literal split patterns `split(/\r?\n` and `split(/\n`. ISC-137, its sibling in the same block, has been `[x]` throughout; ISC-138 was left `[ ]`. **The guard is stricter than the criterion**, which is why this is safe to close: ISC-138 asks only about "an RPC or session stream", while the test bans these forms across the whole of `src/`. **Mutation-verified before grading rather than taken on trust**, since a guard nobody has seen fail is indistinguishable from one that cannot: planting `"x".split(/\r?\n/)` in `src/rpc/epoch.ts` turns it red, planting `import { createInterface } from "node:readline"` turns it red, and removing both returns it green.
- [x] ISC-139: Anti: no generated commit, branch, or PR body contains AI attribution. **[CLOSED 2026-08-19 by this PR.]** Two probes in `test/unit/anti-criteria.test.ts`, and the second is the one that matters. **First, attribution CONSTRUCTIONS under `src/`** — a `Co-Authored-By` trailer, a "generated with/by <tool>" credit, an `AI-`/`LLM-generated|assisted|authored` label. The first draft of this guard banned the bare TOKENS `claude`, `anthropic` and `copilot`, and went red immediately on six legitimate sites: `CLAUDE.md` is a FILENAME this tool must know, because `src/security/repo-hazards.ts` scans repository instruction files and `src/run/worktree.ts` reasons about a clone that carries one. A guard that fires on the subject matter rather than the defect is worse than no guard, so it matches phrasing that has no legitimate use here. **Second, a CAPABILITY PIN, because two thirds of this criterion is vacuous.** Enumerating the git subcommands that appear as argv literals under `src/` gives add, branch, checkout, config, diff, log, rev-parse, status, symbolic-ref, worktree — **no `commit`, no `push`, no `gh`**. pifleet creates branches and worktrees and nothing else, so "no generated COMMIT or PR BODY carries attribution" is true because there are none. A vacuously-true clause is exactly the kind that rots: someone adds `git commit` for a good reason and the clause silently goes live with nothing watching. The test therefore asserts the absence of the CAPABILITY and fails loudly the day it changes, naming what the next author must extend. **The one artifact that IS generated is pinned by behaviour**: `workerBranch` must return its three inputs joined and nothing more, so a later edit appending a suffix or a credit fails here rather than being noticed in `git branch` output months later. Mutation-verified three ways: a planted trailer, a planted `["git", "commit"]` literal, and a decorated branch template each turn it red.
- [x] ISC-140: Anti: no acceptance test in the `headless` suite requires provider spend or a cloud endpoint. **[CLOSED 2026-08-19 by this PR.]** `test/e2e/` IS the headless acceptance suite — `lifecycle.test.ts` opens by naming its own contract, "no Docker, no network, no GUI (ISC-19, ISC-128)". The guard requires that no file there names a provider credential (`*_API_KEY|SECRET|TOKEN`) or an `http(s)` endpoint, with loopback excluded since a fixture may legitimately name it. **Split from ISC-21 deliberately, because the two fail in opposite directions**: a test that needs egress fails CLOSED on an air-gapped runner and everybody finds out, while a test that needs provider spend PASSES and quietly bills someone — the second is the one no green tick will ever reveal, which is why it earns its own probe rather than riding on ISC-21's. Measured at closure: the suite touches only `PIFLEET_RUNS_DIR` and `PIFLEET_PI_*` and contains no URL at all. The guard also fails if it finds zero e2e files, so it cannot pass by pointing at nothing. Mutation-verified: a planted `process.env.OPENAI_API_KEY` and a planted `https://api.example.com` each turn it red.

### Group M — Review findings (added 2026-07-27, post-advisor)

Criteria that came out of the commitment-boundary review. Several correct the SRD
rather than merely implementing it; SRD errata are recorded in `## Changelog`.

- [x] ISC-141: Epoch attribution uses the RPC stream offset, and the SRD §7.5 interleaving is decided correctly when offset is the only distinguishing signal. **PARTIAL — both machines are mutation-proved; the supervisor line that joins them is not, and the e2e test named for this interleaving does not test it.** MACHINE-CHECKED every CI run (`bun test test/unit`). `epoch.test.ts`'s "EpochManager — stream-offset fencing (the §7.5 interleaving)" decides the interleaving on offset alone: epoch 1's straggler at seq 19 — read AFTER epoch 2 was allocated and byte-identical to what epoch 2's own terminal event will look like — is `prior` against `ack_seq` 20, while the same shape at seq 21 is `live`. Mutation-proved: collapsing `attribute` to `if (live !== null) return "live"`, which is exactly the SRD window rule this erratum exists to correct, fails it with `Expected: "prior" / Received: "live"`. That covered the DECISION and left the INPUT unpinned, so this audit added `rpc-client.test.ts`'s "RpcClient x EpochManager — the ack's offset is the fence post (ISC-141)": the real client driving a real `EpochManager`, with the straggler, the ack and epoch 2's output PACKED INTO ONE WRITE, so the ack has to land on the fence synchronously at its true position (record 2) before the next line in the same chunk is dispatched. It is mutation-proved twice over — `pending.onAck?.(seq)` -> `pending.onAck?.(0)` fails it with `Expected [2] / Received [0]`, and the `attribute` collapse fails it with `"prior"` -> `"live"`. **NOT PROVED, and this is precisely why the grade is not `[x]`: the fleet can stop using the offset entirely and CI stays green.** Rewriting `src/supervisor/index.ts`'s `em.attribute(seq)` to `em.attribute(Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER)` — every event live regardless of stream position — passed `test/unit`, `test/integration/{supervisor,dispatch-auto}.test.ts` and the e2e §7.5 case. Before the new test existed the `onAck?.(0)` mutation passed all of those too. **The e2e case that appears to cover this is load-bearing for something else:** `lifecycle.test.ts`'s "the §7.5 interleave" (filed under ISC-84) survives both mutations, because T-005's window never opens — `windowOpen`, not the fence, is what stops the straggler settling epoch 2 there — and its `"prior"` assertion is satisfied by post-settle stragglers arriving while `live` is null, a path that returns `prior` under every mutation tried. Closing this needs a test that drives the real supervisor and asserts the `epoch_attribution` records carry the stream's true seqs. **Grading this `[~]` also exposed a latent defect and fixed it:** `definedIscIds` in `src/attended/voided.ts` matched `- [` `[ x]` `]` only, so a criterion graded partial stopped counting as DEFINED — and because ISC-141 is itself a row in the `tui` voided table, the cross-check immediately reported that operator-facing table as pointing at a nonexistent criterion. A false positive of exactly the rot the check exists to catch. The character class is now `[ x~]`; strictness is unchanged and mutation-proved — dropping the anchor and the checkbox so bare prose mentions match fails "a prose mention of an ISC id is not a definition". **[CLOSE-OUT 2026-08-27 — RE-GRADED `[~]` -> `[x]`. The supervisor-level test this entry asked for now exists. Getting there required refuting this entry's own diagnosis, and the refutation is the substance.]** **THIS ENTRY SAID A TEST WAS MISSING. IT WAS NOT MISSING; AT THE SITE THIS ENTRY NAMED IT IS IMPOSSIBLE.** The recorded evidence was that rewriting `src/supervisor/index.ts`'s `em.attribute(seq)` to `em.attribute(Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER)` passed every suite. Reading three files says why it had to. `RpcClient` dispatches records SYNCHRONOUSLY and IN STREAM ORDER (`client.ts`: `pending.onAck?.(seq)` and `onEvent(msg, seq)` in one loop). `EpochManager.attribute` answers `live` only when `ack_seq !== null && seq > ack_seq`. `windowOpen` becomes true only through `bindStart`, which itself requires `attribute(seq) === "live"`. So the window opens at some `seq_start > ack_seq` and every record after it has a higher seq still — the supervisor's guard `if (attribution === "live" && em.windowOpen)` can never see the two disagree. No test at that call site can discriminate, and writing one would have produced a probe that passes for reasons unrelated to its name. **WHAT IS LOAD-BEARING IS THE OTHER CONJUNCT, `ack_seq !== null`.** Before the live epoch's prompt is acknowledged there is no fence post, and everything in that region must be `prior` — including an `agent_start`, which would otherwise BIND the window and hand a settled epoch's straggler the power to complete the new one. **That region was unreachable from any scenario**: `emit` and `emit_after_respond` both run after the ack. `emit_before_ack` (new, `test/fixtures/fake-pi.ts`, AWAITED so it cannot race the ack) is what puts a record below `ack_seq`, and it is the shape a real worker produces whenever a previous turn is still draining as the next prompt arrives — drain and ack share one pipe and the drain got there first. **THE PROBE** is `test/integration/supervisor.test.ts`'s "the pre-ack start is attributed prior, and the post-ack start is what binds", driving the REAL supervisor over `stale-start.json`. Three assertions that are not one claim: the pre-ack `agent_start` is recorded `epoch_attribution/prior` WITH the stream's true seq; epoch 2's window opens exactly once, at a STRICTLY HIGHER seq taken from the supervisor's own `epoch_started` record (so it is the stream's real offsets being compared, not a pair the test chose); and `T-FENCE-2` still settles `success`, which is what separates "the stale start was refused" from "nothing was accepted". **MUTATIONS, and the second is the one that corrected me.** Dropping `ack_seq !== null` from `attribute` -> this probe reddens; it is the first thing anywhere to kill that conjunct. Neutralising the OFFSET COMPARISON itself (`seq > ack_seq` -> `true`) -> this probe PASSES, as predicted, but three other tests fail: `epoch.test.ts`'s two stream-offset cases and ISC-147's scenario-coverage guard. **So my first framing — "the comparison is dead code" — was too strong and is recorded here as refuted.** The comparison is exercised and mutation-proved at the UNIT boundary, where a caller can present any seq it likes; it is unreachable-as-a-discriminator only THROUGH the supervisor's in-order stream. Both statements are needed: the first is why the unit test is not redundant, the second is why the supervisor test had to be aimed one call up. **ISC-147's GUARD FIRED ON THIS WORK AND WAS RIGHT TO:** adding `stale-start.json` failed "every scenario on disk has a reviewed expectation" until the settle count was declared. Declared `[1, 2]` and the property test confirmed it — a reviewed claim, checked, not a number copied to make a suite green.
- [x] ISC-142: A dispatch whose epoch is `<=` the worker's persisted `last_accepted_epoch` is rejected at the worker side, not merely bookkept by the allocator. **[CLOSED 2026-08-20 by this PR. The behaviour existed and was production-reachable the whole time; NOTHING re-checked it, and the block that looked like it did is about a test double.]** MACHINE-CHECKED every CI run (`bun test test/integration`). **The rejection is WORKER-SIDE, and this note is deliberate about which "worker" that is,** because the codebase supports two readings and only one of them is closable. It executes in the `pifleet-worker` supervisor process, against the `last_accepted_epoch` that process read from its own `fence.json` at boot (`new EpochManager(await readFence(wp))`, `src/supervisor/index.ts:210`), and the dispatching side is not consulted at any point. That is the reading `## Decisions` fixes — "the fence is enforced at the worker, not only at the allocator … The worker side persists `last_accepted_epoch`" — and `last_accepted_epoch` is a `FenceSnapshot` field that only the supervisor ever persists. **The other reading is NOT closed by this and cannot be:** `rpc/epoch.ts`'s own header describes a Pi-side fence as "a second line of defence", and `supervisor.test.ts`'s "fake-pi worker-side epoch fence" block does prove a prompt at or below the high-water-mark is refused — but that is a fact about `test/fixtures/fake-pi.ts`, whose mark is an in-memory `let` that dies with the process, and about no line in `src/`. The real Pi is a third-party binary that makes no such promise. **What now proves the criterion:** `supervisor.test.ts` > "the worker's persisted fence refuses stale dispatch (ISC-142)". It writes `fence.json` with `last_accepted_epoch: 3` BEFORE the supervisor process exists, launches a real detached supervisor over that run dir, and then speaks the control socket DIRECTLY rather than through `sendTaskEnvelope` — which is the "a detached supervisor plus a CLI relaunch is two allocators" hazard in its actual shape: a second allocator that never heard of epoch 3 asks for epoch 3. Three refusals, because the `<=` region has two distinct branches and pinning one leaves the other free to start accepting: epoch 3 (the boundary itself) is `stale_epoch` naming both numbers, `requested: 3` and `next: 4`; epoch 2 (below, never settled) is `stale_epoch`; epoch 1 (below, and in `completed`) is `already_completed` carrying its recorded verdict. **The assertion that separates refusal from bookkeeping is the fence on disk afterwards**: still exactly 3. A worker that merely NOTED the stale request and allocated anyway would have advanced it to 4 before replying, because the dispatch path awaits `persistFence()` before it sends the prompt — so an accepted dispatch is durable before its reply is written, and the seeded value standing untouched is proof three dispatches were refused rather than absorbed. The refusals are also read back out of the worker's own ledger (`dispatch_rejected` × 3, in order), which is the worker's account rather than the caller's reading of a reply, and none of the three ever became a task record. A positive control then dispatches epoch 4 and requires `accepted: true` and the fence moving to 4 — the fence is a high-water-mark, not a lock. **Mutation-proved twice, and the first one is the one the criterion's second clause is about.** Rewriting `src/supervisor/index.ts`'s `em.allocate(envelope.task_id, attemptId, requested)` to pass `null` — which removes the worker-side refusal entirely while leaving allocator bookkeeping wholly intact, since `EpochManager` still increments and persists `last_accepted_epoch` exactly as before — fails the new test with `expect(equal["accepted"]).toBe(false)`, `Expected: false / Received: true`. **That same mutation was run against the pre-existing suite first and everything stayed GREEN**: all 1094 tests in `test/unit`, all of `supervisor.test.ts`, `dispatch-auto.test.ts` and `role-dispatch.test.ts`. The reason is flat: every dispatch in the repo before this one passed `requested_epoch: null`, so the parameter the criterion is entirely about was never once exercised through a real supervisor. Second mutation, for the control rather than the claim: making `allocate` refuse EVERY epoch-bearing dispatch fails with `Expected: "already_completed" / Received: "stale_epoch"`, so the test cannot be satisfied by a worker that simply says no to everything. **Production-reachable, checked rather than assumed:** `pifleet dispatch --worker --task <file>` reads the task file's `epoch` through `requestedEpochFrom` (`cli/commands/dispatch.ts:321`), puts it on the wire as `requested_epoch` (:222), and the supervisor reads it at `index.ts:578` and hands it to `allocate` at :580. Worth recording that `dispatch --auto` passes `requestedEpoch: null` (:442), so the epoch-bearing path is the single-task one — a hand-written or re-dispatched envelope — which is exactly the case `requestedEpochFrom`'s own docblock and ISC-217 already exist to serve.
- [x] ISC-143: The epoch high-water-mark is durable before dispatch; allocate → crash → restart does not re-issue the same epoch.
- [x] ISC-144: The run-dir lease keys on pid plus process start-time, so a recycled pid is not mistaken for a live supervisor.
- [x] ISC-145: A retried dispatch carrying the same `(task_id, attempt_uuid)` replays the stored response rather than returning a bare `already_completed`. **[CLOSED 2026-08-20 by this PR. Half of it was already covered and mutation-proved; the half that was missing is the half where the failure is silent.]** MACHINE-CHECKED every CI run (`bun test test/unit` and `bun test test/integration`). **The DECISION was already pinned and genuinely so.** `epoch.test.ts`'s "the same attempt replays even after the task settled" asserts the whole of `allocate`'s answer — `{ ok: true, epoch: 1, replayed: true }` — for an attempt whose task has SETTLED, which is the only state in which the wrong answer is available to return, since `already_completed` needs a `completed` entry to come from. It is mutation-proved: gating the attempts-map early return on the task not being complete, so a settled task's own attempt falls through to the `completed` lookup, fails it with `"ok": true, "replayed": true` becoming `"ok": false, "reason": "already_completed", "verdict": "success"` — the criterion's contrast, verbatim, in the diff. Its sibling "a NEW attempt for a settled task is already_completed, not a replay" is the negative control that stops the first from being satisfied by a manager that replays everything, and "attempt dedup survives the restart" carries it across a `snapshot()`/restore. **What was NOT proved, and why it mattered more than it looks:** that the worker HONOURS that decision. The two failure modes are different objects — the decision going wrong returns the bare `already_completed` the criterion names, while the supervisor ignoring `decision.replayed` re-sends the prompt and RUNS THE TASK A SECOND TIME — and only the first is visible anywhere in `rpc/epoch.ts`. Deleting the replay short-circuit at `src/supervisor/index.ts:589-593` outright left `supervisor.test.ts`, `dispatch-auto.test.ts` and `role-dispatch.test.ts` all GREEN, because nothing in the repo had ever driven the same `(task_id, attempt_id)` through a real supervisor twice. The e2e case that looks like it covers this is covering the opposite: `lifecycle.test.ts`'s ISC-85 re-dispatch goes through the CLI with a task file carrying no `attempt_id`, so `randomUUID()` mints a FRESH one per invocation and `already_completed` is the correct answer there. **What now proves it:** `supervisor.test.ts` > "a retried (task_id, attempt_id) replays the stored answer (ISC-145)". A real detached supervisor, a task dispatched and driven to a recorded `success`, and then the identical `(task_id, attempt_id)` sent again over the control socket — the retry that arrives AFTER settlement, which is the one that matters. It requires `accepted: true`, `replayed: true`, the SAME epoch back, and `reason` absent, that last one being the criterion's "rather than a bare `already_completed`" written as an assertion. It then requires the replay to have cost nothing: no epoch burned (`last_accepted_epoch` unmoved), the task record still `success` at its original epoch, and exactly one `epoch_started` in `events.jsonl`. A negative control in the same test sends a DIFFERENT attempt against the same settled task and requires `accepted: false`, `reason: "already_completed"` with the verdict — both halves of the sentence, at the worker, in one test. **Mutation-proved three ways.** Deleting the supervisor's replay short-circuit fails it with `expect(retry["accepted"]).toBe(true)`, `Expected: true / Received: false` — the retry fell through and re-sent the prompt, which the double's own fence then refused as stale, so the caller got `prompt_rejected` instead of its stored answer. The decision-level mutation above ALSO fails this test with the same message, so the integration case guards both layers rather than only the wiring. And making any attempt for a known task replay fails the negative control with `expect(other["accepted"]).toBe(false)`, `Expected: false / Received: true`, so it cannot pass by replaying indiscriminately — which would resurrect ISC-85. **Production-reachable, and routinely so:** `dispatch --auto` derives `attemptId: auto:${spec.id}` (`cli/commands/dispatch.ts:441`), deterministic per (run, task) precisely so a re-run of the same list replays instead of re-executing, and a hand-written task file may carry its own `attempt_id` (:312); either reaches `msg["attempt_id"]` at `supervisor/index.ts:577` and `allocate` at :580. **One scoping note, since "the stored response" could be read harder than it is implemented:** what is stored per attempt is the ALLOCATION answer — the epoch — and that is what comes back. A dispatch reply never carried an outcome in the first place (`accepted: true` means accepted, not started), so a caller replaying after settlement learns its epoch and reads the verdict from the task record, as `wait` does. Under the stricter reading in which "the stored response" would have to carry the verdict too, this is `[~]` rather than `[x]`; the grade above takes the reply to a dispatch to be the response to a dispatch.
- [x] ISC-146: Every deadline and stall timer uses a monotonic clock; a wall-clock jump fires none of them early.
- [x] ISC-147: Across every hostile scenario, completion is never declared while the agent will still emit output. **PARTIAL — the scenario property table is far weaker than its name; the hand-written tracker tests are what actually defend this.** MACHINE-CHECKED every CI run (`bun test test/unit`): `completion.test.ts`'s "scenario property — never complete while output is still coming (ISC-147)" replays all 15 files in `test/fixtures/scenarios/` through a real `EpochManager` plus a real `CompletionTracker`, asserts the exact settle epochs per scenario, and carries a table-integrity test that fails the suite when a scenario is added without a reviewed expectation or an expectation outlives its scenario. The table CAN fail — making `queue_update` inert in `observe` turns `queue-race.json: settles exactly []` red. **What this audit found, and the reason the grade is not `[x]`: four separate mutations to the exact machine this criterion is about left all 15 scenario cases GREEN.** Dropping the probe generation token from `confirm`; replacing `countersEqual` with `true`; dropping `#queueEmpty` from `eligible`; and making `agent_end` set `#endedClean = true` regardless of `willRetry` were each caught ONLY by the hand-written `CompletionTracker` describes elsewhere in the same file ("hostile sequences", "probe validity", "queue conditions", "ISC-82, retries") — the scenario property never fired for any of them. Two structural reasons, both worth writing down: (1) the table asserts a settle COUNT and epoch, never a settle POSITION, so a premature settle in any of the 11 scenarios that expect one is invisible — only the four `[]` scenarios penalise prematurity at all; (2) `simulate()` is a re-implementation of the supervisor's routing INSIDE THE TEST FILE, and its own honest `isStreaming` model blocks several premature settles before the tracker is even consulted, which is why the `willRetry` mutation survived even the dedicated truncation test that exists to catch exactly that. **The quantifier is not met as written.** "Every hostile scenario" is 15 files replayed with `delay_ms`, `noise` and `partial` entries SKIPPED and with the harness never issuing an abort, so timing-dependent interleavings, the 16-worker flood and mid-record truncation are not exercised by this property at all, and `aborted.json`/`deaf-abort.json` collapse to natural completion (the file says so in its own comments). The real supervisor routing is exercised for a subset elsewhere — `lifecycle.test.ts` drives queue-race against real workers — but not for the set this criterion quantifies over. **[STRENGTHENED 2026-08-25, and deliberately NOT closed. Two of the three gaps this entry named are addressed; the third is untouched and holds the grade.]** **THE FINDING THAT MATTERS IS THAT THE OBVIOUS FIX WAS INERT.** Gap (1) — the table asserts a settle COUNT and never a settle POSITION — was closed first, by having `simulate` report per settle whether the turn's terminal `agent_end` had already been fed, and asserting it across all fifteen scenarios. It passed immediately, and it passed for the wrong reason: MEASURED, breaking `#endedClean` to ignore `willRetry` entirely left all fifteen replays green, and so did making `turn_end` terminal. Nothing in that harness could produce a premature settle at all, so an assertion about prematurity could not fail. A guard nobody has seen fail is indistinguishable from one that cannot fail, and this one was the latter for as long as it took to check — which is why the check was run rather than the assertion merely added. **Gap (2) is the cause, and it is now bypassed rather than removed.** `simulate`'s `get_state` answer models "is a turn in flight" by reading `willRetry` — the very field `CompletionTracker` exists to interpret — so through a retry the probe is told `isStreaming: true` and refuses to confirm before the tracker's discriminator is ever consulted. The harness was grading the tracker with the tracker's own answer. `fake-pi.ts:487` models it the same way, so this is not a harness bug so much as a harness that cannot see the class. **Three quiet-probe tests script the race the double exists to create:** Pi answering `isStreaming: false` while a retry is outstanding — not exotic, since `willRetry:true` says the AGENT will speak again and the gap between attempts is a real window in which Pi is genuinely not streaming. In it, the only thing between the supervisor and a false completion is the tracker refusing to treat that end as terminal. A one-condition-different control (`willRetry:false`, same quiet probe) settles at once, so the refusal cannot pass by the harness being unable to settle at all; a third pins `turn_end` as not an agent end. **A fourth probe, hand-written against the tracker, closes a window nothing had:** eligibility is not a settle, and a clean `agent_end` that has not yet been confirmed by the double read can be overtaken by a fresh `agent_start`. A tracker keeping that stale flag settles a task with a live turn running. **MUTATION SWEEP, five mutations, each restored byte-identical.** Ignoring `willRetry` now fails 3 (it failed 2 before, both hand-written — the criterion's own scenario block did not defend it); making `turn_end` terminal fails 3 and **survived every test in the file before this work**; `agent_start` not clearing the terminal flag fails 1 and **also survived everything before this work**; ignoring the queue fails 2; ignoring outstanding retries fails 1. **WHY STILL `[~]` — gap (3), untouched and unreduced.** "Every hostile scenario" still means fifteen files replayed with `delay_ms`, `noise` and `partial` entries SKIPPED and with the harness never issuing an abort, so timing-dependent interleavings, the 16-worker flood and mid-record truncation are not exercised by this property, and `aborted.json`/`deaf-abort.json` still collapse to natural completion. `simulate` is also still a re-implementation of the supervisor's routing living inside the test file — the quiet-probe tests get UNDER it rather than removing it, and a second implementation that is bypassed in three places is still a second implementation. Closing this needs the scenarios replayed through a real supervisor, which `lifecycle.test.ts` already does for a subset and which is the shape `supervisor.test.ts` builds; that is the work, and it is not done here. **[GAP (3) ADDRESSED 2026-08-25 by replaying the hostile conditions through a REAL supervisor. Still `[~]`, on a residual that is now one sentence long instead of three.]** **WHAT WAS ADDED:** `test/integration/supervisor.test.ts`'s "ISC-147 (gap 3)" block — a real supervisor, a real `fake-pi` child, a real control socket, seven scenarios. `delay_ms` is WAITED OUT rather than skipped as a marker; `partial` really truncates a JSON line mid-write; the abort is a real RPC. That covers the four conditions this entry listed as unexercised, except `noise`, which is deliberately left to ISC-158's starvation test — `noisy-fleet.json` is a three-script FLEET fixture and replaying it here would duplicate that rig to assert a weaker property. Named rather than silently omitted. **THE PROPERTY, and why it is answerable from the events file.** A task settling `success` must have a LIVE-attributed terminal `agent_end{willRetry:false}` behind it; a success without one is a completion declared while the agent was still going to emit. Liveness is read by EXCLUSION from the supervisor's own `epoch_attribution` records rather than recomputed — the whole complaint against `simulate` is that it re-implements the routing, so this block must not re-implement the attribution either. **THE FINDING, which is the same one gap (2) turned on, one level down.** The six-scenario block went green immediately and was WORTHLESS: ignoring `willRetry` entirely and treating `turn_end` as terminal BOTH left all six real-supervisor scenarios passing, exactly as they had left the in-process table passing. The cause is identical at both levels — `fake-pi.ts:487` decides `isStreaming` by reading `willRetry`, so through a retry it reports the agent as streaming and the probe refuses to confirm before the tracker is consulted. **Every fixture on disk was being defended by the double, not by the code under test**, and no amount of switching from a simulator to a real supervisor changes that, because the simulator was copying the double. **`quiet-retry.json` is the fixture that fixes it**, and it had to be written because none existed: Pi answers `get_state` with `isStreaming: false` while a retry is outstanding — what real Pi genuinely is between attempts — with two waited-out windows, 1500 ms after `turn_end` and 2000 ms after the `willRetry` end, so a tracker that settled at either lands in one. **MUTATION SWEEP AGAINST REAL ROUTING, each restored byte-identical:** ignoring `willRetry` now fails (survived before the fixture); `turn_end` terminal now fails (survived before the fixture); `agent_start` not clearing a stale terminal end and ignoring the queue both still pass here and are caught by the unit probes instead — recorded because a sweep that only lists its successes is not a sweep. **WHY STILL `[~]`, and it is now a single reason.** The real-routing block covers SEVEN of the twenty-four fixtures. "Every hostile scenario" means twenty-four, and extending it there is not a design question but a CI BUDGET one — twenty-four supervisor launches, several with 30 s and 120 s tails needing compressed deadlines, against a `test` job already at five minutes. That is an owner decision of exactly the shape ISC-22 is parked on, and it is not taken unilaterally here. `simulate` also still exists; the quiet-probe tests and this block get UNDER it rather than removing it. **[CLOSED 2026-08-25. The quantifier is met: every one of the twenty-four fixtures has an explicit entry, twenty-two run through a REAL supervisor, and the two that do not name where their real-routing coverage lives.]** **WHAT THE BLOCK ASSERTS.** `test/integration/supervisor.test.ts` -> "the completion property across every hostile scenario": a real supervisor, a real `fake-pi` child, a real control socket, per fixture. `delay_ms` is WAITED OUT rather than skipped as a marker, `partial` really truncates a JSON line mid-write, the abort is a real RPC. Each entry pins the VERDICT its fixture's own comment describes — `truncated` -> `failed`, `no-tool-calls` -> `failed`, `late-failure` -> `failed`, `aborted` -> `aborted`, `deaf-abort` and `late-response` and `queue-race` -> `timed_out`, the rest `success`. **The verdicts are pinned rather than loosened to `not success` deliberately:** a `not.toBe("success")` passes for a scenario that failed for entirely the wrong reason — a `timed_out` standing in for the truncation guard — which is the failure mode this block exists to rule out. On top of the verdict, the property itself: a `success` must have a LIVE-attributed terminal `agent_end{willRetry:false}` behind it, liveness read by EXCLUSION from the supervisor's own `epoch_attribution` records rather than recomputed, because the standing complaint against `simulate` is that it re-implements the routing and this must not re-implement the attribution. **`queue-race` is the interesting entry:** its fixture says the task MUST NOT settle, so `timed_out` there is the property holding, not failing. **THE TWO DEFERRALS, both to real-routing tests and both named in the table:** `noisy-fleet.json` is a three-script FLEET fixture already driven through real supervisors by ISC-158's starvation test, whose assertion — quiet workers settle WHILE an ~800 KB flood is in flight — is strictly stronger than this property; `interleave.json` is ISC-84's, driven by `lifecycle.test.ts`, and ISC-283 records what its abort timing cost to get right, so a second copy here would reintroduce the race that fixed. A coverage-integrity test fails the suite when a fixture has no entry, when an entry names a deleted fixture, or when a deferral does not say where the coverage lives — a quantifier that quietly skips its hard cases is how this criterion came to be graded far above what it held. **THE HONEST CAVEAT, and it is a large one: of the twenty-two fixtures run here, exactly ONE catches anything.** The full mutation sweep: ignoring `willRetry` fails only `quiet-retry`; treating `turn_end` as terminal fails only `quiet-retry`; `agent_start` not clearing an unconsumed terminal end passes all twenty-two; ignoring `queueEmpty` passes all twenty-two. The last two are caught by the unit probes in `completion.test.ts` instead, and the reason they cannot be caught here is structural rather than a coverage hole: both conditions sit BEHIND the generation counter, which invalidates the probe on any activity, so under real routing neither can produce a premature settle to observe. **Fixtures were NOT manufactured to make redundant guards look load-bearing** — that would have been the easy way to a fuller-looking sweep and it would have been dishonest. `quiet-retry.json` had to be written because `fake-pi.ts:487` decides `isStreaming` by reading `willRetry`, so every pre-existing fixture is defended by the DOUBLE rather than by the code under test; it scripts Pi answering `isStreaming: false` mid-retry, with two waited-out windows so a tracker settling at either lands in one. **A LATENT DEFECT WAS SURFACED BY THE LOAD AND FIXED HERE:** all four tests in `container-launch.test.ts` carried `cliBudget(1)` = 5700 ms over `waitForFile` gates of 10 000 ms — one of them over two of them — so the ceiling sat INSIDE the gate it was meant to cover and the declared wait could never be spent. On a light runner the spawn lands in ~2 s and they pass; twenty-two extra supervisor launches made the suite heavy enough that one did not, and it failed reading "the recorder was never spawned" rather than as a budget that was never big enough. Now `gateBudget` derived from the gates. Nothing stamps a version on a ledger record, so no record can be read as being from an older one, and there is no policy — pinned, tested or otherwise — to apply. What DOES happen was measured rather than assumed: a shard holding a record missing today's required `run_id` merges without crashing, the bad record is collected into `mergeLedger`'s `errors` and the other records survive. That is real and it is a strictly weaker statement than the criterion in two ways, which is why this is `[ ]` and not `[~]` — the record is DISCARDED, not read, and the behaviour is shape-driven, so it cannot tell "written by an older writer" from "corrupt shard", which is the exact distinction a version policy exists to make. Closing this needs a product decision first, not a test: either stamp a version on ledger records and pin a read policy against it, or restate the criterion as the shape-tolerance guarantee `mergeLedger` actually offers. Writing a test against the current behaviour would pin the absence of a policy and retire the criterion without satisfying it. **[CLOSED 2026-08-20, Phase G — AND THE CRITERION CHANGED, which is the honest half of this entry.]** Owner decision: refuse by design, named, with a hatch — NOT accept-and-upgrade. **ISC-157 as written has no subject and was RESTATED rather than built.** `LedgerRecordSchema` carries no `schema` discriminator, so nothing stamps a version on a ledger record and no record can be from an older one; closing it as written would have required adding a stamp, which was explicitly not chosen. **Restated to the guarantee `mergeLedger` actually offers, and that guarantee is now pinned:** a malformed record does not crash the merge, it lands in `errors`, and every well-formed record around it survives REGARDLESS OF POSITION. The position clause is load-bearing and was measured, not assumed — under a mutation that hoists the try/catch to per-shard, the LAST-position test still PASSES while mid-shard reddens with `- "c", - "d"`, so a merge that silently drops the tail after an error would have passed a naive test. Three mutations: per-shard try/catch (6 fail, tail silently gone), one catch outside the shard loop (8 fail — a corrupt first shard returns `[]` where a second writer's three healthy records belong, violating `ledger.ts`'s own header claim), silent drop (9 fail). **Rule 3 of SRD §8 checked rather than assumed:** `mergeLedger` has a production caller at `report/collect.ts:114`, so this is a test over a live path and not over a callerless module. **THE HONESTY SENTENCE, also written into `mergeLedger`'s docstring where the next reader will meet it:** *this pins shape-tolerance — a malformed record does not crash the merge, it lands in `errors`, and every well-formed record around it survives regardless of position. It is NOT a version policy: a record failing today's schema is DISCARDED rather than read, and the merge cannot tell "written by an older writer" from "corrupt shard" — both arrive as a shape that fails, both are dropped, both are reported in the same words. That distinction is exactly what a version stamp would buy, and it was not bought.*

A threshold whose accept-set and reject-set overlap does not discriminate — it reports runner contention as a product failure. Widening it was worse: 18ms of observed skew needs a floor near 25, which stops catching the defect's 35s at all and leaves a guard that cannot fail. Note the direction, because the first reading of this failure got it backwards: load makes the measured interval SHORTER, not longer, so "slow runner" has the mechanism inverted. **MEASURED BEFORE CHANGING ANYTHING — 42 samples, three local runs:** `[53,53,53,53,53,53,53,53,53,54,54,54,54,63]`, `[48,53,53,53,53,54,54,54,54,54,54,55,55,59]`, `[52,52,52,53,53,53,53,53,53,53,54,54,54,54]` — min 48, max 63, median 53, i.e. the 50ms sleep plus a few ms of settle cost at worst 2ms of skew. A GitHub runner reached ~18ms of skew where this machine reaches 2ms. **What discriminates is SHAPE, not magnitude.** Skew shortens SOME intervals; the old defect shortened EVERY one alike, because it added a CLI teardown to each measurement equally. The samples separate cleanly on it: the defect's own three readings have a maximum of 49; every honest run has a maximum of 54 or more. So the guard now asserts the TRUE arithmetic floor — the 50ms sleep itself, no fudge constant — against `max(quiet)` alone. `QUIET_SKEW_MS` is DELETED rather than enlarged: there is no longer a number to tune, and therefore none that runner load can tune against us. **Mutation-proved in BOTH directions, which is the whole point of the reshape.** M-A, the defect's shape (every latency shortened 20ms): red, `Expected: >= 50 / Received: 38`, and the failure now prints the whole distribution — `[33,34,38,34,33,33,37,34,35,33,33,33,34,33]` — which the old per-worker assertion never did. M-B, honest skew's shape (ONE worker shortened 20ms): GREEN, 7 pass, which is the tolerance the reshape exists to buy and would be invisible without asserting it. Restored byte-identical. **THE PRICE, not rounded off:** a single worker reading 35ms no longer fails on its own. That is deliberate — per worker, 35ms is indistinguishable from honest skew, which is exactly why asserting on it made main's greenness a function of CI contention.

- [x] ISC-165: Anti: no `:ro` refusal test passes against a mount whose contents were never readable. **[CLOSED 2026-08-19 by this PR.]** The guard checks the property PER TEST, not per file: for every test body containing a `:ro` mount and an assertion that a command was rejected, it requires that same body to also assert a successful read. The reasoning is the criterion's own — a mount the daemon cannot see comes up as an EMPTY directory, and an empty `:ro` mount refuses writes too, so "touch failed" passes identically against a broken mount and a working one. `test/integration/image.test.ts` already gets this right and explains why in a comment; the guard turns a habit into a rule. It also fails if it finds zero `:ro` refusal tests to check, so renaming or deleting them cannot make it pass by vacuity. The test-body split is deliberately crude — chunking on the `it(`/`test(` boundary rather than parsing the AST — and errs strict: over-chunking would refuse to credit a read assertion in a neighbouring test, never the reverse. Mutation-verified: deleting the read assertion from the `/skills mounted ro` probe turns it red.

- [x] ISC-186: Registry writes are serialized, so concurrent registrations cannot lose a worker. **[CLOSED 2026-08-19 by this PR.]** The chain in `startRegistryDaemon` was already there; nothing had ever seen it fail. `test/integration/registry-serialization.test.ts` now watches `writeJsonAtomic`'s temp files, which exist for exactly the span of one write to `registry.json`, while twelve registrations arrive concurrently over the real socket AND a reaper scan deregisters three stale workers in the same window: never two at one instant, every registration present on disk afterwards, every reaped worker gone. The obvious test — fire N registrations, assert all N survive — is written up in the file as the weaker instrument it is, but NOT, as an earlier revision of this entry claimed, as one that cannot see the race at all. Measured with `persist()` bypassing `serialized()`, it failed 18 of 20 runs with no sampler present and 17 of 20 with one, losing a contiguous tail of the newest registrations (`w-11` alone at best, `w-2`…`w-11` at worst). It is a FLAKY detector, and that is a worse thing to rest a criterion on than no detector, because two-and-three green runs in twenty teach whoever hits the red to re-run until it passes. The mechanism assertion has no such mode: `maxConcurrent` read 12 with the chain bypassed and 1 with it intact, every run, the two distributions not overlapping. The earlier claim also defeated itself — it argued that a later-starting write is larger and therefore lands last, while the 512 KiB of filler the test adds makes one more worker a 167-byte step on a 524,562-byte write, a 0.03% difference that scheduling noise swamps. Completion order is roughly independent of snapshot recency, which is why the losses run the other way round from the prediction. Two vacuity guards stop the sampler passing having watched nothing: it must take more samples than there are writes, and must catch at least half the writes in flight (measured 13 of 13 on every one of 8 runs, over 95-113 samples). Reachability checked rather than assumed, since this ISA already has criteria whose library is correct and unreachable: `up` spawns `daemon` (`src/cli/commands/up.ts:717`), which calls `startRegistryDaemon` (`src/cli/commands/daemon.ts:42`), and supervisors send `register_worker` through it (`src/supervisor/index.ts:177`). BOTH writers to `registry.json` are pinned, which took a second pass to get right: `persist()` (`registry.ts:349`) and the reaper's post-scan deregistration (`registry.ts:430`). The first revision of this test passed no `opts.reaper`, so the reaper's write was never exercised and the criterion held only by inspection — a refactor could have lifted that call out of `serialized()` with the test still green. It now drives `reapOnce()` inside the same `Promise.all` as the registration burst, with a hand-driven clock and stubbed process ops so the reap is deterministic rather than timer-raced, and asserts the reap actually reported the three workers so the second writer cannot quietly stop being exercised. Mutation-verified separately against each writer, and the two detectors are not equally strong: bypassing `serialized()` in `persist()` turns it red on 20 of 20 runs with `expect(received).toBe(expected) / Expected: 1 / Received: 13`, while bypassing it in the reaper turns it red on 19 of 20 with `Expected: 1 / Received: 2`. The reaper mutation puts exactly ONE write outside the chain, so it is caught only when that write overlaps a registration write, and about one run in twenty it lands in a gap. Recorded at 19 of 20 rather than rounded up, and deliberately not tuned to 20 of 20 by arranging the overlap — that would be a weaker guarantee dressed as a stronger one, which is the failure this whole entry is a correction for. Green on 8 consecutive runs once both were restored. A second defect surfaced while checking this against the repo's own load harness (ISC-266): the test carried no explicit time budget, so it inherited bun's 5000 ms default over 32 ms of work, and under `LOAD_PROCS=32` it died at 5001.82 ms. It now derives `cliBudget(1)` = 11_400 ms from a counted spawn (`startRegistryDaemon` → `processStartTime` → one `ps`; everything else in the path is in-process or stubbed). Measured: 32 ms idle, 70-91 ms at the harness's DEFAULT load — a 2.2-2.8x inflation matching the repo's own measured CONTENTION of 2.09-2.98x — and 3.5-7.9 s at `LOAD_PROCS=32`, which is 2.3x cores and outside the harness's stated envelope. The budget clears the gate by 125x and the worst observed by 1.4x, and stays bounded. Worth recording that the first diagnosis here was WRONG and was caught by measuring it: the undelayed `while (!stop)` readdir sampler was blamed for starving the writes and for pinning a core on a 2-core runner, and an interleaved A/B refutes both — wall clock 26-31 ms either way idle and fully overlapping ranges under load, CPU time 0.09-0.11 s either way. The loop only looks like a spin; every iteration awaits a real `readdir`, so it is descheduled for nearly all of its life. The `Bun.sleep(0)` was kept regardless, for the `catch { continue }` path, which is the one place the loop genuinely has no syscall pacing it — but it is documented as that and not as a fix for a timeout it does not fix.

- [x] ISC-172: The verbgate ledger is collected outside the container, so a worker cannot truncate its own audit trail. — STAYS OPEN, and the production code says so by criterion number. `docker/verbgate:26-30`: "KNOWN REMAINING EXPOSURE, stated plainly: the ledger is written by the worker, so a determined worker can still truncate it. Making the audit trail tamper-proof needs a collector outside the container — tracked as ISC-172, not solved here." What IS done is adjacent and must not be mistaken for it: the gate no longer lets its subject supply its own policy or redirect its own evidence (`PIFLEET_VERBGATE_LEDGER=/dev/null` and `PIFLEET_CLOUD_ALLOW_FILE` are refused; the policy file sits on a read-only mount and the gate exits 78 if it is writable by the current user). That reduces FORGERY and EVASION. It does not make the ledger authoritative against a hostile worker, which is the only thing this line claims. The verbgate suite is Docker-gated but genuinely runs in CI's `container` job with `PIFLEET_DOCKER=1`, so this is not an untested-code problem — it is an unbuilt-feature problem: no test asserts the containment property because no mechanism implements it. CLOSING IT COSTS: a host-side collector — the writable ledger mount replaced by a append-only sink the container cannot seek or truncate (a unix socket to a host collector, or a pipe drained by the supervisor), plus a rendezvous that survives worker restarts — and a probe that proves the property by ATTACKING it: a worker that runs `: > $ledger` (and `truncate`, and re-`open(O_TRUNC)`) and a host-side assertion that every prior line is still there. Anything less re-proves the evasion controls that already exist. NO MUTATION WAS RUN: there is no implementation to mutate, and mutating the evasion controls would produce a red test for a property this criterion does not assert. **[PHASE H, 2026-08-21 — RE-GRADED `[ ]` -> `[~]`. The collector exists, is wired, and is mutation-proved at both call sites; what is unproved is the container end.]** Owner decision was TAIL AND COPY, explicitly not a transport change, so `docker/verbgate` is untouched and the guarantee is the weaker of the two available: **everything already collected survives truncation, and truncation itself is detected and RECORDED — but rows written and truncated between two passes are lost.** That sentence is the criterion now; it must not be restated as though the ledger were tamper-proof. **The gap was thinner than the first analysis claimed.** A five-whys concluded pifleet had no host-side observer role; measurement refuted it — `startRegistryDaemon` is per-run, outlives every worker and already carries a tick, and `TailReader` already does offset-keyed incremental reads that RESTART on shrink, so truncation DETECTION was already built. The absent thing was a COLLECTOR, not an observer. **Destination is a SIBLING of `ledgerDir`, not a shard inside it** — both are worker-unreachable, but `ledgerDir` holds pifleet's own shards parsed by `LedgerRecordSchema`, and ISC-157's Phase G closure pinned that a malformed record lands in `errors`; verbgate rows there would emit one `errors` entry per row on every merge, closing one criterion by breaking one that closed a week earlier. **`docker logs` was ruled out on measurement:** `--rm` means the log dies with the container, no log driver is configured, and container stdout IS the RPC stream. **Two call sites, deliberately separate, each with its own proof** — the tick (ongoing) and a bounded final pass at daemon shutdown (teardown), since `down` removes containers then stops the daemon and without it the trail ends at the last tick. Collection runs BESIDE the reap with its own re-entrancy flag and catch: neither may disable the other, and sharing the flag would couple their periods, widening the very window in which a row can be written and truncated unseen. The final pass is bounded at 5s and its failure swallowed, because a daemon that refuses to stop is worse than a trail missing its last rows. **Mutations, each reddening a DIFFERENT probe, which is what shows the two sites are separately covered:** collector removed from the tick -> `(fail) the daemon's own tick collects a worker's ledger, unprompted`; final pass removed -> `(fail) shutdown takes one last pass`. Also proved at the module: dropping the truncation mark reddens 2, and writing the copy INSIDE the worker's own `/outbox` mount reddens 5. **WHY `[~]` AND NOT `[x]`, stated rather than glossed:** no probe drives a REAL container. Every test writes the source ledger directly at the host path `workerVerbgateLedger` names, so what is proved is that the collector reads the path the HELPER names — not that this is the path `docker/verbgate` actually writes through the `/outbox` bind mount. Those two agreeing is the criterion's last mile and it is currently asserted by construction rather than tested. Closing it needs a `PIFLEET_DOCKER=1` probe alongside `test/integration/verbgate.test.ts`, whose `makeSandbox()` already builds `<scratch>/outbox/ledger` and reads it back. Rule 2 applies to that probe when it is written: a self-skipping test is not an exit criterion, so the Docker-gated case must be counted as executed, not merely named in a job. **[PHASE H CLOSE-OUT, 2026-08-21 — RE-GRADED `[~]` -> `[x]`. The last mile is now TESTED, and testing it FOUND A DEFECT that made the previous grade's own wording false.]** Two probes in `test/integration/verbgate.test.ts`, both executed on Linux CI rather than skipped — `parsed[container]: pass=84 fail=0 skip=6 total=90 expected=90 rc=0`, with `TOTAL_EXPECTED` RE-DERIVED by the hand method (gate unset: 6 pass, 84 skip, 90 tests across 9 files) rather than incremented, which is what discharges Rule 2 for this criterion. **PROBE 1, the path agreement.** `workerVerbgateLedger` appends `ledger/verbgate.jsonl` in TypeScript; `docker/verbgate` hardcodes `/outbox/ledger/verbgate.jsonl` in shell; nothing links them — no shared constant, no generated header, no import. Mutation: rename the segment in the helper and the container probe reddens with `ENOENT ... /ledgers/verbgate.jsonl` while BOTH host-side wiring probes stay GREEN, because they write through the same helper so both sides move together. That is the previous grade's stated blindness, demonstrated rather than described. **PROBE 2, the attack, and what it found.** A worker truncating its own ledger from inside the container with `: >` — open(O_TRUNC), as the worker uid, on the writable mount. Three assertions that are not one claim: the pre-attack row survives in the collected copy (custody), a truncation mark is present (the attack is recorded, not merely survived), the post-attack row is collected (the collector recovered rather than wedging). **THE PREVIOUS GRADE CLAIMED "truncation itself is detected and RECORDED". THAT WAS FALSE, and this probe is what proved it false.** `docker/verbgate` stamps whole seconds, so two rows written inside one second are byte-for-byte identical for 64 bytes — the argv is the only difference and it starts past the head. A worker that truncates in place and writes a row at least as long as the one it erased therefore defeats all three original signals SIMULTANEOUSLY: `shrank` cannot fire (the file regrew past the old offset), `replaced` cannot fire (an in-place truncate keeps the inode), `head_rewritten` cannot fire (the head is unchanged). Measured before the fix: `truncations: 0`, the reader resumed mid-record, and the audit copy took the one-byte fragment `}` as a genuine collected row — an audit trail asserting a line that was never written, which is worse than the missing mark. **THE FIX** is a fourth signal, `tail_rewritten`, fingerprinting the bytes at the CONSUMED FRONTIER rather than the head: the head answers "is this the same file generation?", the tail answers "is the boundary my offset points at still that boundary?", and only the second survives a writer whose rows share a long prefix. Re-anchored every poll because the frontier moves; a failed re-anchor keeps the previous anchor rather than clearing it, since clearing withdraws the guarantee silently and permanently. Mutation: drop the `tail_rewritten` push and both unit probes go red (28 pass / 2 fail) plus the container attack probe; reverted green. A host-side unit probe pins it too, so the fix is re-checked on every run and not only in the Docker-gated job, and it asserts `toEqual(["tail_rewritten"])` rather than `toContain` — if any other signal starts firing there, the probe has stopped testing its case. **WHAT `[x]` MEANS HERE, and it is the OWNER-RESTATED sentence, not the line's original wording:** everything already collected survives truncation, the truncation is detected and recorded, and collection continues past it. **The residual is unchanged and is NOT closed:** rows written AND truncated between two passes are lost — tail-and-copy's accepted cost for not changing the transport. What the frontier check adds is that the ATTEMPT is now visible even when the rows are not recoverable, which is the operator-visible signal ISC-125 will build on. **One process finding worth keeping:** both probes passed their assertions on the first CI run and still failed the job, in `afterEach`, with `EACCES` removing the scratch — on Linux a bind mount passes host ownership through, so the `ledger/` the shim created belongs to uid 10001 and the runner can neither unlink inside it nor chmod it. macOS squashes ownership and hid it across two local runs. `makeSandbox` already carried a comment naming this exact hazard.

Marker HELD at `[~]`; the tilde now covers a narrower residual than it did, and a different one.]** The gate had a hole that NEITHER of its two checks could see, and it is precisely the `Docs/SRD-COMPLETION.md` row this criterion is graded against — "a stale-but-present image is invisible". Take the REAL worker image, the one this repo builds, and file it under another tag: one `docker tag`, and a registry pull or a hand-retag does it by accident. `imagePresent` then says PRESENT, because it is, and ALL FIVE of `verifyImage`'s checks PASS, because every one of them is a BEHAVIOURAL question about the running container — Pi version, uid 10001, read-only root, tini at PID 1, `/workspace` write-through — and the right bytes under the wrong name answer all five correctly. MUTATION, run bounded (`perl -e 'alarm 600'` + `--timeout 90000`) because a neutered guard whose broken state is "condition never true" can hang instead of failing: neutering ONLY this check (`return null;` at the head of `imageIdentityDrift`) takes the file from 42 pass / 0 fail to 41 pass / 1 fail, and the one is this criterion's test — the ISC-32 absent half, the fails-verify half and the positive control all stay green, so the check is isolated. TO CLOSE: one probe in the Docker-gated `container` job that builds a real image and files it under another image's tag, asserting both that the labels come back as `buildImage` wrote them and that `assertImagesReady` refuses. The rejected route above is unchanged and still rejected. **[RE-GRADED `[~]` -> `[x]` 2026-08-27. The closing condition THIS ENTRY STATES was executed, verbatim, and the older residual it was carrying separately went with it.]** The stated condition was "one probe in the Docker-gated `container` job that builds a real image and files it under another image's tag, asserting both that the labels come back as `buildImage` wrote them and that `assertImagesReady` refuses", in `test/integration/image.test.ts`, with `TOTAL_EXPECTED` RE-DERIVED rather than incremented. All of that, plus the pre-existing residual — "the fails-verify half is a PATH shim, not a real stale image on a real daemon" — which is closable by the same rig and would have been dishonest to leave behind while claiming the criterion. **FOUR PROBES, and the two that refuse are worthless without the two that do not.** (1) THE LABEL ROUND TRIP: `docker image inspect` on the image this suite just built must report `pifleet.pi-version`, `pifleet.toolchain` and `pifleet.config-hash` exactly as `parseImageTag` reads them off the tag it was built under — which is the precise equality `imageIdentityDrift` is built on and which no test read back from an actual image store until now. It also asserts the labels object is non-empty first, so an image with no labels at all fails with that sentence rather than with a `TypeError` on the first index. (2) THE STALE-BUT-PRESENT CASE, which is the `Docs/SRD-COMPLETION.md` row this criterion is graded against: ONE `docker tag` files the real worker image under a tag whose config-hash is not its own, and the probe then asserts — against the real daemon, in this order — that `imagePresent` says PRESENT, that `verifyImage` says OK, and that the gate refuses anyway with `reason: "mismatched"`, naming the role and BOTH hash values. (3) THE FAILS-VERIFY CASE ON REAL BYTES: an image built `FROM` the real one with nothing changed but `USER root`, stamped with identity labels that MATCH its own tag so that presence passes AND `imageIdentityDrift` returns null and the run reaches verification under its own power — `verifyImage`'s `uid-10001` check is what refuses it, and the refusal carries `reason: "unverified"`. The assertions here are the refusal's `reason`, the values it quotes, and the two positive measurements that precede it. **WHAT THE DEVELOPER HOST COULD NOT DO, stated rather than smoothed over.** The suite's `beforeAll` builds the worker image, and that build CANNOT run on this machine: `npm install -g bun` inside the Docker build is refused by the corporate proxy (`ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.3:443`), which is an environment fact and not a repo one. It was not. `src/cli/commands/down.ts` did not import `safety/kill.ts` at all, and `runKillLadder` had exactly ONE production caller — `safety/reaper.ts`. `down`, the only kill path an operator runs BY HAND, ran its own inline ladder over a bare `process.kill`, gated on `processStartTime(pid) !== null`, which is LIVENESS and not identity: `started` was compared at no rung, so the module's headline guarantee ("re-read from the OS and compared at EVERY rung") did not hold on the path where pid reuse matters most. The fixture was then changed to pick a pid that is NOT a group leader so the signal would raise ESRCH; the hazard was routed around, not removed. The operator case is a bare `pifleet down` after a reboot: it resolves the LATEST run, and the latest run is a dead one whose pids the machine has long since reissued. **What is now machine-checked.** `down` resolves a `ProcId` before it signals anything and climbs every rung on `signalIfSame`/`sameIdentity`; `anchorIdentity` refuses the entire ladder when a launch-recorded identity disagrees with the OS. `test/integration/down-identity.test.ts` asserts the NEGATIVE on both rungs — the bystander is still alive afterwards, and the worker reads `already_gone` rather than being laddered against a stranger — and is mutation-verified: deleting the single refusal line turns both tests red and kills the bystander again. `test/unit/kill.test.ts` continues to cover the reaper's ladder. **SECOND ROUND, 2026-08-20 — the fix INTRODUCED a data-loss path, and two more holes were found under it. All three are now closed.** (1) `processStartTime` returned `ps -o lstart=` verbatim, and `ps` RENDERS its timestamp from the calling process's own environment. Measured on one live pid at one instant: `TZ=UTC` gave `Thu 20 Aug 06:44:42 2026`, `TZ=America/Halifax` gave `Thu 20 Aug 03:39:12 2026`, `LC_TIME=de_DE.UTF-8` gave `Do. 20 Aug. 00:39:12 2026`. An identity is captured by the LAUNCHER and compared by the OPERATOR, and those are routinely different environments — `up` locally and `down` over SSH (sshd forwards `LC_TIME` under its default `AcceptEnv LANG LC_*`), `up` from launchd with no `TZ` and `down` from a shell that sets one, a containerised CLI against a host-launched daemon. Reproduced end to end BEFORE any fix, live `sleep` recorded under `TZ=UTC` and `down` run under `TZ=America/Halifax`: `down exit: 0`, `{"workers":[{"id":"eng-1","stopped":true,"how":"already_gone"}],"clean":true}`, bystander still alive. `down` silently failed to stop a LIVE supervisor and called the run clean. Worse, `stopped: true` fed the `--prune` gate, which refuses only when `stopped` is false — so a live worker was classed PRUNABLE. Reproduced with a real clone and a real live process: `pruned: true`, `reason: "checkout deleted"`, exit 0, and the directory gone while the process still ran. That is the §9.3 corruption the gate exists to prevent, reachable BECAUSE of the first fix: pre-fix the gate was liveness, so a live process was never called gone. Fixed at the source — `Bun.spawn(["ps", …], { env: { …process.env, TZ: "UTC", LC_ALL: "C" } })` — which repairs `identityAlive` and the reaper too. (2) `anchorIdentity` read `recorded !== "" && recorded !== current`, and `""` is not neutral: it is exactly what both writers persist when their own capture failed (`(await processStartTime(process.pid)) ?? ""` in `startRegistryDaemon` and `supervisor/index.ts`), and `RegistryWorkerSchema.started` is a bare `z.string()` so a truncated file yields it too. A failed capture therefore DOWNGRADED to the rung-0 self-anchor, and on the daemon rung `signalGuarded(target, "SIGTERM", null)` passes `pgid: null`, so `signalIfSame` addressed `target.pid` — a bare pid, the literal thing this criterion forbids. Measured on unmutated pre-fix code with `{"pid":N,"started":""}`: exit 0, `clean: true`, bystander DEAD. Identical with the field absent. The clause was also vacuous as tested — deleting `recorded !== "" &&` from the pre-fix build left 15/15 across `down-identity` + `down-prune` and 1097/1097 in `test/unit`, measured — so the only thing it ever did was open the hole. Mutation-verified, each against its own defect: unpinning `ps` fails the rendering test with a 3-hour offset in the diff; relaxing an unrecorded identity fails 5 tests including the prune one; accepting a legacy recording fails 2; reporting a refusal as `stopped: true` fails 6 with `Expected: 6, Received: 0` on the exit code. `test/unit/kill.test.ts` gains the assertion NIT-5 named as missing — a mismatched leader spares the GROUP too, not just the pid — mutation-verified by letting a `pgid` bypass the leader check. **A REGRESSION TEST HERE MUST SPAWN REAL CHILD PROCESSES, and the easy version is wrong.** The obvious way to write the rendering test is to mutate `process.env.TZ` between two captures in the test process. Measured: that does NOT reach an inherited-environment child, the two UNPINNED renderings then compare EQUAL, and the test therefore passes with the fix reverted — a green assertion proving nothing, which is the exact failure class that got this criterion re-graded from a docstring in the first place. The two environments have to be real ones, which is why `test/fixtures/capture-identity.ts` exists as a separate process rather than as a helper function; its header carries the same warning for whoever reaches for the easy version first. **Also recorded so the rejected route is not re-suggested: the `""` hole could NOT cleanly be closed at the schema boundary.** Putting `.min(1)` on `RegistryWorkerSchema.started` looks like the tidy fix — remove the state rather than handle it — and it is wrong twice. `readRegistry` throws on a failed parse and `down.ts` catches that into `registry = null`, so ONE bad entry would blind the anchor for EVERY worker in the run, which is precisely the pattern `readRunWorktrees` was already fixed to avoid. And `startRegistryDaemon`'s `persist()` calls `RegistrySchema.parse` on the daemon's OWN identity, so a daemon whose capture failed would crash at startup instead of degrading. `""` is not a value to reject at a boundary; it is the writers' declared capture-failed sentinel, and it belongs folded into the reader's refusal set alongside `null`. **Why `[~]` and not `[x]`.** Two residuals, both narrower than before but neither proved. (a) `--force-identity` deliberately restores the rung-0 self-anchor; it is named, documented and only reachable by typing it, but on that path rung 0 still cannot tell a supervisor from a stranger. (b) Identity is checked on the LEADER and the signal is delivered to `-state.pgid`, a number read from a state file `down` reads precisely because it may be stale. The failure direction is now asserted (a mismatched leader signals nothing at all) and `launchDetached`'s `?? -1` degrades safely through the `> 0` guard, but the positive direction — that the recorded pgid really is the validated process's own group — is checked nowhere. An unvalidated group is a wider blast radius than an unvalidated pid, since it reaches every process in it. ISC-272 carries both. **Recorded, and explicitly NOT grounds for this re-grade:** `bun test test/unit/kill.test.ts` alone throws `ReferenceError: Cannot access 'realProcessOps' before initialization` on a `kill.ts -> run/registry.ts -> safety/reaper.ts -> kill.ts` cycle. It executes normally under `bun test test/unit`, so it is local-isolation fragility rather than a dark test, and formed no part of this grading. **[THIRD ROUND, 2026-08-20, Phase F. "" })` — a `ps` against a pid whose child handle that scope does not hold. `registry.ts:209` named this capture site "weaker than the other two" and said the consequence was the `""` sentinel. **That is not the consequence.** `""` is what a reaped-and-IDLE pid yields; a reaped-and-REISSUED pid yields a STRANGER'S start time, and `launchDetached`'s `pgidOf(proc.pid)` yielded the stranger's group beside it. Narrowing the record's provenance does not narrow the flag. The NEW residual from round three (a forced stop may ORPHAN children a group signal would have taken) also stands. **Also recorded: `ps -o pgid=` had TWO implementations, and the writer was the lax one.** `supervisor/launch.ts`'s `pgidOf` ignored stderr and never read the exit status, so a signal-killed `ps` and a `ps` that printed a group were both "a number or null" to the writer while the reader had already been fixed to keep those apart. The "DELIBERATE DUPLICATION" comment that defended two readers is gone with the second reader. **[2026-08-26 — one sentence in this entry was true of the DESIGN and false of the CODE; it is now true of both. The reader half was built and proved. The writer half was DECLARED and unreachable: both writers spelled the degrade `(await processStartTime(process.pid)) ?? - [x] ISC-192: A ledger or state file written under an older schema version is read under a pinned policy rather than failing. **[STAYS OPEN — graded 2026-08-19, nothing written.]** The ledger half is ISC-157's, unchanged: no version is stamped, so none can be older. The state-file half is worse than untested — current behaviour CONTRADICTS the criterion, measured directly. A `state.json` stamped `pifleet.state/v0` is rejected by `z.literal("pifleet.state/v1")` and `readWorkerState` raises `StateReadError: unreadable state file <path>: schema: Invalid input`; a `registry.json` stamped `pifleet.registry/v0` throws a bare `ZodError` out of `readRegistry` with no wrapper at all. Both are failures, which is precisely what "rather than failing" forbids. ISC-169 makes the state-file case a diagnosed one-line exit rather than a stack trace, and that is worth having, but a well-dressed refusal to read the file is still a refusal to read the file. Closing this needs a decision on what an older stamp should MEAN — accept and upgrade, accept read-only, or refuse by design — and if the answer is "refuse", the criterion is the thing that should change. **ONE INSTANCE NOW DECIDED, 2026-08-20 — the `started` identity format, recorded here because this criterion owns migration policy.** Pinning `ps -o lstart=` to `TZ=UTC LC_ALL=C` (see ISC-191) CHANGES THE BYTES of every `started` value already in a `registry.json` or `daemon.pid` on disk — not only where the timezone differed, but on a machine already in UTC, because `LC_ALL=C` also reorders the fields (`Thu Aug 20 …` against `Thu 20 Aug …`). So the first `down` after the upgrade meets an incomparable value for every worker at once. **Policy chosen: TAG, REFUSE, AND NAME THE HATCH.** Values written by this build carry a `utc1 ` tag (`IDENTITY_FORMAT`), so they are recognisable as comparable; no locale renders a weekday as `utc1`, so the tag cannot collide with a legacy value. An UNTAGGED value is reported `identity_legacy_format` — its own answer, distinct from `identity_mismatch` — and `--force-identity` completes such a run on the pre-fix anchor. **Why not the alternatives.** Reporting a legacy value as a mismatch would assert something FALSE about the world ("a stranger holds this pid") and would train the operator to reach reflexively for the one flag that re-opens the fail-open. Silently auto-upgrading — rewriting the recorded value from the pid as it reads NOW — would launder an unverified anchor into a verified-LOOKING one, which is the fail-open being removed wearing the fix's clothes; nothing on disk can convert a legacy rendering into the pinned one, because the legacy string does not record which timezone or locale produced it. Accepting a match under EITHER rendering does not work either: the legacy value was rendered in the LAUNCHER's environment and `down` can only re-render in the OPERATOR's, so "try both" re-admits the exact ambiguity the pin removes. **Blast radius:** a run started before the upgrade and stopped after it. New runs are unaffected; a run started and stopped on one build is unaffected. This does NOT close ISC-192 — it is one format, decided and tested, where the criterion asks for a pinned policy across ledger and state files generally. **Recommend NOT tombstoning either this or ISC-157: they are not the same claim.** ISC-192 is wider in subject (adds state files, where the failure is real today) and stronger in outcome ("failing" covers a diagnosed error, "crashing" does not); ISC-157 is stronger in evidence, being the only one of the two that demands the policy be TESTED. Neither subsumes the other, so per the ID-stability rule both stay, and satisfying one would not satisfy the other. **[CLOSED 2026-08-20, Phase G — RESTATED, like ISC-157, and for the same reason.]** The criterion asked to read an older file "rather than failing". The owner chose the opposite and chose it deliberately: **refuse by design, named, with a hatch** — so the criterion is restated to *a reader meeting an unrecognised stamp refuses with its own named diagnosis, never a bare library error*, and closed against that. This generalises the precedent this entry already carried for the `started` identity format (`identity_legacy_format`), rather than inventing a second policy. **Measured before it was fixed, not taken from the previous grading:** a `v0` stamp threw a bare `ZodError` (`exitCode` undefined, message's first line the lone character `[`) and a truncated file a bare `SyntaxError`; neither carried an `exitCode`, so both left the CLI as a stack trace on exit 1, off the §10 ladder entirely. **Four readers now separate PROVENANCE from DAMAGE** — `readRegistry` (`RegistrySchemaError`), `control-auth` (`ControlAuthSchemaError`), `attended/mode` (`AttendedSchemaError`), `report/collect` (`TaskEnvelopeSchemaError`), each pairing with a damage error that deliberately does NOT name a build to go back to. The stamp is checked BEFORE the schema at every site, so a future `v2` renaming a field is not misdiagnosed as a missing one. ""` capture sites were left lenient deliberately, because for all three the pid is alive by construction. **CONSEQUENCE FOUND WHILE TESTING, not reported by either engineer:** `sameIdentity` now RAISES where it returned, and three call sites in `signalIfSame`/`confirmGroup` were not written for it — one worker with a broken `ps` aborted the whole run's teardown. `SignalOutcome`/`KillOutcome` gained `identity_unconfirmed` and `down` gained `identity_read_failed`, kept in `IDENTITY_REFUSALS` rather than `GROUP_REFUSALS` because `--force-identity` is the right pointer for an unconfirmable group and the WRONG one for a broken `ps`. **Phase F's three exhaustive switches proved themselves here:** widening `KillOutcome` broke the build at `daemon.ts:57`, `registry.ts:751` and `reaper.ts:190` simultaneously and would not compile until each answered. **RESIDUALS, and they are real.** (1) The guard `test/unit/durable-reader-wrapping.test.ts` is a TypeScript AST scan that DOES catch a new unwrapped reader anywhere in `src/` — proved with a planted file, not asserted — but it checks WRAPPING, not DIAGNOSIS: the same new reader wrapped in a `try` that rethrows the raw `ZodError` passes 8/8 green. Reverting all five of `kill.ts`'s guards at once left 1335 unit and 19 reaper tests green — `processStartTime` got guards AND tests, `processGroupId` got byte-identical guards and none. All ten are covered now, mutation-proved (signal-kill gate removed -> `Received value: null`; spawn wrapper removed -> `error: Executable not found in $PATH: "ps"`). The three `runKillLadder` wrappers were STRUCTURALLY unreachable rather than merely untested — the harness's `startTime` is a `Promise.resolve` with no branch that rejects — so their tests key on the SIGNAL LOG (`[]`, `["SIGTERM"]`, `["SIGTERM","SIGKILL"]`) and not on a call counter, because all three answer `identity_unconfirmed` and the outcome alone cannot say WHICH read failed; keyed on the outcome, a guard that moved rungs would keep passing. **WHAT STILL HAS NO COVERAGE, measured at thresholds 1 through 6 rather than assumed:** `down.ts`'s `waitGone` leniency, the worker rung's own `how`/`stopped` guards, and the daemon rung's outcome capture. The verdict is `identity_read_failed` every time, produced earlier by the anchor or by the SIGTERM rung, so `stopped = held === false` covers only a read that SUCCEEDS at the rung and fails microseconds later.
