One real bug fell out of the audit rather than out of review: the fixture's read-counter used read-modify-write, and `ps` is spawned fast enough to lose increments, so the "fails after N reads" shim never failed at all; one file per invocation, counted with `ls | wc -l`, instead.
- [x] ISC-193: `EXIT.BUDGET` has a producer, or the code is removed from the ladder. **[CLOSED 2026-08-25 by the budget re-grade audit, on ARM ONE — the ladder keeps its rung and the rung now has three ways to stand. Same staleness as ISC-115: correct on 2026-08-19, falsified on 2026-08-20, re-checked five days late.]** **THE STALE GROUNDS.** This entry read *"the only two things that can yield `EXIT.BUDGET` are `BudgetCeilingError.exitCode` and `budgetExitCode`, and `src/safety/budget.ts` has zero importers in `src/`"*, and *"both `worstExit` callers were read in full … there is no budget branch to mutate, because there is no budget branch"*. Both are FALSE. `wait.ts:192` is `if (budget !== null) codes.push(budgetExitCode(budget));` immediately above its `worstExit(codes)`, and `scheduler.ts:877` is the same fold over `budget.manager.snapshot()` — the two call sites the old audit enumerated as empty are now the two that carry it. **THREE PRODUCERS, and each is pinned WHERE IT IS LOAD-BEARING rather than merely where it is convenient — the attribution matters more than the count here, because two of the three are redundant on the path an operator hits most.** (a) `BudgetCeilingError` (`dispatch.ts:929`) on a CROSSED ceiling: it carries its own `exitCode` and is thrown before `exit` is ever consulted, so it — not the fold — is what makes the halted run report 5. Pinned by `budget-halt.test.ts`'s halted run; suppressing the throw turns that test red on its diagnosis (`budget ceiling crossed`, `tokens_ceiling`), which is the half no other producer supplies. (b) The SCHEDULER's refusal fold (`scheduler.ts:891`) on an UN-crossed ceiling — `would_exceed`, which with `fleet.example.yaml` as shipped (6,000,000 ceiling against a 400,000 reserve) is the ORDINARY way a budgeted run ends, since the last reserve-worth is unreachable by construction. Here nothing halts, nothing throws a coded error, every task that ran succeeded, and `worstExit` over the schedule alone yields `EXIT.PARTIAL` from the `ready` tasks: the fold is the SOLE source of the run's integer. Deleting it turns `budget-halt.test.ts`'s refusal run red at 7. (c) `wait`'s fold (`wait.ts:192`), file-driven, which never sees the scheduler at all: a dispatch-then-wait pipeline reports the same 5 off `budget.json`, and deleting it turns the halted run red. **ARM TWO IS CORRECTLY NOT TAKEN.** `EXIT.BUDGET: 5` stays at `contracts.ts:349` and stays in `EXIT_SEVERITY` between `BACKEND_UNAVAILABLE` and `WORKER_DIED`. The disjunction asked for a producer OR a removal; a producer exists, so the rung is not dead code and deleting it would now lose a distinction the CLI makes. **WHY THE OLD `[ ]` WAS RIGHT AND ITS TEST WAS WRONG, kept because the lesson outlived the grade:** `test/unit/budget.test.ts`'s `describe("ISC-193: EXIT.BUDGET has a producer")` asserted that `budgetExitCode` RETURNS `EXIT.BUDGET` for a halted state — true of the function, silent about production, and its comment (*"budgetExitCode is what `wait` folds into `worstExit`"*) asserted a wiring `wait.ts` did not then contain. That comment is now true. It was true-looking for months before it was true, which is why the grade rests on `budget-halt.test.ts` and `budget-wiring.test.ts` — where a real CLI process's integer is read — and not on it.

### Group P — CI portability (added 2026-07-27, found the first time CI actually ran the probes)

The container job had been red since it was added: it read `d.images[0].tag` from
`image list --json`, which emits a bare array, so the TypeError killed the step
before it could tag the image. Every Group C and Group J criterion had therefore
been reported against a job that never executed a single probe. Fixing the
extraction ran them for the first time and seven failed at once.

- [x] ISC-194: The container CI job tags the built image from the real `image list --json` shape and fails loudly on an empty list.
- [x] ISC-195: A host directory pifleet bind-mounts is accessible to the worker's uid, not left at `mkdtemp`'s 0700 or `mkdir`'s 0755.
- [x] ISC-196: The scratch root itself is traversable, since a 0700 parent makes every 0777 child unreachable.
- [x] ISC-197: `WORKER_UID` is pinned against the Dockerfile's `USER`, so the permission widening cannot drift onto the wrong account.
- [x] ISC-198: A read-only mount is made traversable and readable without being made world-writable.
- [x] ISC-199: Anti: no assertion in the suite encodes a platform-specific spelling of a POSIX observation (`ps` printing `??` versus `?`). **[CLOSED 2026-08-19 by this PR.]** The guard bans hardcoded `ps` OUTPUT SPELLINGS in assertions, not `ps` itself — several tests legitimately spawn it, and `src/safety/mlx-training-guard.ts` parses `ps -axo pid=,command=` as a matter of design. What differs across platforms is what it PRINTS: a detached process shows `??` for its tty on macOS and `?` on Linux, and `ps -o sess=` reports 0 for every process on macOS while Linux gives a real session id — a difference `test/integration/supervisor.test.ts` already records in a comment. An assertion pinning either spelling is green on the machine it was written on and red on the other, which is the same "suite you learn to discount" failure as ISC-266, reached through portability instead of load. Mutation-verified: a planted `expect("x").toBe("??")` turns it red.
- [x] ISC-200: Anti: no CI step can fail in a way that leaves its job green, or pass in a way that never executed its probes.

So a `0o300` directory let every durable step run — tmp written, fsynced, renamed into place — and then threw `EACCES: permission denied, open '<dir>'` out of `writeJsonAtomic` with the correct file sitting on disk. A caller told a durable write failed retries it, marks a worker broken, or unwinds a state machine over a file that is already correct; losing the directory entry's crash-durability is the strictly smaller harm. The fix extracts `fsyncDirBestEffort` in `src/util/jsonl.ts`, which swallows the open, the sync AND the close — the close is in scope because a deferred filesystem error surfaces there and would escape a `finally` untouched. Two probes in `test/unit/jsonl.test.ts`: one calls the helper on a directory that does not exist, which no uid can open, so it does not depend on the permission model; the other drives the whole of `writeJsonAtomic` under a `0o300` directory and then asserts the file really did land and no temp was left. The second requires a non-root uid and asserts that precondition rather than skipping on it, so under uid 0 it fails loudly instead of passing having proved nothing. Mutation-verified: restoring the unguarded `dh = await open(dir, "r")` turns both red with `error: Expected promise that resolves`.

- [x] ISC-235: `BudgetManager.admit` is called on the dispatch path and its snapshot persisted; `budgetExitCode` folds into `worstExit` after harvest. **[CLOSED 2026-08-20 — the wiring commission; all three conjuncts built and mutation-proved.]** **(1) `admit` on the dispatch path.** `runSchedule` takes a `ScheduleBudget` (ONE manager per run — not per worker, which would enforce `n × workers`, and not per call, which would enforce nothing) and calls `admit` before every `io.dispatch`. A refusal `continue`s: the task stays `ready`, never failed, blocked or dropped. Every non-`accepted` dispatch answer calls `settle` to release the hold — mutation: dropping the release on `rejected` leaks the slot and fails `Expected: {} / Received: {a: 5}` with the run deadlocking behind a `max_concurrent` of 1. **(2) Snapshot persisted.** New `budgetJson` member in `run/paths.ts` (which had none) written with `writeJsonAtomic`, on the contract `budget.ts` states: the hold reaches disk BEFORE the envelope it authorises, so a crash between decision and dispatch cannot leak an unaccounted slot a restart would double-admit against — mutation: moving the persist after the dispatch fails `Expected: >= 0 / Received: -1` on the ordering assertion. Writes fire only on real state movement (≈ 2 per task), never on a refusal, so no file write sits on the polling path. **(3) The fold.** `worstExit` over the schedule PLUS `budgetExitCode`, after the loop drains — see ISC-193. **Design decisions, recorded where they are made.** RESTART: spend is RECOMPUTED, the halt is CARRIED, reservations are DROPPED (`resumeBudget` in `safety/budget.ts` holds all three with the reasoning). The transcripts are the durable evidence of what was burned and `budget.json`'s `tokens_spent` is a published snapshot of that derivation, not an independent accumulator — carrying it forward while also booking deltas against a fresh observation would double-count every resumed worker, and carrying it without re-observing would lose whatever was spent between the last snapshot and the crash. A crossed ceiling is a VERDICT, so it survives a rotated transcript; a hold belongs to the process that took it, so it does not. Opening spend already past the ceiling halts at construction, because otherwise a resumed over-budget run refuses every admission on `would_exceed`, dispatches nothing, and exits 7 — ISC-114 inverted. A `budget.json` whose `run_id` does not match is refused (`ForeignBudgetError`), never adopted. PER-TASK ATTRIBUTION: there is no per-task usage anywhere in the system; both A6 sources are cumulative per session, so a settling task is charged the DELTA since the last observation, which keeps the run total exact even though no single task's share is independently knowable. The `run.json` writer now lives beside its reader in `run/state.ts` (`runBudgetRecord` / `readRunBudgetPolicy`), round-trip tested — mutation: renaming `tokens_ceiling` in the writer fails `Expected: 777 / Received: null`, which is the silent-fallback divergence that made `max_concurrent` a config key with no reader in the first place, and which does not throw. **[REVIEW ROUND 2 — six defects found INSIDE this fix, five of them the same dead-wiring/silent-fallback class this criterion exists to eliminate. All fixed and mutation-proved; residuals named at the end.]** **(a) The WRITER was unproved.** `runBudgetRecord` was round-trip tested — but only by tests CALLING IT DIRECTLY into a hand-built `run.json`. Deleting its one production call site (`up.ts`, `...runBudgetRecord(loadedConfig?.config.run ?? null)`) left the ENTIRE suite green, and shipped every run at `tokensCeiling: null` — unbounded — with the default cap, silently: `readRunBudgetPolicy` treats absence as normal, `note` is null, no ledger row, nothing on stderr. `tokens_ceiling` would have become a config key with no reader again, one line above the docstring that cites `max_concurrent` for exactly that. Closed by two tests in `up-wiring.test.ts` driving the REAL `up`: the recorded policy reads back 3/4242/11 (all non-defaults, so a budget-less `run.json` cannot satisfy them), and a run `up` created actually HALTS on the ceiling `up` recorded. MUTATION-PROVED: deleting that line fails the first with `maxConcurrent 3→2, perTaskReserveTokens 11→0, tokensCeiling 4242→null` and the second with `Expected: 5 / Received: 0`. `budget-halt.test.ts` writes `run.json` by hand and its header now says what that costs. **(b) `would_exceed` exited 7, and the shipped config makes it the NORMAL ending.** `budgetExitCode` returns SUCCESS unless `halted_at` is set, only `settle` halts, and `exitFor` maps a `ready` task to `EXIT.PARTIAL` — so a run the budget REFUSED reported "dispatch --auto finished with non-success terminal states" at 7 with every task successful. With `fleet.example.yaml` as shipped (6000000 / 400000) admission fails from 5,600,001 spent onward, so the last reserve-worth of every budget is unreachable by construction and this is how a run that uses its budget ends. DECIDED: **exit 5**, on the ground that the run ended because of the BUDGET rather than because of a task outcome — the same reason the halted path reports 5 — with the two kept distinguishable in the diagnosis and in `budget.json` (`halted_at` set vs null) and the message deliberately NOT saying "ceiling crossed", which would send an operator after spend that does not exist. `runSchedule` now records the refusal and folds `EXIT.BUDGET`; the comment claiming "the fold at the bottom turns [ready] into 5" is corrected. **This is the only path on which the FOLD is load-bearing** — `dispatch --auto` raises `BudgetCeilingError` (self-coded) before consulting `exit`, so the halted tests stay green with the fold deleted; `budget-halt.test.ts`'s comment claiming otherwise is corrected too. MUTATION-PROVED: removing the fold fails `Expected: 5 / Received: 7`. **(c) The restart REFUNDED spend whenever observation degraded.** `resumeBudget` rule 1 recomputes spend from observation and rule 1 had no failure mode: `cumulativeTokens` returned a bare `0` on every degradation, indistinguishable from a worker that genuinely burned nothing, and the merge's other input is inert because nothing writes `state.usage`. Rule 2's prose defended only the HALTED case; the common case is un-halted, where a run at 95% of its ceiling crashes, resumes at 0 and gets a fresh full ceiling — **across n restarts, n × `tokens_ceiling`**. Observation now returns `{tokens, degraded}` and the new pure, exported `openingBalance` floors the opening balance at the persisted `tokens_spent` when any observation degraded, while leaving a CLEAN lower observation authoritative (that is rotation, which re-observing exists to catch). MUTATION-PROVED at unit level (`Expected: 950 / Received: 0`) and end-to-end in `budget-halt.test.ts`, which spends 400, renames the transcript out from under the recorded `session_path`, and resumes: floored at 400 instead of 0, with the degradation on stderr and in the ledger. **(d) `unreachable` DOUBLE-BOOKED spend against a ceiling.** `unreachable` is the one dispatch answer that is NOT terminal — the task stays `ready` and is re-offered — and it was routed through `settleBudget` like the four that are. So a task was booked once per ATTEMPT, the tokens came from the worker the dispatch never reached, and because `settle` can trip the ceiling **a run could halt and exit 5 on spend attributed to a dispatch nobody made** (probed directly: two bookings of 100 against a ceiling of 150 halts; one does not). New `BudgetManager.release` gives the slot back and books nothing. The existing suite could not see this because production's `taskTokens` is a per-worker monotone delta that answers 0 the second time, muting the arithmetic — so the regression test asserts the SETTLE COUNT for one task, which survives any change to the fake's token model. MUTATION-PROVED: `Expected: 1 / Received: 2`. A dispatch that THROWS now releases its hold too, instead of stranding a phantom in-flight slot for every concurrent `wait`/`report`. **(e) `persistBudget` could pre-empt the writes non-throwing `settle` exists to protect.** It is `writeJsonAtomic` and can throw (ENOSPC, EROFS, EPERM) from INSIDE the settle pass, before `onChange(graph.snapshot())` — discarding the schedule record of every task that settled in that pass and killing `dispatch --auto` with no stdout. Now log-and-continue via a required-in-practice `onPersistError`, reported on stderr and in the ledger: accounting durability must not outrank the record of what ran. MUTATION-PROVED: rethrowing fails the test with the ENOSPC escaping. **(f) The persist-before-dispatch rationale was justified by a reason rule 3 nullifies.** The docstring claimed a crash between decision and dispatch "must not leak an unaccounted slot that a restart would double-admit against" — but rule 3 DROPS all reservations and spend is re-observed, so a dispatch that never happened has nothing to double-admit. The ordering is KEPT and the reason restated: the live consumer is a CONCURRENT `wait`/`report`, which can only learn the committed slot from this file, and writing first can over-state in-flight commitment by at most one dispatch while writing later under-states it. **RESIDUALS, named rather than left to be rediscovered.** **Filed as their own criteria rather than buried here: ISC-280 (`soft_stop_at` has no reader) and ISC-281 (the `session_present` lag).** (1) `soft_stop_at` is the third key in the `budget:` block and STILL HAS NO READER — `grep -rln 'soft_stop_at\|softStop' src/` returns `config/schema.ts` alone. Stated in the schema and in `fleet.example.yaml` rather than silently shipped two-of-three; wiring it needs a criterion of its own, because what a soft stop DOES is a product decision, not a missing call site. **ISC-280.** (2) The floor is a run TOTAL, not per-worker: `BudgetState` carries no per-worker breakdown, so a run where one worker degraded and another grew gets `max(sum, published)`, which under-counts the healthy worker. Per-worker baselines in the snapshot would close it. (3) `taskTokens`' high-water mark blocks refunds but leaves the ceiling BLIND after a mid-run session switch until the new transcript passes the old mark — an under-count, the direction `combineUsage`'s element-wise max exists to prevent, now stated in the comment as a cost rather than only a benefit. **WHAT THE FLOOR STILL CANNOT DETECT, stated as three things rather than left as a caveat, because the residual matters more here than the fix.** (i) A transcript that reads CLEANLY but under-reports: a switched session that parses fine and starts from zero degrades nothing, so no floor is triggered, and the high-water mark books 0 until it climbs past the old mark. Silent, and the only case in this list with no signal at all. (ii) The floor is a run TOTAL, not per-worker (residual 2 above), so a run where one worker degraded and another genuinely grew gets `max(sum, published)` — which under-counts the healthy worker's growth rather than reconstructing it. (iii) Spend between the last snapshot and the crash is unaccounted BY CONSTRUCTION: the floor is the last thing the run PUBLISHED about itself, so it is a lower bound, not a measurement, and `budget.json` is written at most once per state movement. All three fail toward UNDER-counting the ceiling, which is survivable; the defect that was fixed failed toward refunding it, which is not. (4) **`session_present` is unreliable as the ISC-96 discriminator within its own lag window, measured — now ISC-281, where the evidence and the mechanism live in full.** In brief: `run/state.ts` and `harvest/transcript.ts`'s `classifySession` both document it as what separates `never_created` from `missing_after_present`; a worker that ran a task to completion and whose transcript booked 400 tokens was observed with `session_present: false`. **The flag LAGS the transcript.** `recordSessionPath` sets it from `existsSync` at the instant `get_state` first reports the path — before the file is lazily created, so `false` — and the correction is made by the heartbeat (`HEARTBEAT_MS = 250`), which also flushes. Measured directly: at the instant `dispatch --auto` exits, the on-disk flag is still `false` with the transcript present and readable; it flips true ~400 ms later. Any consumer reading state inside that window sees `false` for a worker that has genuinely spent — and a resumed `dispatch --auto` started straight after the previous one is exactly that consumer. (Recorded precisely because a first draft of this note blamed a "5s heartbeat"; the heartbeat is 250 ms and does flush its correction. The LAG is the defect, not the period, and the wrong mechanism would have sent the next reader to tune an interval that is not the problem.) A first cut of (c) rested on it and mis-classified a real degradation as innocent. The classification is therefore left explicitly ambiguous and resolved where the information exists (is there published spend to lose?). Scope of the knock-on, stated precisely rather than sweepingly: `classifySession` maps `session_present === false` to `never_created`, and during the lag window the file DOES exist, so it answers `present` and is unaffected. It is wrong only for a transcript that vanishes while the flag is still catching up — narrow, but it is the same window this budget path had to stop trusting, and it is the reason the `missing_after_present` / `never_created` split cannot be treated as reliable evidence by anything that must not lose money.

With the comparison the merge is strictly one-directional: it adds files and raises severity and has no expressible way to subtract. That is what makes a PARTIAL allowlist safe here, where this entry — correctly, under the old design — warned that one able to subtract would cap ordinary source files. Measured too: 11 ordinary source and doc paths across five languages produce zero hits. **SIX MUTATIONS, each restored byte-identical (`shasum -a 256`), each caught.** Deleting the graded cap fails 4; collapsing `capFor` so every tier returns `unknown` fails 3; turning the ceiling into an assignment fails exactly 1 — the probe written for it; inverting `strictestTier` fails 2; dropping unresolved commands silently fails 3. **The sixth is the one that mattered most, and it is the RC-1 mutation:** making the harvester write `graded: []` instead of the computed surface fails both new integration probes. That defect — a correct module beside a path nothing exercises — is what ISC-150 itself shipped as, live code reading `facts.harness.touched` which nothing filled in, and it is now recorded ten times in this ISA. **The residual is made LOUD rather than left silent**, which is the other half of the completeness claim: a command whose runner cannot be classified gets no allowlist at all, so `adjudicate` raises a discrepancy saying only the known-partial denylist graded that diff. "I could not determine the harness surface for `npm test`" and "the diff is clean" both certify `success` and must not produce the same report. Proved on the LIVE path — `T-exam-pass`'s real acceptance command is `grep`, which no runner will ever implement. **Three stale docstrings fixed in passing, all introduced by my own 2026-08-25 escape-hatch change and all pointing readers at the wrong semantics for the exact mechanism this criterion is about:** `DEFAULT_HARNESS_PATTERNS`, `harnessSurfaceFor` and `HarnessSurfaceSchema.defaults_missed` each still said `harness.patterns` REPLACES the defaults. It extends them, and has since that commit. **WHAT WOULD CLOSE THIS TO `[x]`:** either the denylist is deleted and every acceptance command in reach resolves to a runner manifest (which needs the (b) work this entry has always named — the transitive closure of `extends`/`include`/`setupFiles` edges, read from the base tree), or the criterion is restated to match what a keyed allowlist can actually promise. Both are owner calls, not engineering ones.
- [x] ISC-244: Validation COST is bounded, not just envelope bytes — array lengths are checked before the schema, so an element-packed envelope cannot allocate an issue object per element.
- [x] ISC-245: A worker-controlled filename cannot forge lines in the harvest report; every refusal is escaped and truncated at one choke point.
- [x] ISC-246: `scanOutboxFiles` returns file DESCRIPTORS, not path strings — a validated path re-opened later is a TOCTOU window, and `nlink` can be raised after the scan. Latent while `safe` has no consumers; arms the moment E3 attaches artifacts. — STAYS OPEN, DELIBERATELY, and the criterion's own hedge is the reason. Current state: `OutboxFileScan.safe` is `string[]` (`src/harvest/outbox.ts:64-69`) — path strings, exactly as the criterion says it should not be. The scan validates with `lstat` + `realpath` on PATHS and opens nothing, so the refactor is genuinely undone, not half-done. **CORRECTION, 2026-08-20:** this note previously read "`nlink` is never read anywhere in the file", which was FALSE — `src/harvest/outbox.ts:537` reads `st.nlink` and refuses any entry with more than one name, and `test/unit/harvest-outbox.test.ts` > "a hard link to a file outside the outbox is refused" pins it (measured: delete the check and that test goes red with the linked private key sitting in `safe`). The correction makes this criterion MORE live, not less. Its own wording — "`nlink` can be raised after the scan" — describes a real read at a real instant rather than a hypothetical one: the scan reads the link count at T on a PATH, and a consumer that re-opens that path at T+1 gets no guarantee the inode still has one name. The path-string return is what leaves that window open, and it is still open. The LATENCY CLAIM IS TRUE AND WAS VERIFIED, not taken on trust: the sole production caller is `src/harvest/index.ts:207`, which reads `scan.refused` only and never touches `scan.safe`; every other read of `.safe` is inside `outbox.ts`'s own `push` calls or in `test/unit/harvest-outbox.test.ts`. Nothing in `src/` re-opens a scanned path, so there is no window to race today — the TOCTOU is armed by a consumer that does not exist. WHY NOT DO IT ANYWAY: the refactor is not small and it does not fully work. Returning descriptors changes the return type, ~10 call sites across the scan's five early-return paths and its bail-out branch, and introduces this repo's FIRST caller-owns-a-file-descriptor contract — every early return and every refusal becomes an fd-leak site, and the scan is explicitly bounded at 10,000 entries, so a leak there exhausts the process table rather than merely being untidy. Worse, it cannot close the window it names: Node exposes no `openat`/`O_NOFOLLOW` relative to a `FileHandle`, so the DIRECTORY walk stays path-based no matter what the leaves return, and the honest outcome is a partial fix carrying a full fd-lifetime tax. The trigger the criterion names ("E3 attaches artifacts") is a consumer nothing in this ISA has specified yet. CLOSING IT COSTS: ~90-110 lines in `outbox.ts`, an fd-lifetime discipline the codebase has no precedent for, and the existing symlink/containment tests (`harvest-outbox.test.ts:309-465`, all of which assert on path strings) rewritten to assert on descriptors — for an array no production code reads. That trade is worth taking WITH the consumer and not before; doing it now would be paying the tax to protect nothing, and re-writing containment tests while their subject has no user is how a real assertion gets quietly weakened. NO MUTATION WAS RUN: there is nothing implemented to mutate, and the existing tests pin the path-string behaviour the criterion wants replaced, so they would go red for the refactor rather than for a regression. **[RE-GRADED `[ ]` -> `[~]` 2026-08-21, Phase H — RESTATED, not built as written, on the ISC-157/192 precedent. `[~]` AND NOT `[x]`, AND THE REASON IS RULE 3.]** **The criterion as written asks for a window that cannot be closed in this runtime, so it was restated rather than built.** Node exposes no `openat` relative to a `FileHandle`, so `readdir` and the containment `realpath` re-resolve names from the root on every call and the DIRECTORY WALK STAYS PATH-BASED no matter how much of the refactor is done. **RESTATED TO:** *the outbox scan validates and then HOLDS each accepted file — `safe` carries an open descriptor, and `nlink` and the regular-file check are performed ON THE DESCRIPTOR rather than on the path, so the inode that was validated is the inode a consumer receives. The walk remains path-based, and the criterion does not claim otherwise.* **What was built** (`src/harvest/outbox.ts`): `OutboxFileScan.safe` is now `OutboxFile[]` (`{path, handle}`) rather than `string[]`; a single choke point `holdIfSafe` is the only place a descriptor is opened and the only way an entry enters `safe`, mirroring the existing `refuse` choke point, so an accept path added later cannot forget to validate on the descriptor or to close on refusal; the open carries `O_NOFOLLOW` (an entry `readdir` reported as a plain file that has become a symlink by open time fails `ELOOP` instead of being followed) and `O_NONBLOCK` (the same swap into a FIFO cannot wedge the open, §12.5); `closeOutboxScan` releases a whole scan and empties `safe` so it is idempotent; and the walk is wrapped so a throw releases every fd opened so far rather than leaking it. **THE GRADE IS `[~]` BECAUSE `safe` STILL HAS NO PRODUCTION CONSUMER, and this was re-verified rather than carried over:** `scanOutboxFiles` has exactly one production caller, `src/harvest/index.ts:207`, which reads `scan.refused` (lines 208-211) and never touches `scan.safe`. The compiler proved it rather than a grep — **changing the element type of `safe` from `string` to `OutboxFile` broke FOUR assertions, all in `test/unit/harvest-outbox.test.ts`, and ZERO lines of `src/`.** Under SRD-COMPLETION §8 rule 3 that makes every test here a test over a callerless module, which proves the module and not the criterion. **The missing consumer, named:** nothing in `src/` reads outbox artifact CONTENT at all; the consumer this criterion is waiting for is the one its own hedge names — "E3 attaches artifacts" — which would read each `OutboxFile.handle` and attach or copy the bytes, and it is unspecified in this ISA. `[x]` requires that consumer to exist and to read the descriptor. **THREE MUTATIONS, and the second is a coverage finding rather than a proof.** **M1 (validate then RELEASE the hold — `await handle.close()` immediately before the push):** the two NAMED descriptor tests go red, `SystemError: Bad file descriptor / syscall: "readFile" / code: "EBADF"` at both `harvest-outbox.test.ts:542` ("an accepted artifact carries a readable descriptor, not just a name") and `:569` ("the descriptor still reads the validated inode after the path is swapped"), 43 pass / 2 fail; reverted, 45 pass / 0 fail / 97 expect(). **M1 WAS NOT A DRILL — it reached `main`'s history.** Commit `ec9cf7e` was taken from a working tree with M1 applied, so it shipped the defect while its own message claimed the scan holds descriptors; `safe` came back full of dead fds. Removed in `8573d8e`. **The lesson is about the SUITE, not the accident:** every pre-existing containment and symlink test stayed GREEN under M1, because they read `safe` through a path projection and a path is still correct when the fd behind it is dead. Only the two assertions that dereference the descriptor caught it. **M2 (`handle.stat()` -> `lstat(target)`, i.e. move the check back onto the NAME) LEAVES EVERY BEHAVIOURAL TEST GREEN — 44 pass, 1 fail, and the one failure is the SOURCE GUARD.** This is measured, not predicted, and it is the honest limit of the `nlink`-on-the-descriptor half: nothing can interleave a filesystem change between the `open` and the `fstat` from inside the same process, so path-stat and fd-stat are not behaviourally separable in-process. That half is pinned by a source scan over `holdIfSafe`'s body ("the accept path stats the descriptor and opens with O_NOFOLLOW"), which checks the SHAPE of the call and not the semantics of the result — a `handle.stat()` whose result was ignored would pass it. Same class of guard, and same class of limitation, as ISC-192's `durable-reader-wrapping` AST scan. **M3 (descriptor budget removed):** "the held-descriptor budget refuses past the cap instead of exhausting the process" goes red, `Expected length: 128 / Received length: 138`, 44 pass / 1 fail; reverted green. **FD EXHAUSTION IS A REAL FAILURE MODE THE RESTATEMENT INTRODUCES, AND IT IS WRITTEN DOWN HERE RATHER THAN DISCOVERED LATER.** Measured, not assumed: a process holding one descriptor per entry reaches `EMFILE: too many open files` after **252** opens under a 256 soft limit — the macOS default in plenty of launch contexts — which is **forty times below `MAX_OUTBOX_ENTRIES` (10,000)**. Uncapped, a large outbox would not merely fail its own scan; it would drain the process table out from under everything the harvester still has to do afterwards, including writing the report that says what went wrong. **Mitigated by `MAX_HELD_DESCRIPTORS = 128`** — half the 256 floor, so headroom survives even in the worst common environment — and exceeding it is a NAMED refusal ("more than 128 artifacts to hold open; scan stopped"), one refusal rather than one per remaining entry, surfaced through `harvest/index.ts` like every other refusal because `refused` IS consumed in production. **It is a bound, not a guarantee:** Node exposes no portable `getrlimit`, so the scan cannot know the ambient soft limit, and where that limit sits below the cap the per-entry open failure is the backstop and reports the errno by name. **The second half of the tax is ownership:** the caller now owns fds, this repo's first such contract, and a scan dropped without `closeOutboxScan` leaks one descriptor per accepted artifact with no finalizer behind it. **WHAT THE RESTATEMENT DOES NOT BUY, stated plainly and also written into `scanOutboxFiles`'s docstring where the next reader will meet it.** (1) **The walk is still path-based, and a DIRECTORY SWAPPED MID-WALK IS STILL NOT CAUGHT** — `files/sub` replaced between the `readdir` that listed it and the `open` of a leaf inside it is not detected by anything here, and no amount of descriptor-holding at the leaves can detect it, because there is no `openat` to anchor the next step to the directory that was checked. (2) Containment therefore remains a PATH-TIME claim: what is pinned is the identity of each accepted FILE, not the identity of the tree it was found in. (3) The criterion's own words "`nlink` can be raised after the scan" are still true — raising a link count after the scan raises it on the inode, and the scan is over; what the descriptor buys is that the link count and the bytes a consumer reads describe THE SAME INODE, not that the count is frozen. (4) The `realpath` containment check on the accept path still has no test, unchanged from the previous grading and for the unchanged reason recorded at `outbox.ts`'s comment block: what it defends against needs root to build. **[RE-GRADED `[~]` -> `[x]` 2026-08-28 — THE CONSUMER WAS BUILT, AND IT IS A REAL FIX RATHER THAN A CHECKBOX.]** The `[~]` rested on one thing only, restated three times above: `safe` had no production reader, so under SRD-COMPLETION §8 rule 3 every test here proved a callerless module. That is now false, and it was closed by fixing a defect the criterion did not name. **The defect:** `ResultEnvelope.artifacts` is the worker's CLAIM about what it produced; `adjudicate.ts` carried it verbatim into the report; nothing ever compared it to the outbox. A worker could name an artifact it never wrote, or write one it never named, and the harvest had no opinion either way. **What was built** (`src/harvest/reconcile.ts`, a new module): `reconcileArtifactClaims(scan, claimed, loc)` reconciles the two directions — claimed-but-absent, present-but-unclaimed, claimed-but-empty, and a descriptor that cannot be read — and `harvestTask` calls it INSIDE the `withOutboxScan` body (ISC-301's window), because the descriptors are alive only for that body's duration. **THE CLAIMED PATH IS NEVER DEREFERENCED, AND THIS SHAPED THE WHOLE DESIGN.** `Docs/SRD.md:1267` names `{"kind":"file","path":"/Users/dan/.env"}` as an exfiltration primitive, and the claimed paths are CONTAINER paths authored by the worker. So a claim is translated through `containerPathToHost` (which already refuses anything outside the mount table, and which had zero production callers until now) and then compared AS A STRING against host paths the scan had already validated; bytes come only from the held descriptors. The guarantee is structural rather than conventional: **the module imports no filesystem API at all**, so an edit that wanted to open a claimed path would have to add the import first, and a claim pins its absence. Only paths under the task outbox `files/` tree are candidates — the worktree is also legal in the envelope and is a repository full of things that must not be hashed into a report. **Set-membership findings are decided in their own pass BEFORE any read**, because emitting them from the digest loop let an artifact larger than the per-artifact cap take its own concealment finding off the report. **Where the findings go:** into `discrepancies`, which §8.4 already publishes, rather than into a channel invented for them. **Where the measurements go:** `derived.artifacts` (`HarvestedArtifactSchema` = `{path, bytes, sha256}`), and that field exists because the first cut computed a sha256 and dropped it. `HarvestSchema`'s own ISC-153 comment had already ruled on exactly that — "the hash was being computed and dropped on the floor, which satisfies neither half of what it is for" — so the digest was published rather than deleted. It is a SECOND schema and not a reuse of `ArtifactRefSchema`: that one is what the worker said (kind + container path, untrusted), this is what the harvester measured, and §12.6 asks for the two to be structurally separated. `kind` is deliberately absent — there is nothing on disk to derive it from, so carrying it would let a claim ride into the derived half wearing a fact's clothes. The published path is the HOST path (matching how `refused` already reports, and resolvable when someone reads the report, which a container path is not once the container is gone) and is `safeForReport`-escaped, while the RAW path stays the matching key, so a hostile filename can neither forge report lines nor evade the comparison; the worker's own spelling survives untouched in `claimed.artifacts[].path` in the same document. Bytes are capped per artifact (8 MiB) and per task (64 MiB); exceeding either is a NAMED discrepancy and the artifact is omitted rather than digested to the cap, because a sha256 over a truncated prefix published in a field called `sha256` is a wrong answer rather than a partial one. **TWO MUTATIONS, both run on this branch, both restored byte-identical (`shasum -a 256 -c` plus an empty `git diff`).** **M4 (read by PATH instead of through the handle — `fsStat(f.path)` for the size and a fresh `fsOpen(f.path)` for every chunk):** exactly three tests go red — "the digest describes the validated inode after the path is swapped", "a symlinked artifact digests its target even after the target is unlinked", and "a descriptor that cannot be read is a named discrepancy, not a throw" — 19 pass / 3 fail. **The other 19 stayed green, including every containment and mount-table test**, which reproduces this entry's own M1 lesson from the opposite direction: a path projection is still correct when the descriptor behind it is wrong, and only assertions that dereference the descriptor can tell. **M5 (`artifacts: reconciled.artifacts` -> `artifacts: []`, i.e. the schema field declared and published but never populated):** 4 tests red across BOTH levels — three in `harvest-reconcile-wiring.test.ts` (JSON round trip, host-vs-container spelling, the escaping probe) and one in `test/integration/harvest.test.ts` ("the harvested outbox artifacts reach both the human and JSON output"), so a `.default([])` field silently emptying is a red build rather than an empty report. **THE OLD CLAIM WENT RED ON PURPOSE AND WAS REPLACED.** `grep -rn "scan.safe" src/` expecting empty was the pin that carried the `[~]`, and its own text said "A hit here is the E3 consumer arriving, and the grade can move." It went red the moment the consumer landed. Three claims replace it: `harvestTask` calls the reconciler, the reconciler reads through the positional descriptor read, and the reconciler imports no `node:fs`. Any one alone hides the others' defect — a caller with no reader, a reader nothing calls, or either of them quietly reopening a name. **WHAT THIS DOES NOT CHANGE, and none of it was reworded to fit the new evidence.** (1) **The `nlink`-on-the-descriptor half is STILL source-pinned, and M2's finding above stands unaltered:** nothing can interleave a filesystem change between the `open` and the `fstat` from inside one process, so path-stat and fd-stat remain behaviourally inseparable in-process. The consumer arriving does not make that observable, and the grade does not claim it does. What the consumer DOES make observable is the other half — that the bytes a reader receives come from the validated inode — and that is exactly what M4 reddens. (2) The walk is still path-based and a directory swapped mid-walk is still not caught. (3) Containment remains a path-time claim about each accepted FILE, not about the tree it was found in. (4) The `realpath` containment check on the accept path still has no test, for the unchanged reason that building its adversary needs root.
- [x] ISC-247: A backslash in an envelope path is refused. Harmless on POSIX, a separator anywhere else; not a control character, so the ISC-240 filter does not catch it.

### Phase 3 — security and cloud identity

- [x] ISC-248a: `up` refuses to start when the configured egress network exists but is NOT internal, rather than adopting it and reporting deny-all it does not enforce.
- [x] ISC-249: A checked-out repository is neutralized BEFORE any worker reads it; each hazard records `detected` and `neutralized` independently. **[CLOSED 2026-08-18, Slice 2]** Was open, blocked on ISC-27/ISC-28 (worktree/bind-mount round-tripping — both since closed) because neutralization needs a per-worker tree to run against, and nothing before Slice 2 created one. `run/worktree.ts`'s clone-based checkouts (SRD §9.2 erratum) close that gap: `up.ts`'s `onCreated` callback runs `neutralizeRepoHazards` against each finished CLONE — not the operator's own checkout, which stays detect-only, per SRD §12.8 — and unlike a linked worktree's pointer-file `.git` (which the scanner explicitly declines to follow), a clone's `.git` is a real directory the scanner acts on completely. Verified end to end, not inferred: `test/integration/up-wiring.test.ts`'s `egress verification and hazard neutralization...` test seeds a root `AGENTS.md` in the operator's repo, runs the real `up` CLI, and asserts a SECOND `repo_hazard` ledger event (`worker: "eng-1"`, `neutralized: true`) distinct from the operator-side detect-only one, that `AGENTS.md.pifleet-quarantined` exists inside the CLONE, and — closing the loop this criterion's own history warns about — that `inspectCloneDirt` reports the resulting checkout CLEAN rather than dirty-from-birth (see the `captureWorktreeBaseline` fix, ISA Changelog and Slice 2 close-out below, for why that last part needed its own fix once this test was written to check for it).
- [x] ISC-250: Every control-socket verb requires the per-run secret, `ping` included; a wrong or missing token is a clean refusal and the server stays up.
- [x] ISC-251: The Google grant is never silent — `up` states per worker which identity it got, or that it got none. Machine-checked in CI (`test/integration/up-wiring.test.ts`); the `token`-mode schema default is exercised here alongside ISC-49's explicit `file`, so the line is proved to REPORT the mode rather than to contain a constant that happens to read right. The identity it names is now resolved from the ADC principal rather than from `gcloud config get-value account` — a different credential store that routinely disagrees; see ISC-49's close-out for the full reasoning, the measured empty-`account` fallback, and the disagreeing-fixture test that pins it.
- [x] ISC-252: Egress host matching requires a label boundary; `evil-googleapis.com` and an empty leftmost label cannot ride a `*.googleapis.com` rule.
- [x] ISC-248: `TokenRefresher` runs on the supervisor's lifecycle and re-injects before expiry. **[CLOSED 2026-08-27 — wired, and probed against a real supervisor, a real container and a real federated credential.]** **What the previous audit got right, kept because it is why this took two phases.** The entry stood at `[ ]` with the first limb FALSE rather than merely unproven: `grep -rn 'security/refresh' src/` returned NOTHING, so the class had zero callers and the criterion's verb — *runs* — had no evidence and could have none. The stated reason for not wiring it was honest and was re-verified rather than carried forward: the refresher attaches to a RUNNING container and the headless path started none, so wiring it then would have attached it to nothing and manufactured the appearance of a grade. That reason stopped being true when the container launcher landed (ISC-286/287). **A larger gap than the entry claimed, found on wiring it.** `injectToken` and `gcloudMinter` had no production callers either — only `test/`. So there was no refresh loop AND no initial injection: the container received the gcloud tmpfs (`gcloudConfigTmpfsArgv`) and the env pointing at `TOKEN_FILE` (`tokenModeStartupEnv`), and nothing ever wrote a token there. A `cloud_access: true` worker had a credential-shaped hole, not a stale credential. **What was built.** The credential PLAN now rides in `WorkerLaunch` — `planCredential`'s output, written by `run/materialize.ts` where the config is known, read by the supervisor where the container is known. That placement is the launch record's own argument, quoted from the docstring above it: `up` resolves config in a cwd and environment a detached supervisor does not share, so a second derivation could differ with nothing looking wrong. The supervisor constructs a `TokenRefresher` after the container spawn and drives `run(signal)`, which ticks due-at-0 — so ONE path serves both the initial injection and the loop, rather than two places for the mint, the record and the failure handling to drift. `refreshAbort.abort()` on the shutdown path tears it down; without it the process holds a live loop and a pending timer and does not exit at all. **The failure policy is an owner decision, recorded as one.** A failed mint DEGRADES the worker loudly and does not kill it: a transient `gcloud` hiccup must not destroy a worker mid-task, but a worker configured for cloud access that silently has none is indistinguishable from a healthy one until some later task fails naming the wrong component. So `state.credential.degraded` is set where `status` reads it, and is cleared by the next SUCCESS rather than by time. **Evidence, and why it is not the unit tests.** `test/unit/refresh.test.ts` (23 tests) drives `tick()` against a fake clock — the right way to pin the schedule, and structurally unable to answer whether a real supervisor starts one. The closing probe is `test/integration/container-launch.test.ts`'s "a compressed token_refresh produces a SECOND injection, not just an initial one (ISC-248)", in the `container` job: a real supervisor process, a real container, a real federated credential, `token_refresh` compressed to 2s. The compression is the only thing faked and it is faked in CONFIG — the field an operator sets — not by reaching into the refresher. It asserts generations `[0, 1]` in `credentials.jsonl`, `state.credential.generation >= 1`, `degraded: false`, no `token` key in any record, and a non-empty token file inside the container's tmpfs. **Deliberately NOT asserted: that the token VALUE changed between generations.** `gcloud auth application-default print-access-token` serves a cached token until it nears expiry, so two mints seconds apart legitimately return identical bytes; asserting inequality would pin gcloud's cache, not this loop. ISC-47 separately proves a fresh token reaches gcloud inside the container. **Mutation-proved on BOTH limbs, which is the point of having two.** Disabling the wiring block entirely fails the probe with `Expected: >= 2 / Received: 0` (nothing *runs*); replacing `refresher.run(signal)` with a single `refresher.injectNow()` fails it with `Received: 1` (it runs but never *re-injects*). A probe that could not tell those two apart would be graded the same by either. **What this does NOT close.** The refresh INTERVAL under real load is still the unit tests' fake-clock territory (ISC-155); the probe compresses it rather than waiting out 45 minutes. And the headless path still starts no container, so a headless run gets no refresher — correctly, since there is nothing to inject into.
- [x] ISC-253: A relay consults `decide()` for live traffic. [STILL OPEN, and narrowed rather than closed by the 2026-08-18 egress relay. A relay now EXISTS and carries live traffic, but it does not consult `decide()`: it forwards a fixed, fully-specified target list (currently the oMLX endpoint alone) at the TCP layer, which is a stricter thing than the policy, not an application of it. Consulting `decide()` per destination only becomes meaningful for a relay that accepts arbitrary destinations — i.e. the Google half below — so this criterion stays coupled to that work. The `*.googleapis.com` rules remain policy-level and unit-tested with no live traffic path: a Docker network alias cannot be a wildcard, so routing them needs an HTTP CONNECT proxy or SNI-based TLS passthrough. Neither is built, and a `cloud_access` worker on the internal bridge consequently cannot reach Google at all. **UPDATED 2026-08-19 (PR #18 review, S13):** the stated reasoning above was half wrong and is corrected here. The relay's target list is NOT simply "fixed": `omlxRelayTarget` pins the HOST to a constant but reads the PORT straight out of `llm.base_url`, and nothing compared that port to `decide()`. So `llm.base_url: http://host.docker.internal:22/v1` produced a relay tunnelling the deny-all bridge to the Docker host's sshd on the alias every worker already resolves. `ensureEgressRelay` now calls `decide()` on every target before building argv and refuses on deny (`assertTargetsAllowed`). **Be precise about what that does NOT do:** `policyFromConfig` derives its llm rule from the SAME `base_url`, so the two still agree BY CONSTRUCTION and the gate does not today refuse the port-22 example — a unit test named `DOCUMENTED VACUITY` pins that fact so nobody mistakes the gate for protection it does not yet provide. What bounds the case today is the host pin: the worst outcome is a port on the Docker host, which SRD §12.8 now records as reachable from the bridge gateway anyway. The gate's value is the SEAM — when the dial side is decoupled from the listen alias (ISC-259), judging the target against an explicit `egress.allow` entry the operator WROTE becomes a change of input rather than a change of design. **This criterion is now BLOCKING for that work: S13 must land before the host pin is relaxed.** **CLOSED 2026-08-19 (ISC-259 branch), and the blocking obligation was honoured in order: decouple, gate, THEN relax.** The vacuity is gone because the two inputs to the comparison are now independent. The dial target comes from a NEW field, `llm.relay_upstream` (host:port, explicit port, defaulting to `host.docker.internal:<port from base_url>` so no existing config changes behaviour), and the policy comes from `relayGatePolicy` — NOT `policyFromConfig`. That distinction is the whole fix and it is not cosmetic: passing `relay_upstream` to `policyFromConfig` would have re-opened the circularity through a different field, because an operator writing `base_url: http://192.168.86.49:8000/v1` gets an `llm` rule that authorizes the very upstream under test. `relayGatePolicy` therefore contains NO config-derived host at all except ones the operator wrote as allow rules: rule 1 is `RELAY_LISTEN_ALIAS` (a compile-time constant, unreachable by editing YAML) at the listen port, plus every `egress.allow` entry. `google_hosts` are excluded — the relay forwards no Google traffic, so those rules must not authorize a relay target. **PROVEN BY MUTATION, not by inspection** (`test/unit/relay.test.ts`, fast `test` job, no Docker): one config with `relay_upstream: 192.168.86.49:8000`, varying ONLY `egress.allow`. - [x] ISC-263: A `cloud_access` worker can actually reach the configured Google endpoints. [SPLIT OUT of ISC-253 on 2026-08-19 so that criterion could close honestly rather than carrying an unmet half. Routing them needs an HTTP CONNECT proxy or SNI-based TLS passthrough, neither of which is built. **The user-visible consequence, stated so nobody rediscovers it from a stalled worker:** a `cloud_access: true` role on the internal bridge cannot reach Google at all, so ADC is granted and then unusable there. SNI-based TLS passthrough was offered and rejected; deferring behind documentation was offered and rejected.]** Recorded with the reasoning, because the choice buys more than this criterion. The relay accepting arbitrary destinations is the case `decide()` was designed for and — as this entry already says — has never actually been exercised against, so building it re-takes ISC-51/57's containment evidence on the path that matters rather than on the set the relay happens to carry. SNI passthrough was rejected on containment grounds rather than effort: routing on a field the CLIENT controls moves the allowlist decision into the handshake, which is a weaker story than a proxy that is asked, in the clear, for a destination it can refuse. **This is the gate on the whole cloud cluster and that is why it was chosen over cheaper work:** ISC-41, ISC-47 and ISC-48 are `[~]` for want of a live path, and ISC-248 cannot be verified end-to-end without one either — its own entry says the Phase 2 credential path "cannot be exercised on this machine", and no CONNECT proxy is the reason. **[BUILT 2026-08-26 — the CONNECT proxy exists, is wired end to end, and is proven LIVE through real Docker networking. `[ ]` -> `[~]`, and the reason it is not `[x]` is this entry's own stated closing condition, not a shortfall in the mechanism.]** **What was built.** `docker/connect-proxy.cjs`, an HTTP CONNECT proxy running IN the existing relay container — which was already dual-homed onto the internal bridge and the NAT'd uplink, already under `--read-only`/`--cap-drop ALL`/`no-new-privileges`/`ip_forward=0`, and already adopted, health-checked and drift-checked by `up`. A second container would have duplicated that entire lifecycle to gain no isolation it does not already have. A third network alias, `egress.pifleet.internal`, is what `HTTPS_PROXY` resolves to; `PROXY_LISTEN_PORT` is 3128. **THE POLICY IS NOT REIMPLEMENTED, AND THAT WAS THE FIRST DESIGN DECISION.** The proxy must decide INSIDE the container — that is what makes it a proxy rather than the port forwarder `egress-relay.cjs` already was — and the pinned relay image is upstream `node:24-bookworm-slim` with no `bun`, deliberately, so it cannot import `src/security/egress.ts`. The alternative was a second copy of the matcher, and the label-boundary rule separating `storage.googleapis.com` from `evil-googleapis.com` is the single thing in this system least survivable as two implementations. So the pure matcher was EXTRACTED to `docker/egress-policy.cjs` and `src/security/egress.ts` now imports it: the host-side policy and the in-container decision are one implementation, not two that agree. The extraction's proof is that the existing 65-test egress suite and 72-test relay suite passed UNCHANGED, and three new probes pin it — `decide()` identity over a 10-case corpus spanning every branch, the `MAX_SHORT` literal the CJS must restate, and the refusal rule names. **HTTP_PROXY is deliberately NOT set, and the reason is a property of the proxy rather than caution:** it answers `405` to anything that is not CONNECT, because cleartext forwarding would put it in the business of parsing and re-emitting requests, so advertising it as an HTTP proxy would advertise a capability it explicitly refuses. `NO_PROXY` names BOTH relay aliases, and that is load-bearing rather than tidy: `proxyPolicyFor` carries no `llm` rule, so a model request that entered the proxy would be denied `default-deny` — every worker stalling with no tool calls, SRD §5.9's exact quiet-failure shape. **PROVEN LIVE, through real Docker, with the BEFORE probe that makes the AFTER mean anything.** A worker container on the real `--internal` bridge cannot reach the destination (non-zero curl, asserted positively rather than as a missing token); the relay comes up; the same container reaches it through the proxy with the nonce returned and exit 0; an unlisted destination through the same proxy is refused `403 Forbidden` by name. Without the BEFORE half a green `curl` is equally consistent with a bridge that was never denying anything, which is a containment test certifying the absence of the control it tests. **The live probe uses a WILDCARD rule, and that choice caught a class an exact-match test would have missed entirely.** `decide()` returns the REQUESTED host on a wildcard match and the proxy dials that, not the pattern. A proxy that dialled `rule.host` would pass every refusal test in this repo and every exact-match tunnel test, and would fail only against `*.googleapis.com` — with an ENOTFOUND for the literal string `*.googleapis.com`. Mutating `decide` to return the pattern turns the live probe red with `CONNECT tunnel failed, response 502`, which is exactly that bug's signature. **A SECOND DRIFT COMPARISON WAS REQUIRED AND IS BUILT (`relayPolicyDrifted`).** `up` adopts a running relay and several fleets share one, so an operator who added a host to `egress.google_hosts` would otherwise get a relay still enforcing the previous allowlist — `up` reporting success and a `cloud_access` worker getting a 403 for a destination the config plainly allows. The forwarding table had exactly this bug and ISC-265 fixed it; adding a second piece of enforced state without extending the check would have reintroduced it beside the fix. Compared as a SORTED set, because rule order is not semantic and a shared relay that cycles spuriously is one an operator learns to work around. **ELEVEN MUTATIONS, each restored byte-identical, each caught.** Allow-everything fails 6; breaking the label boundary fails 4; giving `proxyPolicyFor` an `llm` rule fails 3; dropping `NO_PROXY`'s legacy alias fails 1; removing the policy-drift check fails 1; comparing rules unsorted fails 1; returning the pattern instead of the requested host fails the live probe. **Four of the eleven are RC-1 mutations and each is caught by exactly the probe written for it:** no `HTTPS_PROXY` in the worker env (the proxy exists and nothing points at it), no proxy in the argv (the worker points at a proxy the container never started — caught live as `curl: (7) Failed to connect to egress.pifleet.internal port 3128`), and the relay entrypoint never calling `startProxy` (every loopback test stays green while a `cloud_access` worker gets connection-refused). That last one was a gap found by INSPECTION rather than by a failing test — every probe spawned `connect-proxy.cjs` directly, so nothing exercised the process the container actually runs. **One defect this file shipped with, caught by its own test:** `spliced` covered two distinct states, so the upstream-error branch guarded on `!spliced` could never run and an allowed-but-unreachable destination returned an empty socket rather than a 502. Split into `spliced` and `established`. **And one self-inflicted probe defect worth recording because it made a PASSING assertion vacuous:** adding a bare `echo` before `echo "post=$?"` captured the exit status of `echo`, not of `curl`, so both status assertions became checks that echo works. Only the deny probe caught it, and only because a 403 and a success cannot both be true. `rc=$?` now runs before anything else. **WHY THIS IS `[~]` AND NOT `[x]`, taken from this entry's own words rather than from a judgement call:** it says closing this means "building the proxy, then re-taking ISC-51/57's containment evidence against a relay that accepts arbitrary destinations — which is the case `decide()` was designed for and has never actually been exercised against." The proxy is built and the deny side is probed, but ISC-51/57's containment evidence is an ENUMERATED scan (`what the internal bridge denies — enumerated, not sampled`) and it has not been re-taken with the proxy running. That matters more here than the wording suggests, because `--internal` isolation is FORWARD-chain only and the bridge gateway is already open (SRD §12.8): a sampled probe cannot distinguish what the proxy newly permits from what was reachable anyway. The second residual is smaller and is named for honesty rather than as a blocker — the live probe authorizes `*.docker.internal` rather than `*.googleapis.com`, because whether Google answers is a property of the internet and no test should assert it; the Google case is this mechanism with a different rule in the policy, and the wildcard dial path it depends on IS proven. **NOT RE-GRADED HERE, and flagged rather than claimed:** ISC-41, ISC-47 and ISC-48 are `[~]` "for want of a live path" and ISC-248's Phase 2 credential path "cannot be exercised on this machine". A live path now exists. Whether that closes any of them requires re-reading each against what was actually built, which is separate work and must not be inherited from this entry. **[CLOSED 2026-08-26 — the closing condition THIS ENTRY STATES was executed, and `[~]` -> `[x]`.]** The stated condition was "building the proxy, then re-taking ISC-51/57's containment evidence against a relay that accepts arbitrary destinations". The proxy landed in #80; this is the re-take. **Why a port scan could not BE the re-take, which is the whole reason a new probe exists.** ISC-51/57 bound the reachable set to `{relay listen ports} u {gateway ports} u {sibling ports}` and enumerated each term: the relay's by a full-range scan, the gateway's by a 65535-port scan that must come back EMPTY, the siblings' by `docker network inspect`, which is authoritative for membership. The proxy adds a term none of them can see. `3128` is not a port but a DOOR, and what lies beyond it is decided at request time from the relay's NAT'd uplink: a scan reports `3128 open` and stops, and cannot report that `3128` leads to `oauth2.googleapis.com` but not to `example.com`. The set is therefore `{relay listen port} u {3128 -> POLICY} u {sibling ports}`, and the third term is what the "ISC-263 closing" probe in `test/integration/relay.test.ts` enumerates LIVE. **EVERY DENIAL REFUSES A DESTINATION MEASURED REACHABLE FIRST — that is the design of the corpus, not a detail of it.** This is the lesson ISC-51 was downgraded for on 2026-08-19: the old evidence probed `1.1.1.1` and `example.com` from a container with no route at all and concluded "contained", when what it had measured was a network that could not have reached ANYTHING. [FILED 2026-08-19 by the ISC-259 branch, after a REPORTING ERROR on that branch made the underlying defect visible — the error is recorded here because it is the more instructive half. **What was wrongly claimed:** `test/integration/harvest.test.ts > report honours the same config as artifacts` was reported in PR #20 as a "pre-existing failure on main", on the evidence that it also failed on a pristine `4207b89` worktree. CI completes it in 1235 ms — roughly 4x headroom — and that headroom is not enough on a developer machine under concurrent load. Measured at the time of failure: load average **18.40 on 14 cores**, with three agents running test suites simultaneously and several shells at ~96% CPU. Under that load it failed 3/3 consecutive runs, i.e. it is CONSISTENT under load rather than intermittent, which is why it initially read as a genuine breakage. `materialize.test.ts` and `up-wiring.test.ts` showed the same shape in the same window (hook timeouts under parallel load, green in isolation), so this is a CLASS and not one test. **Why it deserves a criterion rather than a footnote:** a suite that is green in CI and red on every busy developer machine trains its readers to discount red, which costs more than the test ever pays for — the same failure mode as a self-skipping test, arrived at from the other direction. Closing it means giving subprocess-spawning integration tests a budget derived from what they actually do rather than inheriting a default that happens to fit an idle machine, and it should be judged by deliberately running the suite under load, not by re-running it on a quiet box until it passes.] **[CLOSED 2026-08-19 by PR #25 — graded AFTER the CI job below actually ran, not on the expectation that it would.]** **The fix is a budget derived from the work, not a bigger default.** `test/support/budget.ts` computes `cliBudget(N) = max(5000, N * 1900 * 3 * 2)` where `N` is the subprocess spawns a test actually performs. `1900` is not an average — spawn cost is NOT uniform, and that is the fact the model is built around: `report` and `artifacts --all` grade a whole run and cost ~1.3-1.6 s each, while `artifacts --task`, `config validate` and `render` cost ~50-200 ms. `1900` rounds up the worst single expensive spawn measured (1335, 1408, 1618, 1631 ms idle across the four one-spawn tests in `harvest.test.ts`), and charging every spawn at that rate is deliberate conservatism for mixed tests. `3` is the worst per-test inflation actually observed under load (2.09x-2.98x), `2` is headroom for the busier machine this criterion recorded. The result is BOUNDED on purpose: a genuinely hung subprocess still fails, it just fails later. An unbounded budget would trade a flaky test for a hanging suite, which is this same erosion of trust from the other direction. **Why a helper and not a config key:** bun 1.3.11 IGNORES `[test] timeout` in `bunfig.toml` — probed directly, a deliberately-6s test still died at 5001.03 ms with `timeout = 12345` set — and `--timeout` only covers the invocation that passes it, so neither protects a developer running a bare `bun test`, which is precisely the case this criterion is about. The per-test third argument is the only mechanism that travels with the test. (Probed on 1.3.11; CI pins 1.3.12 and was not probed. It does not matter to the fix: a config key that worked would still be a repo-wide number rather than a per-test one.) **What was applied, measured STANDALONE per file** — a full-suite run inflates per-test times through bun's own inter-file concurrency and would have sized every budget against the wrong number. 375 testcases, 23 at or above 1200 ms idle. Eight budgets went where a test was at risk and had NONE: `harvest.test.ts` x5 (including the four-spawn test this criterion was filed over) and `doctor-cmux.test.ts` x3. Eleven at-risk tests already carried hand-picked budgets and **every one of them exceeded its derived value, so NOT ONE WAS REDUCED**; each now records its spawn count, derived value and measured idle so the next reader can see why it stands rather than guessing. **The limits of the model, recorded because they bound what it is good for.** Three slow tests are NOT described by spawn count, and deriving budgets for them would have TIGHTENED tests that pass: `supervisor`'s ISC-212 test measures 11415 ms idle against a `cliBudget(1)` of 11400 — narrower than its own runtime — because its cost is a deliberate 1s deadline plus 5s abort grace, not spawn startup; `acceptance`'s ISC-152 test spawns no CLI at all, its 6006 ms IS the 6s run budget it sets on purpose; and `worktree`'s L443 drives git subprocesses in-process, so no CLI spawn count exists to derive from. All three were left alone rather than given an invented `N`. **The evidence, from both directions.** Before: under ten busy loops on 14 cores, three `harvest.test.ts` tests died at exactly 5001-5003 ms — the timeout, not the work — and the one this criterion names reached 9991 ms once the budget was lifted; it failed 3/3 consecutively, consistent rather than intermittent. After: the full integration suite under eleven loops ran **375 pass / 81 skip / 0 fail in 300.87 s** against 167.76 s idle, a 1.79x inflation with every budget holding, and the same pass/skip/fail split as the idle baseline so nothing skipped its way to green. **Why this earns `[x]` and not `[~]`.** This criterion says explicitly that it "should be judged by deliberately running the suite under load, not by re-running it on a quiet box until it passes", and a script under `.github/scripts/` that a developer must REMEMBER to run would not be a judgement — it would be a suggestion, which is what "just re-run it" already was. `.github/scripts/test-under-load.sh` is therefore wired into a dedicated `load` job in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` that runs `test/integration` under `ceil(cores * 0.75)` busy loops on every PR and exits with the suite's own status, so an inadequate budget — or a test whose spawn count grows without its `cliBudget(N)` growing too — fails a PR instead of a developer's afternoon. Verified green on run `32291463113` before this criterion was marked, and verified to be DOING something rather than merely passing: on that same run and the same commit, `test/integration` took **124.32 s in the `test` job and 222.78 s in the `load` job — 1.79x**, which is the same inflation factor measured locally on 14 cores (167.76 s -> 300.87 s). Two busy loops against two cores is real contention: three runnable threads competing for two CPUs. (The "load average now" line the script prints is NOT the evidence and should not be read as such — it is a one-minute average sampled two seconds after the generators start, so it always reads low, 0.95 on that run. The wall-clock comparison is the evidence.) **What that job does NOT prove, stated rather than implied.** The runner reports **two** cores — not the four this criterion's first draft assumed, and measured rather than guessed — against the 14 these numbers came from, and it carries none of the editor, language server, browser and concurrent agents behind the load average of 18.40 recorded above. It reproduces the SHAPE of the defect — CPU contention stretching subprocess spawns past a fixed ceiling — at a smaller magnitude. It is a floor on the evidence, not a ceiling, and if this criterion ever needs re-opening it will be because a developer machine outruns the runner by more than the 3x contention factor allows, not because the mechanism is wrong. **Not one assertion was weakened**: `git diff` shows zero `expect(...)` lines added, removed or altered across the whole change, and no file under `src/` was touched. **Two residuals observed and deliberately NOT fixed here**, so they are visible rather than lost: `test/e2e/lifecycle.test.ts:197` carries a `3_000` budget, BELOW bun's own 5000 default, and `test/integration/exec.test.ts` carries four hand-picked `30_000` budgets against a 200 ms slowest test — a 150x margin, the same "number unrelated to the work" pattern as this criterion, arrived at from the generous side. **[THIRD INSTANCE, 2026-08-20 — found and FIXED on the container-security branch, and it teaches something new about the LIMITS of `cliBudget` rather than merely adding a site.]** `test/integration/container-env.test.ts` was the only Docker-gated file in the suite still running on bun's 5000 ms default, against two tests that each do `makeDaemonScratch` + `loadConfig` + `materializeWorkerInputs` + `renderWorker` + `ensureControlAuth` + `docker run -d` + `docker inspect`, with a `docker rm -f` in teardown. **The derivation ARGUED AGAINST ITSELF, and that is the finding.** Measured warm on a developer machine at load 3.25 — daemon already up, image already built: whole file 371-391 ms across three runs, per test 170 ms and 152 ms, `docker inspect` 20-50 ms, `docker run -d` plus `docker rm -f` 200-230 ms, three docker spawns per test with the worst single one ~250 ms rounded up. Deriving from those numbers the way this criterion derives `cliBudget` — worst spawn x count x 3 (load inflation) x 2 (headroom) — gives **250 x 3 x 3 x 2 = 4500 ms, UNDER bun's own 5000 ms default**. A derivation that lands below the default it was meant to replace is not a reason to leave the default in place; it is evidence that **the default only LOOKS adequate because the daemon is warm and the image already present**, which is precisely the shape this criterion was filed over — a budget that fits an idle machine and fails elsewhere. **The dominant term is not measurable on a developer machine at all.** On CI the first `docker run` follows a build step against a cold daemon and a fresh overlay, where container creation is orders of magnitude slower than the 200 ms measured here; nothing on a warm box samples that distribution. So the value chosen is `60_000`, matching what every sibling Docker-gated file already uses (`adc.test.ts`, eight times), rather than a tighter number derived from a warm measurement — **which would have been the ISC-267 mistake in a new costume**: a threshold placed confidently on a measurement whose variation was never observed. It remains BOUNDED on purpose, so a genuinely hung `docker` still fails, just later. **`cliBudget` was deliberately NOT used, and the reason bounds the helper generally:** it is calibrated to *pifleet CLI startup* at 1900 ms per spawn, and these tests spawn `docker`, which is a different cost with a different distribution. Borrowing the helper across that boundary would produce a number with a derivation's appearance and none of its substance — the same failure as a hand-picked constant, dressed as arithmetic. The model in this criterion is a model of ONE subprocess cost, not of subprocesses in general, and any future use against a non-pifleet binary needs its own measured per-spawn figure or its own constant.
- [x] ISC-267: A timing assertion in a CI-executable guard test does not fail on the clock's precision rather than on the property it defends. **[FILED AND CLOSED 2026-08-19 by this PR.]** DISTINCT FROM ISC-266, and the signature is what separates them: ISC-266 is subprocess tests timing out on a LOADED DEVELOPER MACHINE, where contention makes a measurement take LONGER. This fired in CI, on an idle GitHub runner, by coming in UNDER a floor — `doctor-omlx.test.ts:246`, `Expected: >= 40, Received: 39`, on a run that was otherwise 374 pass / 1 fail. Load cannot produce that; it is the opposite direction. **Why it matters more than its size.** `test/integration/doctor-omlx.test.ts` is the ONLY CI-executable evidence for ISC-54 and ISC-55 — ISC-260's engineer specifically declined to containerise `doctor`'s probe in order to keep it that way. A guard that fails 1-in-N erodes trust exactly as a self-skipping one does: people learn to re-run instead of read. **Diagnosis, measured rather than assumed.** The assertion compared the reported latency against `COMPLETION_DELAY_MS`, the delay the stub REQUESTED via `await Bun.sleep(40)`. A sleep is a request to be woken no earlier than N, not a guarantee the caller can assert on. Measured 400 trials on macOS/bun 1.3.11: `Bun.sleep(40)` never resumed early (min 40.032ms, zero of 400 below the floor), so the defect does NOT reproduce on the maintainer's machine and appears only on the Linux runner — which is precisely why the fix had to stop depending on timer precision rather than tune a margin. **The fix strengthens the test rather than widening it.** Two changes. (1) The stub now holds via a deadline loop that re-sleeps the remainder until the monotonic clock agrees, so it cannot return early whatever the timer does (measured over the same 400 trials: min 40.001ms, zero early). (2) The floor is now the delay the stub OBSERVED ITSELF TAKING, not the one it asked for. That form cannot be flaky by construction: the client starts its clock before the request and stops it after reading the body, so its interval strictly contains the handler's hold, and `Math.round` is monotonic non-decreasing, so `round(client) >= round(server)` follows. **And it uncovered a real hole while being fixed, found by mutation rather than by reading.** The comment on that assertion claimed a stamped-in constant would fail it. It would not: replacing the measurement with `report.completionLatencyMs = 42` left the suite GREEN, because 42 clears a 40ms floor. A floor is a statement about MAGNITUDE; "the number tracks elapsed time" — which is what the test is literally named for — is a statement about VARIATION, and nothing was asserting it. The probe now runs a second time against a stub holding four times as long and requires the reported figure to move with it, so no single constant can satisfy both floors at once. Mutation-verified after the fix: constant `42` FAILS (it passed before), constant `5000` FAILS (it clears every floor), and a clock read twice with no work between FAILS; the unmutated test passes. The tracking margin is deliberately loose — half the added delay — because the property is that the number MOVES, not that it moves precisely, and a tight margin would re-introduce the very timing-sensitivity this criterion is about. **[SECOND INSTANCE, 2026-08-19 — found by ISC-266's load job, which is the first thing that gate caught.]** `dispatch-auto.test.ts` asserted `gapMs > 100` on the delay between two dependent dispatches, justified by six local runs measuring 237-262 ms. It failed on the load job with `Expected: > 100, Received: 100`. The gap is QUANTISED by `DEFAULT_POLL_MS` in `src/orchestrate/scheduler.ts`: the scheduler re-examines readiness once per 100 ms tick, so a gated dispatch lands one, two or three ticks later and the observed gap is a multiple of 100, never a continuum. Those local runs were 2-3 ticks because 'a' took longer than one tick to settle on 14 cores; on a two-core runner it settled inside a single tick and the gap fell to its FLOOR — which the threshold had been placed exactly on, so a strict `>` called the best possible correct behaviour a bug. The comment's claim that "the margin only WIDENS under load" was the error: load changes how many ticks elapse, not the one-tick floor. Fixed by comparing `>=` against the exported constant rather than a hand-picked number, so the test tracks the scheduler if the interval changes; the discrimination it exists for is untouched, since a same-pass dispatch is ~0-5 ms, two orders of magnitude below one tick. **Recorded here rather than as a new criterion because the property is already stated** — a timing assertion must fail on the thing it defends, not on the measurement's granularity. Only the granularity differs: ISC-267 was the clock's, this is the scheduler's.
- [x] ISC-268: `adc_mode: file` is not silently inert — it either mounts the ADC file through `buildDockerArgv`, or the mode is removed from the schema. **[FILED 2026-08-19, promoted out of ISC-44's prose so the gap is a criterion rather than a caveat inside a closed one.]** ISC-44 is honest about this and the admission deserves its own line: its `file`-mode probe "hand-writes the `-v` itself and inspects a shape it authored", so it pins a CONTRACT that mode must satisfy when wired, not evidence about a launch `up` can perform today. **Measured, not inferred:** `ADC_FILE_PATH` (`/creds/adc.json`, `src/security/adc.ts:69`), `fileModeMaterials` and `fileModeStartupEnv` have ZERO callers anywhere in `src/` outside `adc.ts` itself, and `buildDockerArgv` emits no `/creds` mount at all — a fact `adc.ts:63` already records in a comment. A mode that neither works nor fails is worse than one that is absent, because the failure surfaces as an unexplained permission error inside the container rather than at launch. **Why this is load-bearing and not tidying.** ISC-44's three-relation mount guard carves out exactly ONE documented exception — the single ADC file `file` mode may mount.
