REMOVED — `adc_mode: file` is rejected by the config schema, and all three symbols plus ISC-44's carve-out are deleted in the same change. Leaving the value accepted and inert satisfies neither arm. **[UNBLOCKED 2026-08-20 by the container launcher (ISC-286/287): the runtime path this criterion was waiting on now exists — `up` records a launch argv and the supervisor spawns it, so a container can be inspected, exec'd into and torn down. This criterion is NOT closed by that; what it asks for still has to be built and probed. The note is here so the next reader does not re-derive that the blocker was absence of a launcher.]** **CLOSED 2026-08-25 on the REMOVED arm.** `adc_mode: file` is refused by the config schema, `ADC_FILE_PATH`/`fileModeMaterials`/`fileModeStartupEnv` are deleted, and ISC-44's `allowAdcFile` carve-out is deleted with them. **Why removed rather than wired, decided on what wiring would have MOUNTED.** The host ADC file is `type: authorized_user` and carries a `refresh_token` — a non-expiring grant over the operator's entire Google account, which SRD §12.4 lists as F37 and which §5.8's whole "why token is the default" paragraph exists to keep out of a container. Wiring `file` mode would have made the most dangerous credential path the FIRST one actually built (ISC-248 records that no credential runtime exists at all yet), into a container running model output, on a machine where the production result cannot be exercised. The justification in the SRD was speculative — "some flows … want a credential file" — with no flow in this system having asked. **The carve-out is the part worth naming.** `classifyHostGcloudExposure` permitted exactly one artifact out of the host gcloud store to be mounted. It was the most delicate branch in that guard, it defended a path nothing took, and on the day `file` mode was wired it would have been load-bearing on its first run having never executed against production argv. An exception with no caller is not a dormant feature; it is an untested hole with a comment over it. The launcher's rule and the classifier's rule are now one rule. **Evidence:** `test/unit/adc-file-mode-removed.test.ts` — the schema rejects `file`; the refusal NAMES the field rather than emitting `.strict()`'s "unrecognized key" (which is why `adc_mode` survives as a one-value enum rather than being deleted); `token` is still accepted, so the refusal is about the value; `AdcModeSchema.options` is `["token"]`, narrowed one layer down too because a two-valued type whose second value nothing can produce is the same accepted-and-inert shape; and the guard has no exception left, asserted behaviourally (`hostAdcFile()` -> `inside-the-store`) AND structurally (`allowAdcFile` appears nowhere in the module), with a positive control first that `hostAdcFile()` really is under the store so the behavioural half cannot pass vacuously. **Mutation-proved, three:** P1 restore `file` to the config enum -> the two refusal tests; P2 restore it to `AdcModeSchema` -> the record test ONLY; P3 re-introduce the carve-out -> the two guard tests. **One real COST, recorded rather than absorbed silently.** ISC-251's evidence relied on a two-fixture contrast — `adc_mode: file` set explicitly against `token` arriving from the schema default — to show `up`'s grant line REPORTS the mode rather than printing a constant. - [x] ISC-269: Interrupting `pifleet logs --follow` ends it cleanly, whatever the follower still has to catch up on. **[FILED AND CLOSED 2026-08-19 by this PR, promoted out of a test that had been read as flaky for a session.]** **The defect.** SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers were registered AFTER `await pollAll()` had already returned, so the entire first drain ran unguarded and a signal arriving inside it got Bun's default disposition — terminate, exit 130 — rather than the clean return the surrounding code documents. **Why it was mistaken for flakiness, and why that mistake is the instructive half.** The unguarded window is exactly as long as the backlog takes to render, so the failure is PROPORTIONAL to how far behind the follower is rather than random. Measured on the unfixed code, killing on first output: 200 000 buffered events exits 130 five times out of five, 50 000 the same, 20 000 the same, 5 000 four times out of five, and a single event exits 0 five times out of five. The existing test `SIGINT also ends a follower cleanly` uses a ONE-EVENT fixture — the fastest-draining case there is — so it sat in the coin-flip tail and read as an environmental annoyance. It is not an ISC-266 timeout (that is contention against a fixed budget) and not an ISC-267 clock-precision miss; it is a real product bug that a user hits every time they Ctrl-C a follower attached to a worker with any real history. **The fix** moves both registrations above the first drain and pulls that drain inside the existing try/finally, so listeners are still removed on every path including the `!follow` early return; a signal during the drain sets `stopped`, the drain finishes, and the follow loop is skipped — the same one-final-drain-then-return behaviour, applied to the first drain as well as the last. **Evidence.** A second test gives the follower 50 000 events and requires exit 0. Mutation-verified: it fails `Expected: 0, Received: 130` against the unfixed source and passes against the fixed one. It lives in `test/integration/logs.test.ts`, which the `test` job runs on every PR, so this is CI-executable rather than a hand-run — which is what earns `[x]` here rather than `[~]`. **Scope stated rather than implied.** A signal arriving BEFORE the first drain — during argument parsing or the `stat` calls — still exits 130, deliberately: nothing has been emitted, so there is no session to end cleanly. **On budgets:** the new test measures 120 ms, well under ISC-266's 1200 ms threshold, because it kills on first output rather than waiting out the drain — so it correctly carries no `cliBudget`.

- [x] ISC-283: No e2e test asserts on an outcome that depends on winning a wall-clock race against a fixture's own scripted timeline. **[FILED AND CLOSED 2026-08-20 by the merge-queue pass. Number allocated centrally against the max across all live branches — ISC-282 was taken by `feat/wire-stall-policy` on the same night.]** **A sibling of ISC-274, not an instance of it.** ISC-274 is about a test's CEILING: a spawning test that inherits bun's 5000 ms default times out under load. This is about a test's WINDOW: the assertion is correct, the ceiling is generous, and the test still reports a false failure because the thing it is measuring had to happen inside a gap the fixture chose. No timeout is involved and no budget helper addresses it. **The instance, with the CI evidence that found it.** `lifecycle.test.ts`'s ISC-84 interleave test had to land an `abort` inside `interleave.json`'s 150 ms gap between `agent_start` and the natural `agent_end`, and it spent that gap on `setTimeout(30)` plus a `dispatch` subprocess plus a control-socket round trip. On GitHub's runner the abort arrived after the gap closed, the epoch settled naturally, and the test failed **`Expected: "aborted" / Received: "success"`** — a verdict that is exactly right for the ordering that actually occurred. It passed on every local run, including under the mutation passes that graded this branch. **What the failure was NOT.** It was not epoch attribution breaking, and nothing in `src/` was at fault: the run under test behaved correctly for the event order it saw. It was also not caused by the branch it blocked — `chore/grading-epoch` adds one test file and some ISA lines and touches neither the fixture nor the e2e suite. That branch's 326 new lines of spawning tests simply loaded the runner enough for a latent race to lose, which makes this a defect that arrives on whichever PR happens to be heaviest. **Fixed here, and mutation-proved in both directions rather than asserted.** The window widened to 3000 ms (straggler gap 400 → 1000 ms) and the abort re-anchored on observing `agent_start` in the events file instead of sleeping a fixed 30 ms, so the clock starts where the window does rather than where the test was launched. Proof the change does the work: injecting a 300 ms stall before the `controlCall`, to stand in for the runner's latency, reproduces the CI failure verbatim on this machine — `Received: "success"`, 6 pass / 1 fail — against the old 150 ms fixture, and the same injected stall passes 7/7 against the widened one. A fix that only ever passes is indistinguishable from the bug it replaced. **The class, and why it is graded `[x]` rather than left as a sweep.** The general rule is that an e2e test must derive its timing from an event it OBSERVES, and where it must rely on a fixture gap, the gap is wide enough that runner load cannot close it and the reason is written into the fixture. `interleave.json` now carries that reasoning inline under `_comment_timing`. A sweep of all eleven fixtures in `test/fixtures/scenarios/` found no second instance, and the sweep is recorded rather than summarised because a bare "no others" is not checkable. The only other tests that must land an action inside a scripted turn are `lifecycle.test.ts`'s ISC-83 abort and `abort.test.ts`, and both use `aborted.json` (30 s) or `deaf-abort.json` (120 s) — windows two to three orders of magnitude wider than the latency that closed the 150 ms one, and `abort.test.ts` already says so inline ("the scenario's turn is scripted for 30s — three times the ISC-81"). Every remaining `delay_ms` is waited OUT rather than raced, which is the safe direction: a test that outlives a delay gets slower under load, never wrong. **One fixture was called out here as a deliberate exception, and that call was WRONG — see ISC-284.** `noisy-fleet.json` asserts an ORDERING (quiet 50 ms workers settle while an ~1.6 s flood is still in flight), and this entry originally reasoned that because both sides are scripted, load slows them together and the 32× margin holds. The ordering assertion is indeed fine. What that reasoning missed is the FLOOR assertion underneath it, which compares a supervisor-stamped interval against the child's scripted sleep — two different clocks — and CI failed it at 47 ms within hours of this text being written. The correction is kept visible rather than edited away because the mistake is instructive: "both sides are scripted" answers whether the ORDERING is raced and says nothing about whether the MEASUREMENT is sound, and this entry conflated the two. This is closable now because the instance is fixed and the sweep is empty; if a future fixture reintroduces a raced gap, that is a new instance to file against this criterion, not a reason to have withheld the grade.
- [x] ISC-284: No test compares an interval stamped at EVENT-PROCESSING time against a duration scripted at EVENT-EMISSION time without allowing for the skew between them. **[FILED AND CLOSED 2026-08-20 by the merge-queue pass, immediately after ISC-283 got this case wrong. Number allocated centrally against the max across all live branches.]** **The failure ISC-283 predicted the wrong way round.** ISC-283 swept the fixtures for raced WINDOWS and cleared `noisy-fleet.json` on the grounds that its two racing sides are both scripted. They are, and its ordering assertion is sound. The unsound part is one line below it: `expect(min(quiet)).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(50)` in `scale-16-workers.test.ts`, justified in that file's header by "the quiet script has a fixed 50ms delay, so no honest quiet latency can be under 50ms". **That premise is false, and the test itself is what falsifies it.** The 50 ms sleep happens in the CHILD, between writing `agent_start` and writing `agent_end`. Both ends of the measured interval are stamped when the SUPERVISOR processes those events — `epoch_started` via `logEvent` at `supervisor/index.ts:461`, `settled_at` via `new Date()` at `:348` — so the measurement is the child's 50 ms plus the difference in how long the supervisor took to REACH each end. This test manufactures exactly the asymmetry that makes that difference negative: at the moment a quiet turn starts, the supervisor is draining ~1.6 MB from two flooding workers and can reach `agent_start` late, then catch up and reach `agent_end` promptly. A late start and a prompt end shorten the interval below the sleep that genuinely occurred. **Observed, not reasoned:** CI reported **47 ms** against the 50 ms floor and failed the run, on a branch whose only new content was an unrelated integration test file. The fleet was fine; the clock was read at two moments the scenario deliberately loads. **The file's own header carried the overclaim and is corrected here too:** it said both endpoints "cannot be moved by how busy this test runner is", which is true and is why they were chosen — but it does not follow that they cannot be moved by how busy the SUPERVISOR is, and this test's whole purpose is to make the supervisor busy. **Fixed by naming the residual error instead of hiding it:** `QUIET_SKEW_MS = 10` with the mechanism written out, and the floor derived as `QUIET_TURN_DELAY_MS - QUIET_SKEW_MS`. **The cost is recorded rather than rounded off, because this criterion is about honest measurement and an unstated weakening would be the same sin in a new place:** the three samples that condemned the previous spelling were 35 ms, 35 ms and 49 ms, and a 40 ms floor catches the first two where a 50 ms floor caught all three. The floor is genuinely weaker against a near-miss. That is acceptable only because the floor is a backstop rather than the measurement, and the defect those numbers came from — stamping the start after the dispatch subprocess had exited — is structurally gone now that both endpoints are supervisor-side. **The class, and why `[x]`:** the rule is that a duration asserted against a scripted delay must either be measured on the same side of the pipe the delay was scripted on, or carry a written allowance for the stamping skew. A sweep of the other scripted-delay assertions found no second instance: every other fixture delay is waited OUT rather than measured against, which is the safe direction. Closable now because the instance is fixed and the sweep is empty; a future assertion that compares the two clocks is a new instance to file against this criterion.
- [x] ISC-285: A merge into `main` cannot land an `ISA.md` headline that the merged body contradicts. **[CLOSED 2026-08-20 — branch protection enabled on `main` with `required_status_checks.strict: true`, the owner's decision when the two arms were put to them.]** **The defect, kept in full because the mechanism is counter-intuitive.** `test/unit/isa-frontmatter.test.ts` runs against whatever `ISA.md` sits beside it, so on a PR branch it proves the BRANCH is self-consistent; nothing proved the MERGE was. The tree CI tests and the tree that lands are different trees whenever `main` has moved, and the headline is a derived total over the whole file — the one kind of value a three-way text merge cannot get right, because correctness depends on lines neither side touched. **Observed while draining the queue that filed this.** Merging `chore/grading-acceptance` then `feat/wire-stall-policy`: `git merge-tree` reported the second CLEAN against the new `main`, and the merged tree's headline read `229/281` while its body held 282 criteria. Both branches were individually green and both were honest. **The clean merge was caused by the resolution DISCIPLINE, not by carelessness** — each branch had been rebased and its headline recomputed, and both independently arrived at the identical string `progress: 229/281`. Identical text on both sides is exactly what git merges without a conflict, so resolving the headline correctly on each branch is what REMOVED the conflict that would have forced a recount after the union. The more disciplined the branches, the more reliably it fires. **The fix, and why it is configuration.** `main` had no protection at all — `GET /repos/agileguy/cmux-fleet/branches/main/protection` returned `404 Branch not protected`, so there were no required checks, nothing stopped a red PR merging, and nothing stopped a direct push. Protection is now enabled with `test`, `load` and `container` required and `strict: true` — GitHub's "require branches to be up to date before merging" — which forces each PR onto the current `main` before it can merge, which is exactly the recount cycle this pass performed by hand three times. `allow_force_pushes` and `allow_deletions` are both false; `enforce_admins` is left false so the owner keeps a manual override. **Verified by reading the setting back**, not by assuming the PUT took: `{strict: true, contexts: [test, load, container], force_push: false, deletions: false}`. **What this does NOT do, stated so the guarantee is not overread.** It removes the WINDOW rather than validating the merge: a PR must be current before merging, so the tree CI tested is the tree that lands. It does not check the headline at merge time, and a sufficiently determined simultaneous merge of two PRs that both became current in the same instant is still theoretically the same shape — the protection makes that vanishingly narrow rather than routine. The manual mitigation therefore remains worth knowing and is recorded here rather than discarded: after any merge, `git merge-tree --write-tree` the next branch and count the resulting tree's body before merging it, because a clean merge is not evidence of a correct one.

It was a tripwire awaiting a writer, and `run/worker-env.ts` is that writer. **The contract is not invented:** `docker/entrypoint.sh` states it (`PIFLEET_LLM_PROVIDER`, `PIFLEET_LLM_BASE_URL`, `PIFLEET_LLM_MODELS`, the key named by `llm.api_key_env`) and is the authority because it is the code that consumes those names to render `~/.pi/agent/models.json` before exec'ing Pi. It is not. The probe had put the run dir under `/var/folders`, which is outside Docker Desktop's shared paths on macOS, so the VM had no such file and invented an empty DIRECTORY at the mount source. Re-run with the run dir under `$HOME` the warning is gone and stderr is empty. See ISC-288 — the class is real even though this instance was not.

- [x] ISC-288: `down` removes the worker container, including when the supervisor is already gone. **[CLOSED 2026-08-20 with the launcher, after its own test found the bug.]** **`--rm` does not cover this and the reason is mechanical:** `--rm` is implemented by the docker CLIENT for a foreground run — it removes the container after the container EXITS, with the client still there to do it. - [x] ISC-289: A run started against the `PIFLEET_PI_COMMAND` double writes NO launch record, so the run directory cannot describe two intentions. **[CLOSED 2026-08-20. The design arrived here by refutation, and the refutation is recorded because the first answer was wrong.]** **Conjectured:** the supervisor should prefer the launch record over the double whenever both are present. **Refuted by the existing suite** — twelve `up-wiring` tests went red with `EXIT.WORKER_DIED`, because every integration and e2e test in this repo sets `PIFLEET_PI_COMMAND` AND supplies a config, so a record was written for rigs that have no image and the supervisor correctly launched containers that promptly died. **Learned:** the choice is not the supervisor's to make twice, it is `up`'s to make once. `up` now decides — `PIFLEET_PI_COMMAND` set means the operator explicitly asked for the double, and an explicit override beats a derived default — and passes `writeLaunchRecord` to `materializeWorkerInputs`. The supervisor's rule stays the simplest thing that can work: a record means launch it. **Two properties fall out that are worth naming.** The run directory stays honest: no record means no container was ever intended, which is also what stops `down` issuing a `docker rm` for a name that never existed. And the decision is SAID on stderr, because getting it wrong is quiet in both directions — a stale `PIFLEET_PI_COMMAND` in a shell profile would otherwise run doubles for an operator expecting containers, with every artifact looking like a normal run.

The four tests are plain `test(...)`, NOT under this file's `it = test.skipIf(!LIVE)`, so they run unconditionally in the fast `test` job with no Docker and no oMLX; a comment tells the next reader not to move them. The negative direction — an unshared path producing an empty mount and a raised diagnosis — runs only on a VM-backed runtime. The hazard has a reproducible reader on developer machines and a vacuously-passing one in CI. **[EXTENDED 2026-08-24, Phase F launch preflight.]** The two residuals recorded above are CLOSED, and the criterion's REFUSED half now exists. `assertBindMountsVisible` (`src/container/mount-preflight.ts`) runs at `src/cli/commands/up.ts:1157` — after `materializeWorkerInputs`, the earliest point at which the sources exist at all, which is precisely why ISC-127's guard can sit in `renderWorker` and this one structurally cannot; and before `launchDetached`, so a refusal has nothing detached behind it to reap. ONE container for the whole fleet, because sharing is a property of the daemon and not of the call; EVERY worker checked before ANY is launched, the rule `assertModelsAllowed` states, so no refusal leaves a half-started fleet behind it; exit 3, to agree with `doctor`'s own `misconfigured` verdict over the only channel a machine caller has. **The sharpest finding is that an entry COUNT is not a witness**, and it was MEASURED rather than reasoned: after `-v <unshared>/probe.mjs:/probe.mjs` the VM RETAINS an empty DIRECTORY named `probe.mjs` inside its own copy of the unshared path, so a later directory mount of that same path reports one entry bearing exactly the right name — and a count-based check reads that as shared. The witness is therefore a REGULAR FILE OF A KNOWN SIZE: the runtime invents directories for missing mount sources and never files, so a byte count is a discriminator the silently-empty case cannot fake. The witness is BORROWED from content already present wherever there is any, so nothing is written into `run.repo` or any other path pifleet does not own; a sentinel is written only into a directory that is EMPTY, which is exactly `/outbox` — created empty by `materialize`, mounted READ-WRITE, and the half of the incident where every artifact vanishes with no host-side trace at all. **Reproduced before the fix was written**, on colima 0.9.x / macOS Virtualization.Framework / virtiofs / arm64: `-v /private/tmp/x/probe.mjs:/probe.mjs` gives node `Cannot find module '/probe.mjs'`; `-v /private/tmp/x:/probe:ro` shows `probe.mjs` as a DIRECTORY and `cat` returns EISDIR; the identical content under `$HOME` reads back as a 29-byte file — with `docker run` exiting **0** in all three. It does NOT witness an actually-unshared path. That needs a VM-backed runtime, and the negative direction was produced only BY HAND on this macOS/colima machine, which is local-only evidence that re-checks nothing reproducibly. CI is `ubuntu-latest`, a native Linux daemon where every path is shared, so neither this test nor `doctor-preflight.test.ts` can exercise the negative direction there — `doctor-preflight` still passes vacuously in that direction, for exactly the reason recorded at the Phase F close. NOTHING about the platform limitation changed; what changed is that the criterion's "refused" half now exists on the launch path instead of only its "reported" half in `doctor`. Residuals that remain: only host->container is measured (a sound PROXY, not a measurement, for the other direction — an unshared path is a VM-local directory with no connection either way — while `/outbox`'s real dependency is container->host, which `probeWriteThrough` measures and `image verify` owns); a source ABSENT from the host is deliberately NOT probed, because `docker run -v <missing>:<dst>` CREATES it and probing one would make the diagnostic the thing that materialized the directory it was asked about (that is ISC-188's criterion, and it is loud there); and the negative direction still has no reproducible reader on any runner. **[2026-08-28 — A GUARDED PATH THAT WAS NOT GUARDED, found by enumerating every `-v` construction site rather than by re-reading the ones already covered.]** `up` asserts bind-mount visibility over the finished WORKER argvs at `cli/commands/up.ts:1158`. **Not one of the relay's sources appears on those.** `ensureEgressRelay` mounts `relayScriptPath()`, `proxyScriptPath()` and `proxyPolicyScriptPath()`, all resolved under `repoRoot()` — wherever the operator happened to clone — while the worker mounts come from `run.repo`, the runs root and the scratch root. And `up` calls `ensureEgressRelay` at line 616, roughly five hundred lines BEFORE that assertion, so even a source the workers did share would have been mounted here first. A checkout outside the shared set therefore mounted three invented empty directories where the relay script, the CONNECT proxy and the shared matcher belong; `docker run -d` exits 0 and the relay dies on a missing module milliseconds later, which `ensureEgressRelay` reports as "exited immediately after start" — the false-diagnosis shape this criterion was FILED for, reproduced in a second place. **The refusal now happens at the relay's own launch**, over the same argv `docker run` is handed rather than a reconstruction, and **only on the launch path**: every early return above it adopts a running relay having mounted nothing, so probing there would charge every `up` a probe container's cold start for a mount nobody was about to make. **Placed BEFORE the first thing that changes the machine** — ahead of `ensureUplinkNetwork` and the `rm -f` — which is the one placement decision worth arguing about: both of those mutate, and a refusal issued after them would leave the operator with no relay, an orphan network, and a message about bind mounts, the guard having done more damage than the fault it declined. **`doctor` gains the checkout as a third mount root**, which is the criterion's "reported" half and the one an operator can run BEFORE `up`. Its `env` is `null` rather than a plausible-looking string: the field is the ACTIONABLE half and no variable relocates a clone. **A COST ACCEPTED WITH ITS ALTERNATIVE NAMED.** `probeMountVisibility` writes a sentinel into the directory it measures and removes it in a `finally`, so `doctor` now transiently writes into the operator's own working tree; the file is gitignored and the interrupt window is stated there. A read-BORROW probe (`probeBindMountSources`, which reads a file already present) was considered and REJECTED, and not for effort: it proves a different thing from the write round-trip, so mixing the two would make `visible` mean one thing on two rows of the report and another on the third. One meaning per column was judged worth a transient file. **The grade does not move, and the reason is unchanged:** the new probes substitute the injected `Exec`, so what they re-check is that the guard FIRES when a runtime reports a source invisible — not that a genuinely unshared path on a real runtime is caught. That is still the negative direction, it still has no reproducible reader, and a dind daemon on a Linux runner remains the only route to one that has been identified. **A MEASUREMENT ABOUT THE TEST ESTATE, worth keeping because it nearly shipped green.** The change broke 27 `up` probes in `test/integration/up-wiring.test.ts` and NONE of the unit suite, so a run of `bun test test/unit` — which is what the implementing agent reported — showed 1704 pass and clean. The file drives the real CLI against a PATH shim standing in for Docker, and the shim had no answer for a probe verb that did not exist when it was written, so every `up` in it exited 3 on mounts that were in fact perfectly visible. The shim now answers by running production's own probe script with each `/probe/<i>` rewritten to the host path `-v` was about to mount there — the same liberty the ISC-260 branch takes, and faithful rather than hard-coded, because on a shared path what the container sees IS what the host has. Mutations: deleting the guard reddens 5 of the 6 new probes (the survivor is the adoption case, which holds trivially once nothing probes at all); making the shim's new branch refuse reddens exactly the same 27, which is what proves the branch is reached rather than dead. Both restored byte-identical, `25d175bb866ee162459adcb023eb74d77a6c8f20ece9e0d202ff5907e620e6f8` and `31f4cc1b780297216cf077e55326a0ca5c4adb00d27420f03fcb9d9ce0f9d7ae`. **[2026-08-28 — CLOSED. `[~]` -> `[x]`, on CI run `33149447575`, and the entry's own long-standing premise is REFUTED rather than worked around.]** Every prior note here, including the one immediately above, says the negative direction has no reproducible reader because the hazard is macOS-only. **It is not macOS-only.** It belongs to any daemon whose filesystem differs from the client's, and docker-in-docker is one on Linux — which means it was reachable from a runner for the whole time this criterion recorded it as unreachable from one. The macOS VM share set is one INSTANCE of the class, not the class. **Measured by hand before a line was written**, against a dind daemon (`Alpine Linux v3.24 / 29.7.2`, distinct from the host's `Ubuntu 24.04.2 / 28.4.0`): `docker run -v <client-only-path>:/probe:ro` exits 0 and presents an EMPTY directory; a path the inner daemon really has mounts with real content; and `assertBindMountsVisible` refuses the first with `MountNotVisibleError` and exit 3, naming the witness file and its byte size. **`test/integration/mount-preflight-remote.test.ts` carries three probes and the third is the unusual one:** the refusal; a positive control, without which the refusal passes for any reason at all including a probe that refuses everything; and the RAW HAZARD, asserting `docker run -v` still exits 0 with an empty directory. That last pins the PREMISE rather than the guard — a Docker that begins erroring on a missing bind source turns it red and reports that the guard's justification changed, which is not the same news as the guard breaking. A named volume was rejected for the control: `bindMountSources` does not report one as a host path, so the assertion would have passed having measured nothing. **CI evidence, cited rather than intended:** run `33149447575`, `container` job — all three pass by name, and `parsed[container]: pass=122 fail=0 skip=3 total=125 expected=125 rc=0`. `TOTAL_EXPECTED` was re-DERIVED by the hand method (122 -> 125), never incremented. **TWO CI FAILURES PRECEDED IT AND BOTH ARE WORTH KEEPING.** The first was read as a possible `--privileged` refusal and was not: the daemon started and published a port, and the pull into it died with `connection reset by peer` from 127.0.0.1. Hardening the readiness poll to require two consecutive answers did NOT fix it — and that non-fix is the useful part, because it killed the restart hypothesis and forced the second failure to be diagnosed from the daemon's own logs instead of guessed at again. Those logs named it outright: Docker 28 **deliberately stalls startup** when bound to TCP without TLS (its own words: startup is intentionally being slowed down to show the message), and during that stall the listener is bound and ACCEPTS connections before resetting them — so `docker info` answers, twice over, while the daemon is not yet serving. `--tls=false`, the override that same message names, fixed it; there is no TLS to weaken on a loopback ephemeral port inside a container the test creates and destroys. **The local run fell from 28.9s to 10.3s**, which is the independent confirmation: the same deliberate delay had been paid on the maintainer's machine all along and was merely survivable there, which is exactly why this probe was green locally and red twice on CI. **What this does NOT claim:** the macOS VM-share mechanism specifically is still only reachable on a Mac. The criterion's sentence is about a source the runtime cannot see, and that sentence now has a reproducible reader on every push; the Mac is a second route into the same class, not a second claim.

- [x] ISC-279: `down` never reports `stopped: true` for a worker it refused to signal. **[FILED AND GRADED 2026-08-20 by the kill-path claim review, as the REPORTING gate that no existing criterion covered.]** **Why this is separate from ISC-191, which is about signalling.** A guard and the honesty of the report about that guard are two different properties, and the second is where the damage hid. `down`'s `--prune` gate consumes `stopped` as its INPUT — `down.ts` refuses a checkout only when `stopped` is false — so a false `stopped: true` is not a cosmetic lie about a process, it is a DELETE. This criterion would have caught the §9.3 corruption below on its own, with nothing said about pids, start times or ladders. **The reproduction, taken before any fix, with a real git clone and a real live process:** a live supervisor whose recorded identity was captured under `TZ=UTC` and stopped under `TZ=America/Halifax` reported `{"workers":[{"id":"eng-1","stopped":true,"how":"already_gone"}],"clean":true}` at `down --prune exit: 0`, with `pruned: true`, `reason: "remote already absent; checkout deleted"`; afterwards `process still alive : true` and `checkout after down : exists=false`. The checkout of a container that was still running was deleted, and the command called the run clean. Three different facts — nothing holds the pid, a stranger holds the pid, and the recorded identity disagrees — were all reported as the one that means success, and only the first is one. **What is now machine-checked.** An anchor refusal reports `stopped: false` with a `how` that names WHICH refusal (`identity_mismatch`, `identity_unrecorded`, `identity_legacy_format`), a `worker_down_refused` ledger row, a stderr line naming `--force-identity`, and `REFUSED` rather than `STILL RUNNING` in text output; the command exits `WORKER_DIED` rather than 0. Six tests in `test/integration/down-identity.test.ts` pin it, including `a live worker with no recorded identity keeps its checkout`, which asserts the file is still on disk after `down --prune`. Mutation-verified by making an anchor refusal report itself as a clean stop again: six tests fail, headline `Expected: 6, Received: 0` on the exit code, and the prune test fails on the surviving file. The prune refusal REASON is asserted to differ from the survived-the-ladder wording and to not contain "survived the kill ladder", because no ladder ran and saying so would be a second false report layered on the first. **Graded `[x]` against what is built, and the scope is deliberately narrow:** the claim is about `down`'s worker report only. The daemon rung reports a refusal too (a `daemon` field in `--json`, plus a ledger row) but does NOT fail the command — the daemon holds no checkout, so no prune decision consumes it — and that asymmetry is a decision, not an oversight. **Recorded so the honesty is not re-lost:** `down` can still STRAND an operator — a worker with no registry entry, or an unparseable `registry.json`, cannot be stopped by a bare `down` at all — but it can no longer do so SILENTLY, and `--force-identity` is the named exit. Loud refusal is the intended trade; silent success is the thing this criterion forbids.
- [x] ISC-280: `grep -rln 'soft_stop_at\|softStop' src/` names a production reader outside `config/schema.ts`, or the key is removed from `BudgetSchema` and `fleet.example.yaml` together. **[CLOSED 2026-08-20 on the SECOND arm — the key is removed. The owner was asked which arm and chose removal; this was a product decision and is recorded as one, not as an implementation detail.]** **Why removal rather than a reader.** The criterion was written as a disjunction precisely because what a soft stop DOES — refuse new admissions, warn once, warn per admission, drain and stop, shrink `max_concurrent` — are different products an operator has to live with, and inventing one to close a criterion buys a reader that does the wrong thing INVISIBLY, which is strictly worse than no reader because it is no longer visible as unwired. Deleting the key ends the state the criterion existed to end: the config stops advertising a control the product does not have. **What was removed, in one commit as the criterion requires:** the key and its docstring from `BudgetSchema`, the line from `fleet.example.yaml`, and the line from the config block in `Docs/SRD.md` §, so the spec's example and the schema cannot drift apart. **A consequence worth stating: this schema is `.strict()`, so removal is a BEHAVIOUR CHANGE, not a tidy-up.** Any existing `fleet.yaml` carrying the key — including any copied from the `fleet.example.yaml` that shipped it, which is the likely case — now fails validation instead of silently ignoring the line. That is the intended outcome, but a bare `unrecognized key` would describe it as a typo, and a typo and a removal want opposite reactions from a reader: one should be corrected, the other deleted. New `REMOVED_KEYS` in `config/load.ts` gives the dotted path a message saying it was removed, why, and that deleting the line changes nothing. **The removal is ENFORCED, not merely performed, and both halves are mutation-proved.** `config.test.ts` asserts the key is refused at `run.budget.soft_stop_at` with a message containing both `removed` and `ISC-280`, and — separately — that a genuine typo in the same block (`tokens_celing`) still gets the plain `unrecognized key` wording, so the targeted message cannot leak onto misspellings and send someone to delete a line they meant to fix. MUTATIONS: reverting the lookup to the bare string fails the first test; re-adding `soft_stop_at` to `BudgetSchema` — the restoration-by-merge case, which would otherwise look like a harmless restoration and quietly recreate a key with no reader — also fails it. **The SRD claimed this as a live mitigation, and that is corrected here rather than left standing.** Risk rows F12 (cost runaway) and F24 (budget overshoot between polls) both named an "80% soft-stop" among their mitigations. It was never implemented, so those rows overstated the product's protection against the two risks the budget machinery exists for. Both now say so explicitly and point here. The rows are ANNOTATED rather than rewritten: whether cost runaway needs a replacement mitigation is an owner's call about risk, not a bookkeeping fix, and silently deleting the claim would lose the fact that it was once thought necessary. **Residual, filed as a fact rather than a criterion because nothing is currently broken by it:** the operator experience `would_exceed` lacks is still lacking — a run consumes its budget and then simply stops with a diagnosis, with no warning band beforehand. That was the honest argument FOR wiring rather than deleting, and it loses to the argument that a warning band is a product to be designed rather than a key to be read. If it is wanted later it should arrive as a designed feature with its own criterion, not as a resurrection of this key.
- [x] ISC-281: `session_present` does not report `false` for a worker whose recorded `session_path` exists on disk — or no consumer that must not lose money treats `session_present === false` as evidence the worker never spent. **FILED OPEN 2026-08-20 by the budget-wiring review round.** **A DISTINCT CLAIM FROM ISC-96, which is why it has its own number.** ISC-96 says the absent-to-present transition is RECORDED, so "never started" is distinguishable from "wrong path"; that is met, and the transition is recorded. This criterion says the discriminator is UNRELIABLE WITHIN ITS OWN LAG WINDOW — a different sentence, and one that would be lost as a caveat inside ISC-96's note. **EVIDENCE, measured directly rather than reasoned about.** At the instant `dispatch --auto` exits, a worker that ran a task to completion and whose transcript holds 400 tokens reads `session_present: false` in its own on-disk `state.json`, with the transcript present and readable at the recorded path. It flips `true` roughly 400 ms later. Probed by running a real supervisor and a real `dispatch --auto`, then sampling `state.json` at exit, +400 ms and +1200 ms: `false / true / true`, with exactly one `session_file_present` event in the worker's event log. **MECHANISM — AND THE DEFECT IS THE LAG, NOT THE PERIOD.** `recordSessionPath` sets the flag from `existsSync` at the instant `get_state` first reports the path, which is BEFORE the file is lazily created on the first assistant message, so it starts `false`. The correction is made by the supervisor heartbeat, which also flushes state. **This note first blamed "the 5 s heartbeat", and that was WRONG: `HEARTBEAT_MS = 250` and it does flush its correction.** The mechanism is recorded this precisely because a reader who inherits the wrong explanation goes looking for a slow or non-flushing heartbeat and finds a healthy one — and would then conclude the measurement above was noise. The flag simply trails the file's appearance by up to one tick, and any consumer reading inside that window sees `false` for a worker that has genuinely spent. **THE NARROW REAL CONSEQUENCE, stated precisely rather than sweepingly.** `classifySession` maps `session_present === false` to `never_created` — but during the lag window the file EXISTS, so it answers `present` and is unaffected. The flag is wrong only for a transcript that VANISHES while it is still catching up. **Why that still matters:** a resumed `dispatch --auto` started straight after the previous one sits inside exactly that window, which is the budget path's ordinary resume case, and there the two answers differ by a whole run's spend. ISC-235 (c)'s first cut rested on this flag and mis-classified a real degradation as innocent; the six-worker ISC-109 test caught it by asserting empty stderr. The budget path therefore stopped trusting the flag entirely and resolves the ambiguity where the information actually exists — is there published spend to lose? — which is a workaround, not a fix, and is why this stays open. **Closing it:** either flush the flip synchronously the first time the session file is observed (the write that records the path already happens on that code path), or have every consumer that must not lose money read the transcript rather than the flag. The `missing_after_present` / `never_created` split cannot be treated as reliable evidence until one of those is true. **CLOSED 2026-08-25 on the SECOND arm, and the first arm is improved rather than claimed.** Read that split before reading the evidence, because grading this on arm 1 would have been grading a measurement that any timing change invalidates. **Arm 1 — what was done and what it does NOT prove.** The latch moved out of the 250 ms heartbeat and into `flushState`'s write chain (`noteSessionFilePresent`, one definition, called immediately before `writeWorkerState`), so every `state.json` a reader can observe AFTER ANY ACTIVITY carries a flag computed at that write rather than at the last tick. That is a real reduction — the measured failure was a worker holding a 400-token transcript reading `session_present: false` at the instant `dispatch --auto` exited — but detection is still by SAMPLING, so a reader polling in the gap between two writes can see a value that went stale after the last one. Polling cannot close that, and no amount of test-writing turns it into a proof. **Arm 2 — what actually closes it.** `test/unit/session-presence-consumers.test.ts` asserts, on COMMENT-STRIPPED source, that none of `dispatch.ts`, `safety/budget.ts`, `orchestrate/scheduler.ts` or `cli/commands/wait.ts` reads `session_present` OR `classifySession`. Comment-stripped is not incidental: `dispatch.ts` names the flag eight times in prose explaining at length why it does not use it, so a plain grep FAILS ON THE CORRECT FILE. The decision to distrust the flag was already made and documented in that file; nothing kept it so, and its own documentation invites the mistake by calling the flag "the ISC-96 discriminator". **Non-vacuity is asserted, not assumed:** the guard is a claim about ABSENCE, which passes when the thing it guards is deleted — so `openingBalance` and `taskTokens` are asserted still present, and the same analysis is run against two fixtures that DO read the flag (directly, and via `classifySession`) plus one that mentions both only in prose, so the comment-stripping itself is shown to work in both directions. **Mutation-proved, four, and the SPLIT between the two probes is the point rather than a detail:** N1 latch guard always returns -> behavioural AND structural red; N2 call removed from the write chain -> behavioural AND structural red (the behavioural probe can only catch this BECAUSE there is exactly one call site — with the heartbeat copy still present it would stay green); N3 the heartbeat's own copy re-added -> structural ONLY, behavioural GREEN, which is precisely the regression a behavioural test cannot see and the reason `test/unit/supervisor-session-latch.test.ts` exists; N4 the single-fire guard dropped -> structural ONLY. **One over-claim was found and corrected by N4 rather than reasoned away:** the behavioural probe's "exactly one `session_file_present` event" comment predicted it would catch a missing single-fire guard as a count that grows; it does not, because the sample is taken within a tick or two of the first fire. The comment now says so.
- [x] ISC-282: The stall policy's PRODUCTION inputs and action are covered — `eventSilenceMs` really measures a worker's event silence, and `killWedged` really ends a wedged agent. **FILED OPEN 2026-08-20 by the stall-wiring commission, and filed rather than claimed.** ISC-110 and ISC-117 are `[~]` because `test/unit/scheduler-stall.test.ts` proves the SCHEDULER acts on a verdict, using an injected clock and a fake `eventSilenceMs`. Two production halves are untested: `stat(events.jsonl).mtimeMs` in `dispatch.ts`'s adapter (does an appended event actually move the reading, and does an absent file really answer `null` rather than an infinite silence?), and the `abort` RPC `killWedged` sends (does a wedged supervisor answer it, and does the task then settle?).
