THREE DESIGN POINTS, each of which was a way to get this wrong. (1) IT WORKS ON THE SERIALISED LINE, NOT ON KNOWN FIELDS. The observed leak was in `tool_execution_update.partialResult.content[0].text`, `tool_execution_end.result.content[0].text` and `message_start.message.content[0].text` — the fields SEEN, not the fields that exist. A walker over those three is correct until Pi emits a fourth shape and then fails silently, so the needle is matched against the JSON text, in its ESCAPED form (a string inside a JSON document is escaped; the raw form cannot occur there and matching it could straddle an escape sequence and leave unparseable JSON) plus its double-escaped form, which is how a value survives being embedded as pre-serialised JSON. (2) TRUNCATION IS MATCHED, and this was found by the wiring test rather than reasoned out: a whole-value scrubber sails straight past `head -c 20`, which is the command that actually happened, because a model told not to print a secret truncates it. Any leading run at or above `TRUNCATION_FLOOR` (12) is scrubbed, longest-first. The residual is stated rather than buried — a fragment below 12 characters, or one taken from the MIDDLE or END of a value (`tail -c 20`), is NOT matched, because covering arbitrary substrings costs a needle per window and that is the log-eating failure at scale. (3) NAMES AND VALUES SHARE ONE ARTIFACT. `buildWorkerEnv` declares the granted names in `PIFLEET_SECRET_NAMES` inside the same 0600 env file that holds the values, written by the same call, so the two cannot drift; a sibling names file would fail by arming the redactor against a value it no longer holds while reporting itself armed. That is also the persistence ISC-333 names as its missing half. The marker NAMES the variable (`[redacted:TICKET_API_TOKEN]`) deliberately: a scrubbed leak still happened and the operator's next action is to rotate the credential that reached model output, which an unnamed marker cannot tell them; the name is not the secret and `materialize.ts` already prints `secretNames` to stderr at `up` by design.

It applies only to CREATION — an existing file keeps its mode, so a run directory written before this change is not silently altered under a reader. `<run>/sessions` is CREATED `mode: 0o700` by `mkdir(2)` itself and then widened deliberately, which closes the window between creation and the widen without pretending the end state changed. **WHAT THIS DOES NOT CLAIM, AND THE DRAFT THAT CLAIMED IT ANYWAY.** A first version made the widen conditional on `useDouble`, so a double run left `sessions` at 0700 — and `test/integration/up-wiring.test.ts` went red, correctly. `up` renders and MATERIALIZES a full container mount table on every run, `/sessions` is in it, and that guard asserts every `-v` source exists at the mode its mount needs; skipping the widen put the directory out of step with a table still being produced. The guard was right and the conditional was reverted rather than the guard weakened. MUTATION-PROVED: dropping `mode: JSONL_FILE_MODE` from the append turns the probe red with `Received: 420` — 0o644, the mode measured on the leaking run.

A Linux bind mount passes host ownership through untouched, so a 0400 file is simply unreadable to the worker — and INVISIBLY so on the development machine, because the macOS Docker VM squashes bind-mount ownership to the container user and 0400 reads back perfectly. `makeWorkerReadable`'s docstring in `container/mounts.ts` records exactly this measurement for 0600, and CI is `ubuntu-latest`; shipping 0400 would be re-committing a bug the repo has already diagnosed. Matching uids is unavailable (the image bakes 10001) and `chown` needs a privilege the CLI does not have. **What 0400 was reaching for is bought one level up instead:** `materialize.ts` tightens `<run>/workers/<id>` to 0700, so no other account on the host can traverse to the 0444 file at all. That costs the container nothing, and it is measured rather than argued — the outbox block in the same file records that a bind mount is established by the privileged runtime and the containerized process reaches the path at its MOUNTPOINT in its own namespace, never walking the host chain, and that an operator under `umask 077` has had this directory at 0700 all along with every mount under it working. **Both probes are host-side `stat` calls and are therefore platform-neutral** — they cannot pass on a Mac for a reason they would fail on Linux, which is the specific hazard here. **Mutation-proved separately:** 0444 -> 0644 reddens exactly the mode probe (16/1); 0700 -> 0755 on the worker directory reddens exactly the containment probe (16/1). **WHAT WOULD CLOSE THIS:** an owner decision that 0444-plus-0700-parent is the right trade, or a mechanism that can `chown` the file to `WORKER_UID` — at which point 0400 becomes both achievable and correct. **CLOSED 2026-08-30 BY OWNER DECISION — 0444-PLUS-0700-PARENT IS THE RIGHT TRADE.** That is the FIRST of the two closing conditions this entry named, taken as written; the second, a mechanism that can `chown` the file to `WORKER_UID`, was not built and is not what closes this. If one ever arrives, 0400 becomes achievable and this entry is the place to revisit the mode. **WHAT THE TRADE COSTS, stated plainly so nobody later reads `[x]` as "the file is readable only by the worker uid":** it is not. At 0444 the file is WORLD-READABLE ON THE HOST — every account on the machine that can reach the path can read the credential, and the mode stops nobody. What contains it is not the file mode but the PARENT DIRECTORY: `<run>/workers/<id>` is tightened to 0700, so no other account can traverse to the file at all. The containment is directory-shaped, and it is exactly as strong as the single `chmod` at `src/run/materialize.ts:978` — which is why that line, and not the file mode, is what the registered claim pins. Loosen the directory and the credential becomes readable by anyone on the host, with no other symptom anywhere in the suite. Two consequences follow and are worth naming: an operator whose umask or later tooling widens that directory silently undoes the whole guarantee, and anything that copies the file out from under the 0700 parent carries 0444 bytes with it. **RE-VERIFIED 2026-08-30 BEFORE THE GRADE MOVED, because an owner decision settles a scope question and manufactures no evidence. Both mutations reproduced exactly as claimed.** `SECRET_FILE_MODE` 0444 -> 0644 reddens the mode probe and only it: 16/1 in `test/unit/worker-secret-files.test.ts`, and 2004 pass / 1 fail across the whole unit suite. 0700 -> 0755 on the worker directory reddens the containment probe and only it: 16/1 in the same file, and 2003 pass / 2 fail across the suite — the second failure being the registry claim that pins that exact `chmod` line, which is that claim doing its job rather than collateral. Restored after each, verified by `git diff --stat` returning empty on the mutated file and `shasum -c` against the pre-mutation digests.
- [x] ISC-340: The secret store is bind-mounted READ-ONLY, at a fixed container path, from the path `run/paths.ts` names — and a worker that asked for no secret gets no mount at all. **[FILED AND CLOSED 2026-08-28.]** **`:ro` is load-bearing here for a reason specific to this mount rather than by habit.** The host file is 0444 and the macOS VM squashes bind-mount ownership to the container user, so INSIDE the container that file reads as owned by uid 10001 — the mount flag is the only thing left between a worker and its own credential store. That is the identical argument `/policy/cloud-allow:ro` already makes about the verbgate policy, which is why the mount follows that convention rather than inventing a second one. **The path comes from `workerPaths().secretsDir` and is not joined at the mount site**, on ISC-188's rule: a bind mount whose two sides disagree does NOT fail — Docker creates the missing source — so the worker would come up with an empty `/secrets`, authenticate against nothing, and produce no error anywhere. The same predicate `w.secrets.length > 0` gates the mount in `render.ts` and the directory in `materialize.ts`, for that reason. **Mutation-proved:** dropping `:ro` reddens both ISC-337 probes (15/2) and nothing else, including the second probe that asserts no writable spelling of the same mount is emitted anywhere in the argv. **AMENDED 2026-09-01 — THE SECOND CLAUSE IS SUPERSEDED AND THE PREDICATE SENTENCE IS NOW FALSE, both by design (D8, ISC-407/ISC-408).** `/secrets` used to mean "what the operator granted", and under that meaning "a worker that asked for no secret gets no mount at all" was right: an empty `/secrets` in a worker granted nothing says less than its absence does. It now means "material this worker holds", the Class 1 provider key is delivered into it, and NO worker requests that — so `w.secrets` is empty for most workers that now hold one, and the old gate would have produced a well-formed `PIFLEET_LLM_API_KEY_FILE` pointing into a directory never written and never mounted. That is this entry's own ISC-188 argument turned on the criterion that made it. The gate was therefore deleted from BOTH sides rather than widened on one — no predicate at all, because two conditions that merely agree eventually will not, and a boolean true for every worker is a decision nobody is making. `SecretStoreNotMountedError` (`EXIT.INTERNAL`) is what survives an edit to either side, and it has been made to fire from a real `materializeWorkerInputs` under mutation rather than merely written. **The superseded guard was REPLACED with the positive assertion, not deleted** — `worker-secret-files.test.ts` now asserts a worker with no grants gets exactly one `/secrets` mount, still `:ro`, still from `workerPaths().secretsDir`. **The FIRST clause is untouched and still probed**, which is why this stays `[x]` rather than being re-graded: `:ro`, the fixed container path, and the path coming from `run/paths.ts` rather than being joined at the mount site are exactly what the mutation record above pins.
- [x] ISC-341: **[ANTI-CRITERION]** A worker that runs `echo $TICKET_API_TOKEN` gets an empty string, and `env` dumping the whole environment does not contain the value either. **[FILED AND CLOSED 2026-08-28. So a real `/bin/sh` runs with the plan as its ENTIRE environment (`Bun.spawn`'s `env` replaces rather than extends) and stdout is asserted, with `printf %s` rather than `echo` so a trailing newline cannot be mistaken for content. **The plan under it is built from `fleet.example.yaml`** — the document an operator copies — not from a fixture written to pass, which is the same rule ISC-330 established for this area. **It carries an explicit control as a SEPARATE test:** an empty expansion is also what a broken harness produces, so the same shell with the same environment must expand `$TICKET_API_TOKEN_FILE` to the container path. One going red without the other is a finding; both at once is a broken probe. **`env; set` is asserted too**, because those are the two spellings of the same accident that name no variable at all — a worker running either is doing something entirely reasonable, which is precisely why the value must not be there to be swept up. **Mutation-proved:** restoring value delivery turns all three probes red.
- [x] ISC-342: A granted secret whose file did not land REFUSES the launch, loudly and by name, rather than starting a worker whose environment points at nothing. **[FILED AND CLOSED 2026-08-28.]** **The failure it prevents is §5.9's quiet-failure shape with an extra layer of plausibility on top:** the env file would carry a perfectly well-formed `<NAME>_FILE=/secrets/<NAME>`, the worker would start, and the credential would fail minutes later inside whatever HTTP call needed it, nowhere near the config line or the disk error that caused it. **The verification is a RE-READ and not a trusted return value.** `writeFile` resolving says the syscalls returned; it does not say the bytes are on disk at the right size, in a regular file, at a mode the worker can read, and each of those three produces a container that starts, looks healthy, and cannot authenticate. Replacing the whole read-back with a fabricated `stat` — the writer trusting its own return value, which is the defect the criterion is about — reddens exactly one probe (16/1). The first mutation is reported because a mutation that fails to discriminate is evidence about the probe, and hiding it would make the second one read as stronger than it is.

A fixture that hand-writes what the reader expects proves the two agree with the fixture, not with each other — which is exactly how this defect stayed invisible. **Mutation-proved, three of them, each restored and verified by sha:** reverting the supplier to env-file-only — the bug that would have shipped — reddens 4 probes and leaves the legacy one green; removing the fallback reddens EXACTLY the legacy probe and nothing else, so the two are independent rather than redundant; and changing the WRITER's filename scheme with the supplier untouched reddens 4, which is the binding claim demonstrated rather than asserted. **A limit, stated:** this closes the seam between delivery and the sweep, not the sweep's subject. The same defect then turned up in a second value-reader that this entry did not think to look for, so the lookup moved into `security/secret-values.ts` and both consumers now call it. Everything asserted above still holds and is still probed — the sweep reads the store, falls back to the env file, and the fixture is built by the production writer. What changed is that 'where do granted values live' is answered in one place instead of this one. The sentence about fixing it in place is left standing deliberately: it was true, and it is also the reason ISC-345 exists.
- [~] ISC-344: A ticketing worker asks the SERVER its question and BOUNDS every request, rather than downloading a collection to grep and rather than issuing a call that can hang forever. **[FILED 2026-08-29 FROM TWO MEASURED FAILURES IN ONE LIVE RUN; graded `[~]` because what shipped is INSTRUCTION, and an instruction is not a mechanism.]** **The first failure produced a confident wrong answer, which is the expensive kind.** Asked for one user's tickets in the current iteration, the worker enumerated pages out of 59,616 objects, grepped them locally for the owner name, and reported that a user with THIRTY open tickets had none. Nothing errored. The artifact was well-formed, the verdict was `success`, and the number was wrong — absence in a page you happened to fetch is not absence in the system, and a harvest cannot tell those apart. **The second failure produced no answer at all and no reason.** An unbounded `curl` inside a container does not fail, it HANGS; the only signal reaching the supervisor is that the worker stopped emitting events, so it is killed at its deadline with nothing written and nothing recorded about why. That is real and it is mounted rather than baked, so it reaches a running worker. It is still a prompt. **`[~]` AND NOT `[x]` ON THE STRICTNESS RULE:** the registered claim greps the shipped skill and role for the guidance, which verifies the fleet SHIPS the instruction and verifies nothing at all about whether a worker FOLLOWED it. Grading that `[x]` would record compliance on the evidence of an instruction's existence — precisely the 'reads as coverage' failure ISC-333 was filed against, one layer up. **WHAT WOULD CLOSE THIS, and it is buildable rather than aspirational:** the ticket-ops artifact already carries a `commands` array, and the harvester already parses and reconciles that document. A harvest-side check that every `curl` in `commands` carries `--max-time`, and that a `query` operation whose artifact reports a count does not report one the server's own total contradicts, turns both halves into red builds on real output rather than advice in a prompt. Neither needs a live ticket system to test — both are assertions about a document this repo already validates. **NOT CLAIMED:** the re-run that would have exercised this guidance end to end was aborted when the credential leak was found, so the fix is reasoned from the two failures rather than confirmed against a third live run. **TRANSPORT REPLACED 2026-09-01 — the image now carries `rally-cli` and the skill is written to it, and BOTH halves of this criterion survived the change with one strengthened and one weakened.** *Filter on the server* is unchanged as guidance and unchanged as a claim: the phrase is still in the mounted bundle, still pinned by grep, still weak in exactly the way this entry already said — it verifies the fleet SHIPS the instruction and nothing about whether a worker followed it. *Bound every request* is STRONGER in mechanism and WEAKER in evidence, and both directions are recorded rather than netted off. There are now no examples to count, because there is no request for a worker to shape. That is a named hole in a real guard, which is `[~]`, and it is the same grade for a sharper reason than before. **WHAT WOULD CLOSE IT:** a probe that runs the shipped CLI against a server that never answers and asserts it gives up — which needs a hung listener the container can reach, and is the one shape neither the unit nor the container job has today.
- [x] ISC-345: EVERY consumer of a granted secret's value resolves it from one place, so moving delivery cannot blind one of them while the others keep working. **[FILED AND CLOSED 2026-08-29 FROM A LEAK THAT REACHED A REAL EVENT LOG. This is ISC-343's defect found a second time, in the reader ISC-343 did not look for.]** **WHAT HAPPENED, measured rather than reasoned.** ISC-343 fixed the harvest credential sweep after ISC-337..342 moved granted secrets out of the environment into one 0444 file each. There was a SECOND reader of those values — `redactorForWorkerEnv`, which scrubs them out of `events.jsonl` — and it was not looked for, because the first was fixed in place rather than by asking who else reads this. On the next live run a ticketing worker built its curl config from `$TICKET_API_TOKEN_FILE` correctly and then ran `cat` on the result to check its work; the full 41-character credential landed in `events.jsonl` FIVE TIMES, on a run whose own first log line named that variable as protected. **THE FAILING LINE WAS A `continue`, and its comment argued it was unreachable:** 'A name with no value in the same file is a rotation or an edit between the two halves of one write, which cannot happen while they share a file.' They stopped sharing a file. The impossible case became the normal one, and the redactor armed against three names while able to value one — the LLM key, not either granted secret. `SECRET_NAMES_VAR`'s own docstring had predicted this exact shape: 'a stale name list that arms the redactor against a rotated value and reports itself as armed while scrubbing nothing.' **THE FIX IS DE-DUPLICATION, NOT A SECOND PATCH.** Two readers had been written independently, each with its own `parseEnvFile`, and fixing them one at a time is what produced this. `src/security/secret-values.ts` now owns the question — store first, env file second, for the run-directory-outlives-the-code reason `harvest/patterns.ts` states — and both consumers call it. The next delivery change has ONE call site to follow rather than a set someone has to enumerate from memory. **THE SIGNATURE IS THE ENFORCEMENT.** `redactorForWorkerEnv` takes `secretsDir` as a REQUIRED second parameter. Optional would have let every existing call site keep compiling while silently reading a file that no longer holds what it wants — which is exactly how this shipped. Required turned the change into a compile error at all three call sites. **AND THE BLINDING IS NOW LOUD.** `Redactor.unresolved` carries granted names that could not be valued from any layout — distinct from `skipped`, which means 'found it, not worth a needle'. This means 'told to protect it, cannot see it'. The supervisor writes it into the `redaction_armed` event AND to stderr, because the defect went unnoticed precisely because its only symptom was a value quietly missing from a structure nobody re-read. NOT fatal: refusing to start would trade a degraded log for no fleet, the same trade the absent-env-file branch already declines. **Mutation-proved, two, each restored and sha-verified:** restoring the shipped env-file-only reader reddens both new probes and leaves all 21 pre-existing redaction probes green — which is the measurement that matters, because it shows the old suite could not see this; and changing the WRITER's filename scheme with both readers untouched now reddens FIVE probes across BOTH consumers, where before today it would have reddened none. **A limit, stated:** this closes the seam between delivery and the value-readers. It does not stop a worker deliberately printing its own credential file — ISC-341 says so, and the run that produced this evidence did exactly that. What changed is that the value no longer survives into the log.
- [~] ISC-349: A worker can BIND `<task-id>` to the value it was dispatched under, knows what a guessed directory costs, and writes `result.json` LAST. **[FILED 2026-08-29 FROM A LIVE RUN; graded `[~]` because what shipped is INSTRUCTION, and an instruction is not a mechanism.]** **THE PLACEHOLDER WAS UNBINDABLE, and that is the finding — not the worker's carelessness.** A ticketing worker completed its task and wrote its output to `/outbox/list-tickets-2026-08-29/` — a slug of the job it thought it had done, plus the date — while the id it was dispatched under was `my-iteration-2`. It then wrote no `result.json` at all. Both documents already told it to do neither thing. **WHY A CAPABLE MODEL DID IT ANYWAY, established by reading the delivery path rather than by guessing at the model:** `renderPrompt` (`src/supervisor/index.ts`) builds the worker's prompt from `title`, `brief` and `acceptance` and nothing else, so `task_id`, `epoch`, `outbox`, `worker` and `branch` all sit in `TaskEnvelopeSchema`, reach the supervisor, and never reach the agent. `PIFLEET_TASK_ID` is read by `docker/verbgate` with a `${...:-<none>}` fallback and is SET NOWHERE IN PRODUCTION — `src/run/worker-env.ts` assigns `PIFLEET_LLM_*` and `PIFLEET_HONEYPOT` only, and every file in the repo that exports it is a test.
