A worker that cannot fill two mandatory fields is choosing between an envelope it has been told will be discarded and no envelope — and it chose the option that does not look wrong. **THE COST IS TOTAL RATHER THAN PARTIAL, which is why this is filed ahead of the artifact criterion it caused:** `harvest/outbox.ts` scans `join(loc.workerOutboxDir, loc.taskId)` and only that, so the misnamed directory made the whole outbox invisible — a perfectly-formed `ticket-ops.json` inside it would never have been opened. Meanwhile a missing envelope "downgrades nothing" (ISC-94), so the verdict was rebuilt from a git diff which, for work driven entirely through a remote API, does not exist. Nothing errored, nothing was flagged, and the run recorded a container that produced nothing. **WHAT SHIPPED:** the skill now names the one reachable binding — the `#` heading on the first line of the prompt, because `cli/commands/dispatch.ts` defaults `title` to the task id — and tells the worker to fix that value BEFORE starting work rather than when writing the result, because by then the finished job is the salient name and the dispatched id is not. It forbids deriving one from the work, the role, the date or a sibling directory a previous task left behind. It states the cost in mechanism terms: the harvester opens that directory and reads nothing else, so a wrong name is "not scanned, not reported, and not swept for credentials". It tells a worker that genuinely cannot identify its id to say so in its final message instead of guessing, because the transcript is read even when the outbox is empty and a plausible-looking directory is not. And it closes with a four-check `## Before you stop` list whose first item is the id and whose third is `result.json` — which is now stated as "the last thing you do", with the cost of omitting it written out: it does not fail the task, it removes the worker from the grading. **`[~]` AND NOT `[x]`, ON THE STRICTNESS RULE:** the registered claims grep the shipped skill for the binding, for the stated cost, and for the last-action framing. That verifies the fleet SHIPS the instruction and verifies nothing whatsoever about whether a worker resolved its id correctly. Grading it `[x]` would record compliance on the evidence of an instruction existing — which is the failure ISC-344 was filed against one layer up, and precisely the failure this criterion's own subject just demonstrated against instructions that were already there. **WHAT WOULD CLOSE THIS, and it is a SOURCE change rather than a better prompt:** put `task_id` and `epoch` into the rendered prompt; or set `PIFLEET_TASK_ID`/`PIFLEET_EPOCH` in the worker environment, which the verbgate already reads and currently ledgers as `<none>`; or have the supervisor pre-create `<outbox>/<task-id>` so the value is discoverable with `ls`. Any one of the three makes the id READABLE instead of INFERRED, and only then does a harvest check that reports "the task outbox does not exist" mean a worker disobeyed rather than that it was never told. **MUTATION-PROVED, three of them, each restored with `git show HEAD:<path>` and verified by sha256:** replacing the title-defaults sentence with a vaguer "look for a heading that looks like the string" reddens exactly the binding claim; replacing "not scanned, not reported, and not swept for credentials" with a bare "always use the id you were given, and do not use any other name" — the imperative-without-a-cost form the document was in when a worker disregarded it — reddens exactly the cost claim; and softening "it removes you from the grading" to "is bad practice and you should avoid it" reddens exactly the last-action claim. Each mutation reddened ONE test and left the other 76 green, so the three claims are independent rather than three greps aimed at one paragraph. **NOT CLAIMED:** this branch changed no source, so nothing above is fixed — only described. The binding the document now points a worker at holds ONLY while `title` defaults to the task id; an operator who supplies a human title removes it and leaves the worker dependent on the brief naming the id explicitly. That gap is real, it is stated here rather than papered over, and no edit to a prompt can close it.
- [~] ISC-350: A ticketing worker's output is a PAIR, and the shipped documents state that the filename `ticket-ops.json` is what selects a file for schema validation and for the credential sweep. **[FILED 2026-08-29 FROM THE SAME LIVE RUN; graded `[~]` for the same reason — this is instruction, not mechanism. **RE-READ 2026-08-30: THE MECHANISM NOW EXISTS and this entry is still `[~]`, which is worth separating.** `src/harvest/reconcile.ts` carries an unpaired-`ticket-ops.md` clamp and `src/harvest/index.ts` records it as a second cause of a capped verdict, so a worker writing only the human half no longer "reports clean" — it clamps. That is a mechanism, and it is the one this entry said was missing. What it does NOT do is make the output a pair; it makes a non-pair FAIL, which is enforcement rather than compliance. The criterion as worded asserts the worker's output IS a pair, and only a live run showing a ticketing worker writing both files re-checks that. Re-grading on the clamp would be grading the system's reaction as if it were the worker's behaviour — the same substitution ISC-360 is `[~]` for refusing.]** **THE MEASURED FAILURE:** the worker wrote `files/ticket-ops.md` and no `ticket-ops.json`. `skills/ticket-ops/SKILL.md` already said to write both, in a sentence that had been there the whole time. **WHY THAT SENTENCE DID NOT HOLD, three causes, and the third is the one that did the damage.** It read "the same content, once for a machine and once for a person", which frames the second file as REDUNDANCY — and redundancy is the first thing dropped by anything working against a budget. The only stated consequence attached to a MALFORMED document ("a malformed one is a build failure, not a surprise at read time"); nothing anywhere stated the consequence of an ABSENT one. And `roles/ticketing.md` — the standing prompt, which shapes a worker for its whole lifetime and therefore outranks a reference skill at the moment of deciding what to write — opened by saying the artifact is written "**for the human operator, not for the orchestrator**", and that "the orchestrator reads your result envelope and nothing else". A worker that believed that had been told, by its own role, that nothing machine-readable was wanted. It then wrote exactly one file, for the human, as instructed. The skill's pair rule was not ignored so much as OVERRULED by a more authoritative document saying the opposite. **WHAT THE OMISSION ACTUALLY COSTS:** `harvest/reconcile.ts` fixes `TICKET_OPS_ARTIFACT_NAME = "ticket-ops.json"` and selects on that name deliberately — its own comment explains that a role name is an operator's label changed by editing a string, while a path is fixed by the skill and survives a rename. That one string is what puts a document through `TicketOpsArtifactSchema` AND through the sweep for the credential's literal bytes. The `.md` goes through neither. So a `.md`-only run does not fail: it passes, quietly, with both checks skipped — including the one that exists to catch a worker having put the live write credential it was holding into its own write-up. A malformed `.json` is LOUD and clamps the verdict to `failed`; an absent one is silent, which is strictly worse, and silence is what this run produced. **WHAT SHIPPED:** the skill's artifact section is now a two-row table naming a reader per file, states that the harvester selects on the filename and on nothing else, names both checks that the name triggers, and says in terms that the `.md` "is not the safe half; it is the half nothing inspects". The `no_change_needed` case is called out separately, because a run with nothing to report is the one most likely to skip the `.json` on the reasoning that there is nothing in it worth validating — when the fact that no write happened IS the finding, and the `.json` is where a machine can read it. `roles/ticketing.md` loses the "not for the orchestrator" framing entirely and now opens on the pair, on which reader each file has, and on what writing only the `.md` skips. `skills/pifleet-worker/SKILL.md` gains the general form of the rule, so it reaches every role rather than this one: where a role's skill names an exact filename, that name is load-bearing, and a machine-readable file skipped because a readable one says the same thing is not a tidier output but an unvalidated one. **`[~]` AND NOT `[x]`:** one registered claim greps the skill for the selector statement; the other asserts the ABSENCE of the misleading sentence from the role, so restoring it goes red. Between them they verify what the fleet ships and catch the specific regression that caused this. Neither can observe a worker writing one file where two were asked for. **WHAT WOULD CLOSE THIS, and it is buildable now rather than aspirational:** the harvester already walks the task outbox and already validates any `ticket-ops.json` it finds there. A check that treats a task outbox holding `ticket-ops.md` with no sibling `ticket-ops.json` as a reported finding turns the exact measured failure into a red build on real output. It needs no live ticket system and no new input — it is an assertion about a directory listing this repo already scans, and it is the missing half of ISC-332's wiring, which validates the document when it is present and says nothing when it is not. **MUTATION-PROVED, two of them, restored with `git show HEAD:<path>` and verified by sha256:** reverting the selector sentence to "the two files are the same content, once for a machine and once for a person" — the exact wording that was in place when the run failed — reddens the skill claim; and re-inserting "for the human operator, not for the orchestrator" into the role reddens the absence claim. Each reddened one test and left 76 green. The second is the more valuable of the two: it is a regression guard on the specific sentence that overruled the skill's pair rule, and nothing else in the repo would notice that sentence coming back. **NOT CLAIMED:** no re-run has exercised any of this, so the pair is not known to have been written correctly by a worker since the change; and this criterion does not narrow ISC-341's standing limit that a worker can still read its credential file deliberately, nor ISC-349's, on which it depends — a correct pair inside a wrongly-named directory is harvested no differently from no pair at all.

### Group U — The outbox contract, checked (added 2026-08-29)

`skills/pifleet-worker/SKILL.md` tells every worker where to write and what to write. Nothing
checked either. A live ticketing worker broke the contract three ways in one task and the
harvest reported it clean — not because any check failed, but because every check was keyed on
a file that was never written. These three criteria make the harvest say so.

- [x] ISC-346: An outbox directory under a worker that matches NO dispatched task id is a NAMED finding, and the finding states the consequence — that nothing inside it was scanned, validated, or swept for credentials. **[FILED AND CLOSED 2026-08-29 FROM A LIVE RUN WHOSE OUTPUT WAS ACCEPTED WITH NO COMPLAINT.]** **THE MEASUREMENT.** A worker dispatched task `my-iteration-2` wrote its artifact to `<run>/outbox/tick-1/list-tickets-2026-08-29/` — a directory named after its own idea of the job. The harvester looked in `<run>/outbox/tick-1/my-iteration-2/`, found an empty region, scanned nothing, validated nothing, swept nothing, and published a clean harvest. Every step was correct. The operator's entire signal was an absence, and an absence reads exactly like a quiet success. **THIS IS THE FOURTH SIGHTING OF ONE SHAPE, and naming it is half the entry's value:** a mechanism that is present, tested and invoked, running over an EMPTY INPUT, publishing a clean result. ISC-231 had it at the mount path, ISC-333 at the needle supplier, ISC-343 and ISC-345 at the two value readers. The cure has been identical every time — say out loud that nothing was checked, and why — and it is worth writing down that the repair is never "look harder", it is "report the emptiness". **IT IS A LISTING AND NOT A SEARCH, which is the design decision the whole criterion turns on.** The obvious repair is to find the worker's output wherever it landed and harvest it from there; that is the §12.5 exfiltration primitive with extra steps, because it makes the harvested region the one the WORKER picks. `harvest/layout.ts` therefore reads ONE directory level with `readdir`, compares NAMES, and never descends, opens, or stats a leaf. The output is a sentence, not a widened scan. **IT DOES NOT CLAMP, and that is argued rather than assumed.** An unexplained directory belongs to no task — that is what makes it unexplained — and one worker serves many tasks, so clamping would lower the verdict of every task that worker ran on evidence naming none of them. The diff still speaks for whether the work happened; what was lost is the artifact, and the finding says exactly that. Contrast ISC-348, which DOES clamp, because its file sits inside the task's own `files/` and is therefore attributable. **THE FALSE-POSITIVE SURFACE IS THE REAL RISK HERE and it is closed in three places, each with its own probe:** a worker's OTHER dispatched tasks (compared against every dispatched id in the run, never against the task under harvest — the wrong scoping would report every multi-task worker's whole outbox); the verbgate ledger (`docker/verbgate` creates `/outbox/ledger/` itself on the first gated verb, so a check that reported it would fire on a large fraction of real runs — and the exempt name is DERIVED from `workerVerbgateLedger` rather than typed a second time, on `run/paths.ts`'s own rule); and loose files (only `isDirectory()` entries count, which also settles symlinks by construction, since `readdir` reports a link as a link and never as a directory). **THE CAP IS A SAFETY PROPERTY, NOT TIDINESS.** `HarvestSchema` refuses a `discrepancies` array over `MAX_ITEMS`, and `harvestAll` catches a throwing harvest into a single `unavailable` row — so an uncapped loop would let a worker that created a thousand directories DELETE ITS OWN REPORT. Eight are named, the truncation declares itself, and a probe builds twelve to prove both halves. **Mutation-proved, four, each restored and sha-verified:** deleting the call from `harvestTask` reddens all three ISC-346 probes and leaves 40 green; dropping the ledger exemption reddens EXACTLY the ledger control (1/42); dropping the `isDirectory()` filter reddens EXACTLY the loose-file control (1/42); raising the cap to 1000 reddens exactly the flood probe (1/14). The two false-positive mutations reddening only their own controls is the measurement that matters — it shows those controls are load-bearing rather than decorative. **WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED:** this reports the directory; it does not harvest what is in it, and deliberately never will. It also cannot see an unexplained directory under a worker that has no dispatched task at all, because nothing harvests such a worker — an empty set of dispatched ids makes the check say nothing rather than call everything an orphan.
- [x] ISC-347: A dispatched task with no `result.json` produces a finding in `discrepancies`, naming the task and the container path it was contracted to write. **[FILED AND CLOSED 2026-08-29.]** **THE DEFECT IS A CHANNEL, NOT AN ABSENCE, and the entry has to be precise about that because the commissioning brief was not.** The harvest was NOT silent: `harvestTask` already pushed `no result envelope; verdict rests on derived facts alone` into `reasons`. But `reasons` is where the harvest explains HOW it graded — every line there is procedural, most are benign, and that sentence reads like one of the benign ones. `discrepancies` is the channel §8.4 publishes for things that DISAGREE with the contract, and it is the one an operator scans. So a worker that never wrote its result produced a report indistinguishable from one that did, and the correction is to say it in the channel that means "this is wrong" rather than the channel that means "this is how I got here". **NO CLAMP, ON ISC-94'S OWN AUTHORITY.** A missing envelope is explicitly not a failure — a worker can be killed after committing real work, and ISC-94 says the repository facts stand on their own. Clamping would convert every crash-after-commit into `failed` on evidence that says nothing about the work, which is a worse report than the silence it replaces. The probe pins this as a POSITIVE assertion rather than an absence: the verdict must be `unknown`, which is what the adjudicator reaches with no claim to weigh, and `failed` is precisely what a clamp would have produced. **The container spelling is deliberate.** The finding names `/outbox/<task-id>/result.json`, the path the worker was actually given in its brief, not the host path only the harvester can see — an operator comparing the report against what the worker did needs the string the worker had. **Mutation-proved, and the mutation IS the defect:** moving the statement from `discrepancies` back to `reasons` — leaving the text identical and the harvest still saying it — reddens both ISC-347 probes and leaves 41 green. A mutation that changes nothing about what is said and only where it is said, and that still discriminates, is the strongest available evidence that the criterion is about the channel.
- [x] ISC-348: A `ticket-ops.md` with no `ticket-ops.json` beside it is a finding that says plainly that the schema validation and the credential sweep DID NOT RUN on it, and it clamps the verdict. **[FILED AND CLOSED 2026-08-29. This is the one with teeth.]** **WHY IT IS THE SERIOUS ONE.** `reconcile.ts` keys BOTH the ticket-ops schema validation and the credential-leak sweep on the exact filename `ticket-ops.json` (`TICKET_OPS_ARTIFACT_NAME`), and `skills/ticket-ops/SKILL.md` instructs the worker to write that file AND `ticket-ops.md`, "the same content, once for a machine and once for a person". A worker that writes only the `.md` therefore bypasses BOTH checks — silently. The document is never parsed and never swept for the credential the worker was holding while it talked to the ticket system. It still gets a real `sha256` in `derived.artifacts` and the harvest still reads clean, because a clean report and an unexamined one are the same document when neither says which it is. **SO THE FINDING'S JOB IS THE CONSEQUENCE, NOT THE FACT.** "No ticket-ops.json" is a filing complaint an operator can reasonably shrug at. "The schema validation and the credential sweep did not run on this document; it is unchecked, not clean" is the thing they need, and the probe asserts those words rather than the existence of a finding. **IT CLAMPS, on `TICKET_OPS_FAILURE_CEILING`'s existing argument rather than a new one.** That constant exists because an artifact that cannot be read leaves "nothing known about what the worker did to a system of record other people share"; a document written only in prose is that state exactly, and `reconcile.ts` already grades "too large to check" as distinct from "checked and clean". This is the same distinction reached by an easier route, plus a half the malformed-document case does not carry: a `.json` that fails validation was at least SWEPT, because the sweep runs inside `parseTicketOpsArtifact`, and this one was not. It remains a CEILING and the `rank` guard still applies, so `unknown` (rank -1) is untouched — nothing is weighed on top of evidence the harvest already refused to certify. **PAIRING IS PER-DIRECTORY.** The scan walks `files/` recursively, so both halves may legitimately live in a subdirectory, and a `.json` two directories away is a different document about different work — accepting it would let one validated file vouch for any number of unvalidated ones. **THE CEILING NOW CARRIES ITS OWN REASON, which is a correctness fix and not plumbing.** `harvest/index.ts` printed one fixed sentence for any ceiling the reconciler raised — "a ticket-ops.json artifact failed validation" — and that is FALSE of a document that was never written: nothing was parsed, nothing failed, and an operator told otherwise goes hunting a malformed file that does not exist. **Mutation-proved, four, each restored and sha-verified:** disabling the pairing check reddens 4 probes (39 green); keeping the finding and dropping only the clamp reddens 3 and LEAVES THE FINDING PROBE GREEN, which is what shows the discrepancy and the clamp are independently pinned rather than one assertion counted twice; pairing against any `ticket-ops.json` in the task instead of a sibling reddens exactly the split-directory probe (1/42); and restoring the old fixed sentence reddens exactly the reason probe while `harvest-ticket-ops-wiring.test.ts`'s own ISC-332 reason assertion stays GREEN — the pre-existing suite could not have seen a report misdescribing its own evidence. **A LIMIT THAT MATTERS, AND IT IS ASSERTED BY A TEST RATHER THAN LEFT IN PROSE:** on the LIVE failure shape this criterion does NOT fire, because that worker's `ticket-ops.md` sat inside the unexplained directory and `scanOutboxFiles` walks only `<outbox>/<task>/files/`. ISC-346 and ISC-347 cover that run, and ISC-346's wording carries the credential sentence for exactly this reason. A probe pins the non-firing, so a future change that quietly widened the scan has to face it. **A GAP CLOSED AS A SIDE EFFECT, also pinned:** a `ticket-ops.json` the scan REFUSED never reached the digest loop, so it escaped validation, the sweep and the ceiling together; with the `.md` beside it, the pairing check now catches that shape. **AND A CORRECTION FOUND BY A FAILING PROBE:** an IN-OUTBOX symlink is deliberately ACCEPTED by `scanOutboxFiles` — resolved, opened at the target, reported under the link's own name — so a `ticket-ops.json` symlinked to a sibling is a real validated pair and correctly produces nothing. The first version of that probe assumed a refusal and went red, which is the scan's documented behaviour asserting itself against a wrong assumption.

### Group V — The documentation says what the code does, checked (added 2026-08-30)

An audit of `Docs/SRD.md` against `src/` found eleven divergences. The finding that outranks all
eleven is the PATTERN: documentation currency tracked **proximity to executing code**. `skills/*`
are mounted into workers, `fleet.example.yaml` is built by CI, and both were current. `Docs/SRD.md`
and `CHANGELOG.md` are executed by nothing, and had drifted across eleven merged PRs — including
§5.5's flat "Nothing else is mounted", written while three mounts it did not list were being
emitted, two of them the security-relevant ones (`/policy/cloud-allow`, `/secrets`). These criteria
make the mechanically-checkable half of the document a build failure rather than a reading exercise.

- [x] ISC-351: §5.5's mount table and `src/config/render.ts` name the same set of container paths, checked in BOTH directions — no mount the renderer emits is missing a table ROW, and no row names a path the renderer does not emit. **[FILED AND CLOSED 2026-08-30.]** **Rows, not the section**, and that distinction is the whole probe: the first version searched the §5.5 section TEXT and was decorative — deleting the `/secrets` row left it GREEN, because the erratum immediately below the table names `/secrets` in prose. It passed for a reason that had nothing to do with the table. That was found by MUTATING it, not by reading it, and it is the same "reads as coverage" shape ISC-333 and ISC-343 were filed against, arriving a third time in a probe written to prevent exactly that. Container paths are the key rather than host paths: the host side is a run-scoped placeholder, the container side is a literal both artifacts must agree on. The extractor reads `render.ts` as TEXT and resolves `SECRETS_MOUNT`/`BRIEFING_MOUNT` from their own declarations; importing `buildDockerArgv` would make the probe agree with the code by construction while proving nothing about the DOCUMENT, which is the artifact under test. **Two CONTROLS**, because either extractor silently matching nothing would make the set comparison pass vacuously: emitted ≥ 7 and parsed rows ≥ 7. **MUTATIONS:** dropping the `/secrets` row reddens 1 of 6; dropping the `/policy/cloud-allow` row reddens 1 of 6; adding a phantom `/nope` row reddens the opposite-direction probe alone. Restored and verified clean against `HEAD`.
- [x] ISC-352: §10's command table names every command the CLI registers. **[FILED AND CLOSED 2026-08-30.]** The table listed 20 and `src/cli/commands/*.ts` registers 21; `tui` had never been added, so a command that hands a live worker's pane to a person was absent from the surface an operator reads. The extractor globs the command directory and matches `.command("<name>`, which catches the three registration shapes in use (`"status"`, `"image <action>"`, `"exec [cmd...]"`) without importing Commander. CONTROL: ≥ 20 commands extracted, so a rotted regex cannot pass as "nothing missing". **MUTATION:** removing the `tui` row reddens exactly this probe (1 of 6). Restored.
- [x] ISC-353: §10's exit ladder carries every value in `EXIT`. **[FILED AND CLOSED 2026-08-30.]** `EXIT.INTERNAL: 8` has shipped since ISC-216 and ranks FIRST in `EXIT_SEVERITY` — above every code describing something that happened to the run, because if pifleet itself broke, nothing it reports about the run outranks that. The ladder never carried it, and `contracts.ts`'s own docblock SAID SO ("Not in the SRD §10 ladder") with nothing acting on the sentence for the whole of its existence. **`README.md` had it right, which is the part worth keeping:** the divergence was between two documents as much as between doc and code. **The probe reads the LADDER LINE, not the section**, for the same reason ISC-351 reads rows: this section's own erratum says "`8` was missing from this ladder", so a section-wide search stayed GREEN when `8` was deleted FROM the ladder. Also found by mutation. **MUTATION:** removing `` `8` internal error > `` reddens 1 of 6. Restored.
- [x] ISC-354: Every top-level key of `FleetConfigSchema` is named somewhere in the SRD. **[FILED AND CLOSED 2026-08-30.]** `harness` was a key of a `.strict()` schema — spellable by every operator, and the only lever over the ISC-150 test-harness cap that can turn a `success` into `unknown` — with ZERO occurrences in the design document. It was reachable only by reading `src/config/schema.ts`. §6.5 and §8.2a now carry it. `name` and `version` are excluded from the check as too generic to grep for meaningfully; every other key is a distinctive token. CONTROL: ≥ 10 keys extracted. **MUTATION:** redacting `harness:` and `harness.patterns` from the SRD reddens 1 of 6. Restored.
- [x] ISC-355: The `[~]` count the README states is the count `ISA.md` carries. **[FILED AND CLOSED 2026-08-30.]** The sentence this replaces named ISC-129 as still needing "a run from inside a live cmux pane" ELEVEN DAYS after it was closed and graded `[x]` with live evidence, and described the open set as "a few carried from Phase 3" when every one of the five had an ID above 300. **The probe was exercised for real rather than only by mutation:** it was written while `main` carried five `[~]`, and merging #118 took the tree to seven — the probe went RED on the rebase, named the number, and the README was corrected. That is the mechanism working on its first live opportunity rather than a hypothetical. **Only the countable half is checked**, deliberately: which criteria are open, and why each is `[~]`, is prose no test can grade. **MUTATION:** `Five` → `Six` reddens 1 of 6. Restored.
- [x] ISC-356: The SRD records the two behaviours it was silent about — that granted secrets are delivered as FILES, and that a diff touching the test harness caps the verdict. **[FILED AND CLOSED 2026-08-30.]** Both are user-visible behaviours an operator would reason wrongly about from the old text: §12.4 described only environment delivery, so a reader would conclude `echo $NAME` prints a credential (it prints an empty line, and has since ISC-337..342 on 2026-08-29); §8 described the harvester re-running acceptance as authoritative with no mention that touching `test/**` collapses anything above `blocked` to `unknown`. Registered as greps rather than as a test, because what is being checked is that a PARAGRAPH exists and says a specific thing — a claim a grep answers completely, unlike ISC-344's shape where a grep proves an instruction was shipped and cannot observe a worker obeying it. **NOT CLAIMED: that the rest of the SRD's prose is accurate.** Eleven divergences were found by reading; only the four mechanical invariants (ISC-351..354) are re-checked by a build. The judgement half still needs a reader, and this criterion does not pretend otherwise.
- [x] ISC-357: Every `PIFLEET_*` environment variable the SRD names in normative prose is one the code actually reads. **[FILED AND CLOSED 2026-08-30.]** §15 told a reader the Pi test double is "selected via `PIFLEET_PI_BIN`". No such variable exists: `grep -rnF 'PIFLEET_PI_BIN' src/ test/ docker/` returned nothing, and the name is `PIFLEET_PI_COMMAND` (`src/cli/commands/up.ts:312` decides whether a run is a double run from it, `:481` refuses a no-config `up` when it is unset, `:1356` forwards it to each supervisor). **THIS ONE MATTERED MORE THAN A TYPO BECAUSE OF WHAT THE VARIABLE IS FOR:** it is the only way to run the acceptance suite at all, and §17's preamble says the suite runs "against `pifleet-fake-pi`", so the one document that says how to run the done-condition named a variable nothing reads. `src/supervisor/index.ts:30` had the correct name in a comment the whole time, which is the ISC-115 shape — the source knew and the design did not. EVIDENCE: `test/unit/docs-currency.test.ts` > "no SRD-named PIFLEET_* variable is absent from src/, docker/ and test/" extracts every `PIFLEET_[A-Z0-9_]+` from the SRD and requires each to appear somewhere under `src/`, `docker/` or `test/`. **MUTATION-PROVED, and the FIRST VERSION WAS DECORATIVE IN TWO WAYS AT ONCE — both found by mutating it, neither by reading it.** (1) It scanned the whole document, and an erratum correcting a wrong variable name has to SPELL that name, so the correction was indistinguishable from the error; erratum block-quote lines are now stripped and only normative prose is scanned. (2) Its own docstring names `PIFLEET_PI_BIN` while explaining the defect, and while this file was in the corpus **the test satisfied the probe on the document's behalf** — it went green with the defect still in §15. `test/support/isa-claims.ts` excludes itself for exactly this reason and this file now does too. Proof after both fixes: adding "or `PIFLEET_PI_BIN`" back to §15's normative sentence fails this probe with `the SRD names these PIFLEET_* variables and nothing in src/, docker/ or test/ mentions them: PIFLEET_PI_BIN`, and fails nothing else (8 pass / 1 fail); restored, `git diff --stat` empty. **WHAT IT DOES NOT COVER, stated because the exclusion is real:** a wrong variable name inside an erratum is invisible here, which is the price of being able to write errata about variable names at all.
- [x] ISC-358: §4.1's CLI table has a row for every cmux command `doctor` treats as required. **[FILED AND CLOSED 2026-08-30.]** `respawn-pane` has been in `REQUIRED_COMMANDS` (`src/backends/cmux/capabilities.ts:43`) with §4.1's table carrying no row for it at all, and it is not a marginal command — `capabilities.ts:35-36` says it "is how a viewer starts in a split pane", so without it panes are empty shells and ISC-129 is unmeetable, and `doctor` exits 3 on its absence (`src/cli/commands/doctor.ts:390-391`). The table is the only place an operator reading the design learns which commands that exit means, so a required row missing from it is a diagnosis with no documented cause. `rename-tab` (`src/backends/cmux/client.ts:113-127`, invoked at `index.ts:222`) was also absent and is added as `optional`, which is what it is — `index.ts:221-225` catches its failure because "losing it costs a label, not a fact". EVIDENCE: `test/unit/docs-currency.test.ts` > "every REQUIRED_COMMANDS entry has a §4.1 table ROW" parses `REQUIRED_COMMANDS` out of `capabilities.ts` and requires each name to appear as a `| \`cmux <verb>` TABLE ROW. **ROWS ONLY, and that is what the mutation proves:** deleting the `respawn-pane` row leaves the word `respawn-pane` in the section three times over, in the erratum prose that explains it, and the probe still goes red — `§4.1's CLI table has no row for these commands, which \`doctor\` treats as required and exits 3 without: respawn-pane` — failing nothing else (8 pass / 1 fail). Restored, `git diff --stat` empty. This is ISC-351's and ISC-353's finding applied in advance rather than after the fact.
- [x] ISC-359: §7.6's `state.json` block names every top-level field of `WorkerStateSchema`. **[FILED AND CLOSED 2026-08-30.]** The block omitted two, and both are control-plane state a reader would reason wrongly about from its absence. `proc_started` (`src/contracts.ts:255`) is the launch-time, `ps`-comparable process identity the kill ladder and the reaper compare against so a recycled pid is never signalled (`src/safety/kill.ts:406-407`); it is DELIBERATELY distinct from `started_at`, which the block did carry, so the document showed the wall-clock record and hid the one signalling safety rests on. `credential` (`src/contracts.ts:309-322`) is the ADC refresh loop's durable state — `{injections, generation, degraded, last_failure, last_injected_at}` — and is what `status` reads to say a worker's Google identity has gone stale; §5.8 describes the refresh loop at length and §7.6 showed no field it writes to. EVIDENCE: `test/unit/docs-currency.test.ts` > "every top-level WorkerStateSchema key appears in §7.6's JSON block" extracts the schema's 2-space-indented keys and requires each as a quoted key in the section's ```json FENCE, not in the section — so the erratum explaining the two additions cannot satisfy the probe on their behalf. MUTATION-PROVED: dropping the `"proc_started"` line from the block fails with `§7.6's state.json block omits these WorkerStateSchema fields: proc_started`, while `proc_started` still appears once in the section's erratum prose, and fails nothing else (8 pass / 1 fail); restored, `git diff --stat` empty.
- [-] ISC-360: SRD §5.10 and §17's criterion 59 record that task-scoped cloud authorization is DESIGNED but not BUILT — the verbgate's policy file is written empty at `up` and never rewritten, so the `cloud_allow[]` an operator writes into a dispatch envelope reaches no container. **[FILED 2026-08-30 as a PARTIAL, and the grade is the point.]** THE MEASUREMENT: `src/config/render.ts:272` mounts `${opts.worker.cloudAllow}:/policy/cloud-allow:ro` — per WORKER, fixed at container start; `src/run/materialize.ts:806` is `await writeFile(paths.cloudAllow, "")` and is the only writer in the tree (`grep -rn 'cloudAllow' src/` returns ten lines: one write, one mount, one launch-record field, and seven path/permission lines); `src/cli/commands/dispatch.ts:953` puts `cloud_allow` into the ENVELOPE, which travels to the supervisor and is rendered into a Pi prompt, and no leg of that path writes the mounted policy. **THE CODE SAYS SO ITSELF**, which is why this is a documentation gap rather than a discovery: `src/run/materialize.ts:783` opens "WHOEVER WIRES DISPATCH-TIME REWRITING:" and specifies the procedure that writer must follow — chmod 0644, write IN PLACE, chmod back to 0444, never tmp+rename because a bind mount pins the inode. A correct spec for work nobody has done, and this SRD read as though it had been. **SECOND CONSEQUENCE:** `docker/verbgate:45` and `:78` read `PIFLEET_TASK_ID`/`PIFLEET_EPOCH` for the ledger row's provenance, and `grep -rnF 'PIFLEET_TASK_ID' src/` returns nothing — both are set only by `test/integration/verbgate.test.ts` and `test/integration/image.test.ts` — so the `{task_id, epoch, argv}` §5.10's diagram promises is `{"<none>", 0, argv}` for every row a real run produces, and §17's criterion 59 is unmeetable in both halves. **WHY `[~]` AND NOT `[x]`:** two registered claims re-check the CODE side completely — the empty write is exactly one line, and `PIFLEET_TASK_ID` is absent from `src/` — and neither re-checks the DOCUMENT side, which is prose. Worse, the first claim is pinned on a line whose PRESENCE proves nothing about a second writer being ADDED elsewhere; only the `PIFLEET_TASK_ID` absence catches that, and it catches it only because any real implementation of task-scoped authorization must bind the task id. That is a real guard with a named hole, which is `[~]`, not `[x]`. **WHAT WOULD CLOSE IT:** the rewriter itself, built to `materialize.ts:783`'s spec, plus a probe that dispatches a task with `cloud_allow: ["kubectl scale"]` and asserts the mounted policy contains it — at which point this criterion is retired rather than closed, because §5.10 stops needing an erratum. **WHAT SHIPS IS SAFER THAN WHAT WAS DOCUMENTED**, and that is stated so the gap is not read as a bypass: an empty policy refuses every mutating verb with exit 77, so no mutating verb executes at all rather than the ones an envelope named. `impersonate_service_account` remains the load-bearing control, exactly as §5.10 already said. **PREMISE SUPERSEDED 2026-08-30 BY ISC-366 — the owner DESCOPED the rewriter rather than building it.** This entry's "WHAT WOULD CLOSE IT" named two exits and assumed the first; the second was taken. §5.10 no longer records the mechanism as designed-but-not-built, it records it as withdrawn, and `cloud_allow[]` is refused at parse time rather than accepted and ignored. **THIS ENTRY IS NOT RE-GRADED and stays `[~]`**, for the same reason it was `[~]` on the day it was filed: what it asserts is that a DOCUMENT records something, and its registered claims re-check only the code half. That shape is unchanged by the descope. Re-grading it to `[x]` because the underlying question was settled would be grading the DECISION rather than the EVIDENCE, which is the substitution this ISA exists to refuse. **SECOND CONSEQUENCE CLOSED 2026-08-30 BY ISC-362:** the ledger now carries the real task id and epoch, delivered as a read-only mounted FILE rather than the environment this entry expected any fix to set — so `§17`'s criterion 59 is now unmeetable in ONE half rather than both. The registered `PIFLEET_TASK_ID` absence claim survived that commit GREEN, having predicted it would redden, and is re-worded at the claim site as the record of a guard pinned to a proxy instead of to the property. **[RETIRED 2026-08-30 — PREMISE SUPERSEDED BY ISC-366, under the marker ISC-368 introduces.]** **THIS ENTRY ARGUED AGAINST RE-GRADING ITSELF AND WAS RIGHT; IT HAD NO THIRD OPTION.** The paragraph above refuses `[x]` because closing a criterion on the strength of a DECISION rather than on evidence is the substitution this ISA exists to prevent, and that reasoning is unchanged and is not withdrawn here. What was missing was anywhere else to put it. The criterion asserts that a DOCUMENT records the mechanism as designed-but-not-built; §5.10 stopped recording that on 2026-08-30 and now records it as withdrawn, so the sentence is not under-evidenced — it is about a state of the SRD that no longer exists. `[~]` cannot express that, and this entry sitting inside `8 [~]` is what made ISC-368 worth building rather than worth arguing about. **THE ENTRY PREDICTED ITS OWN MARKER.** Its "WHAT WOULD CLOSE IT" paragraph ends "at which point this criterion is retired rather than closed, because §5.10 stops needing an erratum" — written 2026-08-30 on the assumption the rewriter would be BUILT. The owner took the other exit and the consequence is identical: the erratum went away, and the vocabulary the entry reached for did not exist yet. **BOTH REGISTERED CLAIMS STAY, AT `[-]`, AND ONE OF THEM IS NOW MORE LOAD-BEARING THAN IT WAS.** The empty-write pin still proves the shipped behaviour is the safe one. The `PIFLEET_TASK_ID` absence — which failed as a PREDICTOR of the rewriter being built, and whose failure is recorded verbatim at the claim site — is now a REGRESSION GUARD on a DESCOPE: it goes red if the withdrawn mechanism comes back through the environment carrier ISC-362 rejected. Deleting these two guards along with the grade would have been the exact abuse ISC-368 refuses, and is why the marker's rule is that retirement subtracts from `progress:` and from nothing else. **WHAT THIS RETIREMENT DOES NOT CLAIM.** Not that §5.10's prose is re-checked by anything — it is prose, that was the `[~]`, and ISC-366's own entry carries whatever machine-checkable half exists. Not that §17's criterion 59 is now meetable: it is not, it is withdrawn. Not that the second consequence's history is superseded — ISC-362 closed it, that closure is evidenced there, and none of it is re-opened by retiring the entry that reported it.
- [x] ISC-361: SRD §12.8's reachable set reflects that the bridge-gateway residual was CLOSED, not accepted. **[FILED 2026-08-30 as a PARTIAL.]** THE DRIFT WAS GOOD NEWS GOING UNRECORDED, which is a direction this ISA had not seen before. §12.8's 2026-08-19 erratum measured the residual honestly — an `--internal` bridge implements isolation as FORWARD-chain rules, the gateway is on-link and inside the subnet, so gateway-destined traffic is delivered through INPUT and every port the Docker host listens on is reachable — and concluded "Accepted as a residual, not fixed. Closing it requires either host-side `iptables` DROP rules … or a dedicated Docker host whose gateway serves nothing. Neither is in scope here." The first option was subsequently built: `src/security/gateway-block.ts:110` emits `[op, "INPUT", "-i", bridge, "-d", gateway, "-j", "DROP"]`, applied in the host network namespace by `nsenter` from a privileged short-lived container (`:113-121`), installed from inside `ensureEgressNetwork` (`src/security/network.ts:217`) on the adopt path as well as after create, refusing to start when it cannot be installed or verified (`gateway-block.ts:185-205`). `test/integration/relay.test.ts:554` enumerates the gateway across all 65535 ports and asserts the reachable set is EMPTY, and its own docstring says the result "would be GOOD NEWS to be written into SRD §12.8 and ISC-51 … That is exactly what happened" — to the code, and not to the document, for as long as it took this audit to notice. Three reachable-set unions in §12.8 were consequently overstating the exposure; they now read `{relay listen ports} ∪ {sibling containers} ∪ {one LAN host:port, where authorized}`, and the sibling-container term is still open-ended and still unaddressed. **WHY `[~]` AND NOT `[x]`:** the two registered claims pin the RULE SHAPE (the narrow `-i`/`-d` pair, so a generalisation to a blanket drop reddens) and the CALL SITE inside `ensureEgressNetwork`. Neither can observe that the call is UNCONDITIONAL — wrapping it in an `if` leaves both lines intact and both claims green — and nothing outside the Docker-gated `container` job re-runs the port enumeration that is the actual evidence. The property is real and is proved live in CI; what is not re-checked at unit speed is the mandatory-ness the erratum leans on. **WHAT WOULD CLOSE IT:** a unit-level assertion that `ensureEgressNetwork` cannot return without `ensureGatewayBlocked` having succeeded — the seam exists, and it was not built here. **CLOSED 2026-08-30 — THE ASSERTION WAS BUILT, and the criterion is re-graded to `[x]` on this line.** `test/unit/gateway-containment-mandatory.test.ts` asserts over the comment-stripped body of `ensureEgressNetwork` that EVERY `return` is immediately preceded by an `await containGateway(...)` at the SAME indentation, that the containment calls and the returns are equal in number, and that `containGateway` itself has no `return` at all and ends on `await ensureGatewayBlocked(...)`. Same-indentation is the load-bearing half: the adopt-path call already sits inside `if (before.exists)`, so "is nested at all" cannot be the test — what must not happen is the call becoming conditional RELATIVE TO ITS OWN RETURN, which is exactly a deeper indent than the `return` it guards. Structural rather than behavioural for the reason `supervisor-session-latch.test.ts` gives: `docker()` is a private module-scope spawn in `gateway-block.ts` and `inspectEgressNetwork` spawns its own, so reaching the containment path without a daemon needs two module mocks, at which point the test asserts over a graph it built rather than the one that ships. **MUTATION-PROVED, five mutations, each restored clean:** wrapping the adopt-path containment in an `if` — the gap this entry NAMED, and it reddens; deleting the create-path call; adding a third return with no containment; an early `return` inside `containGateway` before the firewall call; and deleting that call. **THE FIRST VERSION WAS DECORATIVE AND TWO OF THE FIVE FOUND IT:** the return detector matched `/^\s*return\b/`, so `if (x) return y;` on one line — the cheapest possible way to add an uncontained exit — was invisible to it and left the probe green. It now matches `return` anywhere on a line and treats a return sharing its line with a condition as an offender by construction.

- [x] ISC-362: The verbgate ledger names the task that caused each verb, and the worker cannot forge it. **[FILED AND CLOSED 2026-08-30.]** ISC-360's second consequence, repaired. `docker/verbgate` read `PIFLEET_TASK_ID`/`PIFLEET_EPOCH` and `grep -rnF 'PIFLEET_TASK_ID' src/` returned nothing, so every row in every production run read `{"task_id":"<none>","epoch":0}` — an audit trail that recorded THAT a destructive verb was attempted while losing WHICH task attempted it. **THE OBVIOUS FIX WAS WRONG TWICE, AND THAT IS THE FINDING WORTH KEEPING.** Setting the two variables in the worker's `--env-file` fails because (1) the env file is written once at materialize time while a worker container is LONG-LIVED and takes many epochs over its life — a dispatch is a prompt to a running Pi process (`src/rpc/epoch.ts`), not a new container — so the value would name the FIRST task forever and misattribute every later one, which is worse than an honest `<none>`; and (2) `verbgate`'s own header says the variables are "environment the WORKER controls", so a worker could forge the one field an investigator would trust. Provenance is now `/policy/task`, a run-tree file bind-mounted **read-only** beside `/policy/cloud-allow` (`src/config/render.ts`, `src/run/task-policy.ts`), written by the supervisor at each dispatch and cleared at settle. **THE REWRITE FOLLOWS `materialize.ts:783`'s SPEC FOR THE WRITER NOBODY HAD BUILT** — chmod 0644, truncate IN PLACE, chmod back to 0444, never tmp+rename, because a bind mount pins the INODE and a rename swaps the file the host sees while the container reads the old one for its whole life with both sides believing the policy changed. EVIDENCE: `test/unit/task-policy.test.ts`, thirteen tests, and two registered claims. **MUTATION-PROVED, eight mutations, each reddening its own probe and no other, each restored with an empty `git diff --stat`:** rename-based write -> the INODE test alone; dropping the final chmod -> the 0444 test alone; dropping line sanitisation -> the two format tests; reverting `verbgate` to the env carrier -> the file-read test; removing the provenance path from the integrity loop -> the integrity test; deleting the dispatch write -> the ordering test plus the call-site count; deleting the settle clear -> the settle test plus the count; deleting the §5.5 row -> both mount-table directions. **THE ORDERING IS PROBED STRUCTURALLY, on comment-stripped source, and the reason is `supervisor-session-latch.test.ts`'s:** an integration test cannot separate "written before the prompt" from "written after it", because the failure needs the worker to invoke a gated verb in the instant after being prompted and no test schedules that reliably; what IS observable is that the write sits between `persistFence()` and the busy transition, and that there are exactly TWO call sites so neither can cover for a deleted other. **THIS PASS ALSO FOUND A BLIND SPOT IN ISC-351's OWN PROBE.** `docs-currency.test.ts`'s mount extractor resolved container paths that are named CONSTANTS from a hardcoded list of two — `SECRETS_MOUNT`, `BRIEFING_MOUNT` — and silently skipped any other. `${TASK_POLICY_MOUNT}` walked straight through it: a new mount was added, the SRD row was absent, and the probe built to catch exactly that stayed GREEN. It now resolves EVERY `${NAME}` in a `-v` push by searching `src/` for the declaration and FAILS on one it cannot resolve, because silence was the failure mode. Found by a real change failing to redden the probe, not by reading it — the third time in this ISA that a probe's own blind spot was invisible until something moved. **NOT CLAIMED:** that `cloud_allow[]` now reaches a container. It does not; ISC-360's first consequence stands, `/policy/cloud-allow` is still written empty and never rewritten, and every mutating verb is still refused rather than authorized. This criterion repairs the audit trail, not the authorization.
- [x] ISC-363: Every repo path and every pifleet-owned constant the SRD names in normative prose resolves in the tree. **[FILED AND CLOSED 2026-08-30.]** #121 verified §17's 89 criteria by extracting each identifier and grepping for it BY HAND — four were dead, and the pass cost an agent two hours. The operation is mechanical and it generalises to the whole document, which is the difference between this and the judgement half: whether a named symbol EXISTS is decidable, whether a paragraph describes the system is not. It catches the class that audit named "the wrong instrument" — prose that describes a real behaviour while naming a file or constant that does not exist, which reads correctly to someone who already knows the system and is fatal to someone who does not, because the name is the only handle they have. **TWO CORPORA, AND THE SPLIT WAS MEASURED RATHER THAN ASSUMED.** Paths are swept over the WHOLE document including errata, because a path is a pointer and not a claim: an erratum citing `src/foo.ts:12` to prove old text wrong is still pointing at code that must exist. Constants are swept over normative prose ONLY, block-quote lines stripped, because an erratum correcting a wrong constant has to SPELL it — that is ISC-357's finding reused rather than rediscovered. The measurement: over the whole document the constant sweep flags `ADC_FILE_PATH` and `PIFLEET_PI_BIN`, and BOTH appear only inside errata written to say they are wrong; stripping block quotes removes both and removes no true finding. **TWO REAL DEFECTS ON THE FIRST RUN.** §4.2 cited `docker/pi-worker.Dockerfile` as the image's build file; the file is `docker/Dockerfile` and has been throughout (`src/cli/commands/doctor.ts`, `src/security/adc.ts` and `src/harvest/acceptance-container.ts` all name it correctly) — a reader following the design to the build would have looked for a file that does not exist. And §13's control-socket requirement line named three instruments wrong at once: the uid check is not `LOCAL_PEERCRED` but `getpeereid` on macOS/BSD and `getsockopt(SO_PEERCRED)` on Linux (`src/security/peer-uid.ts`, the split MEASURED — glibc does not export `getpeereid` at all); the socket is mode 0700, not 0600; and a stale socket is unlinked unconditionally, not probed for `ECONNREFUSED`. **THAT SECOND ONE IS THE ARGUMENT FOR THE PROBE IN ONE FINDING:** #121 corrected §12.7's account of the same socket four hours earlier and left §13's requirement line saying the old thing, because a section-by-section read fixes the section it is reading. A document sweep does not have sections. **THE ALLOWLIST IS FOUR ENTRIES, EACH WITH A REASON, AND IS ITSELF GUARDED TWICE** — capped at six by an assertion, and every entry required to still appear in the SRD, so an exemption cannot outlive the text that justified it. All four are cmux's own environment (`CMUX_SOCKET_PATH`, `CMUX_SOCKET`, `CMUX_SOCKET_MODE`, `CMUX_SOCKET_PASSWORD`), which pifleet neither sets nor reads; `CMUX_SOCKET_MODE` is named by §17 precisely to record that it does NOT exist, so it is a negative claim a presence check cannot evaluate. **MUTATION-PROVED, five mutations including a MUST-NOT-FIRE case, each restored with an empty `git diff --stat`:** a dead path in normative prose reddens the path probe; a dead path inside an ERRATUM reddens it too (the intended asymmetry); a dead constant in normative prose reddens the constant probe; a dead constant inside an erratum fires NOTHING, which is the behaviour that keeps errata writable; and a stale allowlist entry reddens the staleness guard. **NOT CLAIMED:** that the SRD's prose is accurate. This checks that names RESOLVE, not that the sentences around them are true — a paragraph can name every symbol correctly and still describe behaviour the code does not have, which is exactly what #121 found six times in §13 and what no sweep can decide. Bare lowercase backticked words (`compact`, `blocked`) are deliberately not swept: English prose backticks ordinary words constantly, and the allowlist needed would be longer than the findings.
- [x] ISC-364: The documents MOUNTED INTO WORKERS agree with the code on the two things in them that are decidable — the statuses a worker is told to write, and the container paths it is told it has. **[FILED AND CLOSED 2026-08-30.]** #121 found that documentation currency tracks proximity to executing code, and drew half a wrong conclusion from it: `skills/` and `roles/` were CURRENT in the sense of being mounted and CI-built, and three of the audit's findings were in them anyway. Mounting guarantees a worker READS a document, not that what it reads is true, and these are the worst files in the tree to be wrong in — an SRD that is wrong misleads a human who can push back, a `SKILL.md` that is wrong is an instruction executed by an agent that cannot. The three: `SKILL.md` told workers a guessed outbox directory is "not reported" and "nothing goes looking for it" when ISC-346..348 had built exactly that reporting; it said "a half-written envelope is read as a missing one" when it is REFUSED, which records a discrepancy and caps the harvest at `partial`; and `roles/ticketing.md` said writing only `ticket-ops.md` "reports clean" when it clamps to `failed`. **WHAT IS AND IS NOT CHECKABLE, stated because most of a worker document is not.** Guidance is judgement and no probe decides it. Two things are neither: a worker that writes a status outside `StatusSchema` has its envelope refused, and a worker told it has a mount it was not given wastes an epoch finding out. Both are set comparisons against the code. EVIDENCE: `test/unit/worker-docs-currency.test.ts`. **MUTATION-PROVED, five mutations including a MUST-NOT-FIRE case:** adding a fifth status to `StatusSchema` reddens the schema→document direction; changing `failed` to `bogus` in the instruction sentence reddens BOTH directions; naming a top-level directory that does not exist reddens the path probe; naming `/tmp` fires nothing, which is the behaviour that keeps ordinary container paths writable in prose; and rewriting the sentence so the "`aborted` and `timed_out` are not yours to report" clause reads as part of the enumeration reddens it — the extractor cuts at the first full stop precisely so a probe cannot invert the document's meaning. **THE PATH PROBE WAS DECORATIVE WHEN FIRST WRITTEN, and this is the fourth time in this ISA.** Its character class excluded `<` and `>`, so every path carrying a placeholder was invisible to it — including `/outbox/<task-id>/result.json`, the one the entire envelope contract turns on. Rewriting that path to a directory that does not exist left the probe GREEN. Found by mutating, not by reading, and the mutation that found it is the one now recorded as W3. **NOT CLAIMED: that a worker is told the truth about CONDITIONAL mounts.** `SKILL.md` promises `/workspace` unconditionally while four of seven roles get it read-only or not at all, and this probe cannot see that — it compares against the set of paths `render` can emit, not against what any particular role receives. The conditional half needs the role dimension and is not built here.
- [x] ISC-365: §13's failure table says NOT BUILT in the cells whose mitigation does not exist, and a tripwire goes red on the commit that builds one. **[FILED AND CLOSED 2026-08-30.]** #121 found six mitigations written in the present tense that do not exist and recorded them in ONE erratum below the table. That was the right finding and the wrong placement: §13 is a failure taxonomy, which is consulted DURING an incident by someone scanning rows, and a named mitigation stops the reader looking further. A blank cell sends them onward; a cell naming `skipped:dependency_failed` sends them looking for why it did not fire. Each of the six now carries **NOT BUILT** inline, with what IS real in the same cell where the row is mixed — F11's smaller briefs and report flag are built and its pre-emptive `compact` is not; F35's `exit 2` on a cycle is built and its `skipped:dependency_failed` is not; F36's periodic refresh and re-injection are built and its "re-mints once before failing the epoch" is not. **RE-VERIFIED INDEPENDENTLY rather than taken from the audit report** (`grep -rF` against `src/`): `"compact"` 0 hits, `backoff` 0, `get_last_assistant_text` 0, `dependency_failed` 0, `invalid_grant` 0. F12 needed more care than a count — `get_session_stats` returns NINE hits, and every one is a COMMENT; `src/harvest/usage.ts` states that the only executable `get_session_stats` in the repository is the RESPONDER in the test double, and `src/cli/commands/harvest.ts` says in its own words that nothing sends it, so the 60-second sampler the detection column promised has never existed. F36's mitigation half was checked at the seam rather than by grep: `onFailure` sets `degraded: true` and flushes state — it degrades LOUDLY and does not kill the epoch, which is the opposite of "re-mints once before failing" it. **THE FIVE REGISTERED CLAIMS ARE TRIPWIRES, WHICH IS THE ONLY GRADE-HONEST SHAPE FOR THIS.** Each is an ABSENCE claim on the identifier the mitigation would have to introduce. A presence claim would assert that a document says NOT BUILT, which a build can check and which tells you nothing about whether it is still TRUE; the absence claim goes red on the commit that implements the mitigation, which is precisely when the row must stop saying NOT BUILT. The guard is pinned to the blocker, so removing the blocker turns it red — the shape this ISA has been using since the `[~]` grading rule was settled. **WHAT THE TRIPWIRES CANNOT SEE:** an implementation that introduces none of the five identifiers. `backoff` in particular is a behaviour, not a name, and a retry loop spelled with `setTimeout` and a doubling delay would satisfy F13 while leaving that claim green.
