- [x] ISC-366: Task-scoped cloud authorization is DESCOPED, and `cloud_allow[]` is refused at parse time rather than accepted and ignored. **[FILED AND CLOSED 2026-08-30 BY OWNER DECISION, superseding ISC-360's premise.]** ISC-360 recorded the mechanism as designed-but-not-built and named two ways out: build the rewriter to `materialize.ts`'s spec, or descope it. The owner descoped it. **A DESCOPE THAT LEAVES THE FIELD ACCEPTED IS NOT A DESCOPE, and that is the whole substance of this entry.** `cloud_allow[]` travelled from the envelope into the worker's PROMPT (`src/roles/briefings.ts` composes it; `dispatch.ts` puts it on the envelope) while never reaching `/policy/cloud-allow`, so an operator writing `cloud_allow: ["kubectl scale"]` got a brief telling the worker it may scale, a worker that tried, and a gate that refused with exit 77 — one epoch spent discovering that a grant the document offered does not exist. A field that is accepted and does nothing is not a withdrawn feature; it is a trap with a plausible name. Both `TaskSpecSchema` (what an operator writes) and `TaskEnvelopeSchema` (what the supervisor parses off the control socket) now REFUSE a non-empty value, and the message names the reason and the alternative rather than saying "invalid" — a bare type error would send the operator hunting for a typo in a field working exactly as intended. Both doors, because guarding only the spec leaves the socket accepting a grant it cannot honour, and the socket is the one an out-of-band caller reaches. The KEY stays in both schemas at length zero: the envelope is a wire format and removing a key is a compatibility break for a change whose entire point is that nothing depends on it. EVIDENCE: `test/unit/cloud-allow-descoped.test.ts`, five tests. **MUTATION-PROVED, five mutations, each reddening its own probe and restored with an empty `git diff --stat`:** restoring the plain array on the spec schema; restoring it on the envelope schema; stripping the reason out of the refusal message; adding a SECOND `writeFile(paths.cloudAllow, …)` in `materialize.ts`; and adding a policy write to `dispatch.ts`. **THE LAST TWO ARE THE TRIPWIRE HALF, and a descope needs one.** A descope is a decision, not a state: what would quietly undo it is a second writer appearing, at which point §5.10's "refuses EVERY mutating verb, for every worker, for the life of every run" becomes false with no document changing. The probe pins the write CALL, not mentions of `cloudAllow` — the path definition, the mount and the launch record all name it legitimately, and a claim counting those would be noise nobody could act on. **WHAT SHIPS, STATED PLAINLY BECAUSE IT IS NOW THE DESIGN RATHER THAN A SHORTFALL:** the mounted policy is empty for the life of every run, every mutating cloud verb is refused with exit 77, read verbs are untouched, and the load-bearing control is the CREDENTIAL's scope via `cloud.impersonate_service_account` — which §5.10 always called the stronger of the two, with the verb gate as defence-in-depth on top rather than a substitute. Descoping the weaker half leaves that argument intact. **NOT CLAIMED:** that the verb gate is unnecessary. It still runs, still refuses, and still ledgers every decision with the task provenance ISC-362 gave it; what is withdrawn is the ability to WIDEN it per task.
- [x] ISC-367: The worker's prompt carries the `task_id` and `outbox` it was dispatched under, so the placeholder the shipped documents ask it to bind is bindable. **[FILED AND CLOSED 2026-08-30, from the re-read of ISC-349.]** ISC-349 measured a ticketing worker writing to `/outbox/list-tickets-2026-08-29/` — a slug of the job it thought it had done — while the id it was dispatched under was `my-iteration-2`, and graded itself `[~]` because what shipped in response was INSTRUCTION. **THE RE-READ FOUND THE INSTRUCTION WAS NOT WEAK, IT WAS UNFOLLOWABLE, and that all three routes to the value were closed.** `renderPrompt` (`src/supervisor/index.ts`) took `title`, `brief` and `acceptance` and nothing else, so `task_id` and `outbox` sat in `TaskEnvelopeSchema`, reached the supervisor, and never reached the agent — still true on 2026-08-30, five criteria after the finding. `PIFLEET_TASK_ID` was set nowhere in production, and ISC-362 fixed that for the verbgate's LEDGER by mounting a file the GATE reads, which is not a route to the agent. And `materialize.ts` creates only the worker-level directory that becomes the `/outbox` mount, so `<outbox>/<task-id>` cannot be discovered by listing. A worker asked for a path whose middle component it had no route to, by any means available to it, was going to guess. **THIS IS §5.10's SHAPE FOUND WHERE THE READER IS AN AGENT RATHER THAN A PERSON** — a document asking for something the system does not supply — and it is worse there, because a person pushes back and an agent complies with whatever it can construct. Both identifiers are now rendered into the prompt in a fenced block under its own heading, naming which placeholders they bind — **DELIVERY ONLY, and the first attempt got that wrong.** It also told the worker to write `<outbox>/result.json` LAST, and CI's live chain (ISC-290) went from `complete` to `partial` on it. THE MECHANISM, confirmed in the code rather than guessed: `src/harvest/index.ts` degrades the harvest when `outbox.kind === "refused"`, and `src/harvest/outbox.ts` returns `missing` — which is NOT degrading — when no `result.json` exists at all. A worker that had been writing NO envelope started writing a malformed one, and a refused envelope is worse for the harvest than an absent one, exactly as `skills/pifleet-worker/SKILL.md` already tells workers. **THE ERROR WAS THIS CRITERION'S OWN LESSON APPLIED BACKWARDS:** ISC-349's finding is that the placeholder was UNBINDABLE, and the repair for that is the VALUE, not another imperative. `SKILL.md` is mounted into every container and already says what to write, where, in what order and what it must contain; a terser second copy in the prompt competed with it and added nothing the worker did not have. The block now names the two values and says which placeholders they bind, and nothing else. EVIDENCE: `test/unit/prompt-identity.test.ts`, five tests, importing the shipped `renderPrompt` rather than re-implementing its template — a local copy would drift and the test would keep passing over a prompt nobody sends. **MUTATION-PROVED, four mutations, each reddening its probe and restored with `git diff --stat` empty ON THE MUTATED FILE:** dropping `task_id` from the block; dropping `outbox` from it; unfencing the block; and prepending identity ahead of the brief. **TWO OF THE FOUR EXPOSED A DECORATIVE ASSERTION ON THE FIRST RUN, the fifth and sixth in this ISA.** The fence check took `indexOf("```")` and was satisfied by the CLOSING fence alone, so deleting the opening one left it green; and it checked only `task_id`, so moving `outbox` out of the block was invisible. It now requires a matched PAIR of fences with both identifiers between them. **NOT CLAIMED — and this is why ISC-349 is NOT re-graded:** this proves DELIVERY, that the dispatched value appears in the text the worker is prompted with. It cannot prove OBEDIENCE, and nothing at unit speed can. What changed is that the failure mode is now disobedience rather than impossibility, and only the first of those is the worker's to fix.
- [x] ISC-368: A criterion whose PREMISE was superseded can be RETIRED — marked `[-]`, excluded from `progress:` on both sides, reported by a `retired:` count — and retirement is refused unless it names a closed criterion that names it back. **[FILED AND CLOSED 2026-08-30.]** **THE MEASUREMENT THAT FILED IT.** `ISA.md` had three markers and no fourth, so a criterion whose subject had been replaced stayed at its grade and stayed counted, with the supersession recorded in prose INSIDE the entry. `grep -cE 'RETIRED|SUPERSEDED' ISA.md` found only such inline notes and no marker any counter excluded. Two had accumulated: ISC-307, whose headline had read `[PREMISE SUPERSEDED BY ISC-337 on 2026-08-28]` for two days while the grade stood, and ISC-360, superseded by ISC-366's descope on 2026-08-30. Both sat at `[~]` inside a figure of 8. **THE COST IS ARITHMETIC, NOT TASTE:** `N [~]` had come to mean "N criteria are unproved OR withdrawn", two facts under one number, and the withdrawn ones are invisible unless a reader opens all eight entries — which is precisely what a headline exists to spare them. **WHY `[-]` AND NOT A WORD.** The three counting greps are `^- \[x\] ISC-`, `^- \[~\] ISC-` and `^- \[ \] ISC-`, so any fourth marker had to be one character inside the brackets or every counter in the repo would need a different shape. `-` is the task-list convention for cancelled, renders as an ordinary list item exactly as `[~]` already does rather than as a checked box, and is one character from `[x]` in no direction that a typo produces silently — the accounting assertion in `test/unit/isa-frontmatter.test.ts` fails on any bracket content that is none of the four. **EVERY COUNTING SITE WAS FOUND BY GREPPING FOR THE PARSERS RATHER THAN BY MEMORY, and one of them was a latent false positive nobody would have attributed to this change.** `src/attended/voided.ts`'s `definedIscIds` matched `^- \[[ x~]\]`, and its own comment records that this class was `[ x]` once and that grading a criterion `[~]` made the operator-facing voided table report a real id as nonexistent. `[-]` lays the identical trap: the two criteria retired here are not in that table, so the class would have stayed green today and reddened on the unrelated day someone voided a retired criterion. It is widened to `[ x~-]` now, with a synthetic probe — synthetic deliberately, because a probe reading `ISA.md` would be the green-today one. **THE SITES:** `progress:` and the new `retired:` in the frontmatter; the accounting and headline assertions in `test/unit/isa-frontmatter.test.ts`; the README's count sentence and its ISC-355 probe in `test/unit/docs-currency.test.ts`; the `grade` union and three claim rows in `test/support/isa-claims.ts`; `definedIscIds`. **WHAT THE MARKER DOES NOT MEAN, and these are the clauses the guard exists for.** RETIRING IS NOT CLOSING: no credit is earned, the criterion leaves the numerator and the denominator together, and `retired:` states how many left so the total is reported rather than absorbed. RETIRING IS NOT DELETING: the entry, its text and its id stay, and so do its registered claims — both criteria retired here keep guards over code that still ships, and `test/unit/isa-retired.test.ts` asserts the registry still carries them. RETIRING IS NOT AVAILABLE TO A CRITERION THAT IS MERELY HARD, SLOW OR INCONVENIENT TO EVIDENCE, and it is not a way to make a failing criterion disappear: `[~]` is the honest grade for anything not yet proved, and a red probe is a defect, not a candidate for retirement. **THE GUARD AGAINST EXACTLY THAT ABUSE, and its limit.** A retirement must carry `**[RETIRED <date> — PREMISE SUPERSEDED BY ISC-<n>` in its entry; the named criterion must be DEFINED, must not be itself, must be graded `[x]`, and must NAME THE RETIRED ONE BACK. The last clause is the load-bearing one. Without it a retirement is unilateral — a hard criterion can be retired behind whichever closed criterion is nearest, and the marker parses. Requiring acknowledgement makes the claim two-sided, forces the second edit to land inside a CLOSED entry where a reviewer looks, and puts both halves in one diff. It is NOT proof: nothing mechanical distinguishes a real supersession from a determined forgery of one, and the criterion does not claim otherwise — it claims the forgery costs two deliberate edits in two places rather than one character. Applying it cost a real edit: ISC-337 did not name ISC-307 and now does. **MUTATION-PROVED, THIRTEEN MUTATIONS, each reddening the named probe, each restored from a by-PATH backup, and each restore confirmed with `shasum -c` AND `git diff --stat` empty on the mutated path.** On `ISA.md`: deleting the `retired:` line, and `retired: 2`→`3`, each redden the frontmatter field probe — absence and mismatch are separate branches and both were run; `progress: 353/359`→`353/361`, 361 being the count of ALL criterion lines and therefore what the denominator meant before this change, reddens the denominator assertion, which is the one probe that makes "excluded from the count" true rather than merely intended; `- [-] ISC-307:`→`- [X]` reddens the four-marker accounting assertion; `- [-] ISC-307:`→`- [~]` reddens SIX probes together — the retired-set pin, the denominator, the `retired:` field, both README counts and the claims registry's grade-sync check; deleting ISC-307's `[RETIRED …]` marker reddens the supersession guard with the hard-criterion message; repointing ISC-360's marker at ISC-1 — closed, unrelated — reddens it on acknowledgement; downgrading ISC-337 to `[~]` reddens it on the superseder-must-be-closed clause. Elsewhere: narrowing `definedIscIds` back to `[ x~]` reddens the synthetic definition probe; `Two are retired`→`Three are retired` in the README reddens the ISC-355 count probe; deleting ISC-307's registered claim from `test/support/isa-claims.ts` reddens the guards-are-kept probe; regrading one ISC-360 claim `[-]`→`[~]` reddens both that probe and the registry's own grade-sync check; and weakening the acknowledgement check from a word-boundary match to a six-character prefix substring reddens the synthetic control that exists for exactly it, since `ISC-36` is not an acknowledgement of `ISC-360`. **ONE MUTATION FOUND A GAP RATHER THAN CONFIRMING A PROBE, and it is why the guards-are-kept probe exists at all.** Deleting a retired criterion's registered claim reddened ONE test — the new one. The registry's long-standing grade-sync check did not fire and could not: it iterates the claims that are PRESENT and asks whether each still names a criterion at that grade, so a DELETED claim is invisible to it by construction. Retirement plus deletion would therefore have been a silent way to drop a live guard, which is the abuse this criterion is named for, and no amount of re-reading the registry test would have shown it. **NOT CLAIMED.** That the two retirements performed here are correct — that is a judgement about whether ISC-337 and ISC-366 really replaced those premises, it is argued in the entries, and no test can settle it. That the marker cannot be abused — see the limit above. And that retiring these two improved any evidence: nothing was proved by this criterion, two questions were withdrawn, and the figure got smaller for that reason and no other.

### Group W — `pane_mode: tui`, the attended launch mode (added 2026-08-31)

`pane_mode` was parsed by `config/load.ts` and read by NOTHING: a `fleet.yaml` saying
`pane_mode: tui` validated, rendered an argv identical to `rpc`'s, and launched an ordinary RPC
worker. `.local/TUI-SPEC.md` is the build plan that closed it in four phases. These criteria are
that build, and the grades below are deliberately uneven — **four of the eighteen are `[~]`, and
every one of them is partial for the same family of reason: the mode's subject is a pseudo-TTY,
and a pty is the one thing this repo's test suites cannot stand up.** (This sentence read "five of
the thirteen" when the group closed at ISC-382; the group has since grown by ISC-383..ISC-387 and
ISC-372 was re-graded `[x]`, so the ratio is restated rather than left to rot. It read "five of the
eighteen" for as long as it took to close ISC-380 — the one partial here whose closing condition
did not need a pseudo-TTY. The *reason* is unchanged, and every remaining `[~]` in this group is
blocked on the same terminal.)

The single most important fact, measured rather than read: **there is no `--mode tui`.** `pi --help`
in `pifleet/pi-worker:0.79.6-base` offers `text (default), json, or rpc`. Pi's TUI is its DEFAULT
mode plus a real terminal, so a tui worker is the same argv with `--mode rpc` omitted and the
container given a TTY. Every design in SRD §3.5 that spoke of "a TUI-mode container" was describing
a flag that does not exist.

- [x] ISC-370: A `pane_mode: tui` worker's `docker run` argv carries `-i -t` and its pi argv omits `--mode` ENTIRELY — inventing no value for it — while an `rpc` worker's two argvs are unchanged element for element, and session identity (`--session-id`, `--session-dir`), briefing, tools and skills are identical across both modes. **[FILED AND CLOSED 2026-08-31, TUI spec items 1-2.]** **THE HARVEST IS WHY THE SECOND HALF IS AS LOAD-BEARING AS THE FIRST.** SRD §3.5 promises harvest is *identical* in both modes, and the only reason that can be true is that `--session-id` is chosen before launch — so a tui worker that drifted on session identity would not be a degraded mode, it would be an unharvestable one. `render.test.ts`'s "session identity, briefing, tools and skills are identical across modes" asserts `--session-id`, `--session-dir` == `/sessions`, one and only one `--append-system-prompt` at `BRIEFING_MOUNT`, the `--tools` list, the `--skill` list, the three `--no-*` denials and the sessions mount, from ONE fixture whose two workers differ in id and `pane_mode` only. **THE TUI ARM IS ASSERTED AS A RELATION, NOT AS A SECOND LITERAL LIST**, deliberately: "the rpc one plus `-t`, minus `--mode rpc`, and nothing else". A hand-written second literal would be a second chance to write the bug down, and it would pass while the two argvs diverged in any field the author happened to copy from the implementation. **MACHINE-CHECKED EVERY CI RUN, no gate of any kind** — `test/unit/render.test.ts`'s `describe("pane_mode is binding on the launch argv (SRD §3.5)")`, four tests including "an explicit `pane_mode: rpc` renders identically to omitting the key", in `bun test test/unit` (`ci.yml`'s `test` job). Corroborated off DISK rather than in memory by `supervisor-tui.test.ts:578`, which reads the launch record back and asserts `-t` present for one worker and absent for the other. **NOT CLAIMED:** that the resulting container presents a TUI. That was measured by hand once (`docker run -d -i -t … 'tty; pi'` -> `/dev/pts/0`, `Config.Tty=true`, and the full frame in `docker logs`) and is graded under ISC-378, not here; this criterion is about argv and stops there.
- [x] ISC-371: `docker/entrypoint.sh` installs the RPC stdin redirection (`exec 3<&0` … `<&3 &` … `exec 3<&-`) only for an `rpc` worker, and a `tui` worker that finds no terminal on stdin REFUSES with its own exit code rather than falling back to the RPC plumbing. **[FILED AND CLOSED 2026-08-31, TUI spec item 3.]** **THE REFUSAL IS THE CRITERION, and `evidence === null` is the assertion that carries it:** the probe checks not merely that the exit code is 72 but that the worker binary was NEVER STARTED. A fallback that ran Pi on a pipe would produce a container that looks alive, presents no TUI, answers no RPC, and reports as a worker doing nothing — the failure shape this repo has now met at the mount path (ISC-231), the needle supplier (ISC-333) and the outbox (ISC-346). **72 IS CHOSEN, NOT NEXT-AVAILABLE:** it must not be 71, which is the honeypot-arming failure (ISC-125), or an operator would diagnose a missing tty as a security-shim fault. Asserted in both directions — `test("the tui refusal does not reuse the honeypot's exit code")`. **MACHINE-CHECKED EVERY CI RUN, UNGATED**: `test/unit/entrypoint-pane-mode.test.ts` runs the REAL script under the host's bash with a pipe on stdin, through a `PIFLEET_WORKER_BIN` seam — no Docker and no image — with an rpc arm (`stdin=HELLO-RPC`) and an unset-mode arm (`stdin=HELLO-DEFAULT`) proving the redirection still works where it should. **THE TTY-SIDE HALF IS OUT OF A UNIT TEST'S REACH AND IS SAID SO IN THE FILE'S OWN HEADER** — that a tui worker WITH a terminal starts Pi on it was measured once against a real container and recorded above the launch in `entrypoint.sh`. **A CORRECTION TO A PRE-EXISTING COMMENT WAS FOUND HERE AND IS RECORDED RATHER THAN QUIETLY FIXED:** that file's docblock said "`<&0` alone is not reliable here — the default is applied to the asynchronous list before redirections are processed". Measured in bash 5.2.37 in the real image, `child <&0 &` receives the piped line correctly with both a pipe and a pty on stdin. The block's two stated MEASUREMENTS are both right; the INFERENCE about `<&0`, which was never measured, is not. The RPC path was left untouched — this is a right decision that had the wrong reason written under it, and the next reader should not inherit the reason.
- [x] ISC-372: `config validate` refuses `pane_mode: tui` where there is no pane — paired with the `oneshot` lifecycle, and on the `headless` backend — with a FIELD-LEVEL error naming both the offending key and the reason. **[FILED 2026-08-31 PARTIAL, TUI spec item 4. The bound is the criterion's own, asserted rather than hidden.]** **MACHINE-CHECKED, UNGATED, in `test/unit/config.test.ts`'s `describe("pane_mode: tui is refused where there is no pane (SRD §3.5)")`:** four refusal cases across the three levels a value can arrive from — `roles.pair.pane_mode`, `workers.0.pane_mode`, and tui-from-defaults against oneshot-from-the-role, which is the cross-level shape the `read_only` guard was originally caught getting wrong — plus the headless case asserting `backend.kind is headless` and `docker attach` in the message. THREE NEGATIVE CONTROLS keep it from degenerating into "refuse everything": tui + the default lifecycle on cmux LOADS, oneshot on headless LOADS with the pane mode staying rpc, and **a tui worker with no `backend` block at all is NOT refused here**. **THAT LAST CONTROL IS THE PARTIAL, STATED AS A PASSING TEST RATHER THAN AS A PARAGRAPH.** `backend.kind` is optional and an absent block means UNSET (ISC-271); `up` resolves `--backend > backend.kind > DEFAULT_BACKEND`. So config-validate can only catch the document that SAYS headless — `pifleet up --backend headless` over a tui config is a different surface, reached by a flag this file never sees, and it is not closed in this tree. **WHY THIS IS `[~]` AND NOT AN `[x]` SCOPED TO WHAT IS BUILT.** Rewording the criterion to "in a document whose `backend.kind` is headless" would make it fully evidenced and would be the move this ISA refuses: the requirement is *refuse combinations that cannot work*, and half of a refusal is a refusal an operator can walk around. **CLOSING CONDITION, NAMED:** a check in `up` against the EFFECTIVE backend. That is TUI spec Phase 4 item 12/13 and belongs to `cli/commands/up.ts`, which is outside this change's edit surface. **A CORRECTION TO THE SPEC ITSELF IS RECORDED HERE:** item 4 originally read "`tui` + a role with `pane_mode` unset on a headless backend", which describes a role that is not tui at all. The engineer implementing it caught the garble and built the rule as stated above rather than the sentence as written. **[CLOSE-OUT 2026-08-31 — RE-GRADED `[~]` -> `[x]`. The closing condition this entry named was built, and it is ISC-384.]** This entry said what would close it: "a check in `up` against the EFFECTIVE backend". `assertTuiBackendPossible` now makes exactly that check, `resolveRequestedBackend` reports WHICH input answered (`--backend`, `backend.kind`, or the built-in default), and both are proved in both directions in `test/unit/tui-guards.test.ts` and through the real CLI in `test/integration/up-wiring.test.ts`, which asserts exit 2 AND that nothing was launched. **A criterion that names its own closing condition can be closed by MEETING it** — the rule ISC-361 set and ISC-306/ISC-339 were held to — and no word of the sentence above was changed to fit the evidence. **THE SCHEMA'S BOUND IS UNCHANGED AND MUST STAY UNCHANGED**, which is the half a careless close would have broken: `parseConfig` has no `--backend` and no `DEFAULT_BACKEND`, so a schema that guessed would refuse a perfectly good `up --backend cmux`. `config.test.ts`'s "a tui worker with no backend block stated is NOT refused here" keeps every assertion it had; only its stale closing sentence — "`pifleet tui --worker` is what refuses that worker at runtime" — was corrected, because that describes a refusal of one COMMAND after a fleet is already up with no pane to attach to, which is a different guard from this one.
- [x] ISC-373: A `tui` worker's container is created DETACHED — `-d` inserted immediately after the `run` subcommand, never appended — and an argv that is not `docker run …`, or that already carries `-d`/`--detach`, throws rather than launching. **[FILED AND CLOSED 2026-08-31, TUI spec item 5 / §2.0.]** **THE POSITION IS THE CRITERION, and the reason is a failure with no error message.** `docker run` takes its own flags BEFORE the image and passes everything after it to the container, so an appended `-d` is not a docker flag — it is an argument handed to `pi`. Nothing errors: the container runs in the FOREGROUND, docker refuses `-t` on the supervisor's piped stdin, and the operator gets `the input device is not a TTY` with nothing in it mentioning `pane_mode`. `toContain("-d")` would pass against exactly that bug, so the probe asserts `indexOf("-d") === 2`. **MEASURED, docker 28.4.0, 2026-08-31:** `docker run --rm -i -t <image> true </dev/null` -> "the input device is not a TTY", exit 1; `docker run -d --rm -i -t <image> <cmd>` -> starts, with `Config.Tty=true`, `Config.OpenStdin=true`, `State.Running=true`. **A DOUBLED `-d` THROWS RATHER THAN DEDUPES**, on ISC-188's rule: two places deciding one thing is a defect even when they agree, because the next reader has to work out which one won. **WHY THE SUPERVISOR AND NOT `render.ts`:** `-d` belongs to the CALLER's situation, not the worker's. `pifleet render` emits the command a human could paste, and in a human's terminal `docker run -i -t` in the foreground is exactly right. Keeping `-d` out of the renderer is also what keeps ISC-370's byte-for-byte argv pins meaningful. **MACHINE-CHECKED EVERY CI RUN, UNGATED** — `test/unit/supervisor-tui.test.ts`'s `describe("detachedDockerArgv")`, six tests including "does not mutate its input".
- [x] ISC-374: The supervisor opens no RPC client, sends no `prompt` and allocates no epoch for a `tui` worker; `docker run -d` exiting 0 is a hand-off rather than a worker death; and an `rpc` worker's launch path is unchanged. **[FILED AND CLOSED 2026-08-31, TUI spec items 5-6.]** **THE MOST IMPORTANT PROBE IN THE FILE IS THE `rpc` ONE**, and it is written that way in the source: the risk in this phase was never that tui would fail to work, it was a refactor that quietly routed BOTH modes through the new path. **THESE ARE STRUCTURAL PROBES OVER COMMENT-STRIPPED SOURCE, AND THE CHOICE IS ARGUED RATHER THAN ASSUMED.** A battery of probes that each call the selector directly is satisfied by a refactor that stops CALLING the selector — every test green, no tui worker launched. So the probes pin the call sites: `cmd = tuiMode ? detachedDockerArgv(launch.argv) : launch.argv;`, `tuiMode ? null : new RpcClient(`, `if (tuiMode && code === 0) {` whose body returns without touching `state.exit` or `state.phase = "dead"`, and `detachedDockerArgv(` matched EXACTLY ONCE in the whole supervisor. Two more close the ways a selector can be defeated: `tuiMode` must come from `launch.pane_mode` and never from sniffing `argv.includes("-t")`, and no call site may silence the null client with `client!` or `client as RpcClient`. The dispatch refusal is pinned by source ORDER — `reason = "pane_mode_tui_has_no_rpc_dispatch"` appears BEFORE `em.allocate(envelope.task_id` — because refusing after allocating would burn an epoch on every attempt. **A SURVIVING MUTATION WAS FOUND HERE AND IS THE ENTRY'S REAL CONTENT.** Deleting `pane_mode: w.paneMode` from `materialize.ts` — the single line that puts the mode on the launch record at all — left the entire unit suite GREEN: 82 tests passing on a fleet that could no longer launch a TUI. `WorkerLaunchSchema` DEFAULTS the field to `"rpc"`, so every in-memory fixture kept working. The countermeasure is that `test("a tui worker's record says tui, and a default worker's says rpc")` reads the record BACK OFF DISK through `readWorkerLaunch`, so `parse` runs between the write and the assertion, and it asserts both directions with the tui worker listed FIRST so a wrong-index writer cannot pass by luck. **MACHINE-CHECKED EVERY CI RUN, UNGATED** — `test/unit/supervisor-tui.test.ts`.
- [x] ISC-375: A `tui` worker's completion is TRANSCRIPT-DERIVED — the last assistant entry's stop reason plus a quiet window wider than one poll — and its session file is found by a BOUNDED suffix search: `_<session-id>.jsonl`, non-recursive, no cross-worker collision, and newest-of-several returned WITH the count. **[FILED AND CLOSED 2026-08-31, TUI spec item 6.]** **THIS DELIBERATELY BREAKS ISC-95's NEVER-GLOB RULE FOR ONE MODE, AND THE ARGUMENT IS THE CRITERION.** ISC-95 records the session path VERBATIM from `get_state` because "a glob that finds a file finds SOME file, not necessarily this worker's". `get_state` is an RPC method; a tui worker has no channel to send it on. The choice is therefore not "verbatim or glob", it is "glob or no transcript at all" — and no transcript means the harvest §3.5 promises is *identical* in both modes silently produces nothing for half of them. So the risk is BOUNDED rather than ignored, and each bound is a test: the match is a SUFFIX on a leading `_` (a naive `endsWith(id)` is what `sub-eng-1` breaks — asserted), `eng-11` does not match `eng-1`, a bare `_eng-1.jsonl` with no timestamp prefix is not a candidate, the read is FLAT so a nested file is not found, and with two matches the newer wins and `{matches: 2}` is returned so the caller logs the ambiguity instead of hiding it. **THE QUIET WINDOW IS THE SAME DEFENCE AS THE `rpc` PATH'S DOUBLE `get_state`, WEAKER BY CONSTRUCTION.** Pi appends the assistant entry and its follow-ons in separate writes, so a poll landing between two of them sees a finished-looking turn that is not finished. `TUI_QUIET_MS > TUI_POLL_MS * 2` is asserted RELATIONALLY rather than as a literal — a one-poll-wide window would settle on the first tick that saw no growth, which is the exact race it exists to survive. **A DELIBERATE DIVERGENCE IS PINNED SO IT CANNOT BE TIDIED AWAY:** `verdictForStopReason("endTurn")` is `success` here while `harvest/transcript.ts`'s `reconstruct` answers `unknown` for the same input. The probe exists so that "make them consistent" is a decision someone takes on purpose rather than a cleanup that quietly makes every tui task settle `unknown`. The wiring is pinned too — the turn is read from entries SLICED at the epoch's baseline (`classifyTuiTurn(tuiReader.entries)` unsliced is forbidden), settlement goes through the one `settle(verdict, reason)` and not a private `writeTaskRecord`, and the window is a `Stopwatch` rather than a `Date.now()` subtraction (ISC-155). **MACHINE-CHECKED EVERY CI RUN, UNGATED** — `test/unit/supervisor-tui.test.ts`, 25 tests across `classifyTuiTurn`, `verdictForStopReason`, `discoverSessionPath`, the polling constants and the supervisor wiring.
- [x] ISC-376: A `tui` worker's cost is summed from the transcript's `usage` — abandoned branches included — and its permanently-zero `state.usage` cannot make a worker that spent report as having spent nothing. **[FILED AND CLOSED 2026-08-31, TUI spec item 7.]** **THE JOIN IS THE CRITERION.** Each link existed and was tested — `harvest-usage.test.ts` for the fold, `harvest-transcript.test.ts` for the read — and nothing pinned the CHAIN across `contracts.ts` -> `harvest/transcript.ts` -> `harvest/usage.ts` -> `cli/commands/dispatch.ts`. The failure that gap admits is the ISC-114/115 shape exactly: an under-count feeding a ceiling means the ceiling never trips. **THE PRECONDITION IS ASSERTED, NOT ASSUMED:** `state.usage` materializes at its schema default and IS `ZERO_USAGE` for the life of a tui run, which is what makes `combineUsage`'s element-wise max an identity on the transcript total. **THE FIXTURE CARRIES AN ABANDONED BRANCH ON PURPOSE**, because that is the one place a "sum the transcript" implementation can disagree with itself: an active-path-only sum reports 300/120 against the true 600/210 and undercharges by a third. **AND AN UNPRICED RUN REPORTS `usd: 0` WITH `priced: false`, not a measured zero** — local models have no price table (SRD §5.9), so the flag is what stops a downstream reader averaging $0.00 into a spend report as if it were an observation. **A CONSTRAINT ON A FUTURE EDIT IS RECORDED AT THE DEFINITION** rather than left to whoever wires `get_session_stats`: when source 1 arrives it must stay one ARM of the max and must never become preferred, or a tui worker would read `state.usage`, find the schema default forever, and report every such worker as free. **MACHINE-CHECKED EVERY CI RUN, UNGATED** — `test/unit/tui-cost.test.ts`, six tests, no `process.env` at all. **NOT CLAIMED, and the file says so in its own header:** that a tui worker's transcript can be FOUND. These tests would pass on the day ISC-375 landed and on the day before it.
- [~] ISC-377: `pifleet abort --worker <id>` on a `tui` worker issues `docker kill --signal=INT <container>`, and that STOPS the worker — tini forwards the signal to the entrypoint shell, whose existing `trap forward TERM INT HUP` converts it to TERM, and Pi exits cleanly. **[FILED 2026-08-31 PARTIAL, TUI spec item 8. The routing is re-checked; the signal arriving is not.]** **THE SPEC'S §2.8 WAS WRONG ABOUT THIS AND THE CORRECTION IS THE ENTRY.** It claimed `docker kill --signal=INT` could not reach the worker, because `docker kill` signals PID 1 only and the Dockerfile starts tini WITHOUT `-g`. Both those facts are right; the step it missed is the one after. **MEASURED, one fresh container in the production tui shape per row, 2026-08-31, image `pifleet/pi-worker:0.79.6-base-28cde8879cf9`:** control (no signal) `Running=true`; `docker kill --signal=INT` (PID 1) `Running=false ExitCode=0`; `docker kill --signal=TERM` `Running=false ExitCode=0`; `kill -INT <entrypoint shell>` `Running=false ExitCode=0`; `kill -INT <pi>` single `ExitCode=130`; the same double at 150 ms `ExitCode=130`; `kill -TERM <pi>` `ExitCode=0`. **THE TRAP IS LOAD-BEARING RATHER THAN AN OBSTACLE — dropping `INT` from it would CREATE the no-op §2.8 feared.** Two further corrections fall out of the same table: SIGINT is not an interrupt for Pi, it is a kill, so the double-INT question §2.8 raised does not arise; and a person's Ctrl-C in an attached pane does NOT kill the worker, because Pi's TUI holds the pty in raw mode — measured against a control arm differing in exactly one variable, which binary owns the terminal: `worker = pi` -> `-isig` (ISIG DISABLED), `worker = cat` -> `isig`. §2.8's process-group claim was also wrong; measured pgrp is 7 for both the shell and Pi, not 1. **WHAT IS MACHINE-CHECKED, UNGATED** (`test/unit/tui-interrupt.test.ts`): the argv byte for byte, `INTERRUPT_SIGNAL === "INT"`, `launchPaneMode`'s eight discrimination cases, `planInterrupt`'s four routes, and — the probe that matters most — **the two ends that must move together**: `entrypoint.sh` still traps INT, and `render.ts` still leaves both marks `launchPaneMode` reads. A lexical probe that fails loudly when the other end moves is worth more than a runtime probe that skips itself. **WHY `[~]`, THREE REASONS, NONE OF THEM FIXABLE BY WRITING MORE UNIT TESTS.** (1) The seven-row table is a ONE-OFF LOCAL EXPERIMENT against pi 0.79.6; nothing re-runs it, and the tests compare strings to constants. Having no container is not the same as having no control plane.

it forfeits a check.** It is also not a heuristic: nothing about a VALUE distinguishes a public endpoint from a token above the length floor, so the operator says which, once, in the document that granted it. **THE DEFAULT IS THE SAFE ONE and is asserted as such**: a bare string means `credential: true`, and the long form defaults to `true` too, so an operator who reaches for `{name: X}` to add a field does not silently disarm the sweep for X. **THE DECLARATION IS WRITTEN INTO THE RUN, and that is the criterion's load-bearing half rather than a detail.** `harvest/needles.ts` already states the rule for grants — a harvester is handed a run directory, not a workspace, and a run outlives the config that produced it — so a declaration read from whatever `fleet.yaml` is in front of the harvester would sweep a two-week-old run against today's answer, silently and in both directions. `WorkerLaunch.non_credential_secrets` defaults to `[]`, so every record written before the field existed keeps its sweep exactly as wide as it was. **MACHINE-CHECKED, UNGATED, in `test/unit/non-credential-secrets.test.ts` (11 tests):** the config surface in four (bare string is a credential; the long form defaults to one; `credential: false` names it without touching the grant; one name answering twice is REFUSED rather than resolved by list order; the entry object is still `.strict()`); the supplier in four, each with a control (declared → only the token is a needle; nothing declared → BOTH values are; a declaration naming an ungranted variable changes nothing; a record predating the field sweeps everything, built through the schema and then STRIPPED so it cannot pass by being merely invalid); the consequence in two — an artifact naming the endpoint is accepted while **the same artifact carrying the token is still refused**, which is the pair a change that simply deleted the sweep could not satisfy; and the WRITER in one, reading `launch.json` back off disk so `WorkerLaunchSchema.parse` runs between write and assertion. **THE WRITE PROBE EXISTS BECAUSE THIS FIELD HAS THE `pane_mode` SHAPE**: a correct `[]` default makes a missing write indistinguishable from an old record, and deleting the one line in `materialize.ts` would return the original defect in full with nothing in the failure naming `credential: false`. That mutation survived once on this project already and is not being left to survive twice. **MUTATION-PROVED, seven ways, each restored and verified:** skip nothing (1 red), skip every grant (4), delete the `materialize.ts` write (1), default `credential` to `false` (1), drop the duplicate-name refusal (1), make a bare string mean non-credential (3), and — the one that SURVIVED the first battery — copy the fleet-wide declaration instead of intersecting it with the worker's grant, which passed until a fixture declared a name the worker was never granted. That case is now in the write probe, and the intersection is the reason a hand-edited or migrated run directory cannot switch the detector off for something it never held.

The premise a guard shipped on the same day turned out to be too narrow.]** **"HEADLESS" HAD BEEN STANDING IN FOR "NO PANE EXISTS", and this is the case where those stop being the same statement.** ISC-384's refusal says it in its own message — "A headless run creates no pane, so there is nothing to attach" — and that was true of both surfaces §3.5 knew: pifleet owns the pane (`cmux`/`tmux`), or there is none (`headless`). The operations console is a third. A pane exists, cmux made it, and pifleet is simply not the one that made it — so `--backend headless` is CORRECT there (the console must not have windows opening under it) and `pane_mode: tui` is CORRECT there (the point is Pi's own interface), and the two together were refused. **The guard was not wrong; its premise was**, and a person running `up` inside a pane of their own is what falsified it. **THE EXEMPTION IS A SECOND GUARD, NOT A LOOSER FIRST ONE.** `assertTuiBackendPossible` gains exactly one early return, and everything licensing it is established by `assertAttachHere` running BEFORE it — that ordering is the criterion's load-bearing half. Widening the original condition would have made one boolean answer four unrelated questions, and **a single boolean cannot be reddened one clause at a time**. `adoptRefusal` returns a REASON rather than a boolean for the same purpose. **THE FOUR REFUSALS, each a refusal rather than a warning:** no tui worker (silently ignoring the flag leaves an operator watching a log tail believing it is Pi); more than one (a process has ONE terminal, and attaching to the first of three while calling the run attended OVERCLAIMS for the other two — the one direction `attended/mode.ts` exists to forbid); a pane-owning backend (`--backend cmux --attach-here` would put pifleet's `docker attach` and this terminal on the same pty, SRD §162 violated by a flag pair); and a non-terminal stream, checked on stdin and stdout SEPARATELY because a TUI reads keys and writes frames and either half alone is a half-usable pane that looks like a working one. **WHAT ADOPTION BUYS AND WHAT IT FORFEITS, both recorded.** `Presentation.adopted_terminal` distinguishes an adopted pane from no pane; `surface_ref` stays `null` because there is no id anything could later send bytes to, so **`dispatch` still refuses this worker — correctly, since the person at the keyboard IS the dispatcher** — and that refusal now says so instead of saying "nowhere to go". The attach is a BARE `docker attach --detach-keys=ctrl-]`, not `attachArgv`'s polling `sh -c` wrapper: this path runs after the idle wait so the poll could only ever succeed on its first iteration, and a shell between the process and docker would put a second owner on a terminal §162 gives exactly one. `enterTui` is called BEFORE the attach, so the record may overclaim attendance and can never underclaim it. **MACHINE-CHECKED, UNGATED, in `test/unit/attach-here.test.ts` (14 tests):** each refusal paired with the case that must still be ALLOWED; every refusal kind rendering a message (a lost `switch` arm would print "refusing to start: undefined"); the argv exact, with an explicit assertion that NO shell sits between the process and docker; both guards in both directions including the inert-without-the-flag case across six worker/backend combinations; `adopted_terminal` round-tripping and defaulting `false` for older records; and the two dispatch arms. **PROVEN LIVE, which is the only reason this is `[x]` at all** — the console's pane 1 was rebuilt and read back: `attaching this terminal to tick-1 — detach with ctrl-]` followed by `pi v0.79.6`, the keybind bar, `[Skills] pifleet-worker, ticket-ops` and the model line. `presentation.json` reads `adopted_terminal: true` with a null `surface_ref`; `attended.json` reads `mode: "tui"` with the MODE's 15 voided rows, ISC-85's runs-twice row among them. **MUTATION-PROVED, nine ways, each restored:** allow many workers, allow a pane-owning backend, skip the stdin check, exempt always, exempt never, wrap the attach in a shell, drop `--detach-keys`, default `adopted_terminal` to `true`, and make the empty-worker check unreachable. **THE BOUND:** nothing re-checks that a real terminal survives the handover — the live proof is one machine, one run, and Docker+pty gated exactly as ISC-378 is. What CI re-checks is the argv, the guards and the records.

> **Count reconciliation, 2026-08-28 (ISC-302 filed closed; ISC-300, ISC-259 and ISC-57 restated by owner decision).** `301/303`, RECOUNTED from this file with `grep -c`, never incremented. Arithmetic from main's `297 [x] / 5 [~] / 0 [ ] = 302`: ISC-302 is ADDED CLOSED (closed 297 -> 298, total 302 -> 303); ISC-300, ISC-259 and ISC-57 each move `[~]` -> `[x]` (closed 298 -> 301, partial 5 -> 2). `301 + 2 + 0 = 303`. **Three of the four changes are RESTATEMENTS, and this repository is right to be suspicious of those, so the guard is stated plainly: in none of them is the wording change the mechanism that closed the criterion.** ISC-300's two arms were costed by measurement first — including an attempt to show its trade illusory, which failed in both directions — and the owner then chose; the restatement records the choice. ISC-259's specification moved away from it in two amendments the owner made in August; the criterion was the stale half, not the code. ISC-57's gateway term was FIXED rather than reworded, in `security/gateway-block.ts`, and only the sibling-reachability term — the one nobody intends to build per-worker isolation for — is scoped out, last, after the work. Every clause of all three restated sentences is asserted by a test that already runs on every push; none needed new evidence, which is the argument for the restatement rather than a hole in it. **The one addition is a criterion about the evidence mechanism itself.** ISC-302 exists because a claim's `grep` could not tell code from prose, which had already produced one vacuously GREEN claim and one falsely RED one; it is filed and closed together on the ISC-267/ISC-269 precedent, the defect having been measured twice before it was written down. **What remains is blocked rather than unfinished:** ISC-246 by SRD §8 rule 3, its subject being a module with no production consumer until E3 attaches artifacts, and ISC-301 by the absence of a seam that could induce a throw inside `harvestTask` — one that could be added, and should not be, since a production seam existing only to make a test possible is worse than the honest partial. The apparent duplicate a naive ID check reports at `248` is `ISC-248a` versus `ISC-248`, a pre-existing suffixed ID, not a collision.

> **Count reconciliation, 2026-08-28 (ISC-301 closed, the scan-ownership combinator).** `302/303`, RECOUNTED from this file with `grep -c`. Arithmetic from main's `301 [x] / 2 [~] / 0 [ ] = 303`: ISC-301 moves `[~]` -> `[x]` (closed 301 -> 302, partial 2 -> 1). `302 + 1 + 0 = 303`. The denominator does not move. **The criterion's SENTENCE is unchanged, which is the distinction worth drawing against the three restatements two entries above:** nothing here was reworded to fit the evidence — the evidence was extended to reach the half the entry had already named as uncovered. **The entry asked for a seam and did not get one.** It said closing this needed a way to induce a throw inside `harvestTask`; the answer was that wanting a seam was the error. Expressing the scan's ownership as `withOutboxScan(loc, fn)` makes the release structural, and the throwing path falls out of it — reachable by passing a body that throws, with no hook in production whose only purpose is a test. The mutation that was invisible before this change (release after the `await` rather than in the `finally`) now reddens exactly one probe. **What remains is ISC-246 alone**, still blocked by SRD §8 rule 3 until something in `src/` reads the accepted artifacts.

Live-probe rule: every ISC touching a container, a socket, or a process is verified by running
the real thing, not by asserting on a mock. Mocks are permitted only inside `test/unit`.

## Decisions

- **2026-08-24 — `export_html` STAGES INSIDE THE RUN DIRECTORY and the CLI places the file; it does
  NOT gain an allowlist of permitted roots (ISC-276).** Owner ruling, taken because ISC-276's own note
  said it had to be: *"closing it honestly needs a policy decision taken deliberately"*, and named two
  arms with different consequences for the container phase. The arm not taken was an allowlist of
  permitted roots, which carried two unanswered sub-decisions — configured where, defaulting to what —
  and whose default is load-bearing in a bad way: too narrow breaks `--html ~/Desktop/foo.html`, which
  is the ordinary use, and too wide closes the criterion on paper only. **The arm taken removes the
  question instead of answering it.** Pi's write destination is derived from the run directory and a
  UUID and never from a caller string, so there is no set to get right; the operator's arbitrary
  destination is reached by the CLI, a process that cannot exceed the privileges of whoever typed it.
  **What the implementation added beyond the ruling, and it is the better part:** the verb refuses a
  `path` parameter outright rather than accepting and ignoring one. That was not specified and is
  right — an ignored parameter still advertises influence, and silently dropping an older client's
  `path` leaves it renaming a run-dir file across a filesystem boundary and reporting `EXDEV`, a true
  statement about the wrong subject. **The discriminating case is a path INSIDE the run tree:** every
  containment check accepts it and this design refuses it, which is the clearest available evidence
  that the two arms are not the same control wearing different clothes.

- **2026-08-23 — the bridge-gateway hole is CLOSED by installing a rule, and `up` REFUSES the run if
  it cannot install one (ISC-51).** Two owner rulings, taken in that order. On remediation: install
  the rule rather than document the residual, narrow the criterion, or wait for a runner. On the
  no-privilege fallback: **refuse**, with no `--i-know` escape hatch — a fleet reporting deny-all
  while workers reach the host's sshd is worse than a fleet that will not start, because the first
  failure mode is silent and the second is not. **The privilege question nearly sank the second
  ruling and was settled by measurement, not by argument.** The concern raised before building was
  concrete: pifleet is unprivileged, `iptables` needs CAP_NET_ADMIN in the host netns, and a hard
  refusal pifleet's own CI could not satisfy would break the entire `container` job — a far larger
  blast radius than ISC-51 itself. Three arms were drafted (call `sudo`; require the operator to
  pre-install and only verify; attempt-then-verify). **All three were made unnecessary by a fourth
  that measurement found:** pifleet already holds the Docker daemon, and a privileged container in
  the host's network and mount namespaces runs the host's own `iptables` against the host's own
  tables. No sudo, no operator step, no CI change, and it targets the correct netns on Linux and on
  macOS/colima alike. The lesson is the ordering — the arms were about how to *ask* for privilege,
  and the answer was that the privilege was already held.

- **2026-08-23 — `down` does NOT remove the containment rule, which CORRECTS the ruling as
  originally recorded.** The decision as taken said "`down` removes the rule it added". Building it
  showed that to be wrong in the dangerous direction: `down` deliberately leaves the egress network
  and the relay standing, so a rule whose lifetime ended with the run would leave a still-existing
  bridge uncontained for whatever attached to it next — reopening ISC-51 on every `down`. The rule's
  lifetime is the NETWORK's lifetime. `removeGatewayBlock` exists for the integration suite, which
  is the one caller that actually destroys its networks; without it the host accumulates one dead
  rule per test run.

- **2026-08-23 — containment lives on `ensureEgressNetwork`, not in the `up` command.** Drafted in
  `up.ts` first, and moved after the integration suite showed why: `test/integration/relay.test.ts`
  builds its network by calling `ensureEgressNetwork` directly, so a command-level guard would have
  left the suite — and `doctor`, and every future caller — holding a network that reports deny-all
  and is not. This is ISC-51's own lesson applied to its fix: the posture has to be inseparable from
  the call that claims it. The move closed an import cycle (`network.ts -> gateway-block.ts ->
  relay.ts -> network.ts`), which is why the pinned digest now lives alone in
  `src/security/pinned-image.ts` rather than being copied.

- **2026-08-23 — a Docker-gated probe is NOT a self-skipping probe in this repo, and the strictness
  rule has to be applied by reading CI rather than by inferring from a dependency.** ISC-265's grade
  was drafted `[~]` on the reasoning that its end-to-end assertion needs a daemon, so it self-skips,
  so only the mechanism is re-checked. CI refuted the middle step: the `container` job runs the
  Docker-gated integration suite on a Linux runner with a real daemon, and the probe passed there.
  What no runner has is **oMLX and host ADC** — which is why the two live-inference probes in the
  same file still skip and ISC-258/ISC-262 remain `[~]` — and Phase C's Apple-silicon runner is
  about those, not about Docker. **The correction direction is the interesting part.** The strictness
  rule was written after a criterion was over-claimed, so its failure mode is assumed to be
  optimism; here careful pessimism got it wrong in the other direction and would have left a closed
  criterion open for someone to re-do. The rule's question is "does something reproducible re-check
  what this literally says", and the only honest way to answer it is to look at what the jobs
  execute.

- **2026-08-23 — a drifted relay is REPLACED, not refused, and the concurrent-fleet cost is accepted
  rather than traded away (ISC-265).** Three arms were on the table. (a) Refuse `up` with a named
  error telling the operator to `docker rm -f`; (b) replace the relay whenever the targets diverge;
  (c) replace only when nothing else is attached to the egress network. **(a) is excluded by the
  criterion's own wording** — "takes effect without a manual `docker rm -f`" is not satisfied by a
  path that ends in the operator typing `docker rm -f`; it relocates the defect into an error
  message. **(c) was rejected as a criterion-defeating conditional**: it creates a case where the
  fleet is configured for one oMLX and served by another, which is exactly the state ISC-265 exists
  to abolish, and it makes closure depend on the ambient state of the machine. **(b) chosen.** The
  cost is real and is not minimised here: `pifleet-egress-relay-<net>` is shared, and replacing it
  cuts the model server out from under a concurrent fleet mid-turn. It is accepted because adoption
  never avoided that conflict — with drifted targets, two configs disagree about a single shared
  resource, and adoption resolves it silently in favour of whoever booted first. Both arms are wrong
  for somebody; only one of them is legible. `relay_targets_replaced` is emitted as its OWN ledger
  event rather than a field on `egress_relay_ready`, so the swap is greppable rather than buried in
  a detail blob.

- **2026-08-23 — `scriptSha256` is deliberately NOT a drift input.** It would have been the easy
  second comparison and it would have been wrong: the relay script is bind-mounted from the working
  tree and re-exec'd by `--restart unless-stopped`, so its hash describes the file on disk NOW, not
  the bytes the running container started with. Cycling a shared relay on a hash that cannot be
  attributed to it is a guess dressed as a check. It stays in the ledger, which is what it was
  always for.

- **2026-08-23 — show your math: the E3 delegation floor is not met, and the reason is external.**
  The Algorithm's soft floor asks for ≥2 delegation capabilities at E3; this run used none. The
  session's harness carries a standing instruction not to invoke the Agent tool unless the user asks
  for it, which forecloses the floor rather than trading it against anything. What delegation would
  have bought is named so the gap is legible: a Forge pass over the drift comparator for a
  second opinion on the set-vs-sequence choice, and a sweep for other adopt-without-comparing sites
  in `src/security/`. The first is substituted by four mutation proofs; the second is left undone
  and is worth a follow-up.

- **2026-08-21 — CORRECTION to the same day's "no host-side observer" finding, made by measurement
  before any code was written.** The five-whys at THINK concluded that *pifleet has no host-side
  observer role*, and that was **too strong**. Measured: `startRegistryDaemon` (`src/run/registry.ts:817`)
  is per-run, host-side, outlives every worker, and **already carries a periodic tick** —
  `setInterval` at `registry.ts:946` with a re-entrancy guard (`if (scanning) return`, :949) and
  `timer.unref?.()` (:970), driving `reapOnce` (:906). Further, the tailing primitive also already
  exists: `TailReader` (`src/util/jsonl.ts:217`) does incremental byte-offset reads keyed on
  `dev:ino:birthtime` plus a 64-byte head fingerprint, and **restarts from 0 on shrink or replace —
  truncation DETECTION is already built**, with two production consumers (`logs.ts:251`,
  `transcript.ts:165`). **The refined finding, which is the one that should be carried forward:** the
  gap is not an absent observer, it is an absent COLLECTOR. The daemon's tick watches *heartbeats* and
  reaps; nothing copies the worker's evidence anywhere the worker cannot reach. That is a much thinner
  gap than "a new architectural role", and it changed the ISC-172 design from "build a process" to
  "hang off an existing tick and reuse an existing reader". Recorded because the wrong version of this
  finding would have justified building a second daemon.

- **2026-08-21 — ISC-172's destination must NOT be a ledger shard, and the reason is Phase G's own
  work.** `<run>/ledger/` (`RunPaths.ledgerDir`, `src/run/paths.ts:120,181`) is host-created by `up`
  (`up.ts:275`) and never appears in the mount table (`render.ts:209-238`), so it is genuinely
  worker-unreachable and was the obvious destination. It is the wrong one: that directory holds
  pifleet's own shards parsed by `LedgerRecordSchema`, verbgate rows have an unrelated shape, and
  ISC-157's Phase G closure pinned `mergeLedger`'s behaviour that a malformed record lands in
  `errors`. Writing verbgate rows there would therefore generate one `errors` entry per row on every
  merge — a criterion closing by breaking the guarantee another criterion just closed. A distinct
  location is used instead.

- **2026-08-21 — `docker logs` ruled out as ISC-172's channel, on measurement rather than taste.**
  The container argv begins `["docker","run","-i","--rm"]` (`src/config/render.ts:165`), so the log
  is removed with the container; no `--log-driver` or `--log-opt` appears anywhere in `src/config/`,
  `src/container/` or `docker/entrypoint.sh`; and container stdout is not free — it IS the RPC stream,
  consumed by the supervisor at `src/supervisor/index.ts:383-388` and :596, with stderr already
  mirrored into `events.jsonl` (:600-614).

- **2026-08-21 — Phase H owner decisions, all three taken on the recommendation.**
  **(a) ISC-172 collector = TAIL AND COPY, not a transport change.** A host-side collector reads the
  worker's ledger incrementally and appends to a copy outside the `/outbox` bind mount, on a path
  ISC-127 already proves a worker cannot reach. The guarantee is deliberately the weaker of the two
  available and must be stated as such wherever it is claimed: **everything already collected survives
  truncation, and truncation itself is detected and recorded — but rows written and truncated between
  two polls are lost.** The stronger arm (verbgate writes to a fd or socket the host holds, so the
  worker never owns the file and truncation is impossible) was NOT chosen, because it changes the
  container contract and edits `docker/verbgate`, the security-critical file. A criterion closed on
  the tailer must not be worded as though it closed on the transport.
  **(b) ISC-246 = RESTATE, not build.** Third time this criterion has been examined and the second
  time it has been declined as written. The reason is not cost but reachability: **Node has no
  `openat` relative to a `FileHandle`, so the directory walk stays path-based no matter how much of
  the refactor is done** — the criterion as written asks for a window that cannot be closed in this
  runtime. Restated to the guarantee that IS reachable, on the ISC-157/192 precedent from Phase G:
  descriptors for the files, `nlink` checked on the FD rather than on the path, walk acknowledged as
  path-based. Closed against the restatement with mutation proofs, or not closed at all.
  **(c) ISC-125 seed = REACH THE DOCKER SOCKET.** Chosen over write-outside-mounts and reach-the-
  gateway because it is the only one of the three that cannot produce a false positive: there is no
  legitimate reason for a worker to open `/var/run/docker.sock`, so an observation of the attempt is
  unambiguous, and — the property that matters for rule 5 — **the attempt is recordable whether or
  not it succeeds**, which is what separates detection from prevention. The gateway variant was
  declined for this phase precisely because it is likely to surface a REAL hole rather than a seeded
  one (`--internal` isolation is FORWARD-chain only; the on-link gateway stays reachable), which
  would widen the phase mid-flight.

- **2026-08-21 — ISC-125 DEPENDS ON ISC-172, and the SRD's Phase H table does not say so.**
  Found at THINK on Phase H entry, before any code was written. ISC-125's verb is *detected*, and
  SRD-COMPLETION §8 rule 5 makes this the canonical case of "prevention is not detection". The
  structural argument: detection requires a signal crossing from the event to an observer the event
  cannot reach, so the observer must be host-side. But a host-side **canary** — a file outside the
  container that only a successful escape could touch — detects SUCCESS, not ATTEMPT. Under correct
  containment the attempt fails, the canary never moves, and the probe goes green **having detected
  nothing**. That is a probe which cannot fail, which rule 4 forbids, and it closes the criterion by
  prevention, which rule 5 forbids. Reporting an *attempt* requires a tamper-evident record that the
  attempt was made — which is exactly ISC-172's channel. **Consequence for ordering:** ISC-172 is
  built first and ISC-125 rides on it; they are not independent items in one phase.

- **2026-08-21 — Phase H is one architectural gap, not four features.** Five-whys on why these four
  criteria survived 46 PRs bottoms out at: **pifleet has no host-side observer role.** The supervisor
  is per-worker and exists to run the RPC turn; the daemon is a registry. Nothing watches a container.
  Every other criterion in the ISA could be satisfied inside that model — prevention flags, argv
  assertions, schema checks — which is why these four are the residue rather than an arbitrary set.
  The shared pattern is **evidence whose custody belongs to the worker**: the ledger it writes
  (ISC-172), the paths it can re-point between validation and use (ISC-246), the tree it keeps
  changing after quiesce (ISC-154), and the escape only it can observe (ISC-125).

- **2026-08-20 — the supervisor's launch identity is recorded in its OWN state file, not only in
  the registry, because registration is deliberately optional.** The identity-anchored kill ladder
  on this branch is correct and closed a real hazard (a bare `down` SIGTERMed an unrelated live
  process), but it anchored solely on `registry.json`. `supervisor/index.ts` registers with
  `{ optional: true }` and its own comment states why — "The supervisor must also work alone
  (integration tests, daemon crash)" — so for every daemon-less run the anchor was absent, `down`
  answered `identity_unrecorded`, and the supervisors stayed up. That is not hypothetical: it is
  `test/e2e/lifecycle.test.ts`'s happy path, which asserts `down` exits 0 and observed
  `EXIT.WORKER_DIED` (6) on CI, together with the tmux/headless parity, `readScreen` anti and
  sixteen-worker cases that all end in a `down`. **The identity was never unknown** — the
  supervisor reads it at launch to send to the registry — it merely had nowhere
  daemon-independent to live. `WorkerState.proc_started` is that place, written by the process it
  describes from the same `processStartTime(process.pid)` reading the registry call carries, so
  the two agree by construction. REJECTED: relaxing the anchor to liveness when the registry is
  absent, which is the pre-fix fail-open this branch exists to remove. The fail-closed property is
  preserved intact — `proc_started` is compared, not trusted, and a state file from an older build
  carries `""`, which `isPinnedIdentity` rejects, so it refuses exactly as an absent registry entry
  does. Pinned by two probes in `test/integration/down-identity.test.ts` that both fail against the
  registry-only anchor: one proves the ladder is ENTERED for a daemon-less run (`how: "sigkill"`,
  no `forced_identity`), the other proves a self-recorded identity naming the wrong process is
  still refused `identity_mismatch`.

- **2026-08-18 — Slice 2 real per-worker git isolation: clone, not `git worktree add`, decided
  after a security spike produced a confirmed RCE.** SRD §9.2 specified linked worktrees. Two
  worktree-based designs were built and run against a real container before this decision: one
  fails outright (a linked worktree's `.git` is a pointer file resolving outside the container's
  mounts), the other works and is a confirmed container-to-host RCE (a container with write
  access to the mounted gitdir zeroed the host's `refs/heads/main` and planted an executable
  post-checkout hook that ran as the operator on their next `git checkout`). Presented to the
  user with both findings; the user chose `git clone --no-hardlinks` (plus `--single-branch`,
  origin stripped, a parent-side `worker-<id>` remote for visibility) over abandoning per-worker
  isolation entirely. `--no-hardlinks` is not a hardening extra — a bare local clone hardlinks
  object files by default, and the spike that investigated this feature destroyed this
  repository's own pack file exactly that way before the flag was added; every clone path in
  both the implementation and the test fixtures now passes it, and `test/integration/
  worktree.test.ts` pins `nlink=1` and disjoint parent/clone inodes directly rather than trusting
  clone success as a proxy. SRD §9.2 carries this as an erratum rather than a silent rewrite; see
  `## Changelog` for the full conjectured/refuted/learned record and the Slice 2 close-out below
  for verification.
- **2026-08-18 — `config.run.root` left in the schema, and now read by nothing (ISC-188).**
  Closing ISC-188 meant deciding which of two answers to the runs root is THE answer.
  `run.root` is not a different concept from `runsRoot()` — its schema default is
  `~/.pifleet/runs`, byte-for-byte what `runsRoot()` falls back to — so this was one
  concept with two spellings, unlike its neighbour `run.repo`, which genuinely means
  something else (the operator's working repository). `runsRoot()` won because `up` and
  all nine other run-dir readers already use it and because it is the only one that can
  honour `PIFLEET_RUNS_DIR`; `render` was the sole reader of `run.root`.
  The field is deliberately NOT deleted. It is `.strict()`-validated, set in
  `fleet.example.yaml:27` and documented at `Docs/SRD.md:593`, so removing it would hard-
  fail every existing `fleet.yaml` that sets it — a breaking config change, and out of
  scope for a criterion about computing a path once. That leaves it accepted, defaulted
  and unread, which is honest about today (nothing has silently changed for anyone: `up`
  never consulted it) but is not a resting state — a user who sets `run.root: /data/runs`
  gets no runs in `/data/runs` and no diagnostic. The follow-up is a decision between
  making `runsRoot()` fall back to it BELOW `PIFLEET_RUNS_DIR` (which requires `up` to
  load config before computing the root — it currently does so after) and rejecting the
  key with a named error. Filed rather than chosen unilaterally.
- **2026-07-27 — Project ISA, not task ISA.** cmux-fleet is a thing with persistent identity, so
  the ISA lives at `~/repos/cmux-fleet/ISA.md` as system of record, per Algorithm v6.3.0 §ISA homes.
- **2026-07-27 — 140 ISCs from 89 SRD acceptance criteria.** Compound SRD criteria were split per
  the Splitting Test (e.g. SRD-9's five toolchain probes became ISC-33..37; SRD-58's two verbs
  became ISC-103/104), and Groups A and B were added because the SRD assumes the repo already
  exists and says nothing about the test pyramid the user explicitly asked for.
- **2026-07-27 — `bun test` over vitest.** The SRD constrains the stack to Bun; adding a second
  test runner would need a second config surface and a second CI install step for no gain.
- **2026-07-27 — Manual git worktrees for parallel engineers.** `isolation: "worktree"` forks the
  calling session's repo (paisley), not the target repo. Worktrees are created with
  `git -C ~/repos/cmux-fleet worktree add`, and every engineer brief carries absolute
  worktree-prefixed paths.
- **2026-07-27 — Phase order follows SRD §16 unchanged.** Phases 1–3 are load-bearing; Phase 3
  precedes any real-repo run because the kill ladder and budget ceilings must exist first.

- **2026-07-27 — refined: epoch attribution moves from a wall-clock window to a stream offset.**
  The SRD discards terminal events "outside an open epoch window", which is not a causal order —
  a late `agent_end` for epoch N is byte-identical to N+1's. Pi's events and responses share one
  ordered stdout stream, so a monotonic per-record `streamSeq` plus the `ackSeq` recorded at
  dispatch gives a real happens-before relation. SRD erratum; see ISC-141.
- **2026-07-27 — the fence is enforced at the worker, not only at the allocator.** "Sole epoch
  allocator" is an assumption a detached supervisor plus a CLI relaunch can violate. The worker
  side persists `last_accepted_epoch` and rejects stale dispatch; the run-dir lease keys on pid
  plus process start-time because pid reuse would otherwise resurrect a dead supervisor. ISC-142..144.
- **2026-07-27 — the harvester's independence was overstated.** Re-running the acceptance commands
  executes an artifact the gradee authored: the command string resolves through `package.json`
  scripts, `conftest.py`, `.git/hooks`, `Makefile` — all inside the mutable surface. Acceptance
  now resolves from the base SHA and runs in a fresh clone outside the worktree, and a diff
  touching the harness surface caps the verdict. This is the single largest correction to the
  SRD's §8.2 adjudication story. ISC-148..151.
- **2026-07-27 — gauges cannot prove quiescence.** `pendingMessageCount:0` sampled twice does not
  mean zero in between, and `isStreaming:false` also describes the gap between a tool call and the
  next turn. The stream-offset fence is the primary defence; monotonic-counter equality is the
  secondary one. ISC-147.
- **2026-07-27 — show your math on delegation.** Two engineers per phase rather than four: the
  Phase 1 surface splits cleanly along a config/container seam and an RPC/lifecycle seam with one
  shared contracts module, and a third writer would have to touch one of those two territories.
- **2026-07-27 — SRD Q1 answered by measurement: oMLX batches, it does not serialize.**
  Probed live on `:8000` with `Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-4bit`: a single short request took
  1.51s; four concurrent finished in 1.77s wall (3.40x), and the speedup plateaus near 4.1-4.3x
  at N=8-12. So F40's premise — that N workers queue behind one inference server — is wrong as
  stated. The honest caveat is that these were 80-token requests with negligible KV cache, and a
  real agentic turn carries a far larger context, so the memory-bound ceiling will sit below the
  compute-bound one measured here. `max_concurrent: 2` stays the default as a memory-safety
  margin rather than a throughput necessity, and ISC-158 (16 workers, no starvation) is what
  would justify raising it.
- **2026-07-27 — refined: engineer briefs are sized per subsystem, not per phase.** Both Phase 1
  engineers were truncated at a context ceiling (226k and 241k tokens), not finished — each stopped
  on a statement of intent, and the harness reported it as completion. Engineer B's brief listed 24
  files across seven subsystems. Remaining phases dispatch ~10-14 files per engineer, keep image
  builds in the parent so build logs do not consume an engineer's budget, and treat integration and
  e2e suites as their own dispatch unit because that is reliably what gets cut.
- **2026-08-17 — the "phases done" claim in README/CHANGELOG and the ISA's own done-condition
  had drifted apart.** All six SRD phases shipping every command in §10 did not mean every ISC
  was verified — most of Groups C/D/E/F/G (container image, Google credentials, oMLX, config,
  lifecycle) were unchecked not because the code was wrong, but because no prior session on
  this machine had a running Docker daemon to live-probe against. Fixed by running the full
  `PIFLEET_DOCKER=1` integration + e2e suite once Docker (Colima), vanilla pi.dev 0.79.6, and
  the oMLX key were all available — 54 criteria closed with no source changes beyond one bug
  (below). Deliberately did NOT check off Group E (ISC-50..57, oMLX in-container model calls):
  no dedicated test file exercises them, and "the e2e suite passed" doesn't independently prove
  allowlist refusal or the MLX-training-run guard fire correctly — that's real follow-up work,
  not a documentation gap. Same restraint applied to ISC-44..46, 48, 49, 61(kept — see below),
  74, 32: no test file names them, so they stay open rather than being swept in on file-level
  correlation.
- **2026-08-17 — found and fixed a real bug while unblocking the environment, not part of any
  planned workstream.** `src/harvest/outbox.ts`'s `CONTROL_CHARS` regex and `safeForReport`'s
  replace() were built from literal raw NUL/US/DEL bytes in the source instead of `\x` escape
  sequences. Bun 1.3.11 parses that as "range out of order in character class" and refuses to
  load the file — which took down every test touching outbox.ts, plus `doctor` itself, since
  commands are registered eagerly at CLI startup. Same character class, rewritten with escape
  sequences; full unit suite went from a hard crash to 818/818 green. This suggests the ISA's
  frontmatter `progress: 104/236` (dated 2026-07-27) predates whichever change introduced the
  raw bytes, or predates a Bun upgrade on this machine that started rejecting them — either way,
  nobody had run the full suite on this exact machine+Bun version since.
- **2026-08-17 — vanilla pi.dev installed alongside, not over, an existing fork.** This machine's
  `$PATH` resolved `pi` to `~/bin/pi` → `@oh-my-pi/pi-coding-agent`, a different npm-scoped fork,
  not the pinned `@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent@0.79.6` this project is built against. Per
  explicit instruction, installed the real package via `bun install -g`, which lands in
  `~/.bun/bin/pi` — earlier in `$PATH` than `~/bin/pi` — so `pi` now resolves to vanilla 0.79.6
  without touching the existing oh-my-pi setup at all.
- **2026-08-17 — Workstream 2 (small independent fixes) run as two parallel engineers in git
  worktrees, per the existing manual-worktree precedent above.** Engineer A took the RPC/CLI/
  epoch/supervisor cluster (ISC-214, 215, 216, 217, 228); Engineer B took harvest/container/
  config (ISC-247, 160, 190, 219, 22) — a clean file-disjoint split, so the merge back into
  `workstream-2-small-fixes` was conflict-free. ISC-219's live probe could not run: the worker
  image (`pifleet/pi-worker:verify`) needed by the Docker-gated verbgate suite is the one an
  earlier agent deleted without authorization (see the same-day incident already on record);
  the user's explicit call was "leave it for now," so the image was not rebuilt and ISC-219
  stays open with its test written but unverified, rather than being checked off on the
  strength of the code alone.
- **2026-08-17 — a pre-existing test-isolation flake, not a regression.** After merging both
  engineers' branches, `bun test test/unit` showed one failure in
  `harvest-outbox.test.ts` ("a hard link to a file outside the outbox is refused" — wrong
  refusal reason, consistent with a leftover temp path from a neighboring test rather than a
  logic error). The same file run in isolation, and the full suite re-run immediately after,
  were both 100% green. Recorded rather than chased: neither engineer's diff touched the
  hard-link check or its test, so this reads as ordering/temp-path contention between test
  files rather than something this workstream introduced.
- **2026-08-17 — an independent review pass on the same-day PR found real defects a passing
  test suite had missed, plus two ISA bookkeeping mistakes.** Three reviewers (Claude, Gemini,
  Codex) ran against the diff before merge and converged 3/3 on two issues neither engineer nor
  the orchestrator had caught: `readDockerfile()` threw an undiagnosed error that `doctor`
  reported as `EXIT.INTERNAL`, exactly the "pifleet bug" misclassification ISC-216 exists to
  prevent, aimed at a broken checkout instead; and the `models_allowlist` gate's bare `catch`
  discarded a real config error alongside the one case it was meant to skip. Claude alone (high
  confidence) found that ISC-160's hash covered the Dockerfile's text but not the two files it
  `COPY`s — including `docker/verbgate`, the enforcement point behind the cloud-mutation gate —
  leaving the highest-consequence staleness case still open under a criterion just marked
  closed. **Learned: every fix in this workstream had its own red-then-green regression test,
  and none of those tests were wrong — they each proved the fix did what it claimed. What they
  didn't do was ask what ELSE could go wrong at the same site**, which is exactly the blind
  spot an independent adversarial pass exists to cover, and the same reasoning this ISA already
  applies to worker self-report (`## Anti-criteria`) applies one level up to the engineer
  writing the test. Separately, Gemini's cross-file pass caught that ISC-247 had been fixed and
  tested but its checkbox never flipped, and that ISC-22 had been checked despite not meeting
