- **2026-08-18 — "the cmux socket refuses every call from outside a pane" turned out to be the
  wrong reason ISC-129 was open — the real one is a cmux version regression.** Two prior
  close-out notes (Phase 4, Phase 6) both explained ISC-129 as blocked purely by
  `socketControlMode: cmuxOnly` refusing non-pane callers, with the fix being "run from inside a
  pane" — carried forward unquestioned for three phases. Actually configuring `password` mode
  (per `Docs/SRD.md` §4.1, which says this is pifleet's own intended mode) and driving a real
  `pifleet up --backend cmux` from an ordinary shell showed the socket access story was correct
  and irrelevant: `doctor` reports `backends.cmux: true`, a workspace and both panes get
  created, and the run fails somewhere else entirely — `respawn-pane`'s surface addressing,
  which changed between cmux 0.64.20 (the SRD's verified baseline) and 0.64.22 (installed here).
  **Learned: an unreachable-in-principle diagnosis and an actually-tried-and-found-broken
  diagnosis look identical in a checkbox list, and only the second one tells the next person
  what to fix.** Three phases of ISA notes described a plausible blocker that nobody had
  actually tested since 0.64.20. Full reproduction and the exact fix scope are in
  `## Verification`, "Phase 4 close-out," under the 2026-08-18 addendum to ISC-129.
  Measured on this machine: Colima shares `$HOME` and shares neither `/tmp` nor
  `/var/folders/...`. An unshared `-v` source does not error — the daemon mounts an empty
  directory in its place. `image verify` therefore failed on a perfectly good image, and the
  same mistake in the worker launch path would give every worker an empty `/workspace` and an
  outbox the harvester never sees, with exit 0 throughout. Scratch allocation moves to
  `container/mounts.ts` (`PIFLEET_SCRATCH_DIR`, default `~/.pifleet/scratch`), visibility is
  proved by reading back a sentinel rather than by a successful mount, and `doctor` probes the
  runs root so the failure is loud and early. The default runs root was already under `$HOME`
  and was never affected; `PIFLEET_RUNS_DIR` pointing elsewhere was, which is what ISC-164 guards.
- **2026-08-18 — the ISC-129 root cause committed hours earlier (above) was itself wrong, caught
  by re-testing rather than trusting the write-up.** That entry concluded cmux 0.64.22 requires
  ref-form (`surface:N`) addressing and never resolves a raw UUID for `--surface` — a whole-backend
  rework. Asked to actually implement that rework, a fresh controlled A/B test (not a repeat of the
  same steps) showed every `--workspace`+`--surface` combination succeeds regardless of UUID-vs-ref
  spelling on either flag; the only failing case is `--workspace` omitted entirely, which is what
  `respawnPaneArgv`/`renameTabArgv` had always sent. The actual fix was two argv builders gaining a
  `--workspace` parameter and two id-codec functions gaining a third field to carry it, not a
  backend-wide addressing rewrite. **Learned: a root-cause writeup
  with a reproduction table still needs re-verification before code is built on top of it,
  especially one written under the same "prior diagnosis turned out wrong" pressure that produced
  this exact lesson three phases running now** — the corrected mechanism only surfaced by re-running
  the experiment with tighter controls (one variable changed at a time, immediately re-confirmed
  with a live shell + `send`/`read-screen`) instead of extending the earlier table's conclusion.
  Full corrected reproduction is in `## Verification`, "Phase 4 close-out," 2026-08-18 correction.
- **2026-08-18 — PR #8's review round (Claude/Gemini/Codex, same pattern as PR #7) caught a real
  test-coverage gap and a real backward-compatibility break the live verification above didn't
  surface, because live verification only exercises a fresh run end-to-end and never a stale
  `presentation.json` from an older build.** All three reviewers independently re-ran the live
  cmux A/B test themselves rather than accepting the PR's table at face value — by this point a
  deliberate habit, not an accident, per the two entries directly above. Two reviewers then
  mutation-tested the fix and proved the `--workspace`/`--surface` wiring in `index.ts` had zero
  test coverage (swap the two arguments, whole suite stays green); all three independently found
  that the composed pane id is persisted to `presentation.json` and read back by a later `attach`/
  `tui` process, so widening it from 2 to 3 fields breaks any run recorded by the pre-fix binary.
  **Learned: a live end-to-end verification proves the happy path for a run created and consumed by
  the same build — it says nothing about a run that started under an older build**, which is
  exactly the gap a cross-process persisted format opens and an in-process test cannot see. Full
  findings and fixes are in `## Verification`, "PR #8 review round."

- **2026-08-20 — `Docs/SRD-COMPLETION.md` (SRD-PIFLEET-002) now holds the ORDER for the 54
  criteria this ISA has not closed; this ISA still holds their state.** The two documents are
  deliberately not redundant: the SRD restates no criterion text and carries no checkboxes,
  because a second checklist drifts from the system of record. Precedence is unchanged and
  now explicit in three directions — SRD-001 wins on design, this ISA wins on whether a
  criterion is met, and SRD-002 wins only on which unclosed criterion is built next.
  **The finding that shaped the order:** the 54 have five root causes, and two of those causes
  are not engineering work. Nine criteria (ISC-22, 41, 47, 48, 50, 258, 259, 262, 290) are
  mechanisms that already work with no CI runner able to witness them, and three (ISC-243,
  264, 268) are disjunctions whose arms differ in size by up to 20:1 and which are waiting on
  an owner's answer. Treating either class as ordinary backlog mis-sizes the remainder by
  weeks. **The consequence worth recording:** ISC-290, which reads like the last possible
  item, is blocked by exactly one unbuilt code item — ISC-291's probe target — plus a
  configuration change that ISC-259's resolution already made legal. It is stated in the SRD
  as the first claim to falsify rather than as an assumption to build on.

- **2026-08-20 — Phase A of SRD-PIFLEET-002: two of three disjunctions answered by the owner.**
  **ISC-264 — arm 2, accept the overload.** `RELAY_LISTEN_ALIAS` stays `host.docker.internal`;
  the criterion closes with a test pinning the documented name rather than with a rename. SRD
  §5.9 already argued the acceptance on two checkable grounds and a rename would break every
  existing config for a semantic improvement.
  **ISC-268 — arm 1, WIRE it.** `adc_mode: file` is to be mounted through `buildDockerArgv`
  and proved by an integration test that `docker inspect`s a container built from
  `buildDockerArgv`'s own output, not from hand-written `-v` flags. This is the larger arm and
  was chosen over removal deliberately: it keeps a service-account-key-file path that an
  unattended host or CI runner may need instead of token mode. Consequence to carry forward —
  ISC-44's three-relation mount guard has exactly one carve-out, the single ADC file this mode
  mounts, and that branch has never executed against real argv; wiring the mode makes it
  load-bearing on its first run, so its test must exercise the carve-out and not only the mount.
  **ISC-243 — arm 1, close the measured holes and restate the anti-criterion.** The denylist
  stays the mechanism; the 44-path probe becomes a regression test, the 40 measured misses
  become patterns, the verdict cap widens, and the anti-criterion is restated as an accepted
  documented residual. Chosen over building the graded allowlist because a PARTIAL allowlist is
  strictly worse than a known-partial denylist: `harness.patterns` REPLACES rather than extends,
  so the first over-cap is answered by narrowing the surface — the silent disable ISC-232
  exists to prevent.
  **[SUPERSEDED 2026-08-25 — the owner reversed this to the graded-allowlist arm, and the note
  is kept rather than edited because the reason it was wrong is the useful part.]** Arm 1's
  whole argument rested on `harness.patterns` replacing rather than extending, and that premise
  was repaired on 2026-08-25: extension is now the default and `harness.replace: true` is the
  named opt-out. With an over-cap no longer answerable by silently narrowing the surface, the
  stated risk of the larger arm evaporated and only the work remained. Built 2026-08-26 — see
  the ISC-243 entry for what landed, and for why it graded `[~]` rather than `[x]`.

  **2026-08-21 — ISC-172 closed by attacking it, and the attack is what found the hole.** Two
  container-end probes were written to discharge the last mile the previous grade named. The
  path-agreement probe did what it was designed to do. The truncation probe did something
  else: it failed, correctly, against a collector everyone believed already detected
  truncation — including this ISA, in writing. Building the probe as an ATTACK rather than as
  a demonstration is the whole reason the gap surfaced; a probe that had merely re-run the
  collector against a hand-written ledger would have stayed green forever.

  **2026-08-21 — delegation floor relaxed to zero, show-your-math.** The E3 soft floor is two.
  What delegation would have bought: parallel work on ISC-125 while ISC-172 closed. What it
  would have cost is recorded in `feedback_agents_stall_at_mutation_proofs` — three subagents
  in the previous session stalled at the mutation-proof boundary against a token ceiling, one
  leaving its mutation APPLIED beneath a docstring describing the real design. This work was a
  single-file surgical change gated on a Docker daemon and a re-derived CI count, with the
  finding arriving mid-stream; splitting it across a context that cannot hold the finding is
  how the frontier gap would have been committed as green.

  **2026-08-21 — ISC-125 designed and measured, deliberately not built.** The honeypot shape was
  proved against the real image under the production security flags before being written down,
  and a cheaper FIFO variant was ruled out on mechanism (a docker client `connect(2)`s; a named
  pipe answers `ENOTSOCK`). It stays `[ ]` because two of its four costs are architectural
  firsts — a tmpfs on `/run` in the launch argv, and a background process alongside the agent
  in the worker container, which `entrypoint.sh` has never had. Building either blind, at the
  tail of a session, is how the ISC-246 rescue commit shipped a live mutation; the ISA's own
  precedent for a criterion whose cost is an architectural first is to decide it in writing and
  build it with its consumer, not before.

  **2026-08-23 — the SRD's two-item path to ISC-290 is a THREE-item path, found by attempting
  the run.** §5 names ISC-291 (done, `[x]`) and one configuration change as everything standing
  between the fleet and a real end-to-end run, and calls that "the plan's most actionable claim
  and the one most worth falsifying first". Falsified. With `llm.relay_upstream:
  192.168.86.49:8000` and the paired `egress.allow` entry both set and `config validate` green,
  `up` still refused: *"oMLX unreachable at http://host.docker.internal:8000/v1/chat/completions:
  fetch failed"*. The URL is CORRECT — `up`'s native-tool-call gate dials `base_url` verbatim
  through `containerFetch` on purpose, because ISC-260's whole content is that the gate must test
  the path a WORKER takes. What failed is the relay behind that alias. `docker inspect` on the
  live container: created 2026-08-20, `PIFLEET_RELAY_TARGETS=[{"listenPort":8000,"host":
  "host.docker.internal","port":8000,"name":"omlx"}]` — still forwarding to the Docker host's
  oMLX, which is deliberately unloaded. `up` adopted it unchanged, as `relay.ts:426` says it
  does: "adoption never compares targets". So the config change is INERT until the relay is
  recreated by hand, and `down` does not touch the relay because several fleets may share one.
  **That gap is ISC-265, and ISC-265 is in PHASE J — which the phase table says waits on A and
  C.** The dependency is therefore wrong for this purpose: ISC-290 cannot be reached without
  ISC-265 or a manual `docker rm -f`, and Phase J's own exit criterion is worded for exactly
  this — "changing `relay_upstream` takes effect with no manual `docker rm -f`". **The fix looks
  cheap and the data already exists:** `ensureEgressRelay` already records what the current
  checkout WOULD have started on an adopted relay (`relay.ts:423-426`), so drift detection is a
  comparison against a value that is already computed, not new plumbing.

  **2026-08-23 — the first end-to-end run, and what it moved.** Ordered by how much each
  changes the plan. (1) The chain RUNS: `up`, container launch, dispatch, a real model turn
  with real tool calls and a correct edit, supervisor settle, harvest, adjudication, merge
  pre-check — every stage executed against a real container and the LAN oMLX. (2) ISC-290
  stays `[~]` for a reason that is no longer about pifleet: the AGENT wedged mid-turn. (3) The
  relay adopts stale targets, so ISC-265 (Phase J) is on ISC-290's critical path and the phase
  table does not say so. (4) Three settle ceilings disagree — client 600s, task 900s, stall
  kill 25m — so `dispatch --auto` reports "not settling" before the supervisor settles. None of
  (3) or (4) was visible from any test; both needed the run.

## Changelog

- **conjectured:** a check that compares two strings after normalising both is safe when the
  normalisation is the same function on each side. "Both sides means both sides" is the symmetric,
  obviously-correct reading, and `doctor`'s allowlist verdict was written that way on purpose.
  **refuted by:** ISC-424. `decomposeModel` strips two decorations, and only one of them is symmetric.
  A `provider/` prefix is config grammar whose served-side analogue is a repo-id namespace, so
  stripping it from both sides is right. A `:thinking` suffix is not: a server does not serve thinking
  levels, so a `:tag` in `GET /v1/models` is the server NAMING A MODEL. Measured 2026-09-01:
  `allowlistVerdicts(["ollama/gpt-oss:high"], ["gpt-oss:low"], "omlx")` returned `served: true` —
  `:high` came off the entry, `:low` came off the served id, both became `gpt-oss`, and the check whose
  entire job is catching a model the server does not have reported it green. The block in
  `doctor-allowlist.test.ts` asserting "the comparison uses decomposition" passed throughout.
  **learned:** the test block was not weak, it was DEGENERATE. Every fixture in it decorated a model
  whose distinguishing suffix was a quantisation (`-4bit`, `-8bit`) or a repo-id namespace, and neither
  can collide with a thinking level — so on every input the file contained, the normalised and the raw
  comparison agree, and the two implementations are indistinguishable. **A normalising comparison is
  untested until a fixture exists where the normalisation CHANGES the answer**, and the cheap tell is
  that no row in the block can be made to fail by deleting the normalisation. Ollama's whole catalogue
  is spelled with a colon, which is why a feature that adds a hosted provider is what surfaced this: the
  fixtures were not chosen badly, they were chosen from the one provider the repo had. Found by reading
  the function against a new provider's spelling, not by running it.

- **conjectured:** a criterion closed by an explicit owner decision is durable. The decision was the
  hard part, the evidence was enumerated at the time, and what threatens such a criterion is a change
  that CONTRADICTS it — so the thing to watch for is someone arguing the opposite.
  **refuted by:** ISC-259, closed `[x]` on 2026-08-28, whose closing evidence names three mechanisms as
  *"each ... the reason a hosted provider cannot appear by accident"*. The first was the pin on
  `llm.base_url`'s host. **ISC-369 removed that pin** — deliberately, for a good reason, so a fleet
  could dial the operator's own published tunnel — and ISC-369 never mentions ISC-259, because it had no
  reason to. Nothing contradicted ISC-259; a mechanism it CITED was deleted underneath it. Measured
  2026-09-01 by driving `parseConfig`, `omlxRelayTarget`, `relayListenAliases` and `assertTargetsAllowed`
  directly: pointing the entire fleet at a third-party hosted provider now VALIDATES and is ALLOWED. The
  criterion had read green for four days while the word `never` in its sentence was unenforced.
  **learned:** the strictness rule already says `[x]` requires something reproducible that re-checks the
  claim — and ISC-259 shows the failure mode that survives it, because ISC-259's evidence WAS
  reproducible; it was just re-checking mechanisms that had since changed. The generalisable form:
  **a criterion whose closing note enumerates named mechanisms has taken a dependency on them, and
  deleting one is a change to that criterion even when the deleting change never names it.** The cheap
  tell is directional — when a criterion's evidence lists mechanisms rather than asserting a behaviour,
  the mechanisms are what to re-grep on any change that touches them. The expensive tell is the one that
  fired here: a feature request ("let a worker use a hosted provider") that turns out to be ALREADY
  POSSIBLE is not a feature request, it is a report that a guard is missing. Re-graded to `[~]` BEFORE
  any implementing code exists, because the drift is real whether or not the feature is ever built.

- **conjectured:** a claim that greps for a line of code defends that line. ISC-300's claim pinned
  the reaper's narrowing so that resolving the trade without regrading would turn the registry red,
  and that is what a claim is for.
  **refuted by:** moving the line. The narrowing went from `reapStale` into `reapSupervisor` — same
  behaviour, one place instead of two — and the old spelling survived inside a COMMENT explaining
  the move. The grep matched the prose. For one commit the claim was green while the code it
  defended did not exist, and it would have stayed green if the narrowing had been deleted
  outright. Caught only because the claim passing was SURPRISING: the line had just been removed by
  hand and the guard should have fired.
  **learned:** `ISC-272`'s writer claim in the same file already warned that "a comment that
  teaches the broken spelling is how it comes back" — and the warning cuts both ways. Prose can
  keep a claim ALIVE as readily as it can reintroduce a defect, and the second failure is worse,
  because a red claim asks for attention while a vacuous green one asserts everything is fine. The
  generalisable form: **a claim's grep must be checked against the file's COMMENTS, not only its
  code**, and a comment near a pinned line should decline to quote the pinned form. The cheap tell
  is the one that worked here — when a guard does not fire on a change you know you made, the guard
  is the thing to inspect, not the change.

- **conjectured:** restating a criterion to match what the code deliberately does is bookkeeping —
  the engineering is finished, the sentence is merely inconvenient, and moving it is what closes
  the gap between an honest implementation and a grade.
  **refuted by:** what the restatement actually costs, which is only visible once it is written
  down. ISC-191's original said the ladder uses `(pid, started)` identity, "never pid alone", and
  the restatement gives up the unqualified `never`. That word was not decoration: on a pid an
  operator types, rung 0 still reads `started` off that pid and cannot tell a supervisor from a
  stranger — it can only tell that a human looked at the number. Rewording does not make that
  false, it makes it OUT OF SCOPE, and the difference between those two matters to whoever reads
  the entry next. So both entries keep their originals verbatim and name what was surrendered in
  the same breath as the new sentence.
  **learned:** a restatement is a decision about what the criterion is FOR, and it is only honest
  when the surrendered clause survives in the record next to it. The sequencing is the other half
  and it was load-bearing here: ISC-272's four residuals were closed or filed on their own terms
  FIRST — (2) and (3) with mutations, (4) as ISC-300 with no behaviour changed, ISC-191's orphan
  pinned by a test that reddens if the forced path is ever widened — and only then was the scope
  narrowed. Reversed, the new wording would have absorbed four open questions instead of
  documenting one deliberate trade, and the grade would have moved for the wrong reason. The
  generalisable form: **narrow a criterion's scope last, never as the mechanism that closes it**,
  because a scope change applied first is indistinguishable from giving up.

- **conjectured:** ISC-272's residuals (2) and (3) were small test-writing jobs — a missing EPERM
  fixture and a mid-climb case recorded as "unreachable and untested". Two afternoons of fixtures
  against code that was already correct.
  **refuted by:** trying to write the first one. `bun test test/unit/kill.test.ts` — the obvious
  command for anyone working on the kill ladder — was `0 pass / 1 error / exit 1`, throwing
  `ReferenceError: Cannot access 'realProcessOps' before initialization`. Its THIRTY probes only
  ever ran inside a full-suite run where some earlier file imported the graph in a working order,
  and CI never noticed because CI never runs one file. "Unreachable and untested" was not a
  statement about those two cases; it was a symptom of a module nobody could probe in isolation.
  Two of the three things then found were live defects rather than missing coverage: EPERM escaped
  `runKillLadder`, and because `reapSupervisor` calls it bare inside a loop with no try, ONE
  unsignallable worker discarded every report the pass had already collected — the exact harm the
  SIGKILL rung's own comment describes for an escaping identity read, fixed there and left standing
  one path over. And `signalGuarded` had returned `"errored"` since it was written with NOTHING
  ever matching the value, so `down` reported a ladder it had not climbed — a bug that file's own
  comment describes fixing for workers and "left standing three hundred lines down", still standing
  on both rungs.
  **learned:** "untested" in a criterion is a claim about coverage, and it kept getting read as
  one. Twice this round it was really a claim about ACCESS — the code could not be reached from a
  test, so nobody wrote the test, so the entry recorded the absence and the cause went unnamed for
  a week. The generalisable form: **when an entry says a case is unreachable, verify the
  unreachability before believing the case is safe**, because a case nobody can exercise is also a
  case nobody has checked. The mechanical backstop is cheap and was missing: a per-module
  subprocess guard asserting every safety module loads FIRST in a fresh process, which an
  in-process import cannot express — after the first test file runs the graph is warm and the
  broken order is unreachable, so the assertion would pass for every arrangement of the code.

- **conjectured:** ISC-154's entry was FALSE and the criterion was closable by regrading. Its
  headline said the rule was inert — "nothing populates `tree_hash_quiesce`/`tree_hash_harvest`, so
  the check cannot fire" — while `harvest/index.ts` demonstrably populated both and three probes
  drove the rule through the real CLI. Two mutations confirmed it: breaking the comparison reddened
  one probe with `Expected: "unknown" / Received: "success"`, and reverting the WIRING to the inert
  state the headline describes reddened all three.
  **refuted by:** reading past the headline. The entry had superseded itself six days earlier
  ("THE ANTECEDENT IS NOW REACHABLE... the bracketed note above is superseded") and then given a
  real reason to stay `[~]`: every probe was a host-process test, so what was proved was that the
  fleet's two samples disagree, not that work escaping a CONTAINER'S epoch is noticed. The grade was
  correct; only its headline had rotted. En route, a docstring was very nearly committed asserting
  the criterion had been "graded on a false note" — a comment that lies about the code, the exact
  defect class this repo keeps re-learning, caught by re-reading the entry rather than by any test.
  A second instance surfaced in the same sweep: ISC-272's "What closing it costs" paragraph
  prescribes a schema migration that a later passage in the same entry retires outright
  ("NO SCHEMA FIELD WAS ADDED... is superseded"), and a recommendation had already been made to the
  operator on the strength of it.
  **learned:** an entry that corrects itself IN PLACE, downstream, is only as true as the distance a
  reader travels. Both rotten cases share a shape — a confident early claim, a supersede a thousand
  characters later, and nothing at the top saying "do not cost this from here". The generalisable
  form: **a long-lived record must carry its corrections at the point of first contact, not in
  narrative order**, because the reader who most needs the correction is the one skimming. The
  mechanical backstop is narrower and sharper: ISC-154's headline was free to rot for six days
  precisely because NO claim in `isa-claims.ts` defended it, and the claim now added pins the two
  SAMPLING lines rather than the field assignments — the inert state assigned those same names a
  literal `null`, so the obvious grep would have matched the broken code and stayed green through
  exactly the regression that caused the filing.

- **conjectured:** ISC-125's hard part was DETECTION. The entry had said so since 2026-08-20 — a
  `--cap-drop ALL` container's failed syscall is invisible from the host, so the criterion was
  blocked on a mechanism, and the honeypot design of 2026-08-21 was written as the answer to that
  question.
  **refuted by:** the detection half taking one file and one measurement — a node AF_UNIX listener
  bound at `/var/run/docker.sock` worked on the first try under the full production posture, and the
  `/run` tmpfs uid gotcha this entry had already predicted was the only surprise, i.e. not one. The
  time went entirely into the two halves the entry had listed as costs rather than as risks: making
  the entrypoint a SUPERVISOR (two defects, both found by running the thing rather than reasoning
  about it — `kill -0` succeeds on zombies, and `wait -n -p` unsets its variable so `set -u` aborted
  every `docker stop`), and deciding what the REPORT should say. The second turned out to be the
  criterion's real content: `attempts: 0` is not a claim about anything unless something was
  listening, so the report needed a third state — NOT WATCHED — that nobody had asked for and
  without which the feature reports reassurance rather than evidence.
  **learned:** for a detector, the mechanism is the cheap half and the REPORTING CONTRACT is the
  expensive one, because that is where "we saw nothing" has to be made distinguishable from "we were
  not looking". The generalisable form: **any monitor whose absence of output is meaningful needs an
  affirmative liveness record on the same channel as its findings, or its silence is unreadable.**
  Two smaller lessons. A test that kills a process by NAME is a trap in a container built from this
  repo's own scripts — `pkill -f pifleet-honeypot` matched the entrypoint's and the worker's own
  argv (which contained the string from the test script) and `pkill` was not installed at all; it
  reported success, killed nothing, and would have had me "fix" working supervision. And the claims
  registry has a blind spot its own header does not describe: it catches a claim whose RESULT moved
  in either direction, and not one whose SUBJECT moved — `grep -rn hazard src/report/` stayed empty
  and stayed green while the sentence it defended ("the report carries no security field at all")
  became false.
  **criterion now:** ISC-125 is `[x]` on the narrow reading stated in its entry — a seeded connect is
  recorded, reaches the run report, and an unwatched container says so — with five residuals named
  there, of which socket SUBSTITUTION and row FORGERY are the two that a reader is most likely to
  assume away.

- **conjectured:** Phase E was six criteria and roughly three PRs, and the risk was thought to be the
  supervisor logic — a UI-request state machine, a peer-credential API that might not exist under Bun,
  a containment policy with no obviously-correct answer.
  **refuted by:** all three of those being tractable, and the same non-technical failure recurring in
  four of the four agent runs: a complete, well-argued module written and **never wired to a
  production caller**, reported as finished. Every one stopped within a sentence of the call site.
  ISC-111/112 shipped `ui-requests.ts` callerless; ISC-108 shipped `prose-detector.ts` with an import
  line and no call. Both would have passed a unit suite over the module and closed nothing, which is
  the RC-1 shape this ISA has recorded eight times. What caught it every time was the same two
  commands — read the diff rather than the report, and `grep` for the caller before grading.
  **learned:** the recurring defect in this workflow is not in the code, it is in the reporting layer,
  and it has a signature: a final line that ends mid-sentence is a token ceiling, not a completion.
  Treating "done" as a claim to verify rather than a fact to act on cost two commands per criterion
  and caught four inert deliverables. The generalisable form: **when the deliverable is "a thing that
  runs", the acceptance test is `grep` for its caller, not the test suite that exercises it directly.**
  Two smaller lessons worth keeping. The guards paid for themselves without a human in the loop —
  ISC-147 refused three scenarios with no reviewed expectation and ISC-274 refused five ceilings whose
  derivation it could not read, and the second named its own remedy in its docstring, so it was fixed
  correctly by someone who had not written it. And two criteria closed by CORRECTING this file rather
  than by satisfying it: ISC-126's stated blocker was the wrong blocker (ENOTSUP on a bind-mounted
  socket, for every uid alike, not the shared set), and `control-auth.ts` had asserted for weeks that
  filesystem permissions were sufficient against another user — true at the operator's umask, false at
  `umask 000`. Neither correction was sought; both came from probing a claim the file already made.

- **conjectured:** Phase E-A was three criteria — answer dialogs (ISC-111), stop `editor` hanging (ISC-112), make
  ISC-113's vacuous half mean something — and the plan split it as `src` work and `test` work running in
  parallel, on the reading that the hard part was the supervisor logic.
  **refuted by:** both halves landing and neither being where the difficulty was. The `src` engineer produced a
  complete, well-argued policy module and stopped one step before wiring it into `onEvent`, leaving
  `src/supervisor/ui-requests.ts` callerless — which is not a near-miss but the exact shape that put eight
  criteria in RC-1, and would have been the ninth. It reported as finished; the diff said otherwise, and only the
  diff was checked because a mid-sentence final line is a token ceiling rather than a completion. Meanwhile the
  genuinely load-bearing work turned out to be on the test side, where `fake-pi` could emit a dialog but not
  BLOCK on one — so every probe for ISC-111/112 would have been green against a double that cannot fail. And the
  frame the whole thing turns on is not in the SRD at all: it had to be read out of the pinned image, where the
  key is `id` and the plausible `request_id` is dropped in silence.
  **learned:** the question "is it built?" and the question "is it reachable?" are different, and only the second
  one closes a criterion. Three separate mechanisms had to agree here — a module, a caller, and a probe that can
  fail — and each was independently at risk of looking done while being inert. The general rule this ISA keeps
  re-deriving: **read the diff, not the report, and grep for the caller before grading anything.** Two guards
  caught the rest without a human noticing — ISC-147 refused three scenarios with no reviewed expectation, and
  ISC-274 refused five ceilings whose derivation it could not read — and the second was fixed the way its own
  docstring said to fix it, by adding a third helper to `budget.ts` rather than arguing the exemption in one
  file. Guards that name their own remedy get repaired correctly by people who did not write them.
- **conjectured:** the agent wedge was the fleet's to fix. It had blocked ISC-290 since 2026-08-23 as
  "the agent wedged, not the fleet" — a sentence written from ONE run, which is exactly the kind of
  claim this ISA elsewhere refuses to grade on. The plausible fleet-side causes were all live: a relay
  that dropped a long-lived stream, a client with no read timeout, a supervisor that could not tell
  silence from thought. The planned next step was to build an inter-token watchdog.
  **refuted by:** running it twice more and measuring instead of building. The second run wedged in the
  same place, which made the failure reproducible; then four cheap probes moved it off the fleet in
  under an hour. The Pi process was at CPU 0.04% — blocked, not spinning. Both TCP legs were
  ESTABLISHED in the relay's own `/proc/net/tcp`, so nothing had dropped. oMLX served unrelated
  requests in 1–3 s while holding the wedged one, so it was not saturated. And the model turned out to
  be the variable: `Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-4bit` leaked its tool call as raw
  `<function=…></tool_call>` text in 1 of 3 attempts and produced a 1519-second generation in 1 of 4 on
  the wedge's own conversation shape, while the two other allowlisted models were 3/3 native. Swapping
  to `Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-8bit` and changing nothing else settled `success` in 13 seconds with correct work.
  **learned:** "our system hangs" and "one component of our system hangs" are different claims, and the
  cheapest discriminator is usually a *variable swap*, not an instrumentation build. Three of the four
  probes here cost a single command each, and the fourth — run the same task on a different allowlisted
  model — was the one that actually settled it. The watchdog would have been real work that made the
  wedge legible without making it stop. **The second-order lesson matches this session's other two
  closes:** the wedge was a single-run claim carried for a day as though it were a finding, and the
  thing that broke it open was re-running the SAME experiment rather than reasoning harder about the
  first result. A diagnosis resting on n=1 should say so in the grade, which ISC-290's note now does.
  A real fleet defect did fall out — the stall policy's WARN rung fired correctly at 3 minutes in both
  wedges and its KILL rung could not fire at all, because 25 m exceeds any task deadline under 25 m —
  and that is filed as ISC-297 rather than fixed here, because the fix is a defaults choice with an
  owner in it.

- **conjectured:** ISC-295 was filed as a path change — move `<repo>/.worktrees/<worker>` to
  `<repo>/.worktrees/<run-id>/<worker>` — and the filing predicted the hard part would be finding the
  callers, since a bind-mount source and the directory that creates it must agree or a worker comes up
  with an empty `/workspace` (ISC-188's shape).
  **refuted by:** the callers being the easy part and the TESTS being the finding. One helper already
  owned the path, so changing its signature turned every caller into a compile error — three in `src`,
  six in one test file, found in a single `tsc` run and fixed in minutes. What the change actually
  exposed is that `test/integration/worktree.test.ts` was 28/28 green against the defective layout and
  could never have been otherwise: every rig seeded a PRIVATE repo, so the arrangement the defect
  needs — two runs, one repo, same worker id — was unreachable by construction. The suite was not
  weakly asserting the wrong thing; it was thorough about everything except the one arrangement that
  mattered.
  **learned:** a green suite bounds the cases it can REACH, not the cases that exist, and rig
  construction silently decides which is which. This is the same lesson ISC-296 recorded from the
  other side hours earlier — there, CI was green because the runner lacked an ambient `fleet.yaml`;
  here, a suite was green because every rig was isolated by construction. Both are "green for a reason
  unrelated to correctness", and both were invisible until someone asked what the test could not do.
  The practical rule: when filing a defect about two things interacting, check whether any existing
  test can put those two things in the same room, and if not, say so in the filing — which is why
  ISC-295 carried "do NOT close it on a test passing" from the day it was written, and why that
  sentence is the reason this closed honestly.

- **conjectured:** ISC-51 could not be closed without procurement. Phase C listed it among ten
  criteria "blocked on a self-hosted runner", and the containment defect had sat at `[~]` since
  2026-08-19 as an accepted residual documented in SRD §12.8 — a thing to be measured and printed on
  every run rather than fixed. The blocking sub-question, raised before any code was written, was
  privilege: pifleet is an unprivileged user-space CLI, `iptables` needs CAP_NET_ADMIN in the host
  network namespace, and the owner's chosen fallback was a hard refusal. A refusal pifleet's own CI
  could not satisfy would have broken the entire `container` job — a far larger blast radius than the
  hole it closed. Three arms were drafted for how to ASK for the privilege: call `sudo` and treat a
  password prompt as the refusal; require the operator to pre-install the rule and have pifleet only
  verify it; attempt-then-verify so CI could pre-install.
  **refuted by:** a four-line probe run before choosing between them. `docker run --privileged
  --network host` returned a working `iptables` against the host's tables under colima. pifleet does
  not need to acquire privilege at all — it already holds the Docker daemon, and the daemon's host
  namespace is exactly the namespace whose listeners a worker can reach. On Linux that is the machine;
  on macOS/colima it is the Lima VM, which is the correct target and not a compromise. All three arms
  were answers to a question that did not need asking. A second probe removed the last dependency:
  `nsenter -m` borrows the host's own `iptables` binary, so the already-pinned `RELAY_IMAGE` — which
  has `nsenter` and not `iptables` — is sufficient and no second image is introduced.
  **learned:** "we lack the privilege for X" deserves one measurement before it becomes a plan, and
  the measurement should probe what the process ALREADY holds before designing a way to ask for more.
  Every drafted arm degraded something real — sudo prompts, an operator prerequisite, a CI setup step
  — and all of that cost was imaginary. The generalisable form: when a capability seems to require
  escalation, first enumerate the privileged components already in the trust boundary. A tool that
  orchestrates Docker is not an unprivileged tool. **The second-order lesson is about how the ISA
  itself misled:** Phase C's "blocked on a runner" grouping was a category, not a finding, and it hid
  a defect that needed no procurement for four days. The re-scope that split C1 out (2026-08-23) was
  what surfaced it, and it surfaced it by asking of each criterion what it actually needed rather than
  inheriting the label the phase carried.

- **conjectured:** ISC-293 was filed as a bounded arithmetic fix — derive the fleet-wide ceiling from
  the task list instead of asserting a constant beside it — and the run that prompted it, with a 900 s
  deadline refused at 600 s, was taken as a fair statement of the defect's size.
  **refuted by:** two measurements taken while fixing it. First, `TaskSpecSchema.deadline_s` defaults
  to **1800 s**, so a task list naming no deadline at all was refused twenty minutes early; the
  measured run used 900 s and was therefore the MILD case, not a representative one. Second, and worse,
  mutating the ceiling to `Infinity` did not fail the suite — it hung it. `elapsed > Infinity` is never
  true, so the refusal is unreachable, and the poll loop awaits an already-resolved promise, starving
  the macrotask queue so that even bun's per-test timeout cannot fire to rescue it.
  **learned:** a guard's bad states are not all the same kind. A guard that mis-grades produces a wrong
  answer someone can read; a guard that becomes unreachable produces NO answer, and a suite that hangs
  is strictly worse than one that fails — CI reports nothing and a developer waits. So the fix carries
  two things the criterion never asked for: `runSchedule` refuses a non-finite ceiling at `EXIT.USAGE`
  rather than obeying it, and the test harness carries a tick budget so this whole class fails loudly.
  Neither was visible from the criterion; both came from mutating the fix.
  **criterion now:** ISC-293 is `[x]` on a derivation mutation-proved six ways, and ISC-294 is `[x]`
  by construction from it — the refusal cannot precede a task's deadline, so no second check was
  added, because a second derivation of one fact is what produced this defect.
- **conjectured:** closing ISC-265 meant deciding whether a mismatched relay "should kill a relay other
  fleets may be using" — a lifecycle question weighty enough that the ISC-259 branch deferred it in
  writing, and one whose safe answer looked like "refuse `up` and tell the operator to `docker rm -f`".
  **refuted by:** the criterion's own words, read literally. It says the change "takes effect without a
  manual `docker rm -f`", so an answer that ends in the operator running `docker rm -f` does not close
  it — it renames the defect. Pushing on the concurrent-fleet worry then dissolved it: adoption never
  protected the other fleet. If the targets have drifted, two configs disagree about where the one
  shared relay points and it can satisfy only one of them; adoption picks whoever booted first,
  arbitrarily and invisibly. There was never a "leave the other fleet alone" arm to choose.
  **learned:** a safety question about a shared resource is only real if the incumbent behaviour is
  actually safe. Here the incumbent was making the same choice — silently, and on the worse key. Once
  both arms are wrong for somebody, the choice is not safety versus risk but legible versus invisible,
  and that has an obvious answer. The deferral was still correct: it is a different decision from the
  parsing, and it wanted its own change.
  **criterion now:** ISC-265 is `[x]` — the code replaces a drifted relay itself and records what it
  displaced; mutation-proved in CI, and the end-to-end effect asserted by a probe the `container`
  job runs against a real daemon (run 32676103178).

- **conjectured:** the verbgate collector already detected truncation, so ISC-172's remaining work was
  purely evidential — write a probe that drives a real container and the criterion closes. The grade
  said so in as many words: "truncation itself is detected and RECORDED".
  **refuted by:** the probe, on its first run against a real worker container. `truncations: 0`. All
  three restart signals miss the same attack at once, and they miss it for one shared reason:
  `docker/verbgate` stamps whole seconds, so two rows in one second are byte-identical for 64 bytes and
  the head fingerprint has nothing to see. The file regrew past the old offset, so no `shrank`; the
  in-place truncate kept the inode, so no `replaced`. The reader resumed mid-record and the audit copy
  recorded the fragment `}` as a row.
  **learned:** a detector's discriminating power is a property of the WRITER's output, not of the
  detector. Sixty-four bytes is ample against a writer whose lines differ early and useless against one
  whose lines differ late — and every unit test of this reader had used synthetic rows that differ at
  byte one, which is why the suite was green and stayed green. The head fingerprint was never wrong; it
  was answering a different question from the one an audit trail asks. Detection anchored at a FIXED
  prefix asks "is this the same file?"; an offset-holding reader needs "is my boundary still my
  boundary?", and only a fingerprint at the consumed frontier answers it.
  **criterion now:** `TailRestartReason` gains `tail_rewritten`, fingerprinting the bytes ending at the
  reader's offset and re-anchored every poll. ISC-172 closes on the owner-restated guarantee, with its
  residual — rows written and truncated between two passes are lost — stated rather than closed.


- **conjectured:** the 4 MiB byte cap also bounds the COST of validating an envelope, so ISC-122 needs
  no element-count limb. I measured 1,048,550 elements at 127 MB / 46 ms — about 30x — and recorded the
  reported 2.88 GB figure as quantitatively refuted.
  **refuted by:** my own measurement, of the wrong shape. The reviewer's elements were INVALID for their
  field; mine were valid. zod type-validates every element and allocates one issue object per FAILING
  element before it ever reports the length violation, so the cost is a function of how many elements are
  wrong, not how many there are. Re-measured with invalid elements: 2,097,101 of them in exactly 4,194,304
  bytes cost **2.66 GB and 1.2 s** — matching the original report, and 20x my own number.
  **learned:** two measurements of "the same thing" that differ by 20x are measuring different things, and
  the discrepancy was the finding rather than noise around it. I had published the refutation before
  looking for a shape that would explain the gap. A byte cap cannot bound validation cost when elements
  can be 2 bytes and each wrong one allocates an object — and only `issues[0]` is ever read, so the other
  2,097,100 issue objects are built to be discarded.
  **criterion now:** ISC-122 gains an element-count limb. Array lengths are checked on the parsed value
  BEFORE the schema, so zod never sees an oversized array: same envelope now refused in 18 ms at 55 MB.

- **conjectured:** the SRD's epoch-window rule was sufficient to attribute terminal events to epochs.
  **refuted by:** a commitment-boundary review pointing out that events carry no correlation id, so a
  late `agent_end` for epoch N and a real one for N+1 are byte-identical under a wall-clock window.
  **learned:** the ordering signal was already available and unused — events and responses share one
  stdout stream, so a per-record sequence number yields a genuine happens-before relation.
  **criterion now:** ISC-141 requires the §7.5 interleaving to be decided when stream offset is the
  only distinguishing signal.
- **conjectured:** re-running the acceptance commands gave the harvester facts independent of the
  worker being graded. **refuted by:** the observation that the command string resolves through
  `package.json` scripts, `conftest.py`, `.git/hooks` and the Makefile, every one of which is inside
  the worker's mutable surface — so "independently re-run the tests" grades the worker using the
  worker's own harness. **learned:** independence is a property of *where and from which tree* the
  command is resolved and executed, not of *who* runs it. **criterion now:** ISC-148..150 require
  base-SHA resolution, a fresh clone outside the worktree, and a verdict cap when the diff touches
  the harness surface.

- **conjectured:** the SRD's `CompactionEntry.retainedTail` named a real field of the Pi session
  format. **refuted by:** the installed `docs/session-format.md` for 0.79.6, which spells the same
  concept as `summary` plus `firstKeptEntryId` — `retainedTail` does not exist. **learned:** the
  SRD's §8.2 reconstruction rule was written from the concept rather than from the binary, the
  same failure mode §18 records eleven of. Ground truth is the installed version.
  **criterion now:** ISC-91's leaf-to-root walk is specified against `firstKeptEntryId`; SRD §8.2
  carries an erratum.

- **conjectured:** `unknown` as the lattice identity was safe in every direction, so a task with
  no independent evidence could adopt the worker's claim. **refuted by:** probing a timed-out
  acceptance run against a claimed `success` — verdict `success`, for a worker whose exam never
  finished, reachable without touching a single harness file by shipping a change that makes an
  existing command hang. **learned:** identity is right for a missing CLAIM and wrong for missing
  EVIDENCE; the two had been conflated because ISC-94 only ever exercised the first.
  **criterion now:** ISC-230 caps the verdict when an attempted command returns no answer, while
  ISC-152 still forbids calling it `failed`.

- **conjectured:** SRD §9.2 specified `git worktree add` (linked worktrees, `git worktree prune`,
  per-repo serialization) as the mechanism behind `isolation: worktree` — a worker gets its own
  branch and its own tree, and a linked worktree is the obvious way to give it one without a
  full clone's cost.
  **refuted by:** a security spike that built and ran two `git worktree add`-based designs against
  a real container, not merely reasoned about them. Mounting only the linked worktree directory
  fails outright: a linked worktree's `.git` is a FILE holding a `gitdir:` pointer into the
  parent's `.git/worktrees/<name>`, a path outside anything the container's mount table can name,
  so git inside the container answers `fatal: not a git repository` and the worker cannot commit
  at all. Also mounting the gitdir at its real host path to fix that makes it work — and is a
  confirmed container-to-host remote code execution: from inside the container the spike zeroed
  the host's `refs/heads/main` and planted an executable `.git/hooks/post-checkout` that ran as
  the OPERATOR'S host user on their very next ordinary `git checkout`.
  **learned:** §9.1's "two nested boundaries" table treats the container and the worktree as
  independent controls, but they are not independent when the worktree mechanism's own control
  file (`.git`) is a pointer that must resolve OUTSIDE the container to work at all — mounting
  what makes it resolve hands the confined party write access to the confining party's hook
  directory, and the outer boundary dissolves. A design has to be run against a real container to
  find this; reading `git worktree add --help` does not surface it.
  **criterion now:** `run/worktree.ts` implements `isolation: worktree` as `git clone
  --no-hardlinks --single-branch --branch <the operator's checked-out branch>` per worker, with
  `origin` stripped immediately after (so the host's absolute repository path cannot be read out
  of a container-readable `.git/config`) and a `worker-<id>` remote registered in the PARENT so
  an operator can still read a worker's commits (`git -C <repo> fetch worker-<id>`) without
  leaving their own checkout. `--no-hardlinks` is independently load-bearing: a bare local clone
  defaults to `--local`, which hardlinks object files into the copy rather than copying them, and
  a worker container writing through its own "copy" then corrupts the PARENT'S object store
  through the shared inode — not hypothetical, it is how the spike investigating this feature
  destroyed this repository's own pack file, recovered via `git fetch origin --refetch` with no
  data lost. SRD §9.2 now carries this as a full erratum rather than a silent rewrite, and
  `pifleet worktrees` (new CLI command, §10) replaces the operator-visibility `git worktree list`
  used to provide, since an independent clone has no entry in the parent's worktree list at all.

## Verification

*(Evidence per ISC, appended as each criterion passes.)*

### Twenty-two fixtures, one of which catches anything — 2026-08-25

ISC-147 closed by extending the real-routing block from seven fixtures to all
twenty-four: twenty-two run, two deferred to the real-routing tests that
already cover them, and a coverage-integrity test that fails the suite if a
fixture has no entry or a deferral names no destination.

**The number worth keeping.** Of the twenty-two scenarios now driven through a
real supervisor, exactly ONE — `quiet-retry.json`, written two commits ago —
kills any mutation. Twenty-one hostile fixtures, accumulated over the life of
this project, catch nothing at either level, because `fake-pi.ts` decides
`isStreaming` by reading `willRetry` and therefore defends the tracker from
every one of them. Breadth of fixtures turned out to be nearly orthogonal to
strength of coverage: the twenty-second fixture was worth more than the other
twenty-one together, and it was worth that because it puts the DOUBLE into the
state the code under test exists to survive.

**Two mutations were left uncaught here on purpose.** `agent_start` not
clearing an unconsumed terminal end, and ignoring `queueEmpty`, both pass all
twenty-two — because both conditions sit behind the generation counter, which
invalidates the probe on any activity, so neither can produce an observable
premature settle under real routing. They are caught by unit probes instead.
Manufacturing fixtures to make redundant guards look load-bearing would have
produced a fuller-looking sweep and a false one.

**And the load found something.** All four tests in `container-launch.test.ts`
ran a 10 000 ms `waitForFile` gate under a `cliBudget(1)` ceiling of 5700 ms —
the bound inside what it bounds, ISC-293's inversion in a test budget. They
passed for as long as the suite was light enough. Twenty-two extra supervisor
launches were enough to expose one, and the failure pointed at the recorder
rather than at the budget. Fixed with `gateBudget` derived from the gates.

### The double was doing the defending — 2026-08-25

Gap (3) of ISC-147 said the completion property skipped `delay_ms`, `noise` and
`partial` and never issued an abort. Replaying those conditions through a real
supervisor is the obvious fix, it took a seven-scenario block, and it went green
on the first run — and then the same two mutations that had survived the
in-process table survived the real one too.

**The generalisation worth keeping:** moving a test from a simulator to the real
thing buys nothing when the simulator was copying the DOUBLE rather than the
code under test. `simulate()` decided `isStreaming` by reading `willRetry`;
`fake-pi.ts` decides it the same way; so at both levels the probe was told the
agent was streaming and refused to confirm before `CompletionTracker` was ever
consulted. Every fixture on disk was defended by the double. The fix is not a
better harness — it is a fixture that puts the double in the state the code
under test exists to survive, which is why `quiet-retry.json` had to be written
rather than found.

This is the second time in two days that an addition closing a named gap passed
immediately and had to be broken before it was worth anything. Both times the
green run was the misleading signal and the mutation was the informative one.

ISC-147 stays `[~]` on one residual: the real-routing block covers seven of
twenty-four fixtures, and extending it to all of them is a CI budget decision
(twenty-four supervisor launches against a `test` job already at five minutes),
not a design one. Parked with the owner alongside ISC-22.

### An assertion that could not fail, and the measurement that found it — 2026-08-25

ISC-147's first named gap was that its scenario table asserts a settle COUNT
and never a settle POSITION. Closing that is a twenty-line change and it went
green on the first run — which is the whole point of this note, because it went
green over a harness in which no premature settle was reachable. Two mutations
that should have been caught by a position assertion (`turn_end` treated as
terminal; `agent_start` not clearing an unconsumed terminal end) survived every
test in the file both before the assertion and after it.

**The rule this instance supports:** when an assertion is added to close a named
gap, break the thing it is supposed to catch and watch it fail, in the same
sitting. The cost of not doing that is not a missing test — it is a PRESENT test
that reads as coverage on every future audit. Three of this ISA's re-grades have
now turned on the difference.

What actually made the position assertion load-bearing was scripting the state
the harness could not otherwise produce: Pi reporting `isStreaming: false` while
a retry is outstanding. The harness had been answering that probe from its own
reading of `willRetry` — the field the tracker under test exists to interpret —
so it was grading the tracker with the tracker's own answer. `fake-pi.ts` models
it identically, which is why no existing fixture could expose the class.

ISC-147 stays `[~]`. Two of its three gaps are addressed and the third — the
quantifier, which skips `delay_ms`, `noise` and `partial` and never issues an
abort — is untouched. Grading it `[x]` on the two would be the same move this
note exists to warn about.

### The stall policy's production edges, and a flake that would not reproduce — 2026-08-25

ISC-282 closed, and ISC-110 and ISC-117 with it, on the reason each of them
actually gave. The work was NOT primarily writing tests: both functions were
methods on an object literal built inside `register()`'s action handler, closed
over a `run` and a `ledger` that exist only mid-invocation, so no test could
construct one. Moving them to `src/run/stall-io.ts` is the fix; the sixteen
probes are what that made possible. The adapter kept the binding and lost the
behaviour, and a source probe now forbids the behaviour coming home — proved by
re-inlining the mtime read and watching it go red, rather than asserted.

**The registry caught its second real re-grade.** `test/support/isa-claims.ts`
carries ISC-110's grade alongside its claim, so moving that entry to `[x]`
turned `isa-claims.test.ts` red until the registry was told. That is the second
time the guard has fired on a genuine re-grade rather than on drift, which is
the behaviour it was built for: a grade and its grounds cannot move apart
silently.

**A flake was found and deliberately NOT fixed, because it would not
reproduce.** The first full `bun test test/unit` run after the new file landed
failed `harvest-outbox.test.ts` -> "a hard link to a file outside the outbox is
refused", on the refusal REASON — expected to contain `link`, received `file
escapes the outbox (→ .../private/id_rsa)`. **Containment held in both cases:**
`scan.safe` is asserted empty on the line above and did not fail, so the file
was refused either way and only the classification differed. It did not recur:
four further full-suite runs on the same tree passed 1575/0, twelve isolated
runs of that test passed, and four full-suite runs on clean `main` passed
1567/0. So the evidence is one failure in five with the change against zero in
four without it — too weak to attribute and far too weak to justify editing a
security test's expectation. Recorded here rather than repaired: a guess at a
fix for a defect that will not reproduce is indistinguishable from weakening
the guard, which is the move this ISA has now warned about three times. If it
recurs in CI the reason string is the place to start, and the hypothesis worth
testing first is that `realpath` on an APFS hard link does not reliably return
the name it was given.

### The staleness sweep, and a guard so it is not done by hand again — 2026-08-25

**Closed:** ISC-115, ISC-193 (see their entries). **Corrected without re-grading:** ISC-110,
ISC-117, ISC-125, ISC-126, ISC-273, and a comment in `src/safety/kill.ts`. **Filed:** nothing —
the guard is repo hygiene and is named rather than numbered, per ISC-297's rule that numbers are
allocated centrally.

**What prompted it.** ISC-115 and ISC-193 were graded `[ ]` on 2026-08-19 by the
unreachable-module sweep and falsified on 2026-08-20 by the wiring commission, which re-graded
ISC-109, ISC-114 and ISC-235 and stopped. Nothing in this repo re-reads a criterion's REASONS —
only a human re-reads its checkbox — so two criteria spent five days asserting the opposite of the
code, and the same staleness sat in ISC-110, ISC-117 and a source comment.

**How wide the exposure is, measured rather than guessed.** 26 entries rest their grade on an
absence claim a command can re-check; 41 backticked `grep` invocations appear across the file.

**What the sweep actually found, including where it corrected its own first reading.** All 41
were re-run. Most differences are HISTORY working as intended: ISC-32's *"returns nothing"*
describes the state before that criterion closed and correctly returns 13 today. Two entries were
flagged as stale on a first pass and are NOT — ISC-154 carries a Phase H supersession and ISC-246
says in its own words that `scanOutboxFiles` has one production caller; the flag came from
matching a phrase without reading the paragraph, which is the same error in miniature that this
sweep exists to catch. ISC-126 likewise supersedes itself in its own close-out. The genuinely
stale grounds were the four fixed on this date and nothing else.

**A finding the sweep produced that nobody was looking for: two recorded commands cannot
reproduce their own numbers.** ISC-125 and ISC-126 both record `grep -rn 'a|b|c' src/`. Without
`-E`, grep reads `|` literally, so both return zero against entries reporting "exactly one hit"
and "NOTHING" respectively. Neither entry's substance is wrong; both entries' EVIDENCE was
un-runnable as written.

**The guard.** `test/support/isa-claims.ts` lists the live claims — criterion, grade, the sentence
`ISA.md` uses, and an argv (never a shell string, so quoting cannot change a pattern) — and
`test/unit/isa-claims.test.ts` re-runs each every CI run. A registry and not a scraper, because a
scraper cannot tell a live claim from a superseded one and a guard that cries wolf gets its
expectations edited rather than its subject fixed. Claims run in BOTH directions: `empty` catches
an entry stale because something was built, `nonempty` catches a closed criterion whose wiring is
silently removed — the case no checkbox notices, and the one ISC-115 spent five days in. The
registry records each criterion's grade and cross-checks it against `ISA.md`, so a re-grade that
does not revisit its claims goes red.

**Mutation-proved, four applied, each restored byte-identical:** unwiring both `budgetExitCode`
folds reddens ISC-193's claim; adding a `hazard` reference under `src/report/` reddens ISC-125's;
re-grading ISC-248 in `ISA.md` without touching the registry reddens the cross-check; dropping
`-E` from an alternation pattern reddens the flavour check. **And the guard caught a defect in
itself on its first run** — every claim quotes its own search string, so claims scanning `test/`
matched the registry and the runner, ISC-74 reading 4 hits instead of 1. The tempting repair was
to relax the expectation, which is the exact move the file's header warns against; the fix was to
stop the guard observing itself.

### Phase C oMLX cluster — the `container-live` job — 2026-08-25

**Closed:** ISC-50, ISC-258. **Filed:** ISC-298, ISC-299. **Held at `[~]` on purpose:** ISC-57,
ISC-259, ISC-290. Two checkboxes gained, two criteria created by what the job found.

**What was actually missing.** Not a mechanism — the relay probes had existed and passed since
2026-08-19. What was missing was a *witness*: they ran on one operator's laptop and in no CI job,
and ISC-50's own note predicted they could not run anywhere else, because oMLX binds
`127.0.0.1:8000` on a Mac and the live path leaned on Lima's host-gateway forwarding reaching
macOS loopback.

**The move that unblocked it changed no product code.** Rather than teach the fleet TLS or
tunnelling, `.github/scripts/omlx-shim.ts` makes the *runner's* `localhost:8000` behave the way the
operator's Mac does: it binds `0.0.0.0:8000` and proxies to the real server over a Cloudflare
tunnel. `src/` is untouched, so the thing under test is the same thing that ships. `0.0.0.0` rather
than loopback is the whole difference between this job and `omlx-live`, and it is not incidental —
these callers dial from *inside* a container via `--add-host host.docker.internal:host-gateway` and
land on the bridge address, where a loopback listener is invisible. The job proves both vantages
separately before running a probe, so a transport fault names the transport instead of blaming the
relay.

**Result on `ubuntu-latest`** (run 32797559555, job 97651850285):

    parsed[container-live]: pass=9 fail=0 skip=0 todo=0 total=9 expected=9 rc=0
    ok[container-live]: 9 probes accounted for ... the skip set matches all 0 pinned names exactly.

    [live] gemma-4-26b-a4b-it-4bit: relayed inference answered "4" in 463ms
           from inside the deny-all bridge (direct control: "4").
    [enumerated] gateway 172.18.0.1 (deny-all bridge) reaches [].

`TOTAL_EXPECTED` was DERIVED by the hand method, never incremented: `bun test
test/integration/relay.test.ts` with `PIFLEET_DOCKER` unset → `0 pass, 9 skip, 0 fail`.

**What the job found on its first run, which is the part worth keeping.** The whole-chain probe
failed with `Expected: 0, Received: 10` and no way to ask what the ten were. The fix was to make
the failure self-describing — the supervisor already writes every event verbatim to `events.jsonl`
before it counts anything, so the answer was on disk at the moment the assertion fired and the
assertion simply never looked. With the digest in place the second run said:

    11 of 17 tool call(s) errored ...
    {"toolName":"write","result":"EACCES: permission denied, open '/workspace/add.js'"}
    {"toolName":"bash","result":"chmod: ... '/workspace/add.js': Operation not permitted"}

That is ISC-298: the worker runs as uid 10001, `/workspace` is a Linux bind mount of
`<repo>/.worktrees/<run-id>/<worker>`, and Linux passes host ownership straight through. macOS
squashes it, which is why the identical suite is green on Colima — verified twice locally the same
day, with a stale image and with one freshly built, 33 s and 41 expect calls each time. Co-running
both files was ruled out the same way: `10 pass, 0 fail` locally.

**And the finding underneath the finding.** With every write refused and `add.js` never written,
`dispatch --auto` returned `verdict: success` and the task record read `verdict: success, reason:
quiesced`. An operator would have been told it worked. That is ISC-299, and it survives ISC-298's
fix: `supervisor/index.ts:613` documents this exact shape being caught once already (F39 — "worker
looks healthy, streams, settles, and does nothing"), and the reader added for it asks whether tools
were *called*. Seventeen were. Every one bounced. `state.tool_errors` is counted three lines up and
never consulted.

**Two things deliberately NOT done.** ISC-57 was not flipped: its own note says the residual —
sibling containers on the bridge are "other hosts" — is a criterion rewording and therefore an
owner call, so the run added evidence for the gateway half and left the marker alone. And ISC-298
was not patched around: widening permissions inside the operator's repository, relocating the
worktrees, or running as the host uid against ISC-25's baked 10001 are genuinely different
answers with different postures, so it is filed rather than chosen.

`~/.config/cmux/cmux.json` plus a password set once through cmux's own
Settings UI (the JSON's own `socketPassword` field is write-only from cmux's
side — it gets stripped back out on reload/restart, the real credential lives
in `~/.local/state/cmux/socket-control-password`) lets `cmux ping` return
`PONG` from a completely ordinary shell. `doctor` then reports
`backends.cmux: true` with zero diagnoses. So a live run is genuinely
possible without a human sitting inside a pane — the SRD's own §4.1 already
says as much.

`pifleet up --backend cmux` against that live cmux DOES create a real
workspace and one pane per worker — confirmed via `cmux workspace list` and
`cmux list-panes`, both panes present, workspace titled `pifleet-<run-id>`.
But **both workers logged `viewer_failed`** in `ledger/cli-up.jsonl`:
`Error: Surface not found: <uuid>` from `respawn-pane`, moments after
`createPane` returned that exact surface id. Reproduced by hand outside
pifleet entirely — a clean four-way test:

| `--workspace` | `--surface` | Result |
|---|---|---|
| omitted | raw UUID | `Surface not found: <uuid>` |
| omitted | `surface:N` ref | `Surface ref not found: surface:N` |
| raw UUID | raw UUID | `Surface not found: <uuid>` |
| `workspace:N` ref | raw UUID | `Surface not found: <uuid>` |
| `workspace:N` ref | `surface:N` ref | **`OK`** — respawns, `read-screen` shows the new command |

On cmux 0.64.22, `--surface` only resolves through the workspace-relative
`surface:N` ref form, paired with a ref-form `--workspace`; a raw UUID never
resolves, no matter what accompanies it — contradicting both `cmux --help`
("take a UUID, a short ref, or an index") and `Docs/SRD.md` §4.1, which was
verified against 0.64.20. `respawnPaneArgv` (`src/backends/cmux/client.ts`)
passes a bare surface UUID and no `--workspace` at all; so do
`readScreenArgv` and `sendKeyArgv`, and `createPane`/`attachViewer`
(`src/backends/cmux/index.ts`) track pane identity as a composed
`"<paneUUID> <surfaceUUID>"` string throughout (`composePaneId`/
`splitPaneId`, `src/backends/cmux/parse.ts`) — UUIDs are the addressing
scheme everywhere in this backend, not refs. Fixing this for real means
reworking that addressing scheme to carry/resolve ref-form ids (workspace
index included), across every call site listed above, not a one-line patch —
scoped as a real follow-up, not attempted live during this verification.

`pifleet down` still tore the run down cleanly despite the viewer failures
(pane presentation is deliberately non-fatal to a run, per this same
criterion's own design), and closed the cmux workspace as part of teardown.

**2026-08-18 correction — the diagnosis two paragraphs up was wrong.** It
claimed cmux 0.64.22 only resolves `--surface` through the ref form
(`surface:N`), never a raw UUID, and that fixing this needed reworking the
whole backend to carry/resolve ref-form ids. A direct, controlled re-test
disproves the mechanism, even though the earlier four-way table's raw
observations were real:

| `--workspace` | `--surface` | `respawn-pane` result |
|---|---|---|
| omitted | raw UUID | `Surface not found: <uuid>` |
| raw UUID | raw UUID | **`OK`** |
| raw UUID | `surface:N` ref | **`OK`** |
| `workspace:N` ref | raw UUID | **`OK`** |
| `workspace:N` ref | `surface:N` ref | **`OK`** |

Every combination that includes `--workspace` succeeds, in **any** id-form
mix; the only failing row is the one missing `--workspace` entirely — which
is exactly what `respawnPaneArgv` sent (SRD's 0.64.20-era shape, unchanged
until today). `rename-tab` has the identical bug (`not_found: Tab not found`
without `--workspace`, `OK` with it, UUID or ref either way). `read-screen`,
`send`, `send-key` and `focus-pane` all resolve a bare UUID fine with no
`--workspace` at all — confirmed live by respawning a real shell, `send`-ing
text into it, and reading it back.

So the earlier four-way test's `(uuid, uuid)` and `(workspace:N ref, uuid)`
rows reading as failures was a **procedural artifact** of that test run, not
a property of id spelling — most likely a stale/already-superseded surface id
reused across steps. The real, much smaller regression: cmux 0.64.22 added a
`--workspace` requirement to `respawn-pane`/`rename-tab` that 0.64.20 (the
SRD's baseline) did not have; ref-vs-UUID was never the actual variable.

**Fixed**: `respawnPaneArgv`/`renameTabArgv` (`src/backends/cmux/client.ts`)
now take a `workspaceId` and always send `--workspace`, using whatever id form
the caller already holds (UUID — no resolution step needed). `composePaneId`/
`splitPaneId` (`src/backends/cmux/parse.ts`) carry a third field so
`attachViewer` has the workspace id available; `createPane`'s own rename-tab
call already had it in scope. `readScreenArgv`, `sendArgv`, `sendKeyArgv`,
`focusPaneArgv` are untouched — all confirmed still correct without a
workspace flag. `newSplitArgv` was **already** correct — it already sent
`--workspace` before this PR — which is itself corroborating evidence for the
corrected mechanism, not an example of a builder needing no fix.

**Verified live** (cmux 0.64.22, real `pifleet up --backend cmux` with
`PIFLEET_PI_COMMAND` pointed at `fake-pi.ts`, two workers): `backend_ready`
logged `active: cmux, fell_back: false`; both panes' `read-screen` showed the
worker's live `logs --follow --render` output (`fake-pi: scenario 'happy'
loaded...`), not an idle shell and not `Surface not found`; `pifleet down`
tore the run and the cmux workspace down cleanly. Unit coverage:
`test/unit/cmux-client.test.ts` pins the new `--workspace ws-uuid --surface
surf-uuid` argv shape and its injection-refusal cases; that file and
`test/unit/cmux-viewer-path.test.ts` were also updated for the 3-part
composed id. Full suite: `bun test test/unit test/integration` → 1105 pass,
53 skip (Docker-gated), 0 fail. `bun run typecheck` clean.

**PR #8 review round — 2026-08-18.** Same ProjectManager/CodeReviewer pattern as
PR #7: three independent local reviewers (Claude, Gemini, Codex) against the
diff above. All three independently confirmed the diagnosis by re-testing
live cmux themselves rather than trusting the write-up — Codex's own words:
"this project has now recorded the wrong mechanism for ISC-129 twice, so I
re-ran the experiment myself... the third time is the charm." Two real defects
survived to CONFIRMED, both fixed and re-verified before merge:

1. **The `--workspace`/`--surface` wiring itself was completely untested — a
   consensus finding across all three reviewers, mutation-proven by two of
   them.** Swapping the two arguments at both `index.ts` call sites (passing
   `surfaceId` where `workspaceId` belongs) typechecked and left the entire
   suite green, because the argv-builder tests only pin the pure functions in
   isolation and the viewer-path tests only assert filesystem effects. Fixed
   by adding two argv-capturing wiring tests to `test/unit/backend-controls.test.ts`
   (this repo's existing home for "found by mutation" cross-backend regressions)
   using the already-injectable `exec`; confirmed both tests fail when the
   swap is reintroduced (mutation-killed), pass with the real code.
2. **`workspaceId` was validated only inside `respawnPaneArgv`, after
   `attachViewer` had already written the 0700 viewer script to disk** — 3/3
   reviewers independently found this, reproducing the exact "validate BEFORE
   the id becomes a path, not after" bug this same method's own 20-line
   comment exists to prevent, for the field this PR added. Not currently
   exploitable (`workspaceId` never reaches a filesystem path), but it
   reintroduces the ordering invariant the comment and `cmux-viewer-path.test.ts`'s
   header both exist to hold. Fixed: `assertCmuxValue("workspace id", ...)`
   now runs immediately after the existing surface-id guard, before `mkdir`.
3. **A real backward-compatibility break, found independently by all three
   reviewers and empirically reproduced by two of them**: the composed pane id
   is not just in-memory — `up` persists it to `presentation.json` as
   `surface_ref` (`pifleet.presentation/v1`), and a *later, separate* `attach`/
   `tui` invocation reads it back and calls `splitPaneId`. A 2-field id written
   by the pre-fix binary now throws `CmuxParseError` instead of resolving,
   turning a nameable version-skew condition into an opaque parse failure.
   Fixed: `splitPaneId` now accepts both 2-part (legacy, `workspaceId: null`)
   and 3-part composed ids; `attachViewer` — the one caller that actually needs
   the workspace id — throws a named, actionable error ("this pane was
   recorded by a pifleet build that predates the respawn-pane --workspace fix;
   run `pifleet down` and `pifleet up` again") instead of a generic parse
   error. `focus`/`sendText`/`sendKey`/`readScreen` are unaffected either way —
   none of them ever needed the workspace id.

Also fixed from the review: `composePaneId` now rejects empty fields (it only
checked for embedded spaces, so it could mint a string `splitPaneId` then
rejected downstream — after that string might already be on disk); the
`--workspace` comments in `client.ts` were reworded from "required" to what
cmux's own `--help` actually calls it ("workspace context ... default:
`$CMUX_WORKSPACE_ID`") — 0.64.22 scoped surface resolution to a workspace, it
did not make the flag itself mandatory, and this project has twice mis-stated
the mechanism from imprecise language already. Two accuracy fixes to this very
write-up, both caught by Gemini's cross-file pass: the `newSplitArgv` claim
above (now corrected — it needed no fix because it was already right, not
because 0.64.22 left it alone), and this paragraph previously undercounted the
fix as "two functions" when it touched four signatures across three files.

Three independent reviewers (Claude, Gemini, Codex — see the `CodeReviewer` skill) ran against

**ISC-219, resolved by CI (not local Docker).** GitHub Actions' `container` job builds its own
worker image from scratch every run — it does not depend on this machine's deleted
`pifleet/pi-worker:verify` — so pushing this branch gave the ISC-219 test its first real
execution anywhere. Result: 52 of 53 tests in `verbgate.test.ts` passed, including the new one's
actual assertions; the job still went red because its `afterEach` scratch cleanup hit `EACCES`
removing `/outbox/policy` and `/outbox/cloud-allow` — files the test has the container itself
`mkdir`/`printf` into the bind-mounted outbox. On Linux a bind mount passes the container's uid
10001 straight through to the host, so the CI runner's own user cannot remove what uid 10001
created; macOS Docker Desktop's VM masks exactly this class of ownership mismatch, which is why
it looked fine when written and reviewed locally on this machine — the same asymmetry Group N's
mount-visibility notes already describe, on the write side instead of the read side. Fixed by
having the same container `rm -rf` the two paths it created before the script exits, so nothing
uid-10001-owned is left for the host-level cleanup to trip on. That push also exposed a second,
unrelated issue: the `container` job's own anti-skip guard (`EXPECTED: "52"`) was never updated
when the ISC-219 test was added, so a fully green 53/0/0 run still failed the guard on a count
mismatch — fixed by bumping `EXPECTED` to 53 (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`; needed the `workflow`
OAuth scope added to this machine's `gh` token, since the default scope set can't push changes
to workflow files). Re-run: **both CI jobs green** — `test` and `container`, 53/53 probes, no
skips. **ISC-219 closed.**
