**M1 — `prose` was the fall-through class, so a truncated model was blamed for it.** Any 2xx
with a non-empty `choices[]` that was not exactly `finish_reason: "tool_calls"` with calls
present became "this model answered with prose", exit 2, and the operator was told to point
the role at a different model. That swept in `finish_reason: "length"` with no tool_calls —
what a REASONING model returns when its `<think>` preamble outruns the probe's token budget,
and the budget was 200 while this host serves Qwen3.5-* reasoning models. §5.9's original
`Qwen3-8B-4bit` "prose" observation is itself consistent with truncation rather than template
incompatibility, which is worth knowing before anyone acts on it. `prose` is now identified
POSITIVELY (`stop`, no calls); truncated, filtered, unknown-reason and self-contradictory
answers land in a new `inconclusive` class at exit 3; `max_tokens` is 2048. The gate is
exactly as strict as before — `ok` is false in every one of those cases — but exit 2 is now
reserved for the cases where something in `fleet.yaml` is genuinely wrong.

**M2 — the guard's `mlx_lm.server` negative was trivially true, and the real patterns matched
the inference server.** Patterns were substring-matched against the whole `ps` command line,
so a training entry point's NAME anywhere in the line counted as a running training run.
Verified matching before the fix: an `mlx_lm.server` serving `--adapter-path
/Users/dan/out/mlx_lm.lora`, a `tail -f` of an `mlx_lm.lora.log`, and a `grep` for the
string. The first refused every `up` on a host doing exactly what the fleet requires. The
module comment asserted this could not happen ("Every pattern here has to name a training
verb"); the verb pairing is necessary but not sufficient, and the comment now says so and
explains why. Matching now also asks whether a token is the PROGRAM BEING RUN.

A note on the reviewer's suggested fix, which was directionally right and mechanically wrong:
"consider only argv[0]'s basename and the token following `-m`" would have disabled the guard
for the most common launch shape there is. macOS resolves a `#!/bin/sh` script by exec'ing
`/bin/sh <script> <args>` — measured here, not assumed — so every shebang-launched training
script, and every decoy these suites spawn, arrives with `sh` in argv[0]. The implemented
rule gates on argv[0] being a program RUNNER and then admits `-m` targets and non-flag,
non-flag-value tokens. 27-case adversarial argv corpus through the real matcher: 10 wrong
before, 0 wrong after.

**S1/S2 — two more misdiagnoses in the same function.** A timeout was reported as
`unreachable`, so the operator was told to "Start oMLX" about a server that was up and
cold-loading, which §5.9 records taking longer than the 60s budget on this host. And
`!res.ok` collapsed every non-2xx into "the server is down", including a 404 for a model the
server simply does not serve — a config error reported as an outage. Non-2xx bodies are now
read into the detail, a model-naming 404 is `model-not-found` at exit 2 with its own error
class, and the exit-3 error selects its remedy from the failure class rather than offering
one sentence that cannot be true of all of them. A bare 404 deliberately stays exit 3: that
is far more likely a wrong path than a wrong model, and blaming the model would merely
relocate the misdiagnosis.

**S3 — ISC-54/55 were `[x]` on evidence nothing could re-check.** The reviewer agreed the
live suite's self-skip is correct — CI has no oMLX and never will — so the fix was not to
force it to run but to add the half CI CAN execute.
`test/integration/doctor-omlx.test.ts` drives `doctor --json` as a real subprocess against a
loopback oMLX-shaped stub. The close-out notes for both criteria now state explicitly which
half is machine-checked on every push and which rests on a local run, rather than implying
both are covered. That accounting is the actual deliverable here; the test is what makes it
possible to write honestly.

**S4 — the mandatory gate's default was never proven to reach the CLI.** The up-wiring
fixture emitted `require_native_tool_calls` unconditionally, so no config in the file ever
omitted it and flipping the schema default from `true` to `false` left the whole file green.
Disabling the gate in the four unrelated tests remains right — they assert egress ordering,
allowlist-allow, the ADC grant and mount materialization, and making those need a live
inference server would make four unrelated controls untestable. Only the unconditional
emission was the defect. Fixed narrowly, and one new test omits the key entirely.

**Something the review did not catch, found by fixing one of its nits.** The nit was that
the "launches nothing" assertions were guarded so they passed either way. The guard the
reviewer described (`if (existsSync(run.workersDir))`) is not in this tree — the actual
spelling is `for (const runId of await readdir(rig.root))`, which asserts nothing when the
root is empty. Requiring the loop to be non-empty then turned the ISC-56 test RED, which
exposed the real defect: the MLX guard runs BEFORE `up` creates the run directory, so that
loop had been iterating zero times and proving nothing since it was written. The config
gates run after the mkdir, so an empty existing directory is the right claim there; the MLX
refusal now asserts the strictly stronger thing, that the runs root is empty. The reviewer's
inference — that the directory should not exist — was right for the MLX gate and wrong for
the ISC-53 gate, and the code is what settled which.

**LAN-move flags — filed, not implemented.** The reviewer's LAN-move section was context
only. Its first flag is now ISC-260: the probe runs from the HOST while workers reach oMLX
through the internal egress bridge, and on the current topology both resolve to the same box,
which masks the asymmetry entirely. Move oMLX to the LAN and ISC-53 can pass on the host
while every worker is denied — certifying a model no worker can use and pushing the failure
to runtime, which is the outcome §5.9 exists to prevent. ISC-256 carries a note that its
wording is adjacent to, not a duplicate of, #18's ISC-259, and that both reconcile when the
§5.9/§12 erratum lands.

**Validation.** `bunx tsc --noEmit` → rc=0, zero diagnostics (run explicitly: `bun test`
cannot see these, which is how five type errors shipped to the previous round). Mutation
evidence re-measured rather than carried forward: ISC-53's gate → no-op now turns 4 of 5 red
(was 3 of 4 before the new default test); ISC-56's scan → `[]` still turns 2 of 3 red;
M1's classification → fall-through turns 4 unit tests red; `max_tokens` → 200 turns the
wire-budget test red; the schema default → `false` turns exactly the new S4 test red;
`doctor`'s latency → a constant, and its model list → an echo of config, each turn the new
stub tests red.

**Endpoint discrepancy — flagged, deliberately NOT fixed here.** `fleet.example.yaml:46` sets
`base_url: http://host.docker.internal:8000/v1`, i.e. oMLX on the Docker host, and SRD §5.9 is
categorical about it: *"Every worker's model is served by oMLX running on the same machine as
Docker. No hosted provider is involved, in any role, ever. This is a constraint, not a
default."* But `fleet.example.yaml:50-54`'s allowlist names three models the Docker host does
not serve, all three of which exist on a different machine on the LAN (`192.168.86.49`) — so
the shipped config's model list was written against one endpoint and its `base_url` points at
another. Note also that the allowlist names `Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-8bit` while the local box has the
**4bit** build. Resolving this is a design decision about where the fleet's inference lives —
and it is not free: §12's security argument ("guards a local inference server on Dan's own
machine — carries no value off this host") and §5.9's egress posture both assume local, though
`security/egress.ts` parses the allowed endpoint FROM `llm.base_url` and would follow a change.
Left for the owner. The live tests reach the LAN endpoint through `PIFLEET_OMLX_BASE_URL`,
which changes no shipped default.

## 2026-08-19 — ISC-259: a trusted-LAN oMLX, and the gate that had to land first

**Progress: 209/263 → 210/267.** ISC-253 `[ ]` → `[x]`; ISC-259 `[ ]` → `[~]`; ISC-263, ISC-264,
ISC-265 and ISC-266 filed `[ ]`. Two closed, four opened, net +4 total.

**This closes the endpoint discrepancy flagged at the end of the previous entry**, which was
left for the owner and has now been decided: oMLX need not be on the Docker host, and a trusted
LAN server is sufficient. The SRD was amended to match rather than the config being bent to fit
a constraint nobody wanted.

**The order was the whole job, and it is the part most easily got wrong.** PR #18 landed a
`decide()` gate on relay targets that was vacuous *by construction* — `policyFromConfig` derived
its `llm` rule from the same `llm.base_url` the relay derived its target from, so the two agreed
without checking anything, pinned by a test literally named `DOCUMENTED VACUITY`. That vacuity
was survivable only because `omlxRelayTarget` threw unless the host was literally
`host.docker.internal`: the worst case was a port on a machine the operator fully controls. The
host pin is exactly what this change removes. Relaxing it first would have turned this module
into a TCP tunnel from a bridge running untrusted model output to an arbitrary host:port on the
operator's home LAN, established by editing one YAML string. So: **decouple, gate against
operator-written allow rules, then relax** — all three here, in that order.

**Why a new field rather than more meaning on `base_url`.** `base_url` already serves two
masters (the worker's URL and the egress policy's LLM rule). `llm.relay_upstream` is what the
RELAY dials; `base_url` stays what a WORKER dials and keeps its `host.docker.internal` pin,
because that alias is the only name resolvable on the internal bridge. The default is
`host.docker.internal:<port from base_url>`, expressed as `null` rather than a literal because
it depends on another field's value — a static default would be a second, drifting derivation
of that port. Every pre-existing `fleet.yaml` therefore behaves identically, asserted rather
than asserted-in-prose.

**Non-vacuity is a property of `relayGatePolicy`, not of the gate call.** Passing
`relay_upstream` to `policyFromConfig` would NOT have fixed anything: an operator writing
`base_url: http://192.168.86.49:8000/v1` gets an `llm` rule authorizing the very upstream under
test, and the circularity reappears through a different field. The fix is a policy containing no
config-derived host except ones the operator wrote as allow rules — a compile-time-constant host
at the listen port, plus `egress.allow`. `google_hosts` are excluded: the relay forwards no
Google traffic, so those rules must not authorize a relay target.

**Proved by mutation, because "the gate looks real" is exactly how ISC-253 stayed open across
two PRs.** Source mutated two ways: re-deriving a rule from the upstream turned **5 tests red**;
ignoring `egress.allow` turned **2 red**. The proof test holds `base_url`, `relay_upstream` and
therefore the whole target byte-identical across two configs and varies only `egress.allow` —
first asserting the targets are equal (so the difference cannot be target construction), then
that the with-entry case is ACCEPTED (ruling out the base_url pin, the parser, port validation
and `makeRule` as the refusing party), then that the without-entry case throws `rule:
default-deny` specifically rather than `invalid-host`/`invalid-port`, which would mean the gate
rejected the target's shape and never consulted the policy. A separate test drives
`ensureEgressRelay` with a recording `exec` and asserts **zero docker calls** before the refusal,
because every other assertion would stay green if the production call site were wired back to
`policyFromConfig`.

**`DOCUMENTED VACUITY` was rewritten, not left passing.** It asserted a limitation this change
removes; a green test claiming the gate is circular would actively mislead the next reader. Its
replacement pins the two facts that are now true: `policyFromConfig` still agrees with itself,
and it allows a destination `relayGatePolicy` refuses.

**Two things that would have broken quietly, both handled deliberately.** (1) `--add-host
host.docker.internal:host-gateway` becomes dead weight for an IP upstream and a *bug* for a
hostname one, because Docker's embedded DNS forwards to the host resolver and this machine's
resolver does not answer mDNS/`.local` (`macbook.local` needed `dns-sd`). Resolved on both
sides: a hostname upstream is REFUSED at `config validate` with that reason, and the flag is
emitted only when a target actually dials the Docker host — so it is never inert and never
misleading. (2) The `host.docker.internal` alias becomes a fleet-wide lie. Accepted and stated
in §5.9 rather than renamed, for two checkable reasons recorded in ISC-264; the rename is real
work across four consumers and belongs in its own change.

**SRD.** §5.9 retitled "The LLM is self-hosted — oMLX on the Docker host or a trusted LAN peer";
the no-hosted-provider prohibition is explicitly RETAINED and called out as not what was
relaxed. The verified-topology table was re-measured and per-row dated. §12.4's credential
argument was quoted, retired and restated: it was true *because* oMLX binds `127.0.0.1:8000`
(measured), and a LAN server is bound to a routable interface by definition, so the key crosses
an unencrypted LAN hop on every request and has value on one other host. Documented as an
**accepted residual** with the conditions that would make TLS *required* named up front, rather
than mitigated or quietly dropped. §12.8's reachable set gains `∪ {one LAN host:port}` and
records that this is the first time the relay WIDENS a worker's reach rather than renaming
reachability the bridge already had.

**A helper was written and then deleted.** The LAN upstream falsifies any rule that rewrites
`base_url` into a host-reachable URL, and the first pass added `hostFacingUpstreamUrl` to do it
correctly. Checking the concurrent ISC-260 work rather than assuming showed it deletes
`hostFacingBaseUrl` outright and probes from inside the egress network, dialling `base_url`
verbatim as a worker does — so the probe already follows whatever the relay forwards. The helper
was a duplicate derivation of an endpoint this file does not own, with no caller, and was
removed. Recorded because the absence is a decision.

**What is NOT proven, and why ISC-259 is `[~]` rather than `[x]`.** No test stands up a relay
dialling `192.168.86.49:8000` and confirms a container on the internal bridge reaches it
end-to-end. The endpoint facts are LOCAL measurements, reproducible only on this network, which
alone bars `[x]` under the strictness rule. Docker-gated integration evidence is owned by the
concurrent ISC-261/258 change and still describes the pre-amendment topology — §12.8's new
erratum says so explicitly rather than letting a reader assume the old numbers still hold.

**Container-guard arithmetic: unchanged at `TOTAL_EXPECTED: 72`,** re-derived rather than
assumed by running the documented command with the gate closed — `bun test
test/integration/{image,verbgate,egress,adc,relay}.test.ts` → `0 pass, 72 skip, 0 fail`. Every
test added here lives in `test/unit/relay.test.ts`, graded by the fast `test` job.

**A reporting error on this branch, corrected — and it earned a criterion (ISC-266).** The suite
run here showed `harvest.test.ts > report honours the same config as artifacts` failing, and it also
failed on a pristine `4207b89` worktree, so it was reported as a *pre-existing failure on main*. The
evidence was real; the conclusion did not follow. Running a test on a pristine checkout OF THIS
MACHINE establishes "fails here at that commit", not "fails at that commit". Checked against CI
rather than inferred: run `32268059522` on `4207b89` concluded `success`, with
`(pass) … report honours the same config as artifacts [1235.00ms]` in its log. **main is not broken.**
The accurate statement is that the test is **load-sensitive on this machine**: two sequential `runCli`
subprocess spawns inside bun's default 5000 ms budget, against 1235 ms in CI, failing 3/3 at load
average **18.40 on 14 cores** with three agents running suites concurrently. Consistent under load
rather than intermittent, which is precisely why it read as a real breakage. The conclusion that
MATTERED for this PR is unchanged and was established the same way — reproducing it at `4207b89` with
none of this branch's commits applied shows it is not caused by this change — but "main has a failing
test" and "this test is load-sensitive locally" send the next reader somewhere completely different,
and the second is what is true.
- [x] ISC-369: `llm.base_url` may name a PUBLISHED endpoint the relay answers to on the internal bridge, so a fleet can dial a public HTTPS model server with TLS intact end to end. **[FILED AND CLOSED 2026-08-30, BY OWNER DECISION TO RUN THE FLEET ON `https://inference.agileguy.ca`.]** **WHAT WAS REFUSING IT.** `relay.ts:relayListenPort` threw on any `base_url` host but `RELAY_LISTEN_ALIAS`, and the reasoning was sound for the mechanism that existed — that alias was the only name attached to the bridge, so a `base_url` naming anything else described a listener no worker could resolve. **BUT THE PIN WAS ENFORCING A CONSEQUENCE OF `relayConnectArgv`'s HARDCODED ALIAS LIST, NOT A PROPERTY OF THE NETWORK.** The alias set could not follow the config, so the config was made to follow the alias set. `relayListenAliases` now derives the list from `base_url` itself, which makes the invariant hold BY CONSTRUCTION rather than by refusal: whatever name a worker is told to dial is the name the relay publishes. The schema was never the obstacle — it checks only the scheme — so `config validate` passed and the bring-up did not, which is the shape a refusal should never have. **THE MECHANISM IS A PLAIN TCP SPLICE AND THAT IS WHY IT IS SAFE.** The relay does not parse, terminate or re-originate TLS and cannot; the worker sends the correct SNI and validates the real certificate, because as far as it is concerned it dialed the real name. MEASURED 2026-08-30 from inside `pifleet-egress`: `200`, 229ms, 32 models, `Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-8bit` present, and end to end through the shipped path a dispatched task settled with its artifact written by `Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-8bit` over the tunnel. **THE CONTROL RAN IN THE SAME BREATH AND MATTERS AS MUCH:** an UNALIASED public name from the same bridge still fails to resolve at all (`getaddrinfo EAI_AGAIN example.com`). Publishing one name does not open the bridge; it opens that name, to the one upstream `egress.allow` authorized, and the ISC-253 gate is untouched. **THREE REFUSALS REPLACE THE ONE THAT CAME OUT, each measured rather than reasoned.** An IP LITERAL cannot be a Docker alias, so the dial leaves the bridge and is dropped — a black hole under a relay reported healthy. A LOOPBACK name resolves inside the worker before DNS is consulted, so it answers, as the worker's own loopback where nothing listens. A SINGLE-LABEL name resolves through whatever search domain the container inherited, which is not a promise this code can keep. And a published name may not SHADOW `PROXY_LISTEN_ALIAS` or an `egress.google_hosts` entry, because for those the name already means the CONNECT proxy and republishing it silently re-points authorized traffic into the splice. **TWO DEFECTS THIS CHANGE CREATED AND THE LIVE RUN CAUGHT, NEITHER OF WHICH ANY UNIT TEST WOULD HAVE.** FIRST: `relayRunArgv` runs the relay `--user node --cap-drop ALL`, and a published `https://` endpoint puts the listen port at 443 — which an unprivileged process cannot bind. The container `docker run -d`s fine and dies on EACCES, reported as "exited immediately after start". Fixed with `--sysctl net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start=0` rather than `--cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE`: the cap set stays empty and only this netns's unprivileged floor moves. SECOND, AND IT IS THE INSTRUCTIVE ONE: `worker-env.ts` built `NO_PROXY` from the two relay constants, which was complete only while the relay's alias set WAS those constants. The omission is invisible from every vantage `up` has — a worker without `egress_access` has no `HTTPS_PROXY` to be captured by, and the mandatory §5.9 probe container carries no proxy env either — so the first live bring-up REPORTED SUCCESS while inside the ticketing worker, the one role with `egress_access: true` and the role the operations console runs, `curl https://inference.agileguy.ca/v1/models` answered `curl: (56) CONNECT tunnel failed, response 403`. curl honoured `HTTPS_PROXY`, the request entered the CONNECT proxy, and `proxyPolicyFor` — which deliberately carries no `llm` rule — denied it. **A GREEN `up` OVER A WORKER THAT COULD NOT REACH ITS MODEL SERVER, which is §5.9's exact quiet-failure shape arriving through the one path §5.9's own probe cannot see.** `NO_PROXY` is now derived from `relayListenAliases` minus the proxy's own name, one derivation for what the relay ANSWERS TO and what must bypass the proxy. `hostReachableBaseUrl` gained a matching early return, ordered BEFORE the `relay_upstream` branch: such a fleet always sets `relay_upstream`, so the old order would hand a host-side prober `https://104.21.70.27:443/v1`, and dialing an HTTPS origin by ADDRESS presents no SNI and validates a certificate issued for the name — `doctor` reporting a TLS failure on a fleet whose workers are fine, which is the `hostFacingBaseUrl` mistake ISC-260 deleted arriving through the other branch. EVIDENCE: `test/unit/relay.test.ts` (six new tests) and `test/unit/worker-env.test.ts` (one). **MUTATION-PROVED, EIGHT MUTATIONS, each reddening its own probe, each restored from a by-PATH backup with `shasum -c` confirming all three sources byte-identical afterwards:** reverting `NO_PROXY` to the two constants; dropping the unprivileged-port sysctl; never appending the published endpoint to the alias list; removing the shadow check; removing the loopback/single-label check; removing the IP-literal check; accepting an empty alias list in `relayConnectArgv`; and deleting `hostReachableBaseUrl`'s published-endpoint early return. **WHAT THIS COSTS, STATED BECAUSE IT IS A REAL PRICE AND NOT A ROUNDING ERROR.** `llm.relay_upstream` must be an IP LITERAL, so `fleet.yaml` now pins a Cloudflare ANYCAST ADDRESS that Cloudflare does not contract to keep; the file carries the re-derivation command and names both edits a renumber requires. The hostname refusal is not incidental to that and MEASUREMENT FOUND A SECOND, STRUCTURAL REASON FOR IT the existing docstring did not know: the relay publishes `base_url`'s host and is itself attached to that bridge, so it resolves its own published name TO ITSELF — a splice container aliased `inference.agileguy.ca` and dialing that same name looped every forwarded connection into its own listener and hung the client for the full timeout, with nothing in `docker logs` saying why. The mDNS argument the docstring gave is machine-specific and could be fixed by a better resolver; this one cannot be. **NOT CLAIMED:** that routing model traffic through a public CDN is better than the LAN address for every fleet — it is slower by ~45ms measured, and it is chosen here because `192.168.1.110` is reachable from one network and the operations console is a daily driver that does not stay on it. That the published name is authenticated by anything other than TLS: the bridge alias is a hijack of that name FOR WORKERS ON THAT BRIDGE, and what makes it safe is that the certificate is validated by the worker against the real name and the splice's only destination is the one `egress.allow` authorized. **RE-VERIFIED AND EXTENDED 2026-09-01 BY D7, WHICH ADDED A THIRD CALL SITE.** The claim registry guards this criterion with a COUNT of `relayListenAliases` occurrences, not a presence check, deliberately — its own note says "dropping the worker-env side is precisely the failure that shipped green". D7 gives each provider its own bridge, so `egressBridgePlan` now derives each relay's aliases through the SAME function, and the count moved 4 -> 5. **That is the invariant getting stronger, not weaker:** three call sites, one derivation, and `worker-env.ts` now asks it for the aliases of the provider THIS worker resolves to rather than for the fleet's. **The count had to move for the guard to keep working, which is the interesting part.** At `expect: 4`, deleting the `worker-env.ts` use — the exact defect above — leaves four occurrences (the import survives, unused) and the guard goes GREEN on the failure it exists to catch. At `expect: 5` it goes red. **Mutation-proved 2026-09-01, restore checksum-verified:** replacing the `NO_PROXY` derivation with a hardcoded `["omlx.pifleet.internal", "localhost"]` reddens three probes — both ISC-263 `NO_PROXY` tests and ISC-410's per-provider alias test — and, at the corrected count, the registry guard as well.
- [x] ISC-396: an attended worker names a Pi colour theme in config, that name reaches Pi, and the two panes of the operations console are tellable apart at a glance. **WHY A CONFIG KEY AND NOT A DOCUMENTED `/settings` STEP.** Pi 0.79.6 ships exactly TWO themes, `dark` and `light`, and `light` is not a usable second choice for a pane: a Pi theme defines NO page-background token — `text` resolves to the terminal's own foreground — so the light theme paints light-mode ink onto whatever background the terminal already has. Two attended panes in one dark window therefore cannot be distinguished with what Pi ships, which is why the image carries a bundle. **THE SELECTION MECHANISM IS NOT A FLAG.** Pi has no theme environment variable and `--theme <path>` only LOADS; the only non-interactive selector is the `theme` key in Pi's own `settings.json`. So the entrypoint writes that file — and MERGES rather than writing it whole, which is the load-bearing half: `settings.json` is Pi's live state (model, thinking level, last changelog) on a per-worker named volume that outlives the run, and the `jq -n` shape used ten lines above for `models.json` — correct there, because that file is entirely ours — would discard all of it on every container start, invisibly, with the theme correct and the model quietly reverted. **THE THEMES LIVE OUTSIDE EVERY MOUNT, DELIBERATELY.** `/opt/pifleet/themes`, not `/home/pi/.pi/agent/themes` which is Pi's own custom-theme directory and the obvious place: `render.ts` mounts the `pifleet-piagent-<id>` volume there, and a volume MASKS what the image baked at its mountpoint — so themes copied there would be invisible in real runs and visible in every probe that mounts nothing, which is the worst available way to be wrong. **RESOLUTION IS THREE-LEVEL** (`worker ?? role ?? defaults`), the `pane_mode` shape, and the key is a FREE STRING rather than a `z.enum` of the 16 names: the resolvable set is a property of the IMAGE, and an enum would refuse, at parse time and with no way to say yes, a theme an operator legitimately added to a rebuilt image. An unrecognised name WARNS and the fleet runs. **UNSET STAYS UNSET.** `resolveWorker` does not default to `"dark"` and `worker-env.ts` sends `""`; the entrypoint writes the key only when non-empty, so "config has no opinion" leaves a theme an operator picked inside the pane with `/settings` in place instead of overwriting it on every restart. **EVIDENCE:** `test/unit/themes.test.ts` (7), `test/unit/entrypoint-theme.test.ts` (7), and blocks in `config.test.ts`, `worker-env.test.ts`, `render.test.ts`. **LIVE, not only unit:** image `0.79.6-base-2f317a05ad55` carries all 16 files; Pi's own startup inventory listed all 16 by name in the pane; `docker exec cat` shows `obs-1 → catppuccin-mocha` and `tick-1 → dracula` with Pi's `lastChangelogVersion` still beside them, which is the merge working against the real volume rather than a fixture; and neither container's log carries a theme diagnostic. **NOT CLAIMED:** that the rendered COLOURS were compared. `cmux read-screen` returns plain text, so the last link — two panes that look different on a screen — is the operator's to see and is not asserted here. **MUTATION-PROVED, four mutations, each reddening its own probe, each restored by PATH with a clean `git status` afterwards:** dropping `--theme` from the pi argv; replacing the settings merge with a whole-file write; removing `dracula` from the Dockerfile's build-time assert list; defaulting an unset theme to `"dark"`.
- [x] ISC-397: the theme name list cannot drift from the image that carries it, and turning themes on does not turn the pane's startup text back on. **THE DRIFT PROBLEM IS THE REAL ONE.** `src/config/themes.ts` names 16 themes, and nothing in TypeScript can see inside a Docker image — so on its own that list is a claim nothing re-reads, and a config naming `dracula` against a bundle that renamed it would resolve to Pi's default with no signal anywhere: two panes meant to be tellable apart quietly becoming identical. The chain is `THEME_NAMES ←test→ Dockerfile ←build→ image`: `test/unit/themes.test.ts` asserts the module's names and the Dockerfile's `test -f` list are the same set and that both pin the same bundle version, and the Dockerfile's loop fails the BUILD if a version renamed or dropped a file. Neither arrow alone is worth anything. **THE SECOND HALF IS A REGRESSION THIS CHANGE CAUSED AND HAD TO PAY FOR.** Pi prints an inventory of loaded resources at startup and SKIPS IT when there is nothing to inventory — so putting 16 themes on the discovery path turned a three-line header into an eleven-line one, in the two standing panes whose whole prior complaint was startup text. `quietStartup` is therefore seeded, and it is SEEDED, NOT ENFORCED: written only when `settings.json` does not yet exist, i.e. once per worker volume, so an operator who turns the listing back on inside the pane keeps it. **WHAT QUIET COSTS, STATED BECAUSE IT IS NOT FREE:** the flag gates Pi's whole header, so the logo and the keybinding hint line go with the inventory — `ctrl+o` still expands the full startup help, and the diagnostics that would explain a missing skill still print, because Pi's startup call passes `showDiagnosticsWhenQuiet: true`. **THE BUNDLE WAS READ BEFORE IT WAS TRUSTED,** and the reading is recorded in the Dockerfile above the install rather than in a commit message: the published 0.1.6 tarball is 19 files — 16 theme JSONs, README, MIT LICENSE, package.json — with NO JavaScript at all, no `scripts` block (so no install hook; `--ignore-scripts` is belt to that braces), no dependencies, no `bin`, no `main`. Every theme file is pure ASCII with no control characters, which matters more than it sounds: theme values are emitted to the terminal as escape sequences, so a smuggled ESC would be terminal injection. Every value is a hex colour, an integer 0-255, or a reference to that file's own `vars`. Two files carry `export.background*` keys outside the published JSON schema; Pi's RUNTIME validator is a TypeBox object with no `additionalProperties: false`, so all 16 are accepted — checked by running that validator rather than by trusting the default. **NOT CLAIMED:** that the pin makes a future version safe. It buys one immutable tarball per version; bumping it means reading the tarball again. **MUTATION-PROVED, two mutations, each reddening its own probe, each restored by PATH with a clean `git status` afterwards:** re-seeding `quietStartup` on every start rather than only on a fresh volume; and dropping the rpc filter so the unknown-theme warning names workers that render no pane.
- [x] ISC-398: `pifleet status` distinguishes an attended worker that is mid-turn from one sitting at a prompt, without widening the field every other consumer routes on. **THE DEFECT WAS THREE TRUE FIELDS AND NO FOURTH.** Operations console, 2026-09-01: the status pane read `tick-1: idle task=- supervisor=up` while the pane beside it was visibly mid-turn — a model at 60.9% of its context window, writing files into its outbox, its session transcript 300 KB and still growing. Nothing was stale and nothing was dead. `phase`, `task_id` and `epoch` describe an EPOCH; `dispatch` refuses the socket route for a `pane_mode: tui` worker (ISC-380), so a pane a person types into holds no pifleet task, `em.live` is null on every poll, and `classifyTuiTurn` has nothing to classify against. `idle` was correct and was going to stay correct for the whole life of the run, for the two panes the console exists to show. The state file confirmed it exactly: `phase=idle task_id=null epoch=0 turns=0 last_activity_at=null` beside a `session_path` that was discovered, `session_present=true`, and a file growing on disk — so the poll was RUNNING and had nothing to report. **THE FIX IS A NEW FIELD, NOT A WIDER `phase`,** and that is the load-bearing decision rather than the code. `wait`, `report` and the ledger all route on `phase`; making it read `busy` for a typed-into pane would have made every one of them see a task that does not exist. `WorkerStateSchema.transcript_activity` — `{entries, last_growth_at}`, nullable — answers the OTHER question, is the process doing anything, and nothing routes on it. **THREE STATES THAT MUST NOT COLLAPSE**, which is what the renderer is actually graded on: `null` is NOT MEASURED (an `rpc` worker, whose `phase` is already the honest answer, or a `tui` worker before its first poll) and prints NOTHING, because annotating every rpc worker with a column about a mechanism it does not use would read as an rpc worker sitting dead; a present object with `last_growth_at: null` is WATCHED AND STILL, a supervisor that started against an existing transcript, and prints `transcript no writes yet`; a dated one prints `transcript 3s ago`. **AN AGE AND NOT A BOOLEAN, deliberately.** No threshold in this tree can tell a 90-second gap between writes from a finished turn — a single long `kubectl` produces one and a person walking away produces the other — so `status` reports the age and lets the reader judge. `TUI_QUIET_MS` was considered for the job and rejected: at 2 s it would flap `active`/`quiet` on every tool call, and it is a settlement constant whose meaning would then be two things. **WHAT IS MACHINE-CHECKED, UNGATED, AND IN CI:** `test/integration/tui-transcript-activity.test.ts` boots a REAL detached `pane_mode: tui` supervisor (real `WorkerLaunchSchema` record, real `detachedDockerArgv`, real `transcriptPoll`, real `discoverSessionPath`, real `writeWorkerState`; the only stand-in is a `docker` on PATH that prints an id and exits 0 exactly as `docker run -d` does), writes a session file that appears AFTER the supervisor is up and then GROWS A SECOND TIME, and asserts the field appears, that `entries` reaches 3 rather than freezing at 2, and that `last_growth_at` ADVANCES. The second growth is not decoration: a value written once at discovery and never updated passes every other assertion in the file and is the same defect one field along. In the same test, `phase === "idle"`, `task_id === null` and `epoch === 0` are asserted to be UNCHANGED — the control that keeps this a new field rather than a widened one, and the assertion that goes red if someone "fixes" `phase` instead. `test/unit/status-transcript-activity.test.ts` grades the renderer over all three states, both unit boundaries (60 s → `1m`, 3600 s → `1h`), a future stamp clamping to `0s` rather than printing a negative, and an unparseable stamp printing `?` rather than `NaNs`. **MUTATION-PROVED, and one mutation found something.** M1 — move the recording BELOW `const live = em.live` — turns the integration probe RED with a message that reprints the console's state.json verbatim (`transcript_activity: null` beside `session_present: true`), and turns the structural probe in `supervisor-tui.test.ts` red too. M2 — write the field once and never update it — turns the second-growth assertion RED. **M3 — delete the `void flushState()` — STAYED GREEN, and that is recorded rather than smoothed over.** The heartbeat flushes the whole state file every `HEARTBEAT_MS` (250 ms), which is faster than this poll's 500 ms, so the field reaches disk with or without the call. The flush is therefore a deliberate redundancy, not a load-bearing line; the comment in `src/supervisor/index.ts` says so, the unit probe pins it so a future reader does not delete it as dead, and the reasoning that originally justified it on write-volume grounds was WRONG and was removed rather than left standing. **WHAT THIS DOES NOT CLAIM.** Not that `status` can say whether an attended worker is stuck — an age is not a verdict, and a worker in a 40-minute tool call and a worker abandoned 40 minutes ago render identically, by design. Not that a `tui` worker settles anything: no epoch is allocated by typing into a pane, and this field changes nothing about that. Not that the age is monotonic across a host clock step — it is the one wall-clock subtraction in the tree, it is a display label, `src/cli/commands/status.ts` states why there is no monotonic origin two processes could share, and nothing decides on it.
- [x] ISC-399: The worker image carries a ticket CLI, pinned to a commit, and a worker drives it without ever handling the credential. **THIS REVERSES A DECISION THE SKILL ARGUED FOR, and the reversal is the entry.** `skills/ticket-ops/SKILL.md` opened with "there is no ticket CLI in the image and there is not going to be one", on two grounds. The FIRST is spent: baking one "puts a vendor's name in the image hash and in a public repository" — the repository is private, and the same document had named `rally1.rallydev.com` in its own table since 2026-08-30, so the vendor was already there and a CLI adds no disclosure the endpoint did not. The SECOND is real — it pins the fleet to whatever the CLI calls an update — and is answered by pinning a COMMIT rather than by abstaining: a tag is a moving reference, `v1.2.0` can be re-pointed, and an image rebuilt later would install different code under a Dockerfile whose bytes never changed. **WHAT THE CHANGE ACTUALLY BUYS, which the refusal did not weigh:** the hand-rolled `curl` path had to be TAUGHT the vendor — which URL segment is a user story (`hierarchicalrequirement`, which the URL does not spell "story"), that a `FormattedID` is not an object id, which fields must be in `fetch=` or the reply is tens of kilobytes — and every one of those was a sentence in a document nothing re-ran. One was WRONG for months: it specified `Authorization: Token`, which Rally answers with a 401 and an HTML login page, and nothing caught it because no credential existed on any machine that ran this fleet. **THE CREDENTIAL PROPERTY IS THE LOAD-BEARING HALF, and it is stronger than what it replaced.** The CLI reads `RALLY_APIKEY` from its environment (click `envvar=`), and the fleet deliberately does not put secrets in a worker's environment — so the naive bridges all leak: `--apikey "$(cat …)"` is argv and `ps` shows it; `export RALLY_APIKEY=…` is visible to `env` for the rest of the turn. `docker/ticket-cli` is a shim on PATH as `rally-cli` that reads the four delivered `_FILE` paths in ITS OWN process, exports, and `exec`s. The worker never types the credential and cannot leak it by accident — only deliberately, by reading the file, which it could always do. Same boundary `verbgate` draws, and the `curl --config` construction it replaces had the same property one process further in. **WHAT IS MACHINE-CHECKED, UNGATED:** `test/unit/ticket-cli.test.ts` holds the pin against the Dockerfile (same commit, a full 40-char sha rather than a prefix or tag, installed FROM the ARG rather than a second literal), asserts the build-time `--version | grep` exists, asserts the venv is under `/opt/pifleet` and not under a path a named volume masks, asserts the PATH name is the SHIM and explicitly NOT a symlink to the venv binary — the one substitution that would silently hand the credential back — and asserts `ticket-cli` is enrolled in `BUILD_CONTEXT_ASSETS` so editing the shim moves the image tag. Absence assertions read the shim with COMMENTS STRIPPED, because its header documents the leaking spellings it prevents and the first run of this file fired on the explanation rather than the code. **WHAT IS MACHINE-CHECKED IN THE CONTAINER JOB:** `test/integration/ticket-cli.test.ts` runs the real image — four mounted 0444 files become the CLI's configuration, the base URL is stripped to a hostname, the key arrives (`set via RALLY_APIKEY`) and the sentinel value appears in NEITHER stream, the venv's dependencies are absent from the system python, and — the probe that matters — **omitting any ONE of the four files is a refusal naming that file, not a default.** No live credential is used: the fixture token is the literal `sentinel-not-a-real-key`, because what is under test is the MAPPING and `rally-cli config` reports every mapped value without dialling anything. **MUTATION-PROVED:** making the project fall back to empty instead of refusing — the exact "succeeds at something else" failure — turns the refusal probe RED (`omitting project did not refuse`, exit 0 where 78 was required). That mutation is not hypothetical: measured 2026-09-01, an iteration summary asked without a project returned 49 projects and roughly 180 people and read as a plausible answer, which is why an unscoped query is treated as more dangerous than a missing credential. **VERIFIED END TO END AGAINST REAL RALLY on 2026-09-01**, from inside the built image with only the shim configuring it: 28 rows for the credential's own current-iteration tickets, 8 of them below `Accepted`. **A DEFECT IN THE SKILL WAS FOUND BY RUNNING IT, AND IT IS THE MOST USEFUL THING IN THIS ENTRY.** The first draft recommended `--current-iteration --my-tickets --query '(ScheduleState < "Accepted")'` as the server-side way to ask for unfinished work. **`--query` REPLACES the other filters rather than combining with them**: measured 2026-09-01, the flags alone returned 28 rows and that command returned **19,439** — every non-Accepted artifact in the workspace — in about a minute, exit 0, `success: true`. It is the same failure this entry's own mutation covers, arriving through the escape hatch the document recommended: an unscoped query does not fail, it succeeds at something else. It also reached the document exactly the way `Authorization: Token` did — written from a plausible reading of `--help`, never run — which is the failure the whole CLI change was justified by, reproduced by the change itself within the hour. The skill now leads that section with the override, carries both measured counts, and prefers narrowing with flags and partitioning the result with `jq`; `test/unit/ticket-cli.test.ts` pins the warning, the two numbers, and the absence of any COPYABLE example combining `--query` with a narrowing flag — excluding markdown table rows, because the warning's evidence is a table showing the bad command. **THE OBSERVED SYMPTOM IS WORTH RECORDING TOO:** the live worker ran the bad command and sat at "Working..." for 48 seconds with its transcript static, which is precisely the case ISC-398's activity field renders as quiet — a long tool call and an abandoned pane are indistinguishable by design, and this is the first live instance of that limitation being hit. **WHAT THIS DOES NOT CLAIM.** Not that the pinned CLI is correct — it is third-party code this tree does not test; the pin buys immutability, not quality, exactly as `PI_THEMES_VERSION` does. Not that the credential is unreachable: a worker can still `cat` the delivered file, and the shim removes the casual disclosure only. Not that the fixture token proves the real key is accepted — that is a live-run property, and `rally-cli config` echoing the last four characters is the operator's check, not this file's. Not that 203MB of python and dependencies in EVERY toolchain variant is free: images are per-toolchain and not per-role, so a base-toolchain worker that will never file a ticket carries it too, and that cost is recorded here rather than discovered from a registry bill.
- [x] ISC-400: a SECOND standing console exists beside `operations` — `development`, four EQUAL panes, four attended workers — and building it did not fork the builder or widen the first console's blast radius. **THE OWNER REQUIREMENT** was two engineers across the top and a tester and a reviewer beneath, each pane running Pi's own interface, all four the same size, each on a different theme. **WHY THIS IS NOT A SECOND COPY OF `scripts/operations`.** The obvious implementation is a second script and a second `createOperations`, and it is wrong for a reason the first console already paid for: the BUILD-FIRST-CLOSE-SECOND order in `ensureWorkspace` is a measured lesson (closing first on a machine where `operations` was the only workspace left cmux with no window and no tab manager, so every subsequent call — `workspace list` included — failed, and the flag whose job was to repair a stale console had destroyed a working one). A second builder is a second place to get that backwards. So exactly three things differ between consoles and they are lifted into a `WorkspaceSpec` — name, plan, top fraction — over one `ensureWorkspace`, and `agentPaneCommand` is hoisted so both consoles' panes are built from one copy of the rung rather than two spellings of `--attach-clear`. **EQUAL PANES ARE `null`, NOT `1/2`.** `new-split` halves, so two columns each split once are already four quarters and the correction `OPERATIONS_TOP_FRACTION` exists for is one this layout must NOT apply. `DEVELOPMENT_TOP_FRACTION = null` skips the resize entirely rather than asking for a half and relying on the sub-pixel guard to make it a no-op — a correction that happens to round to nothing is indistinguishable from one computed wrongly, and equal panes are the stated requirement. **THE SPLIT TABLE IS THE ASSERTION THAT MATTERS.** `operations` has ONE pane naming an earlier anchor; this has TWO, and they must name DIFFERENT ones (`splitFrom 0` and `splitFrom 1`). Both pointing at pane 0 — the nearest wrong table, and what "split the previous pane" degenerates to — still produces four panes with four correct commands, stacked three deep in the left column, and passes every assertion about pane COUNT or split DIRECTION. Only the anchors catch it. **MUTATION-PROVED:** re-pointing `splitFrom: 1` to `0` reddens the shape probe; making `attach` unconditionally true reddens the negative-direction probe, which is the one that tells "resolved from config" apart from "always attaches". Both restored by PATH and checksum-verified. **A DISTINCT THEME PER PANE IS NOW LOAD-BEARING, not decoration.** ISC-396 gave two attended panes different palettes as a nicety; this console runs TWO ENGINEERS OF THE SAME ROLE, identical in every other on-screen respect, so the palette is the only thing that says which container a pane belongs to before the title is read. `config.test.ts` grades uniqueness across every `pane_mode: tui` worker with an anti-vacuity guard (>1 attended) and names the offending pair in the failure; mutating `gruvbox-dark` to `tokyo-night` reddens it with `themes were catppuccin-mocha, tokyo-night, tokyo-night, …`. All four are DARK, deliberately: a Pi theme sets no page background, so a light one paints light-mode ink onto whatever the terminal already is — `tick-1` takes that trade knowingly and these do not. **THE BLAST RADIUS IS THE REAL SAFETY PROPERTY.** `operations --recreate` stops EVERY live run, which is right for it because both of its runs are its own. Copying that here would tear down the operations console's containers as a side effect of a command that never mentioned them — destructive, and invisible until the operator switches workspaces and finds dead panes. `src/run/status-runs.ts` filters `status --all --json` to runs holding one of THIS console's workers. It lives in `src/` and not in the script because a script's top level runs `main()` on import, so a helper defined there cannot be unit tested without opening a workspace as a side effect. `status-runs.test.ts` grades the over-matching failures specifically: a worker id appearing in another run's `session_path` must not match (an earlier draft scanned raw text and did), `eng-1` must not claim `eng-10`, an empty worker set stops NOTHING rather than everything, and an unparseable document yields no runs — leaking containers is the only acceptable failure of the three, since throwing refuses the console and defaulting to "all" destroys the other one. **VERIFIED LIVE, and this is the proof that matters:** with three runs standing (`obs-1`, `tick-1`, `rev-1`), `./scripts/development --recreate` stopped `2026-09-01T17-20-26Z-8fd7` and reported it by id, and both operations runs were still `supervisor=up` afterwards. **THE LAYOUT IS CONFIRMED VISUALLY**, which is the one link a text assertion cannot close: the operator's screenshot shows the 2x2 with `eng-1`/`eng-2` across the top and `tst-1`/`rev-1` beneath, all four the same size. **A TOOLING GAP WAS FOUND AND IS RECORDED RATHER THAN FIXED.** `scripts/**` is not in `tsconfig.json`'s `include` — the scripts are extensionless bun files and `tsc` cannot glob them without a suffix — so NOTHING type-checks either console launcher. That is not hypothetical: the first draft of `scripts/development` called a `runOutput` helper it never defined and `bun run typecheck` was clean. Adding `scripts/**` to `include` was attempted and refused by tsc (TS5010, recursive wildcard needs an extension), so the mitigation is executional: `operations-console.test.ts` now execs BOTH scripts through `--dry-run` in the ungated `test` job. **WHAT THIS DOES NOT CLAIM.** Not that the `--recreate` teardown path is integration-covered — `--dry-run` returns before it, so the decision is unit-graded and the wiring to it is not. Not that four attended panes are free: these plus the operations console's two are six Pi processes against one oMLX server, and `run.max_concurrent` bounds each RUN rather than the host, so six panes generating at once is six concurrent requests — a throughput decision the operator makes by opening the console. Not that all four panes CAME UP on 2026-09-01: `rev-1` (base toolchain) runs, and `eng-1`, `eng-2` and `tst-1` refuse on a missing `0.79.6-node-aeeabafa72f2`, because adding the ticket CLI to the Dockerfile (ISC-399) moved every toolchain's hash and the node image cannot currently be rebuilt — `registry.npmjs.org` resolves on this host but its TLS connection fails, while `pypi.org` and `github.com` both answer 200. That is a host network state and a pre-existing consequence of ISC-399, reached by any node-toolchain worker; the refusal is `up`'s own fail-closed guard naming the image and the command that builds it, and the pane's ladder degraded to a shell rather than dying, which is the designed behaviour.


- [x] ISC-401: a `provider/`-prefixed model resolves to the SAME provider name in Pi's argv and in the rendered `models.json`. The two halves now agree. `test/unit/entrypoint-models-json.test.ts` SPAWNS `bash docker/entrypoint.sh` and reads the rendered `models.json`, so the join is exercised end to end rather than simulated. The raw document is where the distinction still exists. Pinned by a test that writes the flat key's OWN DEFAULT VALUE and still expects a collision. Mutation-proved by emptying the key loop: 7 red, including the both-spellings-named message test.

The fallback provider for a bare entry follows the same rule — inside `providers.ollama.models_allowlist`, `gpt-oss` means ollama's, and using the fleet default there would prefix hosted entries with the local provider's name. Both halves of the probe are asserted, in both directions, so neither a function that refused everything nor one that permitted everything passes. - [x] ISC-405: on a `tag_style: true` provider, a model whose tag collides with one of the six thinking levels keeps its tag. The negative direction carries equal weight and is why the flag is per-provider: in ONE fleet, `ollama-cloud/m:low` keeps its tag while `omlx/m:low` decomposes to model `m` + thinking `low`, decided by which provider the worker resolves to — an implementation that kept every colon passes the positive test and destroys the thinking suffix for every existing fleet. Closed by `ensureBridgeRelay`, which takes the target FROM the bridge so there is no optional argument for a caller to omit. **Mutation-proved:** dropping that argument so the `omlxRelayTarget` fallback fires reddens two named tests (`Received: "omlx"`), while `the stamped target still carries this provider's own upstream` correctly stays green — host and port were never wrong. - [x] ISC-410: a provider DECLARED in `llm.providers` that no worker in this run resolves to creates no network, no relay and no alias. *Probe: declare three, use two, assert the third's derived names are absent from `docker network ls` and `docker ps`.* This is a containment property the fleet-wide design could not express at all. **[CLOSED 2026-09-01.]** Closed in two halves at two altitudes, because one of them was reachable by a derivation test and the other was not. The PLAN half: `egressBridgePlan` omits a declared provider nothing resolved to, proved through the REAL config loader rather than a hardcoded provider list — built from `Object.keys(llm.providers)` every assertion would fail, but built from a list typed into the test they would all pass while `up` went on opening the route. Its BOUND is asserted too: the unused provider's upstream address DOES still appear, via `egress.allow`, because §6.5.5 keeps the operator's own allowlist fleet-wide — *"D7 partitions model reachability, not all reachability"* — and an assertion quietly dropped from that sweep is indistinguishable from one nobody thought of. The `up` half: nothing re-checked that `up` CREATES from the plan. Its two loops could have been changed to walk declared providers and every test above would have stayed green, so this was verified by hand on a live three-provider fleet and by hand only — which is not a standard this project accepts. Now pinned in `up-wiring.test.ts`, which drives the REAL `up` against a `docker` PATH shim and therefore needs no daemon: three declared, two resolved, and the unused provider's network, uplink and relay names appear in NO docker argv at all — strictly stronger than absence from the create lines. **Anti-vacuity carried in the same log**, because an absence assertion passes trivially against an empty one: the log non-empty, both used bridges AND their uplinks present, both used relays run, the created-bridge count pinned at exactly 4 so an unpredicted third cannot hide, and the ledger's `egress_network_ready` compared against the same derived pair. In both cases it was the SOLE detector — `relay-provider-bridges.test.ts` stayed 33/33 and the rest of `up-wiring.test.ts` 47/47. Restores checksum-verified. **A harness finding worth recording:** the shim answered `Internal: true` for EVERY name, so `ensureEgressNetwork` always took its adopt branch and `network create` was never issued at all — every claim this file could previously make about network creation was a claim about which names `up` MENTIONED. The absent-until-created behaviour is opt-in per rig, so the ISC-189 positive control, which needs the exists-but-not-internal branch, is untouched.

- [x] ISC-412: the composed relay name is re-checked against Docker's length limit, and an over-long provider key is refused at `up` naming the field. A provider key is operator-chosen, so `pifleet-egress-relay-<network>-<provider>` is the first composed name in this codebase a long config value can push past the limit. *Probe: such a key exits non-zero with the field named.* **[CLOSED 2026-09-01.]** The BOUND already existed — the composed relay name goes through `assertDockerName` and 128 is enforced there — so what was missing was the diagnostic, and the criterion says so: it asks for the FIELD. `providerKeyBudget` reserves `RELAY_NAME_PREFIX` (21) plus the joining dash, and that reservation is what makes the edge bite: a 93-character key composes into a NETWORK name of 108 that Docker accepts and only breaks the limit twenty-one characters later in `relayContainerName`. A budget of `128 - net - 1` misses exactly that gap, and the probe battery straddles the edge on both sides — 92 accepted composing to exactly 128, 93 refused as "1 too long". **A defect the unit battery could not see, found by running the real binary:** the refusal does not arrive through `egressBridgePlan` at all. `renderAllWorkers` (`up.ts:1016`) throws one hundred and seventy lines earlier, outside the plan's `try`, so the message escaped undiagnosed as `pifleet: internal error:` with **exit 8** — the code this CLI reserves for "a bug in pifleet, not a mistake by its caller", handed to an operator with a typo in their own config. `ProviderKeyError` now carries `readonly exitCode = EXIT.USAGE` and so is correct from BOTH call sites rather than from whichever happens to run first; verified through the real binary at exit 2 with the field, the excess and the remedy, and reverted to a plain `Error` at exit 8. The test that asserted the refusal came from `egressBridgePlan` was RETIRED rather than repaired: it was green against a call site that never fires first. **Mutation-proved:** reverting to `assertDockerName` reddens 5 on message content; the naive budget reddens 3 including the gap case. Restores checksum-verified.

Now keyed by the `(provider, model)` PAIR, dialing each provider's own `base_url` through `relayViewForProvider` with its own key through `providerApiKeyEnv` — the same two resolvers the relay and the worker read, so the gate that CERTIFIES a provider and the worker that DIALS it cannot present different credentials. - [x] ISC-424: `doctor`'s allowlist verdict does not collapse a tag-style model id, so it cannot certify as served a model the server does not serve. **LIVE TODAY, no provider map required, and found by review rather than by a test.** Measured 2026-09-01: `allowlistVerdicts(["ollama/gpt-oss:high"], ["gpt-oss:low"], "omlx")` returns `served: true`, because `decomposeModel` strips `:high` from the allowlist entry and `:low` from the served id and both sides become `gpt-oss`. Two independent harms: `doctor` reports green for a model the server does not have, and the allowlist GATE widens — a worker on `ollama/gpt-oss:low` is admitted against an allowlist naming only `:high`, which matters because that list is the fleet's record of which models were probed for native tool calls (ISC-190), so an unprobed tag variant passes. The fix is not simply "pass the predicate here": `doctor.ts`'s own docblock argues against a provider-aware comparison because MLX repo-id served ids (`mlx-community/…`) would break it, so the two requirements have to be reconciled rather than one traded for the other. *Probe: the measured call above must return `served: false`, and an allowlist of `["p/m:high"]` must REFUSE a worker on `p/m:low` — assert both, since fixing only the verdict leaves the gate wide.* **Graded `[~]` 2026-09-01: the VERDICT half is closed and mutation-proved, the GATE half is not.** `allowlistVerdicts(["ollama/gpt-oss:high"], ["gpt-oss:low"], "omlx")` now returns `served: false`; `test/unit/doctor-allowlist.test.ts` carries four rows for it, and restoring the pre-fix `doctor.ts` under those rows turns exactly those four red (measured, restore checksum-verified). Proved in BOTH directions, which matters more than the first: removing the served-side `:level` relaxation instead — so nothing is ever relaxed — turns four DIFFERENT rows red, including `doctor`'s agreement with `up` on `Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-4bit:high`. The tightening and the relaxation are therefore both load-bearing, and neither has quietly absorbed the other; a one-directional proof could not tell that apart from a fix that traded the MLX repo-id constraint away. The served side no longer runs through `decomposeModel` at all: a `provider/` prefix still comes off both sides, so the MLX repo-id reconciliation the entry demands is kept rather than traded, and a served `:level` is relaxed away ONLY for an entry that named no level of its own. What is NOT done is the second assertion in the probe — an allowlist of `["p/m:high"]` still ADMITS a worker on `p/m:low`, because `resolveWorker` eats the tag before `assertModelAllowed` sees it, which is Defect C and needs the `tag_style` predicate wired. That half is pinned by a tripwire in the same file asserting the gate still admits it, so closing Defect C turns it red and forces this re-grade. **RE-GRADED `[x]` 2026-09-01, hours later, when the second half closed.** `resolveWorker` now passes the tag-style predicate, so the tag survives the merge and `assertModelAllowed` has something to refuse on: an allowlist of `["p/m:high"]` REFUSES a worker on `p/m:low`. Both halves of the probe now pass. The gate tripwire flipped from "the hole is open" to "the hole is shut" exactly as designed and was replaced with the positive assertion, with the non-tag-style case beside it — a gate that refused every colon would satisfy the first and break every fleet in this repo. Mutation-proved by dropping the predicate from `resolveWorker` alone, which turns the gate test red from another file.
- [x] ISC-425: a worker's Class 1 key is its RESOLVED PROVIDER's, not the fleet's. *Probe: two providers with distinct `api_key_env`; assert each worker's secret file is named and valued from its own block, and that the fleet default's value reaches neither.* **[FILED AND CLOSED 2026-09-01. Found by inspecting a live run's artifacts — no criterion covered this.]** `buildWorkerEnv` read the fleet-wide `llm.api_key_env` for every worker whatever provider it resolved to. Measured on a two-provider run whose blocks named `OLLAMA_API_KEY` and `VENDOR_B_API_KEY`: `workers/d7a/secrets/OMLX_API_KEY` and `workers/d7b/secrets/OMLX_API_KEY` — both the schema DEFAULT, at mode 0444 behind a read-only mount. `entrypoint.sh` then writes that value into `models.json` under the worker's RESOLVED provider, so a worker dialing a third party held the operator's own local inference key under that third party's name, one request away from sending it. **Nothing about the DELIVERY was wrong, which is exactly why three green criteria closed over it:** ISC-407 asks whether the key is out of the environment, ISC-408 whether the file is 0444 behind a read-only mount, ISC-422 whether it is miscounted as an operator grant. **None of them asks whose key it is**, and all three remain green after the fix — a criterion is only as wide as its question. `providerApiKeyEnv` joins `providerAllowlist` and `tagStyleProviders` as a per-provider resolver in `load.ts`, and REFUSES rather than falling back: `ProviderSchema` already makes `api_key_env` required with no default and argues why — the flat keys' defaults *"describe oMLX on the operator's own machine"* — so a `?? config.llm.api_key_env` would reintroduce that inheritance through the back door, and silently, because the result is a real variable name resolving to a real key. **Mutation-proved, restore checksum-verified:** reverting the one line reddens 3, including the anti-case that pins the fleet default's sentinel out of every surface a key travels on; the flat-fleet case stays green, so §6.1's shorthand is not collateral damage.
